- mr president, the napolitano report on regional and local authorities in the construction of europe has many qualities, and one major flaw: it should not exist. the principle which he himself recalls and which the community has followed since its inception is that the european institutions are based on a union of states. they respect the internal organisations of those states; the only interlocutors are the states and, when the regional level is involved in certain european policies, it is because the states, and behind them their national democracies, have wanted it that way and because they keep and must keep control of the process. in any case, the community does not have to decide - or even suggest - that regional and local authorities will participate more or in some other way in this or that european decisionmaking process, as the napolitano report indicates. on the contrary, as i explained in a minority opinion annexed to the report, the increase in the number of member states through enlargement makes the role of intermediaries and coordinators performed by the states more imperative than ever. it is hard to imagine the european union having direct relations with 250 or more regions, or listening to all their opinions. it would be unmanageable. in any case, national identity and the right of peoples to organise themselves as they see fit must be respected absolutely. the european union has no superior legitimacy to interfere in these matters. and if it does succeed in slipping through, it will open a pandora's box that will eventually lead to disunited nations and an ungovernable europe.
- mr commissioner, mr president, i am in favour of equality between the regions. even if some have legislative powers, this cannot give them superior or additional rights compared to others. otherwise we would have a two-tiered citizenship, with first-class europeans and second-class europeans. it is up to each state to give power to its regions if it so wishes. the question is being debated in several of our countries, in particular but not only in my own country, france. it is up to each state to consult its local authorities and regions in the context of european policies and their transposition. states are not necessarily doing it well, they could be doing it better, but it's a good track. i would remind you that the european union is not an aggregation of regions. it is a union of states and peoples. and each state must remain in control of its internal organisation, both institutionally and territorially. it is the text of the treaties, the current text, and we must preserve both the spirit and the letter of the treaty. no country can claim to have a better system than another. no country can impose its system on another. europe is a contract, not a constraint. so if i had to sum up, i would say: yes to strong and united regions in the european union, yes to regions cooperating across borders, but no to a europe of regions which would then be unequal and with a variable geometry.
commission. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i should like to begin by thanking the committee on civil liberties and the rapporteur, mrs joke swiebel, for the opportunity to discuss the situation of fundamental rights in the european union in 2001 in the plenary today. the report before you is a vast and ambitious document, seeking to provide an overview of the situation of fundamental rights in the european union and its member states and calling for concrete action by national authorities and the european institutions. as an example, i can mention the need to pursue a consistent policy of combating discrimination - against all forms of discrimination - and to promote integration into european societies in order to avoid manifestations of racism and xenophobia and to defend the rights underlying european citizenship. the european parliament's annual report on the situation of fundamental rights in the union is an important instrument for ensuring respect for these rights, both at european level and at the level of each member state, whether in the present union or in a union of 25 member states in the future. the commission, for its part, has a direct interest in the report which parliament is going to vote on, because, as mrs joke swiebel has just said, it requires us to take a series of concrete actions. i am committed to carefully considering the various recommendations which parliament may wish to make to us and we will of course take the appropriate measures to ensure that they are followed up. the commission has always responded to the challenges which parliament has put to it, and i believe that we have taken them up in a positive way so as to develop fruitful cooperation between the two institutions in this area. a good example of this cooperation is certainly the creation by the commission, following parliament's resolution of july 2001, of a network of experts on fundamental rights. in this resolution, based on the parliament's report for the year 2000 drawn up by mr cornillet, parliament clearly stated its commitment to a serious and concrete approach to the charter of fundamental rights of the european union, calling for the creation of an appropriate instrument for monitoring and assessing the situation of fundamental rights both in the member states and in the european union. the commission, like parliament, is convinced that it is essential to know the situation regarding the protection of fundamental rights in order to be able to assess the quality of such protection, which must always be a rigorous and efficient assessment. this is the mission of the network of experts on fundamental rights. this network will enable both parliament and the commission to remain vigilant and ensure that the charter of fundamental rights is respected and enforced. we believe that the network must be allowed to function and begin to produce its results before moving on to more complex institutional solutions, such as the establishment of an observatory. the network is also responsible for informing parliament and the commission on the sensitive issue of the balance between security and freedom in the context of the fight against terrorism, a subject which will be given special attention in the report being drawn up as part of the network's work. this network of experts on fundamental rights became operational in october 2002 and in its report it should take into account developments in national legislation and the way in which it is applied, as well as developments in the case law of the court of justice of luxembourg and the court of justice of strasbourg, and the relevant case law of the national courts and constitutional courts of the member states. in this context, the important role which parliament and the commission are called upon to play has two aspects: on the one hand, to have an even clearer view of the situation of fundamental rights in the member states in order to take the necessary actions and decisions in this area in a targeted and precise manner within the framework of the powers conferred by the treaties on the european institutions; the commission has also proposed that the european parliament should be consulted on the draft directive on the protection of the environment. in this connection, i would like to recall that placing fundamental rights at the heart of the european project means defending the thesis that the convention on the future of europe and the subsequent intergovernmental conference should incorporate the charter of fundamental rights into the constitutional treaty of the union and give it binding legal force. the european union is an area of freedom, security and justice which lacks strict protection of fundamental rights. the drafting of a constitutional treaty, of a genuine european constitution which takes up the charter of fundamental rights as an integral part of it and which at the same time and in parallel authorizes the accession of the european union to the european convention on human rights, is a major challenge which we are facing and which we must overcome. but at the same time, the quality of the protection of fundamental rights must be assessed in a pragmatic and effective way. this report, the debate in this house and the final resolution of parliament will certainly make an important contribution to the commission's work on fundamental rights in the following year.

the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the rail network is not affected by the current crisis. it is also a key issue for railway europe in the 21st century. although mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the reports on the development of rail transport contain excellent points. mr jarzembowski is right to be concerned about the decline of rail transport compared with road and air transport. the commission notes that, in the freight sector, the railway market share fell from 21% to 8% in europe between 1970 and 1998. yet the amount of goods to be transported has increased dramatically and more people are travelling. this has had disastrous consequences in three areas. the environment, because the road and the airplane pollute more than the railway; traffic, with the congestion of the road network and the air corridors; and finally, the safety of people, because the train is a safer means of transport than the road, on which tens of thousands of people die every year in europe. the french are particularly affected by these consequences. if there are more accidents in france, it is not, as the french government claims, because the french are more careless than their european neighbors. the reason is that the main roads on our network, which are used by lorries connecting the mediterranean countries with those in northern and eastern europe, are now congested. these trucks can occupy the road for many miles and cause many accidents and traffic jams. the ordeal experienced by the thousands of motorists stuck in -5°c overnight on january 4th and 5th is of course the consequence of the snowfall, but also and especially the failure of the motorway services and the presence of trucks blocked on the road by the snow. however, the proposals contained in the reports of our colleagues, which are those of the commission, do not always seem to me to be adapted to the situation. the commission has also proposed that the european parliament should be consulted on the future of the railway system. why is the french government not doing what the swiss authorities have done? to set up a railway network and to require lorries to use it when crossing french territory. why do many french companies rely on trucks and not trains to transport their products? why do millions of french people take their cars instead of public transport? because the sncf, under the control of the unions, is performing less and less of its public service mission. because the french no longer feel safe on public transport because of the insecurity that sometimes exists and the thugs that are rampant. because the automobile is, in an increasingly regulated society, one of the last instruments of freedom. these are realities our leaders ignore; with public cars, they dream of what was the rule under mao - and many maoists have converted to ecology - that the people take the old public transport or bicycles and continue to use the means that the community makes available to them.

mr president, this second opportunity to speak gives me the opportunity to speak perhaps a little more specifically on the proposal by mr jarzembowski. the commission's proposal is based on two very important innovations: the first is to abolish the transeuropean rail freight network and to anticipate a total liberalisation of the international, national, local and regional freight networks by 2006, and the second is to open up and liberalise rail passenger transport. as regards the first proposal, i am one of those who believe that a strong political move is needed in the direction of the railways, and if it is not advisable to change the dates constantly, i would personally follow my colleague jarzembowski on the matter of freight, since the situation is so worrying today. on the other hand, i would be infinitely more reserved about international passenger transport. i do not consider this to be a top priority for railways, unlike freight. and i, who often travel by train, have no particular difficulty crossing borders. what i do know is that there is considerable commercial greed involved, and i am not one of those who are confined here to creating a railway market; i am one of those who wish to see a move towards a european transport policy, which is a little different. to conclude, in a way, on the whole of today's debate, what is clear is that, whether there is openness or not, the construction of a railway europe cannot be reduced to liberalization, competition or openness of networks. or else we will have market shares that will substitute for each other within the same modal share for rail without being able to substitute rail for the car. there are therefore other aspects of transport policy to be implemented. there is pricing and in particular the reduction of the social and fiscal gap between the different modes and, in particular, between road and rail, which seems to me to be a priority if we want openness to be a gain on the road, rather than simply the construction of a rail market. there's also an investment policy. personally, from this point of view, i hope that this debate will be a very strong message from the european parliament to the council. for several months now the council has been completely deadlocked on the financing of the transeuropean networks, it has been sticking to a regressive approach, it does not want to hear about taxation, fuel taxation or large european borrowings. i think that, in the absence of a large, ambitious policy and rail infrastructure, the opening-up efforts we are making will be a fight between railway companies rather than a conquest on the road. that, ladies and gentlemen, is the message i wanted to convey to the council, also on behalf of the european parliament.
mr president, the increasing opening up of the european railway network to competition, as advocated in the jarzembowski report, is a retrograde step, seriously damaging both the interests of users and railway workers. voting in favour of this report is tantamount to behaving like vulgar agents of the private interest lobby, which wants to dismantle the public service railways. it is well known that private companies which are only interested in their profits will save on investment or on labour. it is well known that the privatisation of the british railways has led to disasters. we refuse to sacrifice the interests of the community so that a few private groups can make money off the backs of users, perhaps even risking their lives. the railway must be a unified public service throughout the continent and we reject this report and any proposal for privatization.

in writing. - the european commission proposes in this 'railway package' a new version of directive 91/440 which aims to further liberalise rail transport, mainly for freight. the committee on regional policy, transport and tourism of parliament has added, by its amendments, the liberalisation of passenger transport. i'll vote against both. why this acceleration of liberalization when the 1991 directive has just been revised? why go back on an agreement, a balance, that was hard-won just over a year ago, before member states had even completed transposing the revised 2001 directive? this means that the effects of the liberalisation that has been initiated will not be assessed until further steps are taken which will create an irreversible situation. it is simplistic to claim that the loss of competitiveness of rail freight compared to road transport is mainly due to the lack of liberalisation. it was not necessary to liberalise rail passenger transport in order to achieve successful cooperation between national operators in respect of thalys. what works for passengers could be developed for freight transport. the will must still exist, and european and national investments must be on hand. let's really choose the rail instead of the truck! in writing. - under the pretext of overcoming the national fragmentation of the european rail network, which should have been unified long ago, you are imposing a fragmentation, even more serious, between private interests competing with each other. the pretense of developing a 'community security system' is at best a reflection of your own concern at this obvious fact: private interest groups, concerned with maximising their profits, will not give priority to investing in people and equipment to ensure adequate security. but in reality you only invoke security to oppose the possibility of 'complementary national rules' 'limiting the opening up of the market'. the security you speak of is minimal security, which will lead to disaster. we reject the report and say that the public service nature of rail transport should not be affected. we are also opposed to the idea of a public service being emptied of all content in the race for profitability.
in writing. - we are of course in favour of the interoperability of the transeuropean rail system and of some of the measures proposed in this report. but this interoperability is proposed in a railway package which aims to generalise competition in rail transport and open it up to privatisation. the report stresses long-term profitability, is concerned about the loss of railway competitiveness, but does not expressly oppose privatisation and competition or the dismantling of the public service that this implies. this is in line with the policy of abandoning public service. we therefore abstained on this report.
in writing. - i want to congratulate sylviane ainardi on her excellent work. the report is part of the 'railway package' which aims to promote rail development by creating an integrated railway area. this is achieved in particular through the interoperability of the trans-european rail system, which is a prerequisite for smooth international traffic. until now, very different national technical specifications and standards, often incompatible with each other, have created obstacles to the use of the train as a means of transport. i regret this as a railway activist for reasons of both environmental protection and public safety. i therefore welcome the european commission's proposals to try to coordinate the different tsis (technical specifications for interoperability). however, harmonization must not be done from below in the field of security! it will therefore be necessary to carry out an assessment of the benefits that can be expected from each its project in terms of market share, traffic development, and also environmental, safety and social aspects. given the prevailing ideology in this area, public service advocates must be vigilant!
in writing. - i would first like to express my satisfaction with the report by mr markov, which supports the commission's proposal for a new regulation on road transport, which was presented in october 2001. the report includes improvements made by the new regulation to the present situation, with the dual objective of improving road safety and improving the working conditions of drivers. the measures such as the abolition of the possibility of splitting breaks, the extension of the scope of application and the strengthening of penalties for infringements of the regulation, which were included in the commission proposal and are included in the report, represent important milestones. the markov report further strengthens the regulation, for example by opposing the creation of a flexible week, introducing a limit on working hours, giving a definition of driving time or by encouraging the involvement of the social partners. i would particularly like to stress the importance of the measure to extend the scope of the regulation to all road drivers who drive in europe, whether they are eu nationals or not. this measure will have the effect of reducing social dumping considerably, while encouraging third countries to strengthen their national legislation in favour of the working conditions of their road hauliers. (parliament adopted the legislative resolution)
in writing. - the proposed text is probably a step forward for countries where there is no legislation at all or where legislation is extremely unfavourable to workers in this field. but it is revolting that a text entitled 'social provisions' should envisage 56-hour driving weeks! we also consider it unacceptable that in order to improve things in some countries, they are made worse in countries with the highest levels of protection. the only acceptable harmonisation is to standardise the highest level of social protection and working conditions. this is the only way to prevent transport employers in france from employing workers who are less well paid and less protected, and who come from countries whose legislation, particularly as regards the length of the driving day, is either non-existent or unfavourable to lorry drivers. furthermore, laws which protect workers in some way should not be left untouched, as is often the case, but should be imposed on employers by force.
in writing. - the aim is to simplify the rules governing the organisation of driving and rest periods in the union, in order to improve road safety and the working conditions of the persons covered by the regulation. the proposal also aims to make the current rules compatible with the use of the new digital tachograph, in order to improve compliance with the existing rules. the report by my colleague helmuth markov is in line with the positive proposals of the european commission: the abolition of the possibility of splitting breaks, the reduction of exemptions, the abolition of the provisions on the minimum age of drivers, the strengthening of penalties for infringements of the regulation. but the rapporteur has also succeeded in getting through amendments which i think are essential. the report rejects the provisions on the flexible working week, it strengthens controls and sanctions in the event of non-compliance with the provisions of the regulation, and it strengthens the involvement of the social partners. the rapporteur, however, was unable to get the amendment to be voted on, which rightly proposed a reduction in the working week to 45 hours. so it was reintroduced in plenary and i voted in favour of it, of course!
in writing. - we fully support the need to harmonize social standards in road transport. our concern is not to solve distortions of competition with third countries, but to guarantee road workers the best working conditions, status and pay. but in this area, there are no half measures to be taken in a sector abandoned to liberal savagery. it is right to oppose the flexible working week, to limit working hours, to specify the minimum age of drivers for the transport of goods. the controls must be strengthened, employers must be sanctioned for breaches of the rules and the social partners must be involved more closely. but the markov report is insufficient in terms of weekly driving time and the possibility of splitting breaks. reducing the weekly driving time from the current 56 hours to 45 hours is not satisfactory. it is unacceptable to allow the division of rest time. both of these measures perpetuate the fact that road workers are wage-earners outlawed for the greater benefit of the market. that is why, while we are in favour of progressive social measures, we have not voted for this report.
in writing. - during yesterday's debate in this house i pointed out that the participation of the regions in the european decisionmaking process advocated by the napolitano report would open a pandora's box from which many surprises would then emerge. we have had some glimpses of this at the meeting of the committee on constitutional affairs, which, no doubt carried away by its impulse, voted for strange provisions, such as the right of regional and local authorities to adapt european legislation to local needs. of course, the members of the committee who voted for such provisions were subsequently repudiated by their groups, and parliament has just made corrections in plenary. but he only corrected the most obvious flaws. the rest, which tends to circumvent the states more subtly, has been retained. these false maneuvers only showed in the open what this report would lead to if it were implemented. the house also voted an amendment stating that the union would now be based on the legitimacy, not of the 'peoples' (taken as a whole), but of the 'citizens' (taken individually). such a development would change the nature of the union and bring it closer to a nation state. we therefore voted against this report.
in writing. - in addition to being an unacceptable interference in the constitutional organization of the member states, this report is sewn together with a white thread: as always, it is a matter of destroying nations by upsetting the internal political order of the states, in order to build a federal europe. the argument put forward to bring the union closer to the citizens is a fraud. complementing the work undertaken at supranational level, the work of transferring the powers of the states from above to the european union, parliament is in reality only seeking to empty the nations of their sovereignty from below. the naïve who are sensitive to the sirens of local democracy or new governance, concepts fabricated by the ruling techno-structure, should know that the decentralisation promoted by and for the federalists will be nothing but a zero-sum game: in the end, it is brussels which, by absorbing the new prerogatives provisionally granted to local entities, will benefit from a process which it will have wisely controlled. let the candidates ponder this moral of la fontaine: "whatever eats you, man or wolf, all flesh seems to me one in this respect; "one day earlier, one day later, it doesn't make much difference".

- report (a5-0431/2002) by mr andria, on behalf of the committee on economic and monetary affairs, on the communication from the commission to the council and the european parliament entitled 'clearing and settlement mechanisms in the european union - key issues and future challenges' (com (2002) 257 - c5-0325/2002 - 2002/2169 (cos)).
- mr president, first of all i would like to thank our colleague mr andria on behalf of my group for his work. the subject is complex and mr andria has used every means at his disposal to reach a compromise. our group is very satisfied with the method of work and the results obtained. the report as voted on in the committee on economic and monetary affairs is very balanced. we would like to make two minor amendments to clarify the text and not to change its substance. i shall not repeat here the importance of our work on the establishment of a european-wide integrated financial market. our parliament has already examined some aspects of this market and laid down some of the many common rules which will be necessary for its proper functioning. a single and transparent framework for clearing and settlement is one of these essential rules. that is why, in parallel with our work on the investment services directive, our parliament is asking the commission to draw up a draft directive on clearing and settlement. in the absence of any regulation, market players have organised themselves, creating a system that, while it works, is far from optimal. moreover, this system naturally tends to create a private monopoly and to distort competition by confusing infrastructure functions with banking functions. we cannot seriously accept it. of course, we could, as some of my colleagues suggest, let the market organize itself. we can also take up our responsibilities as co-legislators and ask the commission to establish rules to ensure transparency and free competition. as you all know, markets can only achieve a healthy balance if they are organised in a transparent and secure way. that is not the case today, and that is what my group is asking for. we support the rapporteur on three main points. first, the removal of all obstacles to the creation of a single market for clearing and settlement. the obstacles, whether technical, fiscal or legal, impede the outcome of individual crossborder transactions and must be removed. secondly, free exercise and transparency of competition. we are asking for open and fair access to settlement-delivery infrastructures. we believe that these settlement-delivery infrastructures should be considered as a service of general interest. this should not prejudice their private or public status, but allow them to be managed as non-profit-making entities and be accessible without discrimination to all users. finally, the current state of confusion between infrastructure and commercial functions must be brought to an end. we cannot accept that certain players, motivated solely by the prospect of profit, expose infrastructure functions to banking risk. this is particularly relevant at a time when the us is strengthening its market protection measures. that is why our group will support mr andria's request for a clear separation of roles. we will thus protect our markets and put an end to the dumping which is so often masked by confusion. the european commission has asked us to comment on this matter. it is not by presenting an empty recommendation that we will be able to play our full role as co-legislators. for this reason, our group will reject all the delayed amendments and will support the rapporteur in his clear and constructive positions. we tabled two amendments; the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. we only think that the wording of the current paragraph 11 no longer corresponds to the state of market forces and would cause too great a disruption if the settlement services were to be owned by their users. we also took the liberty of adding to the compromise agreed by all the groups on paragraph 12 our commitment to transparency and the exercise of free competition. i think that should not be a problem for my colleagues.
- mr president, i congratulate my colleague mr andria on his excellent work, firstly, and on his political courage on a difficult issue, secondly. in the financial market action plan, this subject of clearing and settlement was not given the attention it deserved from the outset and this omission must now be corrected. the post-market infrastructure is essential for the successful completion of the transactions. you said something about trust, security. there are also systemic risks associated with this type of activity, which are therefore clearly in the public interest. on the other hand, these are activities with increasing returns. and it is for these two reasons that, in all historical logic, regulation in the public interest is indispensable. we know that these regulations exist at national level, whereas at european level the fragmentation of infrastructure and rules was predominant until recently. it is therefore time to draw up legislation in line with our objective of building the internal market. we find that, in the absence of appropriate legislation, the current trend is biased and dangerous, because we are seeing the creation of entities that combine clearing settlement activities and competitive banking activities, without a framework of general interest and at the risk, obviously, of distorting competition. the rapporteur is therefore absolutely right, both for reasons of substance and experience, to choose a public service or, i would say, public utility approach, the terms do not matter - in the united states, we speak of public utility, it is the same thing. hence the proposals to separate non-profit activities from cost-based pricing practices. and in conclusion, i would say that now is the time to legislate. i don't see why we have to consult again. we have clear positions from the rapporteur which our parliament should adopt without any sweeteners in order to have a positive line. we therefore believe that the commission should now, for the sake of the credibility of all our work, prepare the draft directive.

- mr president, madam commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, the work of the european commission, the work of the rapporteur, whom i thank, and the work of our european parliament, whose representatives spoke this evening, is based on two central facts. a very positive fact: the human life span is steadily increasing with a real decline in the outward signs of aging. another factor which is of great concern to economists and especially to budgetary officials of all stripes is that this increase in life expectancy is accompanied by an increase in the cost of health and care, which is also increasing and will increase considerably in the coming years. consequently, if one does not believe that the single market and free competition will solve all the problems in this respect too, one must expect that, in order to guarantee a high level of quality of care for all, significant financial efforts will have to be made in terms of contributions and taxes, which will of course have to be distributed fairly. some people deny it, they're wrong. some people regret it; i feel sorry for them because one day they'll be old too. others, including myself, think and say that it is a matter for the individual. this is the only way to prevent the extension of life from being merely a step back from death and to ensure that this extension represents the maintenance of real life, without forgetting that experience is also a factor of progress. this means high-quality care and services adapted to all situations. this requires public research into new medicines and treatments, changes in mindsets and different priorities for our society and, most importantly, public budgets that meet the needs. at the beginning of the new millennium, mr president, everyone knows this, and some of us even regret it: we are far from having met all these conditions and criteria.

council mr president, commissioner, members of the european parliament, on the one-year anniversary of the signing of the bonn agreement in 2001, in taking stock of the progress made towards its full implementation, i would like to point out that this agreement laid the foundations for the creation of a modern and modern afghan state, for which one could express a moderate satisfaction with the progress achieved so far. in particular, we note that after the establishment of a provisional authority and administration, the extraordinary loya jirga was convened and the president subsequently elected by it. a judicial committee and an independent human rights committee were set up. a central bank was established and the country's currency was issued. a drafting committee was set up as a precursor to the constitutional committee. a proposal for a national development framework was adopted to serve as a guide for reconstruction and the promotion of a better situation in the country. president karzai issued a decree establishing an afghan national army, which is an important step towards afghans taking responsibility for the security and stability of their country. on 22 december 2002, afghanistan and six neighbouring countries signed the kabul declaration on good neighbourly relations and non-interference in the internal affairs of other states, an important development for peace and stability in the region. in general, we could say that president karzai and the afghan transitional government have achieved enough to put the bonn process on a proper track. i would like to point out that at the meeting held in st petersburg on 2 december to confirm the will to implement the bonn agreement on afghanistan and to give a new impetus to the reconstruction effort in that country, a declaration was adopted which clearly states the objectives and timetable for implementing the bonn agreements, introducing the new constitution and the 2004 elections. however, there are still many transitional challenges that the afghan transitional government and the international community must address. in the last six months, there have been few reforms, little visible reconstruction, limited restoration of the balance of power both within the central administration and between the centre and the periphery. progress in these areas is necessary to boost the confidence of the afghan people, which is ultimately the key to supporting the government. the basic philosophy of bonn was, moreover, precisely based on supporting the entire transitional scheme on the traditional, local, national and religious structures of the country. and representativeness must be safeguarded at all costs, but it must be governed by rules which are entered into centrally by the government. the european union must not be allowed to continue to be a mere spectator, but must be a witness to the fact that the european union is a political force, a political force which is not only a political force but also a political force, a political force which is not only a political force but also a political force. the government is inherently fragmented, with members drawn from all regions of the country, and so it is of particular importance to try to support and accelerate the pace of reconstruction in the country. a useful means of supporting the central government is to channel aid exclusively through the government, in order to assert its authority throughout the country and to ensure the commitment of neighbouring countries and local leaders. the european union is also committed to the development of a common foreign and security policy, which will be based on the principles of the united nations charter and the united nations charter. we share the views of the afghan people that although insecurity still exists, the desired progress has not been made to the extent that we would like. the economic reconstruction of the country should also be a priority. the afghan authorities should, in cooperation with the international monetary fund, establish an effective and coherent macroeconomic and monetary framework within which to establish stable economic growth and to enable donor offerings to be invested. in this context, tokyo's international donors should be encouraged to actually commit the pledged resources through the national investment budget presented by the afghan administration. the community's assistance to afghanistan will certainly continue to be based on conditions dictated by the basic principles and values which we share as members of the western community. our conditions are aimed at the success of the bonn agreement and, consequently, at the compliance of all parties in afghanistan with a process that has been put in place and aims at peace, representative government, stability, the condemnation of terrorism and the curbing of the illicit production and trafficking of drugs. community assistance should be directed towards national stability and reconstruction, improving food supplies and supporting the return of refugees and displaced persons. the strengthening of democratic values, pluralism and respect for human rights, including women's rights, is a necessary condition for social and political development in this country. we encourage the afghan transitional government to work closely with the international community to establish verifiable benchmarks and timetables so that the full implementation of the bonn agreement can be ensured. the council has already expressed its satisfaction at the role turkey has assumed in the management of the international security promotion force. we congratulate germany and the netherlands on agreeing to take over the leadership of isaf for the next six months and wish them every success in the difficult task they are undertaking. i would like to reiterate the european union's commitment to help afghanistan, in cooperation with the united nations, to eliminate the production and trafficking of illicit drugs by accelerating the implementation of reconstruction programmes, including in the areas where the drugs are cultivated, by developing law enforcement institutions and by providing alternatives to the local population to gain a better prospect. for afghanistan to develop into a modern state requires success in a series of reforms in the areas of security, administration, justice, economy, social welfare. we support the establishment of committees for the drafting of a constitution, for the modernisation of the judicial system and for the protection of human rights. however, we note that the committee on public administration is not yet fully operational. the european union is committed to contributing to the work of these bodies. the committee on the judiciary must also be strengthened to enable it to make progress in the procedural system. we welcome italy's contribution to this by hosting the conference on justice in afghanistan in rome last december. in this context, timetables and milestones are necessary to ensure the implementation of the provisions of the bonn agreement. in particular, the activation of the committee responsible for drafting a new constitution and the adoption of an electoral law to hold elections by june 2004 are immediate priorities. the presidency will continue to follow these issues through the european union special representative for afghanistan. the year 2003 is crucial for this country and will probably determine its future shape. during this year, president karzai should undertake the reforms needed to bring reconstruction and reconstruction to a rapid pace, to substantially reduce the power of local leaders, to draft a modern and functional constitution based on the principles of good governance, to convene a constituent assembly and to advance preparations for the 2004 elections so that the afghan people can see their aspirations fulfilled for peaceful conditions in afghanistan, for progress, and where afghans themselves can determine their future without violence and fear. we reiterate the european union's continued commitment to make a substantial contribution to the reconstruction of afghanistan. finally, we recall that the council, in its conclusions of 4 december 2002, has already invited the high representative and special representative of the european union, mr vendrell, to monitor closely the implementation of the petersburg commitments and, in cooperation with the commission, to make recommendations on further actions that the european union can take in support of the afghan transitional government.
commission. – mr president, i very much welcome this opportunity, with my colleague mr ionitsis, to discuss progress in afghanistan over the past year. as i said to the foreign affairs committee in december, the changes have been in many respects dramatic, and do offer a real chance to build a stable democracy. but timing is critical; there is – as the minister properly underlined – a limited window of opportunity which we have to exploit. unless president karzai and his government manage to strengthen their position throughout the country, then there is a risk that these early gains will be lost. but before turning to the substantial challenges that lie ahead, i would like to say something about the successes of 2002, successes accomplished in extremely difficult circumstances. only a year ago donors met in tokyo to pledge over usd 1.8 billion for 2002. much has since been achieved in afghanistan. in the summer, president karzai was elected by an emergency loya jirga to lead the afghanistan transitional authority; constitutional and judicial commissions have been established; a new currency has been introduced, and the process of recovery and of reconstruction is well under way with increasingly strong leadership from the afghan government. the international community has not only honoured the pledges made at tokyo, but, not least in comparison with some problems we have experienced in the past, the speed of disbursement has been remarkable. the track record of the european union and the european commission has been, i think one can fairly say, particularly impressive. by early december, eur 755 million of the total european union commitment of over eur 830 million had actually been disbursed. the commission has played a leading role in co-ordinating the european union effort and we have been actively involved in building up a strategic dialogue on afghanistan with the united states and other g-8 partners. i must say that i am very proud of the quality of the ec assistance programme and the speed with which it has been delivered. it is a fine example of a successful linkage between relief and recovery, and it has been a good test case for the reform of the management of the external service. it is also fair to pay tribute to the excellent staff we have at the newly set-up ec office in kabul. i would also like to pay tribute to the special representative, who brings so much knowledge and so much expertise to his extremely challenging work. in more concrete terms, our development programme of over eur 205 million in 2002 has helped to finance: firstly, the operation of 238 health clinics and over 450 primary schools as part of the government’s 2002 back to school campaign; secondly, the clearance of landmines and unexploded bombs from more than 8 000 square kilometres of land; thirdly, the return of some 17 000 key public sector workers, including the return to service of over 2 000 teachers and 2 000 nurses and doctors and fourthly, the creation of jobs. through our rural recovery and urban rehabilitation programmes, we are financing over 3 million person days of work this year alone, and i should also refer to the rebuilding of infrastructure. the commission, along with the swedish government and pakistan, has already started the emergency rehabilitation and reconstruction of the kabul-jalalabad-torkham road and full reconstruction will start next year. in addition, our humanitarian aid has helped to support the return of over 1.8 million refugees to afghanistan. over eur 70 million has been spent by echo in 2002. that means that the money which we have spent in total in afghanistan over the last twelve months, the money which is voted by this parliament, now stands at eur 275 million. i do not think anybody can suggest that we have not played – or are not still playing – our full part so far in the reconstruction of afghanistan. for 2003, the challenge will be to consolidate this early progress. the commission will continue to play a leading role. we anticipate total development assistance of about eur 185 million, and there will also be continued humanitarian assistance from echo of between eur 45 and 55 million. that means that we will be spending in afghanistan this year, on present estimates, between eur 230 and 240 million. colleagues will recall that at tokyo on behalf of the commission i pledged eur 1 billion over five years in reconstruction assistance. that is not including the humanitarian assistance figures that i have mentioned, so the total contribution of the european commission, from your taxpayers' money, to afghanistan, quite apart from contributions from member states, will be well in excess of eur 1 billion for the reconstruction of afghanistan. some people in the past have derided that sort of work as nation-building or social work. frankly, when i look back, i think if we had done more of it in the 1980s and 90s, we would not have the problems that we have had recently in afghanistan. (applause) success in 2003 will hinge on three key issues. first, the need to improve internal security. second, the need to ensure human rights are fully respected, including those of women and minorities. when i visited kabul last year, one of the most moving visits that i paid was to a school in the extraordinary bomb site that is southern and western kabul, where young women had returned to schooling for the first time in six years and were sitting in classrooms without blackboards, without textbooks, being taught physics. i must say the commitment and dedication of the staff, and of those young women, was remarkable: anybody who ever thought that it would have been right for us to stand by and allow taliban rule to continue indefinitely should perhaps have been present on that occasion. the third key issue for us is the need for continued long-term commitment from donors and for effective coordination. the argument about coordination is one which has been extremely well made by members of this parliament, and i will say another word about it a little later if i may. internal security is critical not only for the future of afghanistan but also to the delivery of aid. aid workers must be able to work without fear of recrimination. in this context, i would like to express my strong concern about the death of one aid worker, and the serious injury of two others, in kabul just before christmas. i think sometimes we underestimate the amounts of courage and commitment which are required for aid workers working in these sort of circumstances. president karzai’s commitment at the 2 december bonn ii conference to form an afghan national army is a welcome step forward, as is the recent signing of the kabul declaration on good-neighbourly relations. the government must press on quickly with the creation of a national army, but clearly this will not be achieved overnight. in the meantime, the international community must do everything possible to support president karzai and to strengthen the government’s position across all regions of the country, including in the fight against opium poppy production. the minister has already referred to our concern about this. if you look at the present un figures, there is very considerable reason not just for concern, but alarm. there has been a substantial increase in the amount of hectares under opium production, a rapid increase in the farm-gate price of poppies, a ballooning in the production of heroin with implications not only for surrounding countries, but for european countries, and for the funding of organised crime and terrorism in the region and beyond. i believe that we have to give far more attention to this problem in the next year or so, a problem which directly affects political authority in afghanistan itself. overall, as agreed at the bonn ii meeting, we need tangible benchmarks to measure progress. these are critical not only to shape our vision of afghanistan’s future, but to provide support to the reformers within the government. this is of critical importance for human rights. recent reports highlight the unacceptable situation faced by minority groups, and women, in some parts of the country. we must secure fundamental change by ensuring that the establishment of the independent human rights commission translates into tangible change on the ground, and that the new constitution enshrines human rights for all, including women. clearly, these issues are vital in view of the general elections which are scheduled for mid 2004. we also cannot hope to deliver sustainable change without good donor coordination. we must all continue to give a strong and consistent message to the afghan government about the need to tackle internal security, to respect human rights for everyone and to set benchmarks for progress. i would like to finish by stressing that we must be prepared for the long haul – regardless of other events that may unfold in 2003. rebuilding a cohesive state will take time, as will improving the unacceptably low levels of education and healthcare. i want to assure parliament of my personal commitment to these tasks. i paid a first trip to kabul in may 2002 and will be returning this february as part of a trip to the central asian republics. i intend to make one of the priorities of my visit the discussion of the better coordination of donor efforts, including the work done by ngos. the support received from this house has been very reassuring, especially in helping to secure funding for afghanistan for 2003. i look forward to an equally rewarding working relationship with parliament over the coming year and i want to express my great gratitude for the informed and thoughtful contribution which parliament has made to the discussion of these issues. it is sometimes difficult for the international community to focus on more than one or two blips on its radar screen at any one moment. there is a real danger of us assuming that, because we do not read as much about afghanistan on the front pages of the newspapers, our job in afghanistan is, as we would say colloquially in english, done and dusted. it is far from that. there is a huge job for us to do in afghanistan. there are worrying tasks for the international community in the central asian republics and there are reasons for concern about the situation in pakistan. so i hope that we can continue to focus on this work in the years ahead, whatever the tragic distractions may be elsewhere.

- madam president, the conciliation has produced a result which, in the end, satisfies no one. animal rights campaigners say the text does not go far enough, industry does not think it can meet deadlines and consumers do not understand what has been decided, particularly on animal testing, which is at the heart of the directive. by prohibiting, without any possibility of derogation, the testing and placing on the market of products tested on animals six years after its entry into force, the directive is putting the cosmetics industry on the back foot and undermining its capacity for innovation. however, we all wanted, from the very beginning of the negotiations, to bring healthy and anallergic cosmetic products to the market, to save animals from unnecessary suffering and to preserve the employment, competitiveness and know-how of our export-oriented companies. however, the deadline agreed will lead, in our view, to the safety of products on the market no longer being guaranteed - these products will not have been subjected to comprehensive tests offering the same guarantees as tests on animals - to the penalisation of european products on the markets of third countries which continue to carry out animal testing, the only fully reliable methods today, and to the risk of a wto sanction, which may perceive this ban as an obstacle to the marketing of cosmetic products manufactured outside the european union. it is generally accepted that few alternative methods will appear within the next ten years and that the complete replacement of animal testing could be envisaged within the next fifteen years. i think it would have been more realistic to agree to a ban in ten years' time, with a derogation for three types of tests, those on reproductive toxicity, on toxicokinetics and on toxicity in case of repeated application. despite this, there are some positive points, such as the indication on the packaging of the durability of the use of the products and the possible presence of allergenic ingredients, which are concrete measures that improve consumer protection. finally, i note that some directives are now in their seventh revision, while others, such as the birds directive, which dates from 1979, and the habitats directive, which has just celebrated its tenth anniversary, have not yet been revised.

in writing. - this seventh amendment to directive 76/768/eec on cosmetic products is essential because, in addition to the fact that it seeks to approximate the different laws of the member states relating to cosmetic products, its main purpose is to establish a permanent and definitive ban in the european union on the carrying out of animal experiments for finished cosmetic products. this objective could have remained a wishful thinking if parliament had not demanded that both an immediate ban on animal testing for finished products and ingredients, where alternative testing methods have been validated by the european centre for the validation of alternative methods, and a ban on the placing on the market of cosmetic ingredients tested on animals be put in place simultaneously. i believe that only the coexistence of these two prohibitions is a really effective way of stimulating the development of alternative experimental methods. finally, with reference to the precautionary principle, i think it is necessary that carcinogenic, mutagenic or toxic to reproduction substances, classified according to their hazard in categories 1, 2 and 3, should be banned from use in cosmetic products.

in writing. - while the commission, in its communication of 7 may 2002, sought to lead the member states in the unrealistic direction of supranational (so-called 'integrated') management of the external borders, the governments have brought it back to reality by adopting a plan for the management of the external borders based on practical and useful measures: exchange of good experience, operational coordination, joint continuing training, compatibility of equipment, joint risk analysis... the pirker report of the european parliament is rather following this path, and so are we, as we said at the european council in seville (june 2002). however, the report seems to regret - hence our abstention in the vote - that the council has rejected the idea of an integrated european border guard corps. such supranationalisation of the guarding of the external borders would in fact be highly counterproductive, since it would relieve the member states of responsibility. it is essential that each of us remain in control of our boundaries. on the other hand, it would be useful for those states which, because of their geographical position, incur substantial expenditure in this respect, which benefits their neighbours in the union, to receive substantial technical and financial support from the union. european solidarity should find useful expression here.

council mr president, ladies and gentlemen of the european parliament, the debate on lebanon is indeed a direct reference to the discussions on the middle east, both on the issues of israel and on the discussions we have had over the last 24 hours on iraq. the situation in lebanon remains extremely complex, mainly because of the coexistence of many communities, which makes a multi-ethnic, multi-lingual and multi-religious approach to the problems necessary, without forgetting that lebanon also hosts a large number of palestinian refugees, some 370 000. these communities are represented at institutional level. the implementation of the provisions of the thaad agreement of 22 october 1989, which provide, inter alia, for the stationing of syrian forces in certain areas of lebanon, is in principle part of the relations between lebanon and syria. the council is closely following the internal political dialogue in lebanon. the israeli withdrawal from southern lebanon in may 2000, accompanied by the partial redeployment of the lebanese-syrian army in june 2001, is a first step. at the same time, hezbollah's presence in the south of the country risks being a destabilizing factor for lebanon in its relations with israel. the parliamentary elections of 3 september 2000, which were held in a free manner, represent a step in the right direction towards the normalisation of the situation in lebanon. the destabilising effect of the middle east conflict in lebanon can therefore be underlined. the council has on many occasions reaffirmed that the fight against terrorism is its priority. in this connection, the recent terrorist act in bali has once again underlined the need for close multinational cooperation against terrorism. the implementation of the action plan decided by the european council in september 2001 is progressing well. as regards its external dimension, the council decided to include the fight against terrorism in the framework of the agreement concluded by the european union with third countries. the fact that lebanon is among the first countries to sign the agreement with the european union on this issue demonstrates its willingness to actively cooperate with the eu, including in the area of information exchange. the link between the cooperation agreement on counter-terrorism and the association agreement was underlined by the fact that the two agreements were signed on the same day, on 17 june 2002 in luxembourg, and will enter into force simultaneously - and i hope very soon. the council is closely monitoring the respect for human rights. the council expressed its concern at the action of the lebanese army against christian activists in august 2001 and the closure of the independent television station mtf last september. the association agreement will also strengthen the monitoring capacity of this issue and encourage the lebanese authorities to respect human rights more. i would remind you that the agreement makes respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms a key element in the internal and external policies of both sides. it will also institute a regular political dialogue at various levels, notably in the association council, on all issues of interest. the european parliament has already expressed its views on the association agreement, and i would like to ask the commission to give its assent to it. the signing of the association agreement was a significant development and the beginning of a new chapter in our relations with lebanon. the agreement is mainly about intergovernmental relations, but it also provides a framework for business and civil society to operate. this agreement is important for the whole of the eu's mediterranean policy and is a further step towards the creation of a euro-mediterranean free trade area. i would point out that lebanon has just ratified both the association agreement and the interim agreement, which will enter into force on 1 march 2003. the existence of good channels of communication between the policies of the two sides of the mediterranean is an important factor in a constructive eu relationship with our mediterranean partners. at bilateral level, the association agreement provides for the possibility for the council of the european union - lebanon to facilitate cooperation and contacts between the european parliament and the parliamentary institutions of lebanon. the members concerned must, however, define the framework for this dialogue, which, as far as the council is concerned, should be complementary to the wider euro-mediterranean dialogue. i welcome the results of the last meeting of the euro-mediterranean forum in bari in june 2002, which underlined the parliamentary dimension in our cooperation with the mediterranean countries. we are currently examining the cooperation mechanisms for the creation of a euro-mediterranean parliamentary assembly. the european parliament has started work on the creation of such a euro-mediterranean parliamentary assembly, bringing together members of the 27 national parliaments and the european parliament. the euro-mediterranean conference in valencia proposed strengthening the parliamentary dimension of the euro-mediterranean dialogue by creating a euro-mediterranean parliamentary assembly. i welcome the recent meeting of the euro-mediterranean parliamentary forum in bari on 17-18 june 2002, which voted in favour of the creation of a euro-mediterranean parliamentary assembly and decided to set up a working group to set up such an assembly. the high-level officials responsible for the barcelona process also agreed to set up a working group to coordinate with the baris group. the greek presidency aims to exploit the potential of euro-mediterranean cooperation and strengthen its parliamentary dimension. this is one of the priorities of our presidency in order to achieve new levels of integration and to strengthen the credibility of euro-mediterranean cooperation. to this end, we are currently examining the cooperation mechanisms and the measures necessary to set up the said assembly. it is desirable, if not necessary, for the euro-mediterranean parliamentary forum to take a decision at its next meeting in crete on 27 march 2003 on its conversion into a parliamentary assembly. in this case, the conference of foreign ministers in crete on 26-27 may 2003 could welcome this decision, so that this new institution becomes a reality.
commission. – mr president, the house is considering today a very important resolution on the adoption of the association agreement signed with lebanon in june last year. this agreement is not only important for our relations with lebanon – it is also crucial in the overall european union-mediterranean partnership since it represents another step towards the completion of the grid of association agreements within the barcelona process (the only agreement still being negotiated is the one with syria and i am hoping to have the opportunity next month of trying to persuade the syrians to go ahead themselves more seriously to negotiate an agreement). lebanon is a key partner in the euro-mediterranean structure. when prime minister hariri was elected to office in september 2000, he set his government an ambitious deadline – to conclude the negotiations with the european commission by the end of 2001. i am very pleased that he has delivered on this promise and i call upon members of the house to vote favourably on the resolution, and to endorse the agreement. parliament has before it, in my judgment, the means to provide lebanon with a firm foundation for building its future. the country has experienced a terrible civil war. it has been the victim of outside interference, it still remains vulnerable. lebanon is now grappling with recovery and with modernisation under difficult economic circumstances, faced with poor immediate prospects for peace in the middle east, smouldering tensions along the border with israel and the unsettling possibility of a military conflict in iraq. there is broad support in lebanon for this new strengthened relationship with europe. the lebanese parliament ratified both the association agreement and the interim agreement in december. the interim agreement allows both sides to start the 12-year transition period from march 2003, leading to the gradual introduction of free trade. this is a clear sign that lebanon is serious in meeting at an early stage its commitments to opening up large areas of its trade and approximating its legislation to that of the european union. it will also be bound by its engagements on respect for the fundamental principles of human rights and democracy from this date and i want to return to that in a moment. the free-trade area will bring about profound changes to lebanese commerce. lebanon is rightly prized for the entrepreneurial skills of its work force. its economic strategy is already liberal. world trade organisation membership has been requested. the opening of markets and economies will bring benefits through economic liberalisation and increased competitiveness. lebanon will benefit immediately from market access for its agricultural and processed agricultural products. and the union will gain from improved access to service sector industries in lebanon, once these arrangements have been concluded. by signalling lebanon’s commitment to economic and social reform, this agreement will send a clear and positive message to the international and european investment community of the opportunities for direct foreign investment in lebanon. the successful outcome of the paris ii donor conference in november last year, organised with great commitment and success by president chirac, suggests that this message has already struck home. of the 18 governments participating, six were member states and the commission was also represented at its highest level. there is a clear interest in seeing that lebanon weathers the economic storm of post-war recovery, and reduces its debt. the amount pledged to assist in debt relief matched expectations (about $ 4.3 billion were pledged in all). but, the association agreement is first and foremost a political agreement, which is why it devotes so much importance to political dialogue. the agreement is a potent expression of shared values and common objectives. it is through dialogue that members of this partnership can pursue the shared commitment to achieving peace in the middle east. our dialogue, and this was a point which mr galeote quecedo referred to, will embrace the fundamental principles of human rights and democracy with an honesty and appreciation born, i hope, out of close partnership. lebanon’s pluralist society, embracing numerous sectarian and religious groups, has functioned most effectively when there is consensus, tolerance and open debate – a unique feature in the region. we are, however, conscious of the concerns expressed by the parliament’s foreign affairs committee on specific points of the human rights situation in lebanon. the agreement provides an additional forum for tackling these concerns. by ratifying the association agreement, the european union will trigger the important commitments from lebanon concerning human rights and democracy, migration and re-admission, money laundering, the fight against organised crime and illicit drugs, and judicial cooperation. and i know too the concerns which have been expressed about freedom of the media. i can reassure you that the commission will continue to monitor and follow these concerns wherever and whenever possible. the agreement will also, as the minister pointed out, trigger lebanon’s undertakings on cooperation in counter-terrorism, set out in the exchange of letters to which he referred. our partnership will extend well beyond trade and politics, and will be wide-ranging, covering areas as diverse as cooperation in the fields of science, education, energy, tourism, the environment and industry. social and cultural cooperation is also central to the agreement, in terms of rights of workers, and social dialogue. our partnership will be sustained by contributions under the meda programme which i hope will be focused, as far as possible, on implementation of the agreement. so we are moving towards our overall ambitions in the southern mediterranean with the agreement that we have put before parliament with the lebanon and i very much hope that we can move on from this to completing the grid of association agreements by successful negotiations with syria. i commend this agreement most warmly to parliament.
mr president, this morning we are discussing here the fate of the afghan people, who have been torn apart by decades of war and fratricidal strife, and i cannot forget that when i take the floor in this new debate. i am not forgetting that the lebanese people have gone through the same trials and i am pleased that at the end of those trials they were able to find the resources necessary to begin rebuilding the model of multiethnic and multicultural cooperation which you spoke of, mr president-in-office of the council, and which the whole world admired before the disease of fear of the other, of fear of being dominated, which was to spread later in the balkans, where i was personally able to see the ravages, was unleashed there. i do not forget the 'balkanization' of lebanese territory, which was as destructive as the later 'lebanonization' of the former yugoslavia. that is why i can only welcome the progress made in concluding this association agreement with the lebanese republic, which you were right to say, commissioner, would be political first. it will be approved tomorrow, i am sure, by a large majority in our parliament, as proposed by our colleague gerardo galeote. i do, however, recognise the difficulties which remain and which have been raised in this debate by you, mr president-in-office, by the commissioner and by our colleagues elmar brok and gerardo galeote. i personally say that the lebanese model -
