the rapporteur. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, everyone will understand that at the beginning of this debate i express my regret, my deep sympathy and my solidarity with the fishermen and aquaculture workers of the atlantic coast with whom i deal on a daily basis. the year 2003 begins with very sad omens. i would like to return to the growing importance of the aquaculture sector. over the last ten years, aquaculture has experienced a meteoric rise in the world, as well as in the european community, becoming a fast-growing sector in the field of world food production. aquaculture accounts for almost 30% of the total value of fisheries production in the union, almost €3 billion a year, and 60 000 jobs. there are many advantages, but i would like to focus on three of the most important ones. the commission has also proposed that the european parliament should be consulted on the proposal for a directive on the protection of the environment in the event of a serious accident at work. it is a source of employment in areas where there is little alternative, and i am convinced that it will also help to preserve the natural resource if we preserve wild strains. the report i have been asked to present to this house today focuses on what i believe is the most important aspect of aquaculture: sustainable development. in many cases, certain aquaculture activities are considered to be polluting or to be detrimental to the environment. this is less and less true, as professionals respect the european rules, which are sometimes drastic. on the contrary, this sector is particularly and unfortunately too often directly affected by external pollution: nitrates in fresh water, degassing, hydrocarbons, chemicals, toxic algae in seawater. too often, the actors suffer helplessly from tragedies like the prestige. that is why i have focused my report on sustainable development, which is structured around four concepts: environmental, social, economic and governance. i shall not go into the themes that everyone knows well. i would like to emphasize, however, a fundamental aspect of aquaculture, namely research, which must enable us to produce products of unquestionable quality for consumers, to bring new products to the market, to find innovative forms of exploitation such as offshore sites, but also, and why not, as i have proposed, to conserve and develop wild stocks, particularly for fish, with a view to repopulation which in a number of cases may allow the resource to be maintained. i 'll see you later . i shall not go into my report either, which i am very pleased to have unanimously adopted in the committee on fisheries. i would rather take this opportunity to express once again my sympathy for the fishermen and fish farmers who have been so permanently affected by the sinking of the prestige, which clearly shows their vulnerability. they are not polluters, they are sufferers. this disaster, which began with pollution of the galician coast, also affected the french atlantic coast, including the arcachon basin, a major centre of oyster farming. behind aquaculture sites are men, men who have worked tirelessly to ensure the quality of their products and who risk having all their efforts, even their lives, reduced to nothing. the prestige case has thus plunged all members of a profession, and their families, into moral and economic distress for an indefinite period. it is intolerable that oyster fishermen should once again be the victims of the insecurity of the sea and the oil spills on our coasts. in this connection, i would like to congratulate the commission, which at the time proposed the start of the necessary measures, under the cover of the erika 1 and erika 2 packages, and i would like to express my regret, and i am addressing this directly to the presidency, that these measures have been postponed for some, not taken into account for others, under the pressure of a limited number of member states, which are more likely to rely on economic incentives than to devote themselves to the essential thing: the survival of the planet. what can we do in the short term? it is true that resources already exist in the framework of fifg programming and a whole range of measures can be implemented; the commissioner has answered me on this. finally, i would stress the importance of combating flags of convenience and the need to create a european coastguard; although its creation would be difficult in the short term, the benefits of such a body would include improving the efficiency of controls and thus enhancing maritime safety. i do not forget that, beyond the prestige, the sea bandits pollute our seas every day with a crime that is too little sanctioned, the dumping of gas. i strongly urge the greek presidency to put maritime safety and disaster response as a priority on its agenda. this report will be adopted under very sad circumstances; but let us look resolutely to this sector of the future. it is important that the commission implements what my report recommends, particularly in its research and innovation aspects. consumers and the whole industry will be involved.
- mr president, first of all i would like to congratulate mr hugues martin on this excellent report, which he has drawn up in consultation with the professionals. at a time when the demand for fish is expected to increase considerably and when the sound management of fish stocks should be an objective, aquaculture has a de facto complementary role to play in supplying markets. however, as the rapporteur points out, its development requires a number of precautions. in view of the experience gained, we would like to stress the need to strengthen research, because it is not conceivable to base this development on systems of breeding which show their limits. research must therefore be equipped with the means to provide answers to the key questions arising, such as the impact on the environment, the reduction of the use of fishmeal in the diet, the development of less carnivorous species, the control of diseases, the genetic risks to natural populations linked to escapement and the development of new products. i also support the rapporteur in refusing the introduction of genetically modified fish into the european union. livestock products and fishery products are different. they must therefore be identified accordingly in order to give consumers the freedom of choice. but the expansion of aquaculture production can only be envisaged as a complement to traditional production, which, let us not forget, actively contributes to the economic activity of our coastal regions.
- mr president, this is a good report, solid and well-worked, concerning an important sector in which we are very short of funds - we import more than half of the fish we consume - where traceability can only be better ensured by domestic production and where, with a resource ceiling, aquaculture can create essential complementary jobs in our coastal regions. the rapporteur is right to denounce the silence of the green paper on aquaculture and to point out the shortcomings of the commission's communication of september 2002. the aquaculture sector is characterised above all by the size and duration of the research effort, which is often disproportionate to the financing possibilities of young, family-run, low-capitalised enterprises operating in a context of intense competition and unstable prices. for example, the french company which created the european turbot industry, headed by michel adrien from vendée, had to invest chf 2.5 million per year in pure research for ten years before it was able to master the technique of turbot breeding in captivity. should and can such heavy, costly research programmes, involving considerable technical and commercial uncertainties, and dealing with questions of fundamental biology be undertaken entirely by companies? i don't think he did. i believe, on the contrary, that this type of research must be carried out, to a large extent, with the help of public funds, just as the permanent renovation of the work equipment of the small-scale fishing enterprise, that is, its vessels. it is clear that in such cases state aid cannot be considered to distort competition. i am thinking in particular of research into new vaccines to eliminate the risks associated with the use of antibiotics. this is a crucial issue for the future and the perception of the sector. strong financial incentives, both at national and community level, must therefore be put in place. i also support the idea of adjusting the rules of the fifg, and i will add those of the eaggf, to allow the financing of aid for the settlement of young people, the transfer of holdings, consumer information. i share the rapporteur's concern about the risk of genetically modified fish and it is clear that this practice must be completely banned both for production in the european union and for import. finally, mr president, we must be very vigilant about unfair competition practices by certain third countries, since dumping must be absolutely prohibited in an emerging and volatile market. the import of aquaculture products which do not comply with the standards imposed on producers in the european union must be strictly prohibited and this prohibition duly controlled.
mr president, our colleague mr martin's report deals with a scientifically exciting and exciting subject, including economic and social issues, and it is also a topical issue. the prestige case in galicia, where spain is the leader in shellfish farming, or arcachon, where france is the leader in oyster farming, showed that this was indeed a very fragile activity, both in terms of continental aquaculture, which our colleague van dam seems to have forgotten, and in terms of marine aquaculture, that is to say fish farming, but also oyster farming. it is an activity that is very closely linked (you have to know it well to understand it) to the environment, these are extremely subtle balances. not just water, not just currents, not just chemistry, not just biology. consider that in enclosed environments, such as coastal ponds, the mediterranean, lake thau, the mere painting of boats can disturb the environment. that's why the sea farmers are doing sustainable development without knowing it all along. it is a future activity, because we are moving out of the harvest to carry out noble activities with noble fish - whether bars, daurads, turbot - and high-tech activities; to undertake major scientific breakthroughs, research on gmos, on diploid or triploid oysters, on vaccines. with, of course, limitations that must be taken into account. it is certain that fish are used to feed fish. the quantities of fishmeal are therefore greater than the quantities of fish produced and there is a risk that the fishery will be fed by the meal; hence the need for research. health problems: these are not just problems of antibiotics or bacteria, but of mysterious, microscopic algae, like dinophysis. hence the need to avoid intensive farming, to control gmos, especially genetically modified salmon, and the need to have deep-sea farms, as in japan. but we must not do bambi, walt disney, and talk about fish welfare; otherwise, you'll have to stop opening the oysters because it's cruel or putting lemon in them because they're suffering. the establishment of young people must therefore be encouraged by training, investment in sewage treatment plants and bars, cutting-edge scientific research, perhaps even nanobiology, and the creation of quality labels (for example for oysters from arcachon, but also for those from bouzigues, which may be superior, or from the thau pond). finally, mr president, with ten thousand years of delay, ten thousand years of delay on the peasants of the earth, perhaps we should consider cultivating the sea.

- mr president, famines are increasing in africa. we're moved by the children who are starving, but we don't address the causes. beyond the climate hazards, famines are the result of structural policies, including agricultural and trade policies, which have led farmers in poor countries to produce for export rather than for local consumption. food aid is not a viable solution. in the name of good conscience, it has often become a means for rich countries to dispose of their agricultural surpluses and also to legitimize their devastating policy of overproduction. the united states is therefore rushing to sell its boycotted gmos on the european market, not only in the form of food but also in the form of seeds. cynically, they accuse governments of allowing their people to die if they refuse to provide such aid. this blackmail of vulnerable populations is indecent. it is contrary to the fundamental right to food which recognizes that every human being has the freedom to choose his food. who are the most guilty ? the countries suffering from famine that refuse to feed their populations with potentially harmful products, or those that offer only genetically modified seeds to help poor people, whose consequences for the environment and biodiversity will prove to be disastrous? in some of these countries or regions, food shortages are not widespread. the problem is not necessarily a lack of food, but an equitable distribution of it around the world. only local production and intra-regional trade are sustainable and can guarantee access to food for all. the european union, on the other hand, advocates free trade at the global level and forces developing countries to open their markets. in return, it promises to open its market to all products, except arms, but of course also, except bananas, except sugar, etc., from the least developed countries. not only has this measure created competition between developing countries, instead of increasing their market shares, but it has also promoted export crops at the expense of self-sufficient food crops. in the same vein, the current crisis in coffee farming reminds us that free trade leads to the ruin of small farmers and the prosperity of large multinational firms. free trade is not fair trade. in fact, there is no reference to fair trade in the new commission communication on trade and development, which we shall soon have the opportunity to discuss in this house. president lula has made the fight against hunger his priority. it proposes the creation of an international fund for this purpose. this is also the aim of the fao, whose recent summit seems to have had no significant impact. the greens believe that only sustainable development of food production based on the needs of local people and fair trade between north and south, that is, trade that pays its fair price, reflecting the social and environmental costs of production, resources and workers in poor countries, can eradicate hunger in the world.
- mr president, commissioner, the integration of the economies of the poorest countries into the world trade system remains a decoy if the revenue envisaged does not take account of the difficulties these countries face in trading and, above all, in developing. the fight against poverty and food insecurity, and the prevention of the conflicts that often follow, must target the structural causes and free ourselves from failed economic, agricultural and trade policies. the main economic obstacles to meeting the food needs of billions of people are well known: the obligation to sell at prices below production costs, the quasi-obligation imposed on the agriculture of these countries to target export products useful to the northern countries before they are needed by the populations of the south, the liberalization of trade promoted by international institutions such as the world bank, the imf and the wto, to the detriment of the right of peoples to define their own policy. the commission could decide to tackle these problems. unfortunately, i fear that the path taken is, once again, not the right one. indeed, the undp report in 2002 reminds us that if the process continues at this turtle-like pace, it will take more than 130 years to eliminate hunger. world hunger deserves better than a pressing appeal from rich countries to poor countries to rely on the rules of the wto. when 60 percent of zambia's population is in need of food aid and the multinational monsanto, with dupont, controls 93 percent of the market for its seeds, it deserves better than short-sighted, short-term private investment. when world trade is worth $7 trillion a year, when financial transactions are worth $1.5 trillion a day and when the world bank itself considers it necessary to double global development aid, which is capped at $50 billion a year, when is a useful tax levied on international financial transactions to finance this aid? that is where the european union could be useful. the fight against poverty requires that developing countries gain the right to set their own priorities, their own strategies to support sustainable food production by mobilising their natural and human resources, local know-how, investing in the structural transformation of their economies, and also benefiting from legitimate guaranteed prices. free trade agreements between unequal parties, based on the abolition of customs tariffs, regardless of the level of development of each, have exacerbated poverty and have a negative impact on food security. there is an urgent need to encourage local agriculture and food production, by promoting access to land, water and biodiversity resources. there's an emergency to cancel the debts.
- mr president, today, of the six billion people in the world, more than 800 million suffer from malnutrition. three quarters of them are rural people, people whose vocation is to provide not only for themselves but also for their fellow citizens. these 600 million poor farmers are unable to feed themselves or their fellow farmers, because they are the direct victims of the fall in agricultural prices dictated by the liberalization of trade, and they have no choice but to cut off their own stocks of food in an attempt to preserve, often without success, their production potential. how do we get them out of this hell spiral ? by adopting a new approach to the globalisation of agricultural and food trade, the core of which must be the recognition of the principle of food sovereignty. this principle states that each country or group of countries is free to determine its own food supply. food sovereignty is the recognition of the right of peoples to feed themselves and the right of peoples to feed themselves as they wish. it is the opportunity for developing countries to achieve food self-sufficiency by developing their agriculture. it is not enough to proclaim the right of the developing countries to develop their food crops, but the rules of international trade in agricultural products must not prevent them from doing so in practice. these countries must therefore be given the clearest possible recognition of their right to protect their agriculture and to open their markets only selectively, as europe itself has done to end its food dependence. the countries that have been most successful in reducing hunger are those where responsible governments have been able, through policies of supporting agricultural prices and subsidies for inputs and infrastructure, to enable their farmers to access their own internal markets, thereby increasing their purchasing power and productivity and thus their production. if we are to tackle the problem of hunger seriously, it is therefore urgent to put an end to the fall in agricultural prices: the farmer's access to a profitable local market is the first condition for the growth of agricultural production, which is itself the key to the reduction of hunger. the total and unchecked liberalization of agricultural trade does not serve the interests of the hungry countries, it serves the interests of the structurally agricultural exporting countries, but it ruins the poor farmers of the developing countries. it makes no sense to want to put the chadian peasant in direct competition with the farmer in minnesota, the shepherd in the andes and the latifundia in new zealand. if the european union is to make an effective contribution to the eradication of hunger in the world, it must therefore be particularly vigilant in three key areas. first, all agricultural development projects financed by the community in the developing countries will have to include a component of aid for the marketing of food products. secondly, the european union will have to help developing countries or groups of countries with similar production costs to protect their internal market against the dumping prices of the world market, with the help of instruments without which their producers will be ruined. thirdly, the european union must finally exert its full weight in international trade negotiations to ensure that the right to agricultural exception is recognised, that is to say, the right of nations to protect their farmers, who feed them and whose prosperity is a condition for their take-off.

- mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i am the rapporteur for the implementation, through an article 169 programme of eur 600 million, of a partnership between europe and developing countries in the field of research against aids, malaria and tuberculosis. i would like to congratulate mr wijkman. we are all aware of the urgency and the seriousness of the situation. five million people die every year from one of these three diseases; almost 40 million people are infected with aids: 90% of them live in developing countries, with a large proportion - 70% - in sub-saharan africa. there is also a resurgence of tuberculosis. malaria, which reappeared in the 1970's, is again affecting countries where it was eradicated. the european union must therefore adopt a strategy to combat these diseases effectively and quickly. the regulation under discussion here defines the framework for community action. it also creates the legal basis for europe's contribution, with the aim of stimulating research to develop medicines, treatments and vaccines and facilitating access to them. this is absolutely vital because only 10 percent of research activities are on the diseases that are responsible for 90 percent of the conditions around the world. so we need to do public research and encourage private sector investment. it is also important that these medicines are adapted to the living conditions in the countries concerned and that they can be distributed through health systems worthy of the name. finally, prices must not be prohibitive, and this brings us back to the problem of intellectual property. i therefore support this report, mr president, and i hope that it will be adopted in one reading.

- the next item is the report (a5-0009/2003) by mr santini, on behalf of the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs, on the proposal for a european parliament and council directive on the right of citizens of the union and their family members to move and reside freely within the territory of the member states (com (2001) 257 - c5-0336/2001 - 2001/0111 (cod)).
commission. – madam president, first of all i would like to thank the rapporteur once again for his excellent report and confirm that the commission will be able to incorporate the vast majority of the proposed amendments into our amended proposal, which we will present shortly. let me turn to the two controversial issues during this debate. first of all, concerning article 2 and the concept of family, one has to recognise that harmonising the conditions of residence for european union citizens must not result in our imposing modifications on member state legislation defining family status. i understand this debate and the difficulty of, on the one hand, ensuring compatibility with article 13 of the treaty, which is the legal basis for combating discrimination, including discrimination against unmarried couples or same sex couples when, on the other hand, the treaty excludes family law from the scope of competences of the european union. in this very sensitive field, the community must respect the developments introduced in member state legislation and must be flexible in this. there is no universal legal solution for this kind of de facto partnership or for registered partnerships or same sex marriages. i would like to draw your attention to the fact that we should not exaggerate the extent of the practical difficulties that unmarried couples or same-sex couples encounter in exercising the right of residence. in fact, when the two people are citizens of the european union, they both enjoy the right of residence by virtue of article 18 of the treaty, independently of the nature of their relationship. however, i recognise that the problem arises when one of them is a third-country national. for the time being, the commission's proposal is to define marriage with reference to the term 'spouse', and we do not seek to define this term. in fact, at present, the legislation of only two member states recognises union between persons of the same sex as marriage. under the case law of the court of justice, the term 'marriage' designates a union between persons of the opposite sex. the commission prefers, at the present stage, to follow the case law of the court of justice, and to use a formula that allows progressive interpretation of this concept on the basis of future developments in the legislation of member states. as regards unmarried partners, including registered partners, the commission also considers that the recognition of these situations will have to be made by reference to the host member state legislation. i understand the argument of mutual recognition, but one has to be very careful when using it. the recognition for the purpose of residence of unmarried partners on the basis of the legislation of member states of origin could pose problems to those member states whose family legislation does not recognise these possibilities. in addition, the principle of non-discrimination requires that the host member state treat unmarried couples of other member states in the same way as its own nationals. i believe therefore that everyone will agree, particularly in this field, that we should not create reverse discrimination. that would be the actual outcome of such a proposal. i will follow your deliberations tomorrow and the negotiations with council very closely. i am sure that all of you are aware of the difficulty of this debate and the different approaches of the member states. the rapporteur has suggested an amendment to article 21 concerning equal treatment which aims to exclude inactive people from social assistance during the first six months rather, than the first four years of residence, until they acquire permanent rights of residence, as provided for in the commission's proposals. i am aware that the commission's text needs to be adapted in the light of the recent judgment of the court of justice in this field, which stated that any citizen residing legally in another member state must enjoy equal treatment with its nationals in matters of social welfare. however, despite the fact that mr santini's amendment goes in the right direction, it is not possible to accept it in its current formulation as it is not completely in accordance with the judgment of the court of justice to which i have just referred. the commission considers it preferable to reconsider the proposal and to better scrutinise the content of the court of justice judgment. we will bring forward an amended proposal as soon as possible.
commission. – madam president, mrs ludford is of course right, but her remark raises a second problem, which is that of the legislation of the host country discriminating against unregistered couples. one has to recognise that partners who do not lose the privileges they have in the country of origin, will enjoy a privilege which the citizens of the host state do not have. that is the heart of the issue. i respect your opinion, mrs ludford, and i look forward to the discussion with the council under the co-decision and qualified majority voting procedures, with which you are much more familiar than i am.

- the next item is the report (a5-0010/2003) by mrs terrón i cusí, on behalf of the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs, on the commission proposal for a council directive on the conditions of entry and residence of thirdcountry nationals for the purpose of employment or selfemployment (com (2001) 386 - c5-0447/2001 - 2001/0154 (cns)).
- madam president, ladies and gentlemen, the proposal under discussion today aims to establish a harmonized legal framework for the conditions of entry and residence of third-country nationals. it is clear that the european union is still very lukewarm on this issue. we can only deplore the hypocrisy of european policies. while all countries see development aid as a means of combating illegal immigration, cooperation budgets are being reduced, and brains are being smuggled out of the country without any training being provided. we do not hesitate to select the right immigrants, those who serve our interests, and for the rest we use the readmission clauses of the cooperation agreements to better expel those undocumented people who are already rooted in their social and professional life and are fully involved in the construction of europe. the economic and demographic needs of the member states are met by the exploitation of controlled immigration, which is primarily used to overcome the lack of labour and to compensate for the demographic imbalance, which can be exploited and managed at will, without concern for the future of these people, their protection, or even the respect of their fundamental rights: the right to health, education and housing. yes, mrs. terrón and cusí are right. the question of immigration must be part of a long-term, global vision of the union's community policy. in this context, it is necessary to address issues relating to the management of flows, including visa policy, essential policy, family integration policy, in particular the rights linked to european citizenship, the new definition of development aid involving genuine cooperation. although one of the conclusions of tampere is to ensure fair treatment of third country nationals, this is far from the case when we look more closely at the conditions of entry and residence, but also at the rights of citizens, in particular the freedom of movement, the right to live with one's family or the rights which should be linked to residence and not to nationality. if european legislation makes workers from third countries cheap labour, a kind of cannon fodder for precarious work, the european union will lose all the credibility that its anti-discrimination programmes have taken years to build, programmes that its ideals of justice and freedom require it to defend. everyone knows that the europe of citizens cannot be built on discrimination which is the basis of injustice, exclusion and racialism. it is therefore our responsibility to work towards a community and humanist immigration policy, respectful of fundamental rights and reaffirming that immigration is an opportunity for europe.
mr president, the proposal for a directive under consideration today is aimed at harmonizing the rules for granting work permits to third-country nationals at european level. it poses a first major problem: what exactly is it for? the explanatory statement gives three reasons. firstly, the current rules on the admission of thirdcountry workers would differ from one member state to another. but what 's the difficulty ? on the contrary, it is good and in line with subsidiarity that each state can adapt the rules for the acceptance of foreign workers to the needs of its society and its labour market. the second reason given in the explanatory statement is that applicants and employers would be confronted with national administrative procedures which are sometimes - we are told - very complex. but again, this is a problem for the member states and the community institutions have no business getting involved. the third reason is that the regulation of immigration of workers from third countries would be a cornerstone of the general immigration policy. this proves nothing, because the amsterdam treaty has not communitized immigration policy in general. moreover, the cornerstone, in my view, mr commissioner, would be the fight against illegal immigration rather than the granting of work permits. in the end, this community harmonization of work permits is not justified. it would only serve to open up immigration policy a little more when we already have too many unemployed. for example, i will quote the astonishing provision in article 29 (4) of the proposal which provides that a member state's refusal to grant a work permit to a third country national should contain - and i quote - 'a justification based on objective and verifiable criteria'. i believe that the granting of a work permit to a third-country national is a royal right and that the states should not be prevented from doing so, especially in the present economic situation, where they need to safeguard their essential interests. the proposal for a directive would also lay the foundations for even greater centralisation in the future. the committee on civil liberties of this house has understood this so well that it is now entering the breach by proposing to remove other powers from the states, for example the right to suspend the issuing of licences for reasons connected with the lack of reception capacity. we can see where all this would lead if this directive were adopted. but it is so blatantly violating the principles of subsidiarity and proportionality which we are being told every day that i hope someone in the council will be able to stop it.
commission. – mr president, first of all concerning the legal bases – the issue raised by mr pirker – our assessment is that article 63(3) of the treaty on conditions for entry and residence is the correct legal basis for this proposal for a directive that deals with common definitions, criteria and procedures regarding the conditions of entry and residence of third-country nationals for the purpose of employment. i recognise this is a difficult debate. to be frank, mr nassauer and i have been discussing these issues for a very long time, and we all know that there is no magic solution to this very complex problem of immigration. i accept the criticisms, i can even admit that i can be wrong. however, what i find difficult to accept is being criticised for things that i have never said and that are not written in my proposal. i have never said that there is a right to immigration. there is no right to immigration. i will repeat it hundreds of times: there is a right to asylum, but there is no right to immigration. immigration is only a possibility. our proposal states that very clearly. the decision on admission is exclusively that of the government of each member state or even of the regional or local authorities of the member states - brussels does not decide on one single entry. i recognise that the link between migration and unemployment is very complex. evidence shows that migrants might affect and disrupt the internal labour market. the first victims of new waves of migrants, as far as the functioning of our member states' labour market is concerned, are previous waves of migrants, because there is direct competition between newcomers and the earlier migrants. that is a source of concern, because the existing migrants will be a burden for the social welfare state. is there a direct link between the arrival of migrants and the re-entry into the labour market of our own european citizens? there the connection is much more complex, because in certain cases the difficulty of re-entering the labour market is more connected with the specific characteristics of the welfare state and social security systems that benefit our own citizens. it is unfair to say that migration policies are the reason why european union citizens have difficulty re-entering the labour market. in fact, it is the lack of reform of the welfare state that is responsible for the difficulty of encouraging people to re-enter the labour market. of course, that lack of reform varies from one member state to another. i do not want to harmonise anything with regard to reform of the welfare state. as far as the report is concerned, the commission welcomes and fully agrees with amendments 6, 11, 8 and 12, but we cannot make any commitment today on those amendments concerning rules on intra-corporate transfers and contractual service suppliers. those rules are very interesting and we will bear them in mind. however, they are closely linked to international trade issues and we have to wait for the ongoing world trade organisation negotiations to see what the impact of those negotiations will be on migration policy, above all as far as services are concerned. i would urge you to keep the reference to the eures system before being able to recruit third-country workers, because keeping that system will guarantee the principle of preference for the european labour market. that is a fundamental principle in our proposal. i look forward to seeing parliament's amendments and thank you for this very interesting and stimulating debate.
in writing. - i commend the quality of the work of mrs terrón i cusí. the commission's proposal for a directive on the entry and residence of thirdcountry nationals again focused on legal and illegal immigration and put employment as a prerequisite for granting stable status. i welcome the improvement made by the committee on civil liberties to the proposal for a directive, but i would also like to stress that the rapporteur has shown great lucidity and has approached the subject without demagogy. i note some interesting proposals and progress, including more transparency, simplification of procedures and greater consideration of the interests of third countries. the rapporteur generally favours improving the rights of holders of residence permits for workers and stresses the need for all foreigners to have equal access to education, training and housing assistance. i regret that these proposals were not properly quantified and that the report did not place more emphasis on access to citizenship. let us do everything we can to guarantee the principle of free movement, to increase the chances of workers finding employment and enriching their professional experience, to promote mobility with a view to a closer union between peoples. in writing. - the proposal for a directive on the right of citizens of the union and their families to move and reside freely within the territory of the member states is gradually changing the meaning of this right in all its chapters. in the treaty it means that the citizens of each member state may a priori move or reside in the territory of the others, but it does not mean that the states of residence do not have a right of control or a right to a reasoned refusal. the directive proposed by the commission is based on the case law of the court of justice, but goes beyond it, and the necessary clarifications have not been introduced into the treaty after a democratic debate. this text would lead to the member states being disarmed and losing a little more control over their territory, which we reject. even the french government, although usually lenient towards the community institutions, has protested in particular against the abolition of the right to expel a community national after a permanent residence of four years, provided for in the directive. in these circumstances, we voted against this text.
in writing. - the right of free movement within the territory of the member states was decided in principle when the treaty of rome was signed in 1957 and was to enter into force at the same time. the mere fact that 45 years later resolutions are still needed to make this right effective is really a sign that for the decision-makers of european unity, only the free movement of capital and goods counts, and not the right of men. and even in this proposal for a directive, this right is partial and carefully framed. for example, it will be up to the host member state to decide whether or not to grant social assistance benefits or student grants. but we are constantly being told about european citizenship! we have nevertheless voted in favour of this report because its recommendations are likely to significantly improve the directive currently being prepared on the right of citizens to move and reside within the territory of the european union, particularly as regards the rights of spouses and children.

provisions of the member states relating to the advertising and sponsorship of tobacco products, which was the subject of a political agreement in the council in december 2002, provides for a ban, as from 31 july 2005, on sponsorship of events involving or taking place in more than one member state or having other cross-border effects, including, of course, formula 1 races. the directive takes distortions of competition. the directive aims to eliminate these problems and to approximate the relevant provisions.

the rapporteur. - mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, if i may say so, it is indeed eeurope that is on the agenda this evening, and i shall deal in particular with the full deployment of third generation mobile communications. the debate was organised somewhat like the third, in disorder, commissioner, since we started with the van velzen report, which is rather complementary in that it deals with information which will be included in the third generation gsm, such as weather information or road conditions provided by the public sector. after all, this is not a very serious matter, since, moreover, the third generation of gsm is also about avoiding the digital divide, which my colleague paasilina will strongly denounce. so, all in all, it's quite normal that we can have this debate of a collective kind. it may be worth recalling that the barcelona council in march 2002 stated: 'technological convergence offers all businesses and citizens new opportunities to access the information society. digital television and third generation mobile communications will play a key role in widespread access to interactive services". however, this third generation sector seems to be in rather difficulty. perhaps, in order to avoid the digital divide and not break the continuity of eeurope, it is necessary to say that 3g services must be part of a global logic, but important issues of consumer health and environmental quality must also be added. in addition, lessons must be learned from the current gsm market so that the mistakes which may have been made in the past are not repeated. one of the crucial issues in the development of mobile telephony is the interoperability of terminals. in this respect, the commission recalls that progress was made in the development of 3g terminals in 2002. the first models are ready. they are also ready in china, i would point out, since we received the information last week. in addition, the existing 2g networks have been upgraded to 2.5g. there may still be some technical problems, but let's say it all works. as regards the market situation, the current availability of 3g services in europe is not clear. they are available in japan, but the operators are confident, and after all, since there are about fifty capable of offering these services, the problem of competition is solved, it can take place. as regards regulatory issues, the commission notes that the procedure for granting 3g licences has been initiated in all eu countries. this number of licences is sufficient. so there is no problem for the competitive environment. following consultations with stakeholders interested in the deployment of 3g mobile communications, a three-point consensus was identified. first, the phase of deployment of 3g services does not require any intervention at the legislative level, market forces must be allowed to play a role. secondly, 3g communications will have to become, in the long term, one of the service platforms offered by a universal information society. finally, public authorities must be involved in the deployment process by providing ongoing support. three factors are identified: a stable, harmonised and transparent regulatory environment, taking into account the interests of consumers; the proactive supporting role that the union can provide; and, thirdly, long-term initiatives, taking into account what has happened in the 3g communications sector, particularly in the run-up to enlargement. so we need to strengthen the coordination of all these choices. the commission foresees that no amendments will be necessary for the granting of licences and that the duration of licences will not be subject to changes in the short term. however, there is still a need for regulatory clarification on the sharing of network infrastructure. as rapporteur, i therefore believe that the commission has put the matter in the right economic context, but that a number of points should have been added. it is a costly technology and this technology can be competed with, for example, wifi, that is to say, today we are wondering whether 3g will integrate some of what computing does or whether it is the opposite, that computing will gradually replace what gsm does. after all, it is the market that will decide, but it is good to ask the question and to take the lead. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the 3g network is not used for commercial purposes. finally, we must protect the security of payments, otherwise the consumer will not trust us. i come now to the precautionary principle, which my colleagues on the right wanted to abolish. i want to talk about the health problems that can arise because they are being raised by several scientists today. it was asked, with a great deal of consensus, to respect, at least at european level, the demands of the world health organization. we are told that today it is, but we will have to evaluate it. finally, the installation of 3g relay antennas will have to be carried out in a manner which respects the environment and urban planning. member states shall ensure that the authorizations of town planning services are subject to a clear procedure and to public scrutiny. the third generation requires four to sixteen times as many antennas as the second generation. so the co-location or sharing of antennas, as recommended by the commission, is something extremely important. in conclusion, regulatory stability will allow for the harmonious development of this technology if the european union takes into account social and environmental parameters as well as economic parameters.

in writing. - this text calls on the european parliament to give its blessing to an economic agreement between the european union and the chilean state. once again, commercial concerns are presented as acts of generosity. the new association agreement is expected to strengthen relations between the eu and latin america at a time when the region is experiencing serious difficulties. but it was precisely the predatory actions of european companies that brought argentina to its knees. and we are being led to believe that identical economic exchanges will have beneficial results! there is no doubt that this trade will be profitable for europe's big capital. but for the chilean people? a few large chilean families of wealthy people will continue to get rich, like those who made their fortune in wine. but this enrichment of a few will not bring any benefits to the great mass of the population. the agreement also provides for cooperation in the fight against terrorism. the fact that this is a country where one of the greatest criminals in recent history, pinochet, is living in peace, with the general indifference of the great powers, is yet another reason to reject this draft recommendation!
in writing. - we're not going to vote against the fact that the public can have access to public sector information. but even when they are in favour of transparency, the european institutions are in favour of public sector documents being used by commercial companies for private profit. it is not transparency, it is information for the benefit of some and misinformation for others. the only transparency which could be of use to the whole population in this area would be to oblige large companies to make their accounts available to everyone. thus, when firms are preparing to lay off workers, workers and the population of the regions concerned would be able to see that the profits of the firms in question or, failing that, the personal fortunes of their shareholders would allow the threatened jobs to be maintained and that consequently the dismissals are not justified.
in writing. - i have already said in the debate that the commission's proposal on the harmonization of work permits for third country nationals violates subsidiarity and would give brussels essential powers to the states to regulate their respective labour markets. more specifically, this centralisation would have several disadvantages. it would make rigid a system which must remain flexible and flexibly adaptable to the local needs of each state. it would put the member states in a position of perpetual defendants, as is shown by the provision in article 29 (4) of the proposal for a directive which i quoted in the debate, which provides for the mandatory statement of reasons for refusal of work permits. finally, it would open the door to further harmonisation in the chain, as the european parliament has very well understood, which has outbid by its amendments, in a lax perspective. the rapporteur himself has given evidence of this, calling at the beginning of his explanatory statement for the 'end of the policy of stopping immigration which has been widely practised up to now'. at least with such statements, the hidden intentions of the text become clear. we denounce this policy of centralisation to disarm ourselves better, and we obviously voted against it.
in writing. - the rapporteur makes no secret of the fact that his main concern, when he deals with the conditions of entry and residence of third-country nationals for the purpose of gainful employment, is to satisfy what he calls 'labour market requirements'. it therefore shares with the commission the concern to provide capitalist enterprises with the labour they need. in other times, we talked about slave traders. we did not vote against this report because some of the amendments proposed would make things a little easier for immigrant workers. but we reject the spirit of the approach. the report proposes relaxations compared with the commission's draft because the strict regulations contained in the latter, in particular the impossibility for the so-called undocumented workers to legalise their situation, or the requirement of stable employment for a sufficiently long period of time to obtain a work card, eventually become burdensome compared to the demands of the employers themselves. as regards the regularisation of the situation of the undocumented, which is timidly addressed in the report, we reiterate the demand for immediate and unconditional regularisation of the situation of all those who live and work in the territory of the european union.
in writing. - from the reduction of administrative or legislative restrictions on applicants when they arrive on european territory, to the extension and simplification of the conditions for the residence of non-community nationals in europe, to the broader definition of 'family members' or the possibility of issuing collective visas at the border, the list of immigration-related incentives included in the three reports presented to us yesterday morning is long. but beyond this philosophy of increasingly destructive national identities and economies, we must bear in mind that the worst is yet to come. as from may 2004, the council will no longer be able to reach unanimity on asylum, immigration and free movement, but will be able to do so by qualified majority and co-decision with the european parliament. so tomorrow, with this reform announced in the amsterdam treaty, the nation states will no longer be in control of the management of their migration flows and their immigration policy. other states will be able to decide for them and force them to apply measures which run counter to their own national interests. therefore, without a reaction from the european people and leaders, we will witness the voluntary sinking of all the nations of europe, which have become totally dependent on europe's suicidal immigration policy.
in writing. - i voted for the joint resolution tabled by the left, which was in the direction of the social movement and against unbridled globalisation! our text was rejected "by a landslide" in favour of a liberal-conservative text which goes against the demands of those who demonstrated in porto alegre and davos. our european parliament has once again confirmed that it is right-wing by majority. and let us not forget the preparations for the european elections in june 2004!
in writing. - i voted against the european parliament's resolution on the forthcoming opening of agricultural negotiations in the wto for two reasons. firstly, the resolution endorses the commission's general approach of agreeing to start comprehensive negotiations in the agricultural field, with an accelerated liberalisation perspective, even though the content of the reform of the european cap will only be decided at a later stage. in other words, the commission is trying to force its hand on us. secondly, the negotiating proposal tabled by the commission on behalf of the european union proposes to reduce export subsidies (which is acceptable, given the harm they can cause to poor countries), but also to reduce our import protections by an average of 36%. in other words, we would be dismantling the community preference a little further. on the contrary, a general principle of regional preference should be established, with each country or group of countries having the right to preserve its agricultural model. this would require removing agriculture from the wto rules. once again the commission is trying to manipulate us, and we can only deplore the approval given by the french government to the general affairs council on 27 january.
in writing. - the european union's proposal for wto negotiations is not compatible with the objectives of the cap. the joint resolution does, however, remind the negotiator of some essential points on which he must not make any concessions, in order to preserve the countries' freedom of choice, whether it be in ensuring their independence in terms of supply or in determining their agricultural model. however, we do not support it. firstly, because the opinion of the european parliament no longer has any significance after the council's decision. the resolution does not, however, call into question the substance of the decision. how can we maintain agricultural activity throughout the whole of the territory, protect designations of origin, reduce subsidies, open up borders more and more, when we have no positive sign that our partners are prepared to accept the compensation and limits proposed. the convergence of world prices below production costs will not offer the countries of the south any more prospects than those of the north. it can already be concluded that the present proposal, even if it is presented to us without any assessment of its consequences, will oblige the european union to adopt the principle of decoupling of aid.
- mr president, the white paper on transport is undoubtedly an event to which we owe a great deal to commissioner loyola de palacio in that, for the first time, it does not simply lay down market rules but offers us a voluntary strategy in favour of a transport policy, of sustainable mobility, more favourable to non-polluting modes of transport. we welcomed the fact that our proposals for european loans to finance the transeuropean networks, which are currently out of order in the council, were accepted. but we ultimately abstained on this report for a simple reason: we believe that there will be no fair competition in transport in europe without a policy of social and fiscal convergence. the tax and social differences between member states today, particularly on the eve of enlargement, are likely to create flag transfers, particularly in road transport, which distort competition and render ineffective and ineffective our efforts to open up markets and to shift modal from road to rail.
in writing. - the need for a transport rationalisation policy at european union level is obvious, since the organisation of railways, major road or river routes at national level is anachronistic, not to mention air transport. it is still necessary to know what policy is involved. the main concern of the report is to deliver more public transport to the private sector, even when it is still a public service, by proposing subsidies and tax incentives for private capital. we reject this policy as a whole, where the pretense of rational transport planning is nothing but a deception. the fact that this sector, which is essential for social life, is based on competition and the pursuit of maximum profit leads to waste, aberrations, insecurity for users, if not to disasters. a european transport policy should be based on the public service of the main means of public transport. the essential public transport, which is essential for the population, should not generate private profit but be organised according to needs. we therefore voted against this report.
in writing. - last night i had the opportunity to express my strong reservations about a white paper and a report which illustrate the gap between the objectives and the means used to achieve them, in the field of transport as in many other areas in europe. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the use of the term 'competent authority' to cover the whole of the european union. the right wing has united, often with the support of the socialists. i therefore voted against a report which fails to address the serious problems of spatial planning, the environment and social issues.
in writing. - i heard a colleague of mine talk about "a revolution in transport culture", and i agree! we agree to encourage the development of clean transport, we agree to limit road traffic, we agree to a european transport policy which contributes to economic and social cohesion. but let us not forget one thing: there are real geographical and cultural differences between the countries which explain the history of transport in each of them and which europe must not ignore. for example, in france there is a great diversity of landscapes, particularly in mountain areas and rural areas. if we want equal treatment of citizens wherever they are in france, and more broadly in europe, we cannot reason in a dogmatic way as the commission did in its proposal. this proposal lacks pragmatism and does not take sufficient account of disparities in treatment at local level. when i see the glaring lack of transport infrastructure in certain geographical areas which are already suffering from isolation, depopulation and neglect, i cannot accept the guidelines in this white paper which continue to respond to the liberal concern alone. in writing. - i voted for the report. transport policy is essential both for economic development and for the preservation of the environment and the living environment, which requires a long-term vision. improving transport quality means increasing alternatives to road, in particular by supporting rail and the effective implementation of north-south links (rhine-rhone-mediterranean via frankfurt/lyon/perpignan/barcelona) and european interconnections (lyon-turin, etc.). in this area, the political will of governments is sometimes lacking. improving transport efficiency also means paying particular attention to trans-european waterway networks. all too often these projects are blocked. improving transport safety also means avoiding predictable weather events that block roads, airports, leaving citizens to fend for themselves, without adequate responsiveness, equipment, or effective warning systems, even though the appropriate techniques exist. finally, i am not in favour of the creation of a european road safety agency. i do not think that the problems we are facing today can be solved by multiplying this type of structure. in writing. - while supporting the auroi report and the work of our rapporteur, i wanted to stress throughout the debate that if the precautionary principle were applied in the field of mobile telephony, we would stop using mobile phones. i can see why. so at least we should do a proper research to limit the potential dangers of this technology and ban the most dubious installations or equipment very quickly! we need not wait for another asbestos-type tragedy to make us aware of the dangers that threaten us.
in writing. - the agenda for the european council in march, which has just been presented to us, contains such a multitude of economic and social priorities that it will inevitably lead to confusion. we see three negative effects in particular. firstly, there is a complete lack of public awareness, especially since many of the subjects considered to be priorities at european level are in reality very secondary in the eyes of our fellow citizens. secondly, the subliminal message that we do not accept is that the european union is a superstate that takes care of everything and touches everything. finally, and above all, it is guaranteed to be ineffective, because in the face of so many priorities, the action of the union and the states can only be dispersed. as i said in the debate, many of the proposed actions are very interesting, but we must concentrate on a few key ideas: the european union must not add an additional layer of cumbersome and restrictive management; it must remain flexible and differentiated; it must make life easier for member states on the international stage by helping them to limit immigration and by fighting at the wto so that we can maintain our security as the identity of our societies.

- mr president, the fifteen are faced with a test of truth. the attitude they adopt in the coming days, faced with the prospect of a new gulf war, will in fact shape the outline of a vision of europe and a conception of the world. they will have to assume their responsibilities in a context which will leave no room for any of those soft consensus to which the cfsp has so often accustomed us. between the pressure of the bush administration for a rally to the war and the demands of european public opinion, which is massively opposed to it, there will be no medium term: we will have to choose. what message does parliament have to convey to the european council in these circumstances? its resolution of 30 january was clear on the essentials and remains fully up to date. let me add a few points drawn from the impressive experience of the delegation of more than 30 meps from 11 countries and four political groups who have just returned from iraq. i would like to begin by sweeping away the insidious remarks of those who have tried to portray us as being in the service of saddam hussein. in the opinion of the journalists present, it was the most independent delegation in recent times. moreover, our links with the democratic opponents of the regime in baghdad and our absolute rejection of saddam are well known enough that i shall not dwell on this little trial of intent without foundation. i hope that the european parliament's ad hoc delegation to iraq will not stop in new york but will go on to baghdad. conversely, our delegation will be traveling quickly to new york and washington, where the antiwar movement is spreading day by day, right into congress. so what did we see and hear in iraq, and what collective conclusions did we draw from that? first, there are the impressions and the accumulated information about the lives of the population, from baghdad and its poorest suburbs to basra in the south and mosul in the north with its gigantic kurdish refugee camp in turkey. poverty is rampant everywhere and social regressions are spectacular, according to those who lived in iraq before the gulf war, and even more so before the war against iran. there is no economy, except for oil, whose exports have fallen by half, due to lack of investment. in rural areas, activity has collapsed, desertification is increasing, exodus is accelerating. un officials are sounding the alarm: one third of the population is chronically malnourished, one third of children are severely underweight. infant mortality has exploded in the last decade. more than 8,000 schools are in a state of disrepair and would require rehabilitation that is currently too expensive. the students are deprived of books. a teacher earns the equivalent of a few euros a month. in iraq today, people are not living, they are trying to survive with the meager assistance of the oil-for-food programme, financed by hydrocarbon resources and managed directly by the government. this is the result of 12 years of embargo. ending this intolerable collective punishment is an absolute imperative. we will also get a sense of the memory of the war by visiting, as we did, the so-called demilitarized zone in the south of the country. there, a pile of countless carcasses of tanks, cars, jeeps, buses reminds us that in the final hours of the conflict, even as iraqi troops were retreating, a final bombing left more than 30,000 unnecessary victims. today, in this context, fatalism, resignation, and silent trauma are dominant. a new war would inevitably lead to a dramatic disruption of the food and water supply. it would be a humanitarian disaster. this reason alone, in our view, radically forbids any new use of war, whatever the circumstances. there is another reason for this, namely the risk of destabilisation of the whole region, starting with the middle east, where the palestinian people are facing one of the worst situations in their history. the other highlight for us was our meeting with the spokesman for the inspectors and the director of the un inspection centre in baghdad. what they told us is common sense. first, as long as the inspectors are on the ground, saddam will have little chance of manufacturing banned weapons. secondly, it is absolutely impossible to accomplish such a mission in two months, but with time, resources and the cooperation of the authorities, the objective of the international community to ensure that iraq no longer represents a threat to the world can be achieved. that is why we have publicly stated on the spot that we believe that the only chance for iraq today is to cooperate fully with the un inspectors. this is also why the franco-german proposals to strengthen the inspectors' resources are, in our view, the only acceptable solution to this crisis today, to the exclusion of any military operation. this is the position our group expects from the member states, and especially from those of them who sit on the un security council, all the more so since they have the right of veto, which they have, if necessary, the duty to use if that were the only way to refuse an unworthy bail to a power-drunk team which today endangers the balance and peace of the world. what credit would the un have if the rule of the stronger led a handful of states to violate the spirit of the un charter in such a cynical way? next saturday, around the world, an unprecedented backlash in many countries will rise up to say no to war. we want as many members of the european parliament as possible to be visible in these demonstrations, because europe has a duty to say no to an imperial machine, the nature and scope of which are illustrated by the new strategic doctrine published by the bush administration on 20 september: the cult of military force, the desire for domination, the claim, i quote, 'to act alone, if necessary, as a preventive measure' to achieve objectives which have nothing to do with the security of the world. allies but not allies, we said the day after 9/11. we must remind this principle to the quartet of leaders among the fifteen who are ready to divide europe at the whistle of the white house. as for the applicant countries, i think it is time to tell them frankly, before the ratification of the accession treaties, that we must be clear about our common ambition: let us not confuse the new europe with a remake of nato. let us rise to the occasion of a european public opinion that is gaining ground throughout the continent. in the eyes of a growing number of our fellow citizens, what the united states has gained in power, it is losing in confidence because of the messianic and megalomaniacal drift of its leaders. this situation gives the european union a historic responsibility, not against america, but against the dangerous hegemony of those who claim to rule the world in its name, even if it leads to chaos. we are, as i said, facing a test of truth. history is not written. let those who hold the cards in their hands consider the weight of their responsibility. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, there are many aspects to this sad iraqi affair. we've covered a lot of them, but what strikes me at this point is the incredible power of propaganda, and particularly the mechanism of demonization. indeed, there are today throughout the world a very large number of men and women, probably in all sincerity, who believe that saddam hussein is threatening world peace, or even, as mr poettering said earlier - if the situation were not so dramatic, it would make one smile - that saddam hussein is starving his people, whereas the truth is exactly the opposite and so simple that it is almost embarrassing to formulate it in its simplicity. it is the american and british governments which have for years imposed a terrible embargo on a population which has been reduced to living, or rather surviving, in a ghetto. as a result, iraq is a bloodless country, now unable to wage any war. karl ritter, who headed the inspection which ended in 1998, said it was impossible that iraq could have built any weapons of mass destruction. i repeat, propaganda must be very powerful to make us eat painful lies. and even if iraq were armed, what right do we have to deprive it of any means of defence? this is the second trick of propaganda: to blind us to the condition of a world of order, that is, a world of sovereign nations cooperating with each other and balancing each other. no, iraq's armament is no more dangerous than that of other nations, especially its neighbors, saudi arabia, iran and syria, who are not necessarily motivated by the best intentions. i simply believe that we have no right to disarm iraq, any more than any other country, as general de gaulle pointed out in 1963 when he refused to sign the nuclear non-proliferation treaty. another trick: to make it appear that what the propaganda calls the international community has the right to overthrow a regime, which is absolutely contrary to international law, and even, i will say this as a conclusion, mr president, to the most fundamental truth in the world, which is the freedom of peoples. we shall see that little by little, i hope, during this century.
