council mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the european union is particularly concerned about the deaths and injuries caused each year by unexploded ordnance left over from armed conflicts. in addition to direct civilian deaths and injuries, the presence of explosive remnants of war often impedes humanitarian aid, peacekeeping, post-conflict reconstruction and development in general. the union has therefore played an active role in the discussion on explosive remnants of war in the context of the convention on certain conventional weapons. let me give you some examples of the union's activities in this field. in june 2001, the union distributed a discussion paper on explosive remnants of war to the meeting convened on the subject of such explosives in preparation for the second review conference of the convention on certain conventional weapons. the general affairs council on 19 november 2001 adopted conclusions on the promotion of the convention on certain conventional weapons, in which it requested the second review conference to establish a working group on explosive remnants of war. thirdly, the european union submitted a working document to the second review conference of the convention on certain conventional weapons in geneva in december 2001 calling for the establishment of a legal instrument to deal with explosive remnants of war, which would seek to prevent the formation of explosive remnants, including by requiring greater construction reliability and self-destruct mechanisms, and to prevent bodily injury caused by explosive mechanisms that have been in explosive remnants of war. the union also submitted a reflection paper on explosive remnants of war to the governmental expert group set up by the second review conference. at the meeting of states parties to the convention on certain conventional weapons, the presidency, on behalf of the european union, stressed that the establishment of a legally binding instrument on explosive remnants of war under the convention is a matter of priority for the union. the council did agree to the recommendation of the governmental experts group to begin negotiating a means for these explosives. the relevant council working party will discuss future union action in this area. i would like to point out on behalf of the council that there is no unanimity among the member states of the union on the declaration of an immediate moratorium on the use of all types of cluster munitions. the council has also received no information on the possible use of cluster bombs by any nato member. the first three articles of the november 1997 joint action of the union address the issue of the universality of the mine ban treaty, by which the member states of the union have committed themselves to the objective of the complete elimination of antipersonnel mines throughout the world. the joint action shall empower the presidency to take appropriate measures. these measures have so far consisted of political visits to countries not yet party to the treaty, including associated countries, and also of calls to accede to the treaty. these steps are taken by the presidency. the union has also promoted the universality of the treaty in all appropriate forums, in particular at the united nations. the decisions of the general assembly on the implementation of the treaty have been unanimously supported by the member states of the european union. in addition, the regulations of the european parliament and of the council of 23 july 2001 on action against anti-personnel landmines in developing countries and third countries other than developing countries have a common article 3 according to which any union-funded cooperation in the field of mine action should in principle be directed to countries that are parties to the mine ban treaty. exceptions can only be made for humanitarian reasons. this attitude of the union has created a strong incentive to join the mine ban treaty. the european union and its member states are the leading international funder of mine action, which in turn is an important way of promoting compliance with the treaty. i would also point out that no report has been submitted to the council on the use of depleted uranium munitions by american and british forces in the intervention in afghanistan. the council has not dealt with the question of the implementation of the protocol on untraceable fragments, a protocol to the convention on certain conventional weapons to which all member states are parties. the council has also not held any discussion of the ongoing work in the united nations on this subject. finally, the council does not have at its disposal a list of munitions containing depleted uranium currently in use. decisions on the use of different types of ammunition are taken by member states under their national sovereignty. all member states are parties to the geneva conventions. nor has the council received any information on the possible use of depleted uranium munitions in chechnya, nor has it discussed the question of considering the use of cluster bombs or depleted uranium as a war crime under the statute of the international criminal court.
commission. – let me start by saying that serious scientific studies have shown that there is no reason for anxiety in relation to the issue of the harmful effects of depleted uranium ammunitions on health. from the commission perspective, i want, in particular, to refer to the opinion of the euratom treaty article 31 expert group which was convened in early 2001, with the participation not only of member states experts but also representatives of unep, the iaea, the who and nato. the group focused on the lasting contamination from the use of depleted uranium ammunitions in the balkans and the potential post-war radiological risk for the health of the local population and the international assistance teams. the group did not look at the actual health effect on soldiers who had been on mission in that region, this being outside the community remit and to be handled in other fora such as nato. again i refer parliament to the conclusions of its own stoa report of may 2001, when it came to much the same conclusion in relation to this issue. on 6 march 2001, the opinion of the article 31 expert group was released to the press. in a nutshell, it concluded that there is no major concern, from a radiological point of view, either in terms of inducing short-term cancer, or in terms of a wide impact on the environment. widespread intervention in the concerned regions was not required. other reports issued by unep on 13 march 2001, the who on 1 may 2002 and the uk royal society on 12 march 2002 present similar conclusions. in addition, the latter two reports also address the chemical toxicity of the uranium, concluding that it is not expected that adverse effects on the kidneys or any other organ will occur. at the end of march 2001, my colleague, commissioner wallström, concluded that no further actions seemed to be required with regard to the application of the basic safety standards for the protection of the health of workers and the general public against the dangers arising from ionising radiation. as mentioned above, further investigations into the chemical toxicity not addressed in the report of mrs wallström have since been analysed in the who and the uk royal society reports. while the article 31 expert group had concluded that there was no need for individual monitoring of the commission's own staff and contractors sent to the region, the commission's medical services nonetheless proposed a check-up and urine analysis programme for the staff members concerned. no single health effect related to depleted uranium has been observed. coming now to the commission's activities related to anti-personnel landmines following the european parliament and council regulations 1724/2001 and 1725/2001 on the reinforcement of the european union contribution to the fight against apls, the european union has taken a leading role in fostering better coordination of programmes and in providing momentum, predictability and effectiveness for cooperation between partners on the ground. this is very strong support by the european community for the implementation of the mine ban treaty that is the ottawa convention, according to which all apls should be eliminated by 2009. in 2001, under the new apl regulation providing for a dedicated legal basis for coordination at european union level, the community budget contributed up to eur 30 million for demining actions. using various community instruments such as geographical, echo, apl and rrm budget lines in an integrated way, the european commission has mainly supported surveys, clearance, assistance to victims, as well as the economic and social rehabilitation of the demined regions and the resettled populations. at european union level the european community efforts and the member states' activities combined total eur 143 million. the european union is, therefore, with the us, the top contributor in the fight against apls, including stockpile destruction and creation of local capacity-building. in order to ensure sustainability over the years, the commission approved in december 2002 the european commission mine action strategy and multiannual indicative programming for the period 2002-2004. this document was prepared on the basis of strong coordination with the member states, the united nations, the us, and the wider mine action community. the commission will, in the coming weeks, make the necessary arrangements to present this strategy to the european parliament committee on foreign affairs, human rights, common security and defence policy. finally, coming to the issue of cluster bombs and other forms of unexploded ordnance, the convention on conventional weapons (ccw) is the current international framework that provides the basis for the prohibition and elimination of weapons which operate in an indiscriminate fashion or cause excessive injury and suffering. most eu member states are parties to the ccw and are working on the revision of the convention to further prohibit certain designs of weapon, such as explosive remnants of war, anti-handling devices, and to establish common principles on fuse insensitivity, self-destruction or self-neutralising weapon modes. these principles, if agreed, would be applied to anti-vehicle mines and submunitions – or munitions delivered by a remote carrier such as an aircraft, missile, minefield launcher and so on. the revision of the ccw is still at the level of working groups: one on anti-vehicles mines, the other on submunitions. the commission closely follows the debates of both groups. this revision would lead to a new protocol to the ccw to address the problems caused by explosive remnants of war, thus covering cluster bombs and submunitions, so that these weapons are detectable and equipped with effective self-destruction mechanisms. the work being carried out in view of the new protocol is strongly sponsored by the eu through a common position and a number of joint démarches requesting that concrete steps be undertaken to address this issue under the ccw framework. currently, the opportunity to prepare a further common position on the suggestions tabled is being explored. let me conclude by mentioning that, in addition to its participation in the international framework of the ccw, the commission, on a concrete and operational level through its activities related to apls, is already providing an indirect but tangible contribution to the reduction of the threat posed by cluster bombs and other unexploded ordnance. mine-clearance encompasses de jure and de facto clearance of other unexploded ordnance, although this is not a specific submunitions instrument. we are already engaged in such broader clearance activities in countries such as laos, kosovo and afghanistan, where the apl problem is inextricably connected to unexploded ordnance pollution.
- mr president, mr president-in-office of the council, mr commissioner, i thank you for this essential update which you have just made and which shows the seriousness of the commission's work. it is the technician who, for once, will be speaking in this house, particularly on depleted uranium weapons. we must not, more or less consciously, keep in mind - in the minds of the public and, as i have seen in this house, in our own minds - the confusion between the use of depleted uranium weapons and the use of nuclear weapons. in this connection you have given us very important information and i would simply like to give you my personal testimony. depleted uranium weapons are weapons that have been developed to allow the penetration of new armor. the armor of world war ii was pierced by chemical-powered hollow-bore shells. the new armor can only be penetrated by kinetic energy weapons. they're arrow shells. it is necessary to be able to give them a high initial speed. they must also have heavy cores. that's why we took the depleted uranium. but again, the confusion i'm talking about is not innocent. i heard a television reporter covering our colleagues' mission in iraq speak twice - so it was not a slip - of enriched uranium in relation to these munitions. i was involved in the experimentation, the development of these weapons in the technical directorate of land armaments, where we have very powerful unions, which protect our workers and our engineers. i can therefore testify to you that, if there had been any risk, the precautionary principle we apply in our arms industries in france would have consistently disposed of these munitions.

of course, you referred to existing legislation that must be enforced. however, i think that new measures must be taken to inform trade union organisations and works councils about the aid received. measures should also be adopted to oblige these companies to report on the use of the funds granted and to repay them in the event of non-compliance with the commitments made. the commission has also proposed that the european parliament should be consulted on the future of the steel industry, and that the commission should be consulted on the future of the steel industry. if we do not do this, commissioner, we are not moving towards a union of solidarity but towards a union of terrible oppositions between workers and citizens. while we are talking about social governance, we need even more legislation. i believe that new european legislation must be put in place to make it easier for companies operating in the union to assume their responsibilities. the commission and the member states must adopt a more proactive approach to industrial restructuring and its social impact. i think it's also a matter of ethics. in a europe which intends to defend the fundamental rights of its citizens, can we stand by while thousands of workers are thrown out onto the streets like mere commodities? the opposite approach is precisely what we need to promote for a new industrial dynamism in europe. employees must be given new rights within the company at all levels. of course, reference is made to the legislation on european committees. but i think that democratization of the boards would avoid many restructuring and liquidation measures imposed by management which are essentially driven by financial pressures and are far from meeting industrial requirements. in this sense, i think the union should force the companies concerned to take better account of the alternative proposals of the trade unions before any decision is taken.
- commissioner, you said that restructuring in the steel industry, but also in the metallurgical industry, is an old one. it's been going on for 25 years. what i would like to stress is the difference in nature that now exists in these restructurings. you know, 20 years ago, we downgraded entire territories, depriving workers of their jobs in the name of modernization, productivity. it was extremely painful, but there was a sense of understanding a certain evolution, rightly or wrongly considered necessary, and so one felt detached from a story whose meaning one understood more or less. the problem we have today is that all this no longer makes sense, that is to say that we now realise that in restructuring it is the law of anything, and in particular the law of shareholders, that imposes itself in this way, in a brutal, wild, arbitrary, unforeseen way. these stories have no meaning, and the fact that they have no meaning makes them utterly hopeless. that is, people are either revolted or totally desperate. and they are particularly desperate for europe, because all these restructuring are taking place on this scale. and you have - as in the case of the arcelor group - this kind of ping-pong game: i close here, i buy elsewhere, in poland in this case for this company. so, everyone feels like they're competing with everyone else. and i strongly insist on this. how can you expect citizens to give europe any credit or even to desire it if europe first appears to them as a field of warlike competition, with shareholders who are sometimes totally dishonest and who make the law? do we need to speak, since there are people here in this chamber who do not like the name of glencor, that crooked shareholder, being mentioned? can we leave industrial and economic development strategies, thousands of jobs in the hands of a crooked shareholder, who can run down the prestige, buy up profitable jewels within the metaleurope group, and leave a region in an unacceptable state of pollution? and i think we must also talk about the terrible pollution of the sites, the very serious damage to the health of the workers, their children and their families. who's responsible? who 's paying ? are corporations these predatory species that squeeze the lemons under the shareholder law and leave all the damage in the hands of the government? or does europe want to have the means to regulate all this and impose certain things? there are some very simple things to do. it is essential to strengthen the power of employees at european level. employees must be able to think, participate in company strategies, coordinate, fight their battles together. everyone here deplored the commission's lack of ambition in its statement. it's true she's unambitious, i'm not gonna say she isn't. but it must also be realized, ladies and gentlemen, that while the commission can say no to a merger in the name of a monopoly situation, of non-respect of competition law, it cannot say no to a restructuring which is carried out in defiance of legislation on information and consultation of workers. i would ask that this be considered in the debate on social europe in the convention. a newspaper recently carried the headline: 'the convention is destroying social europe'. let's think about all of this. do we want the people to lose all hope in europe? i want the commission to be able to say no to restructuring which is carried out in breach of european legislation. but it is not the commission that has not wanted to do so, it is our member states in the council that have chosen to reserve to themselves the legal and administrative means of imposing sanctions or not. how do you want this to work? i want the commission to have the power to say no to restructuring which violates the rights of workers, which disregards the environment and the requalification of sites. and that is, in my view, within the framework of the convention. i would ask you, ladies and gentlemen, to put pressure on all your mainstream members in your groups, on all those with whom you have relations, to promote social europe. otherwise this europe will be hopeless and i ask you to believe that the citizens will not vote for it when they are consulted by referendum.

- mr president, the planned plant closures by arcelor are outrageous. the most powerful steel group in the world, collapsing under the weight of profits, coldly announced that it would close a total of six blast furnaces in belgium, germany and france, throwing thousands of workers out of work, condemning their families to poverty and ruining whole regions. the fact that such a decision can be taken in the secrecy of a board of directors, obeying the demands of a handful of financiers, shows how much the system you defend corresponds to the dictatorship of money. the fact that this can happen without even the reaction of the political authorities, except for a few hypocritical groans, shows how much the workers cannot rely on the authorities to defend them. we are told that periodic restructuring is inevitable in industry, but why is it always the workers who are made to pay for these restructurings, and never the shareholders or the owners of the companies? commission. – mr president, i have listened with great care and attention and interest to this crucial debate. one cannot but be moved by the strength and passion with which members of parliament have expressed their views on this unfortunate issue. a number of interesting ideas were developed throughout the debate and the commission will study all of them with great care. most of the points raised were dealt with in my introductory remarks and i will not go into detail on them now. let me underline again the basic principle according to which decisions on corporate restructuring are a prerogative of management, but also its responsibility. a wide consensus seems to exist in europe on the way to address crises resulting from the need for companies to adapt, from industrial change and from corporate restructuring. let me reaffirm again the importance of effective, timely and comprehensive information and consultation of workers' representatives. you have nevertheless expressed other types of concerns to which i would like to give you the commission's preliminary view. before i do that i would like to pick up one or two points that were made. there were references, for instance, to the european coal and steel community, and i was asked whether articles 3 and 5 have any application in these circumstances. it appears to be the case that articles 3 and 5 no longer have application because the ecsc is no longer operational. nor indeed are state aids possible. we all know that. there is no competence at eu level to deal with many of the issues that have been raised by honourable members in this debate this afternoon. i can only quote what mrs zrihen said in her contribution just a moment ago, when she said the legislative arsenal is insufficient. that is indeed the case. there is not a lot that can be done in many circumstances in relation to some of the issues that you have raised because of the very point that mrs zrihen has raised. i shall now deal with some of the issues you raised. firstly, with regard to the trade dispute in the steel sector between the usa and the eu, the commission is pursuing a very active line with regard to the unilateral measures taken by the us to protect its steel industry. those defensive measures include, besides intensive bilateral contacts with a view to solving the conflict, retaliation measures and using the wto disputes settlement mechanism. my colleague, commissioner lamy, is forcefully pursuing that particular issue. another issue that was raised in the debate was the issue surrounding the issue of enlargement. for the steel industry, as well as for many other industries, enlargement is above all a window of opportunity for them to develop their businesses in the interests of themselves and in the interests of their workers. there are issues related to compliance with standards in the new member states, notably in the social and environmental fields. those issues are, however, being dealt with through technical assistance to help their industries to adapt, as well as through the assurance that those new members will have to comply with the relevant community law from the date of accession. a number of members made reference to social funds and so on, and particularly to the free use of community funds, notably the european social fund, to support the training and professional reconversion of workers affected by restructuring. i should like to make a few points on that. after the expiry of the ecsc treaty, the only possibility lies in the european social fund and in interventions from the structural funds. the main goal in the long term must be the reconversion of local industrial activities. this will have a much greater impact on the regions than direct social aid to the employees, although some transitional measures can be considered. we should recall that aid for the rescue and restructuring of companies in difficulty remains prohibited, in principle, for the iron and steel industry, as does any investment aid. the same rules apply to the countries applying for accession and with regard to new aid. there were also references to making public aid dependent upon the maintenance of employment. generally speaking, public aid to companies is already subject to those kinds of conditions. a number of the existing instruments specifically link the obtaining of state aid funds to the obligation to keep people employed during a minimum period. the guidelines on national regional aid make it clear that aid for job creation must be made conditional on maintenance of the employment created for a minimum period of five years. similarly, the commission regulation on state aid for employment contains provisions stipulating that such aid can only be granted if the employment is maintained for a minimum period of three years, or two years in the case of smes. continuous employment should also be granted to workers in the case of aid for the recruitment of disadvantaged and disabled workers. the structural funds regulations do not contain similar conditions, but it is clear that in so far as structural funds are used to cofinance state aid schemes, relevant obligations to keep people employed for a minimum period of time have to be respected. some reference was made to the alleged ambitions of one of the companies involved to make acquisitions in poland. possible acquisition by arcelor of certain factories in poland or other third countries would be the subject of a survey by the commission, pursuant to regulation 4064/89 on the control of concentrations between undertakings. the commission underlines that it only permits concentrations which are compatible with the common market. in its evaluation the commission comes to a conclusion only about the competitive aspects without intervening in the industrial policy of a private company. i should also say that the commission has no information to the effect that any such plans for acquisition by that company have been successful. finally, industrial change has economic implications and an impact on employment and social cohesion. however, it also provides opportunities when anticipated, prepared for and managed. dialogue, transparency, proper worker involvement, anticipation, risk prevention and the development of employability are the key elements of our european response to this phenomenon. let us do our best to build the instruments of a legislative or other nature which can promote these principles.

commission. – mr president, over the past years, democratic conditions in most of the countries of central asia have deteriorated. however, the commission understands why the focus of parliament’s attention in this debate is on kazakhstan. once considered one of the ‘hopefuls’ in the region, the past two years have seen a crackdown on political opposition and critical media. especially hard hit were those who had the courage to criticise corruption at the highest level, involving the president and his family. the commission agrees that the court cases on corruption charges against mr ablyazov and mr zhakianov, the two leaders of the opposition movement democratic choice for kazakhstan, had every appearance of being politically motivated. the commission has furthermore viewed with great concern the campaign of intimidation that has been going on against a great number of critical media in kazakhstan. this has included the firebombing of offices, the vandalising of transmitter equipment with a machine gun, a decapitated dog nailed to a newspaper office door and physical attacks against individual journalists. the perpetrators of these crimes have never been apprehended, and many cases have simply been closed. a number of newspapers, furthermore, have been subject to judicial proceedings, endless tax and safety inspector visits and heavy fines, in a number of cases resulting in closure. the commission also agrees that the recent court case against mr duvanov on rape charges was marred by grave irregularities. we therefore strongly believe that the trial should be reviewed. it is against this background that president nazarbaev’s recent statements that kazakhstan will seek its own pace of democratisation – to be achieved by 2030 – and that western standards should not be automatically applied to kazakhstan, are to be met with due caution. president prodi underlined our deep concern over kazakhstan’s recent democratic record during the president’s visit to brussels on 29 november 2002. on the other hand, it is important to take a number of positive developments in kazakhstan into consideration as well. prisons have been transferred from the ministry of the interior to the ministry of justice, and we hope that pre-trial detention facilities will soon follow. a law on the humanisation of prison conditions has been passed and a serious effort seems to be being made to implement prison reform. kazakhstan, as well as other countries in central asia, has also established the post of human rights ombudsman, although much remains to be done in terms of strengthening their mandates and facilities. a 'standing council' for further democratisation and development in civil society was approved by presidential decree on 29 december 2002. it is to be hoped that its recommendations, for example those on the law on political parties, will be followed up. the commission notes that parliament’s resolution focuses on kazakhstan only. the commission believes, however, that the matter of human rights in kazakhstan is to be viewed in its regional context. it cannot be denied that there has been a crackdown on non-governmental media and opposition in kazakhstan. but the commission does not believe that the state of democracy and human rights in kazakhstan – nor, for that matter, in kyrgyzstan or tajikistan – is beyond repair. we believe that the eu can continue to have an impact on democratic conditions in these countries through critical but constructive dialogue under the partnership and cooperation agreements. we have deeper concerns regarding uzbekistan and turkmenistan, on which parliament’s resolution remains silent. uzbekistan has no independent press, whereas turkmenistan has no press at all worthy of the name. opposition parties do not exist in these two countries. kazakhstan and kyrgyzstan have been under the close scrutiny of human rights watchdogs for some time now because of the deterioration in democratic conditions. this scrutiny has certainly been justified. but let us not forget that in uzbekistan, and certainly in turkmenistan, for years there has been no democracy at all left to deteriorate. in these countries, any opposition activist, critical journalist or simply any muslim practising his belief, risks ending up in a torture chamber, a penal colony or on death row on charges of terrorism, religious extremism or an attempt on the life of the president. opposition and civil society in kazakhstan, kyrgyzstan and, to an extent, tajikistan, are under pressure, but this has, at least so far, not made them less resilient or vocal. through constructive dialogue and targeted support, the eu can still make a difference in these countries.

will have an impact far beyond trade rules on the internal rules of wto member countries. when we talk, for example, about the water supply or the postal sector, not about cross-border mail but about the internal organization of the postal sector, it is clear that we are looking beyond international trade alone. this raises the question, for this agreement as for the trips agreement on intellectual property, whether the trade organization is not going beyond its legitimacy. the problem with this agreement is precisely that it puts everything on the same level: banking services, insurance services, but also water supply, energy, postal services, education and health, potentially. in this respect, it is europe's negotiating line which will make the distinction and indeed some areas will not be brought under the purview of the wto and its dispute settlement body. the first question i would like to raise is about protecting european public services because we have seen a dangerous shift in the last few months. the commission's position and statements were initially that there would be no liberalization offers for european public services. secondly, it was said that health, education and audiovisual services would not be the subject of liberalization offers. but european services, public services are much broader than that. and we do see that there are offers in the postal sector and that, subject to clarification and classification at the wto, there could be offers in the energy and water sectors. we therefore say to you that the commission must take a clear stance and exclude european public services from any liberalization proposal, which must be the responsibility of the member states, the council and the european parliament and not the responsibility of the trade organization. secondly, there is no automatic reciprocity, but there must be coherence and the union cannot, on the one hand, ask others to liberalise public service sectors and, on the other hand, think that the argument will not be returned to it. we have already made requests for liberalization, for example in the field of water, to countries such as tanzania, mozambique and bangladesh. i think we should not put that kind of pressure on developing countries. we must instead encourage cooperation, investment in the sectors where these countries need it, but within the framework of cooperation, leaving them in control of the rules they impose on foreign investors in environmental, social, etc. matters. thirdly, mr lamy, i think that what you have said about excluding public services by revising the agreement and article 1 (3) is not right. it would be enough to amend the paragraph which restricts the definition of government services to those which are not offered on a commercial or competitive basis and to say that wto member states are free to exclude their public services from this negotiation.

- madam president, i do not think that the round of negotiations that is about to begin should call into question cultural diversity. culture, as defined by unesco, is the sum of the distinctive spiritual and material, intellectual and emotional features that characterize a society or social group. it includes, in addition to the arts and letters, lifestyles, fundamental human rights, value systems, traditions and beliefs. the right to culture is a fundamental human right. it is enshrined as such in the universal declaration of human rights. this cultural diversity must not only be defended but also supported and encouraged. this applies, of course, to all the member states of the union, but also to the developing countries, because cultural diversity is an integral part of the heritage of humanity. to avoid the risk that culture will one day be regarded as a commodity like any other, we must give it a new legal framework to exclude it from the negotiations on world trade. culture is not a commodity like any other. the wto cannot and should not be the venue for cultural debate. commissioner reding has recently stated that any conceptual discussion on cultural diversity and cultural policies which might take place in the wto must be strongly opposed, since the wto is not a competent organisation, nor is it mandated to deal with the substance of this matter. we therefore need to create a new binding international legal instrument, not only to support and promote cultural diversity but also to set the rules of trade in cultural goods and services. several ministers of culture agreed to draw up this instrument so that in future the states may have the means to determine, from a cultural point of view and in accordance with their own situation, the policies they need to ensure the preservation and promotion of cultural diversity. unesco is the most appropriate body to assume this responsibility. i therefore wish that this process will be completed as soon as possible.

- oral question (o-0003/2003 - b5-0084/2003) by mr stevenson, on behalf of the committee on fisheries, on the socioeconomic crisis in the white fish sector. (if the author is not present, the president shall give the floor to the commission first)
mr president, there must be no ambiguity about the objective pursued by the drastic measures proposed by the commission and endorsed by the council on the north sea cod stock. the aim is to restore stocks in a sustainable way so as to preserve as many jobs as possible in the fishing communities that have long been fishing for whitefish, which must be compensated temporarily and fairly and not permanently reconverted. but to achieve this objective, we must go beyond these draconian measures to limit fishing days. it is imperative that we learn from the canadian experience, which we must study with the greatest care. the moratorium imposed in the north atlantic for the past 12 years has unfortunately not had the desired effect: the cessation of fishing has had no influence on the state of cod stocks off newfoundland, nova scotia and the gulf of st. lawrence; the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used to the full. canadians now recognize that fishing is just one factor in the evolution of the resource. other factors play a decisive role and need to be studied much more closely and taken into account as much as fishing: climatic factors, changes in water temperature, the importance of natural mortality, the significant sampling carried out by seals whose population is exploding, as well as by mackerel and herring which are proving to be large consumers of cod eggs. it also appears that in canada fishermen have not been sufficiently involved in the preparation and management of recovery plans. if we are to have any chance of success, it is therefore essential to define quickly a framework in which local experience and scientific expertise can be constantly confronted and not be limited to fishing bans, to keeping boats at the dock, as if this alone would automatically result in the replenishment of stocks. this rudimentary means of action must be urgently and rapidly supplemented - and financial resources must be made available for this purpose - by in-depth multifactorial analyses including the effects of the fishing industry, which will make it possible to implement a much more elaborate management policy and thus to preserve as much as possible what must remain our primary objective: the future of the fishing communities concerned.
the commission. - mr president, madam president, i would like to thank the commissioner for his reply. i am happy to be able to discuss these matters with the committee on fisheries. i would just like to point out right now that we have to think very carefully about this, because you know that the funds available under the fisheries structural fund are very limited, and if we start by setting aside money for emergencies, then of course that money is not available for the normal programme, and that could then ultimately lead to us leaving money, so to speak, unused, because we can hope that in the future we will not just be dealing with a chain of disasters, but on the contrary that we will be able to deal with the matter with these replenishment plans. we shall be dealing with this matter in great detail this year and there will also be proposals to parliament for additional recovery plans. but as i said, this is certainly a question worth exploring, and i'm happy to do so. perhaps we can have an informal debate on this subject in the committee on fisheries, on the basis of a sort of non-paper.

in writing. - the aim of the directive, which is to establish, through transparent access to port services, common rules for maritime ports in order to strengthen their role in transport and to give them a leading position in intermodality, must not be achieved at any price, that is to say by giving up a high level of maritime safety, effective environmental protection and satisfactory employment conditions for workers in this sector. the directive under consideration, however, calls into question the social rights of workers, the issue of self-help being the paradigmatic example: it would be to allow self-help to be entrusted to 'fixed shore' personnel employed by ship owners, which would probably lead to the removal of this work from professional dockers and other qualified technical personnel to be carried out by unskilled and cheaper labour. the risks of social dumping are obvious. i shall therefore vote in favour of rejecting this directive, a position which will certainly not be the majority in the ep. i shall therefore vote in favour of any amendments which seek to strengthen the text in the direction of greater protection for workers.
in writing. - parliament, the council and the commission remain firmly committed to the liberalisation of port services. the few advances, such as the exclusion of pilots and sailors from the directive, do not reverse the process that has begun and we fear that the respite for these professions will be short-lived. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the port authorities are able to take account of the needs of the port community. dockworkers, threatened by self-help, i.e. the possibility for shipowners and charterers to have their ships loaded and unloaded by their own staff, have shown the way by organising several eurogroup strikes and demonstrating in thousands in front of the european institutions. we have been and are in solidarity with their mobilization. that is why we voted against the directive. it is preparing, as has the liberalization of rail transport, for human, social and environmental disasters. these disasters will not take place off our coasts, as in the case of the erika and prestige, but in the ports. against liberalisation, we must promote a public port service coordinated at european level, guaranteeing the highest level of safety and social standards.
in writing. - after opening up maritime transport to ultra-liberal competition, with the consequences we all know: polluted beaches, french fishermen killed by a norwegian chemical tanker piloted by sri lankans, the european commission is now going to hand over port services, from piloting to handling, to private services, in the name of competition between ports, competitiveness and cost reduction, as in the air and rail sectors. the opening of the market, which is apparently limited to the major ports, and whose capacity is not known to be 3 million or 45 million tonnes of cargo, involves, for example, 'self-help', i.e. the ship's own crew will be able to handle the cargo with, as one might guess, its underpaid men from south-east asia, thus providing new slaves for world capitalism in the service of social dumping, all under the flag of complacency. the debate is only about whether safety concerns will allow piloting and towing to be excluded from the port's privatisation. for the rest, our dockers in marseille, sète and other major ports will be handed over to the pirates of ultra-liberalism. the destruction of fishing jobs will be supplemented by the destruction of port jobs. the revolt and despair of these men against a directive produced by the hawks of economic globalisation is understandable.
in writing. - this directive is far from perfect - states must be able to require that the rules in force for shore-based personnel apply to seafarers carrying out (self-help) activities referred to in the annex to the directive - but it is nevertheless welcome. the reluctance of some companies is in fact a simple refusal to open up port services to competition. this self-sufficient logic does not only reflect a rejection of the market economy in principle. solemn declarations on the maintenance of public service obligations, the guarantee of jobs or the preservation of the safety and environment of ports - objectives which are perfectly legitimate and which no one disputes - conceal a desire, much less noble, to defend monopolies, especially trade unions, which some believed to be untouchable. the completion of a major project such as port 2000 in le havre, the first french port for the transport of container cargo, clearly shows that our ports and the companies in the sector are not afraid of the introduction of a more competitive dynamic in port services. on the contrary, by equipping themselves with the necessary infrastructure to prepare for the future, ports will be able to meet the challenge of opening up the market and win it.

mr president, the debate on the violation of the stability pact, which mainly concerns three countries - france, germany and portugal - leads us to recall that, in budgetary matters as elsewhere, the tree must not hide the forest. the three countries with the largest deficits have one thing in common. in the past they have had a period of socialist government - from which germany has not yet emerged - which has been lax on public spending and inert on reforms that could have brought savings. in all three cases, the room for manoeuvre provided by the growth of 2000/2001 was wasted, and we are now reaping the bitter fruits. but this tree must not hide the forest, i.e. the general deterioration of public balances in the euro area, which in 2002 reached an average of -2.4% of gdp, thus approaching the 3% mark. the main reason is that growth has slowed down and has not yet started up again, even slowly, contrary to what is being said, somewhat unrealistically, in the various reports presented this evening. the reason for this slowdown may be the inevitability of the economic situation, but also and above all the heavy burden of public taxation and the structural rigidities which have not yet been remedied. in this respect, we are bound to break a taboo by asking whether the euro itself is not one of those rigidities which penalize growth. in any case, the differences in performance between the euro and non-euro areas raise the question. in view of these shortcomings, should the stability pact be given more flexibility? i note that the commission, the european central bank and even the last ecofin council are saying rather no, with a few minor amendments. as always, with regard to the stability pact and foreign policy, the european union tends not to want to face reality and to oppose paper walls to the deviations from the fundamentals. we believe that, without losing sight of the objective of eliminating public deficits altogether, which is certainly a good thing, france is right to maintain its programme of tax relief in order not to aggravate the crisis at the moment. we are forced to assume an inheritance that we did not create. let's at least try to do it smart.
- mr president, it is clear that the european institutions, which are so inclined to lecture the small countries of europe when they do not respect the convergence criteria, are using a moderate tone when it comes to two of the great powers of the european union, france and germany! maastricht criteria or not, these two states take it for granted that they have the right to increase their deficits in order to help capitalist enterprises in their countries. but we can also see from the attitude of the french government how these two states will respond to the demands of the european institutions, if they do respond. the commission has already taken a number of measures to reduce the deficit, but it is not yet ready to take action. in france, these amounts represent at least 10% of the budget. there is plenty of room to make a deficit of 3.4% disappear. but in order not to reduce the sums paid to businesses, the french government is attacking the state's expenditure, that is, in reality, the public service. the call for a return to budgetary balance will, in these circumstances, result in less funding for hospitals, less funding for schools. the whole population will pay so that the richest don't have to pay. although it is not the european authorities but the national governments which actually draw up their budgets, we are voting against this report which is used as a cover and justification for austerity measures or attacks on public services.
- mr president, ladies and gentlemen, a directive on supplementary pension institutions should have been designed to serve a social protection mandate, but the union does not have that mandate. the project is therefore part of the objective of creating an internal market for financial services: the bias is obvious. the main purpose of the act is to enable the supplementary pension industry in britain and elsewhere to benefit from its position in offering crossborder services. we have not voted on the report of the committee on economic and monetary affairs at first reading. while it sought to correct shortcomings in social obligations, it increased investment risks. the council's common position preserves the possibilities of prudential rules in investment matters better, but it is lagging behind parliament's social demands. we have therefore tabled a motion to reject this common position. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the social security system is not disrupted by the crisis. trust in these pension fund systems will not be restored without strict management rules and mutualisations for guarantees. these schemes should also be the subject of european collective agreements between the social partners. i must say that mr karas has done a good job and has taken care to ensure that the text is balanced. however, in the end, compromises between the various components of the political groups and with what seemed acceptable to the council to avoid conciliation led to amendments of limited scope. compared to the common position, this is an improvement, and the amendment tabled by the green group strengthens the prudential investment rules, but the essential and fundamental bias of the text remains.
- mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the greens will vote against the gue/ngl group's proposal to reject the common position. it is not that we take a principled position of refusing to finance supplementary pensions by capitalisation. a pension, as mr kuckelkorn said, is a pension, it is not a savings instrument. it's something that's characterized by its life-long form; the insurance covers the survival of a worker, the return to the surviving spouse and certain guarantees in the event of incapacity. it's not a financial product. it is quite possible that some financial products and financial institutions contribute to the management of certain pension schemes. but from that moment on we are jointly looking for the first time at european level for definitions of pension instruments and social mechanisms, and then we are asking ourselves the question of the conditions under which a financial institution can contribute to them. in the present situation, it is only a savings product that is dressed vaguely but very vaguely, and i thank mr karas for all the efforts he has made to make this dress as similar as possible. we dress it up to look like a retreat; the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. these are purely and simply savings products which should be treated as such and it is selling false goods to say that these are retirement products.

in writing. - in voting on the karas report on occupational pension institutions, the french socialist delegation voted in favour of the motion for a resolution tabled by the gue group. we believe that the financing of pensions is based on the principle of sharing. moreover, the text proposed to us at second reading is not acceptable and the subsequent proposals of commissioner bolkestein or the amendments voted by the economic and monetary affairs committee do not sufficiently improve the balance of the text. the occupational pension institutions cannot be treated as mere financial instruments; they must be based on a social protection logic. the aim here is not to infringe the prerogatives of the member states in social matters but to underline the social importance of the text by the european parliament, the body representing the citizens. since the first reading we have fought for the basic principles of biometric risks, regular information for members and control over these institutions to be incorporated into the text. today, under the singular pretext of avoiding the conciliation stage, the rapporteur, with the complicity of the commissioner, is forbidding our assembly, as a co-legislator, to defend the interests of the citizens. we refuse this coup.
in writing. - is the wto the organization for the "districting" of public services? this is the impression given by the general agreement on trade in services (gats). although article 16 of the ec treaty clearly defines the role of public services in the social and territorial cohesion of the union, they are still on sale. post office, power, railroad, everything goes through here. when will culture, education and health care be competitive? i would like the mandate given to pascal lamy, the union's negotiator, to be clear and extremely well defined. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. the mandate given to the commission should be decided by unanimity of the member states, not by qualified majority. it should be public too. no one has been able to read it, not even national parliaments, which have not been able to debate it. they voted to create public services. only a few meps were able to access the mandate document in a room specially prepared for them, with a formal ban on taking notes. this is a good illustration of the democratic deficit.
in writing. - we voted against the parliament's resolution which gives the commission a guarantee to negotiate the liberalization of trade in services in the so-called 'gats' cycle. this guarantee is granted on far too vague a basis, the commission will exploit it as usual in the broad sense, and the peoples will find themselves a little more disarmed by those very people who claim to make them 'stronger'. our fears are heightened when we note that the convention chaired by valéry giscard d'estaing intends to include trade policy among the exclusive competences of the union, dealt with by qualified majority, and to abolish the exceptions (cultural and audiovisual services, education, social services and human health) which article 133 (6) tec still required to be dealt with unanimously. such a development would make the gats trap worse for us. it is noted with some amusement that the french government protested and asked for unanimity to be maintained on these 'very sensitive' matters. but why should these areas be considered more sensitive than others, such as water production or nuclear engineering? and if unanimity really does provide such good protection, why is it demonized in all european affairs?
in writing. - trade agreements which advocate the liberalization of international trade, deregulation, imply that more and more sectors of public services are being left to the market, to competition, that is to say to the appetites of private interests. this is a disastrous development for the vast majority of society. it's a regular attack on the working classes. but it must be stressed that it is conducted with the agreement of governments, or even on their own initiative, even when they pretend to be different from the wto or other similar bodies. the problem is not only to preserve cultural diversity, although it is legitimate to say that culture should not be a commodity. but how can we accept that health, health care, education, which are essential to social life, should be left to the stupid laws of the market and competition? how can we accept it for water, electricity, postal services or railways and other sectors important for social life? we, for our part, oppose all this and oppose any opening up of public services to competition and profit-making, any attack on their staff and any job cuts.
in writing. - the liberals and conservatives of all colours, who signed a joint resolution, have thwarted all attempts to defend cultural diversity and reject the 'commercialization' of culture! all the amendments by the gue/ngl group which went in this direction were rejected. that is why, like the members of my delegation from the republican, radical and citizen left, the gue/ngl group and a few other socialist members, i voted against this resolution by the epp-pes-liberal group. this is not the kind of europe that corresponds to the european europe for which i have been fighting for 40 years!
in writing. - i regret that on a subject so decisive for the future of the european citizens, we have to content ourselves with a resolution procedure. a commissioner should only speak on behalf of the european union after negotiating his mandate with the elected representatives. the constitution will have to take account of this democratic deficit if it is to succeed in bringing europe closer to its citizens. the amendments proposing a political reorientation of the text having been rejected, i shall vote against the resolution. public services should not be part of the negotiations, a suspensive moratorium on any new agreement would allow a genuine impact assessment with regard to other market services. some say that developing countries are asking for such agreements. they have no choice but to privatise their public services, the level of their debt preventing them from borrowing for the development of these services, especially for water. the wto must no longer be the trojan horse of a liberalism which has shown its limits and its inability to improve the quality of life of the majority of the world's citizens. international trade is essential, but it must be conditional on the adoption and observance of environmental and social rules.
in writing. - as is often the case in the european parliament, the joint resolution on the gats tabled by the right (epp-de), the liberals (eldr) and the socialists (pse) is a mixture of negative and positive proposals (publicity for the negotiations, defence of cultural diversity, etc.). but the general line of the project is clear: to pursue the liberalisation of services and to strengthen the role of the wto in the context of unequal globalisation. the joint resolution defends the theory, contradicted by the facts, that opening up the market for services benefits everyone and aims to 'convince poor nations that the success of the wto is decisive for the economy of all countries, rich and poor' (recitals a and c). instead of calling for the suspension of the doha round and a moratorium on the gatt negotiations - conservative measures without which there is no possible exercise of democracy - it wants more liberalisation in a number of sectors, including telecommunications and maritime transport (articles 3 and 8). the authors of the joint resolution are aware of the general concern raised by the gats. but the formal precautions cannot hide the fact that the adoption of this resolution would represent a further step in the commodification of services. we voted against it.
in writing. - services, particularly public services, are the key issue, not only because they represent two thirds of european gdp, but also because they touch the very foundation of the identity of peoples with culture. should we then privatize, commodify global public goods like health, literacy, knowledge, water? the wto says yes. everything is merchandise. the european commission says yes, but behind the scenes, because brussels ideologically adheres to the philosophy of the 'libertarians', for whom everything is for sale, including the police, the army and humanitarian aid through echo. we pretend to preserve cultural diversity. culture and audiovisual are not "marketable", while agriculture, the foundation of civilization, has been marketed since the uruguay round. it is also said that no offer of liberalization has been made by europe for health, education and the audiovisual sector. but already american chains of intellectual "fast food" are buying a university in madrid. the audiovisual of berlusconi, bouygues, murdoch, is a commodity. there is water, which the former imf managing director, camdessus, says is the major factor in corruption, especially in the french lyonnaise des eaux. the confidentiality of the negotiations, the uncertainty about the services involved and the byzantineism about the distinction between globalized trade and nationalized regulation make the gats an agreement behind the backs of the peoples.
in writing. - once again the fishermen disagree with the commission. the cod seems to be the guinea pig for the commission to experiment with the new instrument it has managed to impose on the council in the context of recovery plans for endangered species: limiting fishing effort. this instrument is naturally susceptible to the widest extensions. we are already talking about cod and sole in the bay of biscay. the commission proposal on cod is based, as always, on the most recent opinions of the international council for the exploration of the sea, which includes many non-european partners and many of whose positions have been controversial in the past. it is undeniable that certain cod stocks are in a vulnerable situation in several areas. but by attributing the origin of this situation exclusively to fishing, the commission risks condemning the fishermen without restoring the resource. we abstain on the stevenson resolution only because it advocates codecision in the cfp, which in our view does not need an additional factor of uncertainty and unpredictability. we are of course supporting the rest of the resolution.
in writing. - the explanatory statement of this report welcomes the decline in unemployment at european level. the 13 million unemployed figure proposed in the text is not to be welcomed, however, and is certainly an underestimated figure which, moreover, does not take into account those who have to content themselves with precarious work with low pay. in addition, for several months now, the number of unemployed has been rising again in all the countries of the union. how could it be otherwise, even as the continent's most powerful industrial groups announce major job cuts and close one factory after another? speaking in terms of employment strategy, to use the title of the report, may seem rather ominous to those millions of workers who are being pushed into poverty simply so that the firms that lay them off can ensure their shareholders higher dividends by paying lower wages. we voted against this text because its philosophy is that it is for employers to decide sovereignly whether or not to maintain jobs, even though it is obvious that, without coercive measures forcing companies to withdraw from their current or past profits what is needed to maintain jobs and wages, the number of unemployed will continue to increase and poverty will increase.
in writing. - the commitment made in lisbon to a european future characterized by a quantitative and qualitative improvement in employment and greater social cohesion seems to be seriously threatened by this report, if it is now amended in the way proposed by mr mann. these amendments, which have been reintroduced for the plenary, also completely call into question the work done by the committee on employment to rebalance the rapporteur's text in favour of an employment policy which is concerned not only with greater flexibility and a reduction in taxation but also, and above all, with the speedy achievement of quality employment for all: training and education must therefore be the focus of our policy, second-class jobs and other unskilled work must disappear. the report, as amended, ignores the principles of solidarity and social cohesion, which are essential and objective principles for anyone who is seriously seeking to implement a new strategy for employment, a generous strategy which puts people at the centre of all its concerns. i am therefore opposed to this report, which, with its amendments, embraces neoliberal principles and, in other words, advocates a policy of employment which ignores the human factor.
in writing. - following the conclusions of the lisbon summit, we have always insisted on the necessary balance between quantity and quality. we have made real progress and we must fight the scourge of unemployment. but we must be careful about social plans, restructuring, relocation and mass redundancies. we cannot be satisfied with the precarious situation that is afflicting more and more of our fellow citizens. the european parliament has a real duty in this warning. mr mann has given the opposite message, and that is unacceptable, by presenting to us an exclusively neoliberal profession of faith. we need a real fight against poverty and for employment today. we do not accept low-skilled jobs, and we do not accept workers being precarious. instead, we need to focus on training, on skills, and on supporting the most vulnerable. we must be very vigilant about women's work, we must allow young people to enter the labour market with hope. we do not want deregulation and uncontrolled opening up of the markets for trade in services (gats). we will not accept sacrificing all our hard-won social gains. in writing. - while stressing its commitment to respecting the provisions of the stability pact and to accelerating the reforms adopted in lisbon, the garcía-margallo report remains deaf to the criticism and deep divergences that are increasingly being heard in public opinion. he remains blind to the rise in unemployment, mass layoffs, and the sudden closure of businesses. what crime did the employees of metaleurope commit ? what kind of 'stability' is this when lives are being destroyed for the sake of 'compatibility with monetary policy'? the old adage is well known: liberalisation of markets requires sacrifice ! i would have liked the eu to set itself the ambition of a genuine pact for employment and growth, based on meeting the needs of the people, a rise in wages, a genuine policy for creating jobs and wealth. i can therefore only object to the logic of the report not to call into question the macroeconomic stability which means that bosses receive public funds, can close companies, without being held accountable. i cannot support the call for 'strengthening liberalisation in the services of general interest ... including postal services, telecommunications, gas and electricity, rail and air transport and broadcasting'.
in writing. - this report is of no interest to the european parliament except to give its unconditional support to the commission's proposals. apart from the inevitable catalogue of good intentions - promotion of the spirit of enterprise, increased investment in human resources and research and development - which we can only endorse, this report perfectly illustrates the pavlovian spirit which reigns in this house: it is enough for the commission to become the champion of european integration on the liberal and federalist model for parliament to automatically agree with it. the same is true of the demand to make the commission the economic government of europe, and of the desire to liberalize services of general interest and the network industries, the main ones being postal services, telecommunications, gas and electricity, and rail transport. while greater convergence of the economic policies of the member states is obviously desirable, to be viable it must be achieved within the limits of their competence and, in so doing, naturally result from free economic competition between states, and not from technocratic decisions ignoring national realities.
in writing. - the trentin report welcomes the extremely satisfactory implementation of the stability and growth pact, which was recently denounced as stupid by the president of the commission, romano prodi. the report also stresses the need to ensure that the eu's external relations are not distorted by the threat of a crisis. the trentin report, like the garcía-margallo and dos santos reports, which were also put to the vote, is in favour of the intelligent application of the pact and the adjustments that this implies. but intelligence and stupidity meet in incoherent speech, which would make things that are not compatible compatible. in short, the structural reforms mentioned mean increased precariousness of work, financialization of pensions and new privatizations. in the face of rising unemployment, the alternative is to abandon the stability pact altogether in favour of a policy focused on job creation through a profound change in the distribution of income. it is because there is no trace of such a perspective that we voted against this report, which only proposes inconsistent revisions of the pact.
in writing. - the report, which is faithful to the orthodoxy of monetarism and federalism, calls for an even more rigid interpretation of the pact for stability and growth, which is not so well named. it is not so much a question here of drawing lessons from the observed reality as of examining the case of states guilty of not complying with the obligations of a text which today constitutes an unsustainable snare for economic recovery. above all, it is clear that the absolute status of the stability pact is not only motivated by purely economic reasons, but that it is now a genuinely political issue. indeed, who does not see that budgetary balance is not only seen as an economically laudable objective - which is common sense - but that it is erected as a dogma from which no one must deviate, on pain of calling into question the whole of an edifice (the emu) built for primarily political reasons (to set up the first genuinely federalist european structure)? the rapporteur therefore, rather than analysing the current economic realities, wants to make the stability pact more rigorous, in particular by increasing the commission's autonomy in the supervision of the member states. this logic is unacceptable.
in writing. - the european parliament is once again the channel for the urgent requests of the brussels college. a majority of this parliament may wish to see the stability pact applied intelligently and flexibly in the manner proposed by the commission, or it may support the commission in arbitrarily initiating inquisitorial proceedings against states which cannot submit to a zealous interpretation of the provisions of the stability pact, but i cannot go down that road. if i consider that the alleged adjustments introduced by the european commission - adjustments which recognise the existence of a structural component and a component linked to the economic cycle in the budget deficit - are in fact based on the fact that they strengthen the growth pillar without compromising the stability component, i do not forget that this dramatic turnaround is also part of a more general strategy to make the commission the economic government of the union. it goes without saying that i cannot accept such a hypothesis.
- mr president, commissioner, this operation in macedonia has just been presented as a historic milestone in the european union's commitment. i think we need to do a little bit of a downgrade on this ambitious presentation. first, because, quantitatively, it is a relatively small number. this is a mission, if i understand correctly, of less than 500 men, including the commander. secondly, because we have not been able to agree on very specific objectives. we are not even able to agree on the name of this country and i am happy to speak to the greek foreign minister. i ask myself why we should not allow this country to use the name it had when it was a federal republic within the yugoslav entity, since that name would of course not imply any territorial claims or changes in borders. secondly, and above all, the presence of our forces has no really very clear purpose. we are not told in what context this mission might end, because the causes of the conflict are still there, including the gradual albanization of this territory, which was until then predominantly populated by slavs. finally, contrary to what the committee on foreign affairs and security claims, the mission is not really a nato mission. it will be led by the supreme allied command europe from its headquarters, shape. it uses nato's resources. it seems that the united states, which needs its troops in the middle east, has outsourced this operation, now secondary, to its european vassals. i don't think there's much to be proud of.
council on a similar issue, i would like to stress to the honourable member that, like the european parliament, the council reacted swiftly after the prestige accident off the coast of galicia in november 2002. the council takes note of parliament's resolutions and shares most of the principles set out in them. in particular, the council agrees with the objective of avoiding the presence of non-compliant vessels in european union waters. among the measures included in its conclusions of 6 december on ship safety and pollution prevention, the council expressed its support for the work being carried out within the imo framework to develop a flag state code and a mandatory standard control system, with a view to ensuring that flag states fulfil their obligations under international conventions. in general, the council stressed the need to review international rules on the law of the sea and maritime transport, rules which allow certain open-minded experts to tolerate irresponsibility and negligence. the commission may take the initiative and, where appropriate, propose specific measures for ships bearing the so-called 'opportunity seals'. however, the council is convinced that the objective can be achieved by better-designed measures against non-compliant vessels, such as by strengthening port state control. the current legislation allows for the strengthening of port state control based on criteria for the classification of non-compliant ships, which were laid down in the paris mou. this includes the ship's flag. moreover, according to the port state directive, which will enter into force by 22 july 2003 at the latest and is part of the erika i package, member states refuse access to ports to ships of different categories if they fly the flag of a state included in the blacklist published in the annual report of the memorandum of understanding and have already been deposited in the past.
- thank you, mr president, for your input, but let me also stress that the european parliament has also followed all the initiatives of the commission and the council to speed up the implementation of the erika i and erika ii packages. you are referring to the new provisions concerning the imo. but if the european parliament has proposed a ban on flags of convenience, it is because everyone here knows well, from the debates we have had following maritime disasters, that the flag of convenience has this peculiarity that, in the event of a problem, there are enormous difficulties in locating those responsible. it is well known that throughout the chain between the flag, the state, the ship's pilot and the various crews, it is no longer possible to determine who will ultimately be criminally and financially charged, hence parliament's proposal. i'll allow myself to insist. it is true that the commission must take the initiative, but i would like to know how you, as president of the council, will support this proposal from the european parliament.

equality policies. it is extremely difficult to implement what the european parliament is proposing with gender mainstreaming, which i translate as transversality in french. first of all, we must recognize the difficulty of making specific policies for women - which is why there is a committee on women's rights in parliament - and at the same time ensuring that these policies have a cross-cutting effect in all committees and in all policy areas. that is what this report proposes. once again europe is a pioneer in this field and we must be extremely attentive to this double challenge. we must walk on two feet and not one: on the one hand, equality, with the committee on women's rights and equal opportunities, and on the other hand, transversality and gender mainstreaming, which is extremely difficult. we both check this every day in our respective committees, apart from the committee on women's rights and equal opportunities. this report, and i thank mrs gröner again, proposes a two-level laboratory. on the one hand, it is a question of touching the decision-making process, of ensuring that, as is already the case, i believe, in the commission, gender mainstreaming is applied at all levels within parliament. secondly, the emphasis is not on parity but on gender equality in all areas, thanks to this report which will be voted on in plenary, which i and because it highlights the difficulty of this policy. the informal council last week had already virtually adopted some of the proposals in this report, and i am pleased to see that. i am, however,
