- mr president, we shall vote for this report because it contains a number of good intentions concerning equality between women and men, which it proposes that the european parliament should already be sweeping away at its own door. not only are there half as many women as men in parliament, but in the governing bodies of parliament, the bureau of parliament, the conference of presidents, etc., women are outrageously underrepresented. i would like to stress, however, that to act only at this level would be to touch only the surface of things. in companies there is always a significant difference between men's and women's wages. why do the european institutions, which are able to propose binding directives to facilitate trade and business, not do the same to ensure real wage equality? why do they not impose on all member states, including the most backward ones, this elementary right of women to dispose of their bodies? it would not be enough to stop the development of misogyny and barbaric behaviour towards women, which are growing on the basis of the impoverishment and ghettoization of working-class neighbourhoods, but it would stop the deterioration of women's living conditions.
- mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, speaking this morning on behalf of my group in the debate on consumers and consumer protection, i would like to say once again, as many of my colleagues have done, that if we can agree with the european commission's objectives - a high level of protection, effective enforcement of the rules and effective participation of consumer organizations - we must again note that the proposals made to us are still far too vague and not sufficiently concrete. i therefore largely support the proposals by mr whitehead and mrs patrie, in particular on safety, transport, chemicals, electronic commerce, prior information to be provided in all cases to enable effective defence mechanisms and appropriate remedies to be activated where necessary. i would also like to make a special mention of the readability of the eco-label and, above all, of the very comprehensive information needed on gmos, which, as we know, is a matter of debate among us. i would like to emphasize the toy directive and the control of ce marking. as rapporteur on these matters for several years, i know that the toy directive needs to be revised very quickly and that the ce marking has often lost all meaning because of the lack of sufficient controls. i have written to the commission several times on this subject, but unfortunately i have not received very satisfactory answers. i would also like to make two very clear concerns in the form of substantive criticisms at this stage of the debate on consumer policy and protection. first concern: whatever their interests, consumer protection policies are too closely linked to, and therefore too dependent on, the objective of forcing the way towards the completion of the single market. these policies are rarely objectives in themselves but are more often the consequences of free competition. secondly, these policies are often, if not always, a pretext for erasing, drowning or even eliminating the concept of public service, which is much broader than consumer protection by taking the long term into account, integrating solidarity and spatial planning, particularly through pricing and access conditions. in some countries and in some political groups, the best advocates for consumers are often the best opponents of public services, in the name of free competition and private domination. i therefore wanted to point out this morning, while welcoming the efforts of the european commission and supporting the proposals of our rapporteurs, that there are differences, even fundamental differences.
- mr president, the green paper presented by the commission and the reports presented this morning are moving in the right direction. all the elements necessary to ensure a high level of consumer protection must be established rapidly. they must be sure that their rights are everywhere equally and fully respected. in order to achieve this high level of protection, it is therefore essential to involve representative consumer organisations in the formulation of both community and international policies. as many changes are taking place in the commercial sector, it is imperative that civil society be consulted. it must be able to participate in the debates and influence decisions which are of primary interest to it. the consumer must play an active role through his consumption. it is no longer a question of consuming unconsciously, but of making informed choices. the consumer must therefore be protected, but he must also be informed. to this end, he must be able to access any information he considers essential, for example by being able to obtain information on production processes, including the working conditions of employees. the logos for fair trade or for companies that respect a social charter, established at community level, therefore appear to be valuable and effective instruments, as are those for organic farming. if we want to have an ethical and fair trade, we must remember our commitment to quality products that do not compromise human dignity, in fields as varied as coffee or children's toys, and that meet all the criteria that satisfy the precautionary principle. in this context, the traceability of gmos appears, once again, to be of the most fundamental importance. we must not, as some amendments suggest, allow consumers to trust gmos more and more. on the contrary, our duty is to protect consumers and to provide them with comprehensive and unmistakable information enabling them to make informed and conscientious choices for themselves and their children. we must also stress the need for citizen consumers to participate in the establishment of a sustainable model of society. we must not reduce the citizen to a mere consumer. on the contrary, it must be a full participant in determining the needs which then constitute a real choice of society.
- mr president, with the legal protection of consumers we are tackling a vast and ambitious project which must lead to a high level of protection. a high level does not necessarily mean uniform protection. we believe that it must respect the principles of subsidiarity, necessity and proportionality. i am in favour of minimum harmonization, which does not prevent each member state from introducing legislation which best suits its identity. i also share the idea of systematically using article 151 (3) of the treaty, which should become the sole legal basis for legislation. we must stop systematically using article 95 which deals only with the single market. ensuring universal and affordable access to high quality services for all citizens is one of our key demands. let's demand that the wto not dismantle our public services. i also approve of the wto labelling as a means of providing information on origin and method of production. i am, however, reserved about the creation of a european consumer centre which would work in tandem with the national organisations, which are playing their part well and would benefit from networking. i am also concerned about the content of the thyssen report: asking the commission to carry out an impact study on the possibility of maximum harmonisation seems unrealistic. similarly, a link should be made between consumer protection and the sales promotion regulation. as far as the introduction of codes of conduct is concerned, the idea does not seem to me to be a viable one at present. where do these codes of conduct get their legitimacy? and how do we ensure their sustainability ? these are all questions which justify not pursuing them further.
mr president, i think we can look forward to the discussion we have today on the green paper and the strategy proposed by the commission on consumer policy. we welcome this because, with enlargement and therefore the extension of the internal market, it is clear that it is important to harmonize community legislation on consumer matters. we also know the role of consumption in the economy. god knows we need it today! however, studies have shown that, outside crossborder areas, the european consumer does not know how to use the benefits of the european union. then why did you do it ? simply because it still lacks confidence, because it does not always have the relevant information and data on products and services and because it does not always have the means to know the quality of products, price references; because, especially in the event of a dispute, he does not know which court will be competent. so all this means that the consumer does not take advantage of these possibilities offered by europe, whereas, on the other hand, he needs knowledge, information and is quite willing to behave as a citizen, respectful of eco-labels for example. the commission has also proposed that the european parliament should be consulted on the draft directive on the protection of consumers in the event of a dispute between the consumer and the consumer. we therefore support better, clearer consumer information in the consumer's own language, so that he can make a fully informed choice. developing a framework strategy for the consumer also means ensuring his legal protection, putting an end to litigation which is linked to unfair business practices and protecting the companies themselves. we therefore welcome a high level of consumer protection, the transparency that will be achieved through the associations and we expect a lot from the commission. we can assure you, commissioner, that we will be behind you in monitoring this consumer policy.
- mr president, i welcome the in-depth work done by my colleagues whitehead, patrie and thyssen on the implications of the green paper for consumer protection. we support the call for simpler and more targeted legislation to facilitate the implementation of the internal market legislative arsenal, which we believe is lacking in transparency and is too fragmented to inspire consumer confidence. we welcome the emergence of the concept of citizen consumers and i would remind you that their fundamental rights are the right to safety, information, freedom of choice, representation, redress, satisfaction and a clean environment. the consumption of the future must take account of the three pillars of sustainable development: economic, ecological and social, the latter two being still too often neglected. i propose that we consider the feasibility of a general directive on the environmental quality of consumer products and services, taking account in particular of a european label and a high level of protection. we believe that the citizen consumer must become a central element, not only as a consumer but also as a decision-maker, as an engaged consumer concerned about the ethical level of the product he consumes. in this sense, it will become one of the main and indispensable actors in this development which we want to be sustainable.

in writing. - the friedrich report is right on two counts: firstly, that the current voting system in the governing council of the ecb ("one member, one vote") will be unmanageable after the enlargement of the euro area; the reform proposed today by the ecb itself (the system of allocating countries into groups, with differentiated rotations) is obscure, complex and very difficult to make work too. but this report omits two important points: firstly, the 'one governor, one vote' system was deliberately inserted into the maastricht treaty to present the model, supposedly attractive to the voter, of a monetary union which operates on an egalitarian basis; secondly, this model, which did not wait for enlargement, is already working very badly today, and it is largely responsible for the ecb's inertia in dealing with the problems of the largest economy in the euro area, germany. the reform proposed by the ecb is therefore, with technical exceptions, far from trivial. the alternative suggested by mr friedrich (the introduction of a weighting of votes according to the population) calls into question an essential principle of equality solemnly adopted by the peoples. that is why we are asking for more than a debate that has been sent to the cleaners.
in writing. - we voted for the bösch report on the protection of the communities' financial interests because it is a serious and solid report, which lists some of the commission's dysfunctions or some very impressive cases of fraud, confirming what we have been saying for a long time. during the session it was revealed that documents had been withheld from the european parliament in the andreasen case (contested dismissal of a commission accounting officer who had complained of practices which were out of line with normal accounting standards). we protest against this cover-up. it is therefore possible that this scandal will worsen and add to the burden of the bösch report. we are, however, wary of reaffirming the traditional call - which is also discreet in the bösch report - for the establishment of a european public prosecutor. without entering into the debate here, i would just like to point out that the working party concerned within the convention, despite its good federalist intentions, also found this proposal questionable. we can also be effective through other means (eurojust, etc.) which will have the merit of not creating institutional problems in the chain.
the commission. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i have to say that i am very pleased with the way the commission has been working. the problem of closing down companies that have received financial aid from the european union is unfortunately a frequent - and increasingly frequent - headline item in the newspapers. this problem is not new, but it is true that cases of closures, often followed by relocations, have been increasing recently. the commission therefore fully understands that this problem, which rightly concerns our fellow citizens, is of great importance and considerable interest to the european parliament. my colleagues, mrs anna diamantopoulou and mr michel barnier, have asked me to explain to you the commission's position on this complex problem. it is clear that several different aspects are involved: firstly, the policy of economic and social cohesion through co-financing from the structural funds; secondly, european social policy; but also, thirdly, the rules of the european internal market, which are intended to enable our companies to develop in a climate of fair competition. i would like to concentrate on these questions in my statement, but first i would like to address two other points. firstly, the problem of closures of firms - even if it also directly affects the community as a result of the financial aid granted - is not a purely european phenomenon but one which must also be considered in an international context. unfortunately, our companies often succumb to the temptation to move their operations to low-wage countries, sometimes in defiance of any social or environmental considerations. the european parliament has already expressed its views on the situation in the middle east, and the european council has already expressed its views on the situation in the middle east. secondly, the commission pays particular attention to this problem in the context of enlargement. the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos is a very good one. in a single market such as ours, the decision on the location of a company is left to the management of the company. we know that investors base their decisions on the comparative advantages of the location: these include wage costs, social climate, quality of infrastructure, applicable legal framework, but often also public aid and tax benefits. the subsidies which may be granted to investors are freely negotiated with the public authorities within the framework of community and national state aid legislation. the commission's proposal for a regulation on the application of the principle of equal treatment for men and women in matters of employment, vocational training and promotion of equal opportunities is a good one. the regional aid granted for productive investment is therefore intended primarily to compensate for the handicaps of the assisted regions, in order to enable them to compete more effectively with the more developed regions. in this field, the commission can only ensure the implementation of the general provisions on the structural funds, which have been adopted by the council in agreement with the european parliament. this is also in line with the practice at national level, where each region is constantly trying to attract new enterprises and direct investment. it is also the commission's responsibility to prevent unfair competition between states, economic operators and social actors. the structural funds have therefore provided for a number of preventive measures for the 2000-2006 programming period, which i would like to recall briefly. the guidelines on national regional aid provide that the beneficiaries of such aid must maintain their investments for a period of at least five years. this period begins when the investment is first put into operation in the undertaking concerned. the general structural funds regulation of 1999 is moving in the same direction. it states that the funds will continue to contribute to productive activities only if the location of those activities does not change during the five years following the decision on the structural funds' contribution. finally, the new regulation on employment aid, which was adopted in 2002, is somewhat more flexible. the commission has also proposed that the council should adopt a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to carcinogens at work. all these rules must also be applied in the future member states from the date of accession. for the sake of completeness, i would point out that the five-year rule just mentioned concerns only the programming period 2000-2006. for the period 1994-99, community assistance may be reduced or withdrawn if the conditions for implementing the measure no longer exist. in all cases, neither the commission nor the member states may refuse to grant a subsidy if the necessary conditions are met. however, if it is found that a beneficiary company has not complied with the community rules on state aid, it must repay the aid it has wrongly received. the commission is therefore prepared to accept its responsibility if an undertaking has unlawfully received subsidies under an aid scheme co-financed by a community programme. this is, however, subject to the authorities of the country from which the company has migrated having first established an infringement on the basis of the points described above. the commission has already taken a number of measures to combat the problem of unemployment. although closure of a plant is undoubtedly a matter for the management of the company concerned, we must not forget that the many restructuring operations currently carried out in europe are not all comparable. some are the result of clear economic decisions which have been openly discussed with the workers and their representatives, others are unfortunately carried out in defiance of labour law and sometimes push people into unemployment. the commission's position is clear: while companies are free to make their economic choices, they must always be aware of the social dimension. when redundancies seem inevitable, every effort must be made to increase the mediation capacity of the employees concerned. this requires a forward-looking and thoughtful policy on the part of companies, and they must also demonstrate social responsibility. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. the framework within which this dialogue must take place is laid down in several community directives. in particular, the directive on the establishment of a european works council imposes specific obligations on multinational groups established in europe to inform and consult employees' representatives. finally, the social measures accompanying restructuring are also an important issue for the social partners and for the new european observatory for industrial change. but here too the commission is dependent on the member states. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's labour law is respected. the commission will, however, exercise its control function fully, in particular to prevent the directives on information and consultation of workers from being insufficiently implemented. (applause from the centre)
mr fischler, whose analysis i do not share, is with us because i believe that the union has strong levers to influence the companies which are subsidized by europe and which are relocating. i also - mr president, i should like to begin by welcoming the work of our colleague, mr gérard caudron, on this report on the first application of article 169 of the treaty to the sixth edf. his work has helped us to work together very well and to make this wonderful proposal a success. this is due to the courageous initiative of commissioner busquin and consists of allocating a total of €600 million to major research, with the aim of fighting hiv/aids, malaria and tuberculosis, under the edctp programme. the importance of the objective and the means employed require us to stress the need to respect ethical rules in the context of this research; to stress also the need to be able to use the results in the general interest, to collaborate with developing countries and to promote the scientific and technical emergence of these countries. ethical principles are those set out in article 6 of the treaty on european union and in the charter of fundamental rights, and those defined in the declaration of helsinki of the world medical association on ethical principles for medical research in human subjects. the european and developing countries' clinical trial partnership programme shall apply good clinical practice as defined in directive 2001/20/eec for the conduct of clinical trials on medicinal products for human use in the european union. the edctp programme should promote specialist training and capacity building in developing countries, step up technology transfer to these countries and mobilise additional funds to combat these diseases. the community will ensure that policy decisions and the implementation of programmes are geared to the objective of bringing to market effective products which are accessible at the lowest possible price and easy to use and adapted to the specific conditions of developing countries. they must therefore involve, in an active process, the actors of the developing countries, scientific experts from the north and the south, representatives of patient groups, ngos and the who. finally, our green/efa group wants the results obtained under this programme to be considered as public property and therefore not subject to the intellectual property rules as defined in the trips agreements, in order to ensure access to the treatments resulting from this research at the lowest possible price for developing countries.
the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial interests are protected. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, fraud and economic and financial crime, as has been said, cause considerable damage to the financial interests of the european community, estimated at over one billion euros a year. enlargement will certainly not improve this situation, since it will increase the fragmentation of the judicial area, increase the number of administrations involved in the management of community funds and thus increase the risk of fraud. this fraud and this crime have, as we know, been a long-standing concern of the european parliament and article 280 of the treaty of amsterdam has already given the community the power to take effective and equivalent measures in all the member states. i therefore fully support the commission's green paper on the creation of a european public prosecutor for the defence of the community's financial interests and the report by mrs theato. i support the inclusion of a new article 280a in the future constitutional treaty, an idea which, moreover, was rejected by the last intergovernmental conference, despite the support of our assembly, in 2000. the institution of a european prosecutor is indeed necessary, but its democratic legitimacy should be ensured by appointment with the assent of the european parliament; it is also necessary to emphasise the need to provide the prosecutor and the delegated prosecutors with a status ensuring their complete independence from the parties to the proceedings, the member states, the community institutions and bodies. it is also essential to ensure that the court of justice acts in a uniform manner throughout the european judicial area by affirming the principle of equal prosecution and by strictly regulating cases of conditional dismissal. in this connection, support should be given to the principle of the creation of a community court, attached to the court of justice, to deal with criminal cases. finally, there will of course be a need for better coordination, the best possible coordination, between the european prosecutor and the structures of olaf, eurojust and europol. as mrs theato has just said, we have appealed to the convention, and we hope that it will take up the matter.
mr president, on the fight against fraud, i would first like to say that there is a problem which needs to be dealt with urgently. there is no judicial institution today with the power to conduct investigations within the community administrations, because of the privileges of the latter. if there is a justifiable mission for a european prosecutor, it is this one. as for the rest, that is to say the possible creation of a supranational body responsible for conducting investigations and bringing legal proceedings against member states in the case of offences affecting the financial interests of the communities, the proposed operation seems to me to have more disadvantages than advantages. of course, differences in national judicial spaces can in some cases impede prosecution. but eurojust is designed to remedy this problem in accordance with national competences. let him act first and develop. we'll judge after that. as for the supranational european prosecutor proposed by the commission, it would lead us into an endless maze, since not only would it be necessary to harmonize charges, sanctions, time limits, all kinds of procedural acts, including the admissibility of evidence, but it would also be necessary to look at the question of the protection of individual freedoms for all the coercive acts that the european prosecutor would require: search, seizure, listening, arrest warrant, judicial control, provisional detention, not to mention, of course, the huge question of democratic control that would have to be created. it is enormous, mr president, and i urge my colleagues to follow the eurojust approach instead, which can achieve the same results without destabilising anything.

the rapporteur. - mr president, madam commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, in the difficult times we are living in today, the commission's desire, reaffirmed on several occasions and over the past few years, to make the europe of knowledge a strategic priority for the union seems to me more timely than ever. the erasmus world programme, which we are discussing tonight, is perfectly suited to this objective. so this is very good news for europe. the main objectives of this programme are twofold and closely linked: to make higher education in the european union more attractive to students and teachers from the rest of the world and to strengthen links between european universities in order to improve the quality and competitiveness of european higher education. indeed, it is by developing, on the one hand, their links with each other and, on the other hand, their links with the rest of the world that our universities will improve the quality of their offerings. as mrs reding said, erasmus world is the instrument europe needs, both internally and externally, to emerge victorious from the globalisation of education. by opening up our universities to the world, we are also opening them up to europe. a word here about the name of the program. we propose that this programme be renamed erasmus mundus. in this way the principle of cultural diversity, which we all deeply cherish and which is a great strength of our union, will be respected and preserved. this programme covers the period 2004 to 2008. it proposes four actions, all of which are very concrete. first, the creation of masters, which we will call erasmus mundus masters, numbering 250. these masters will be selected for a period of five years and will involve at least three higher education institutions from three different member states. they will lead to the award of officially recognised diplomas. these master's degrees will be open to students and teachers from third countries and i hope they will be open to students and teachers from the european union so that they too can benefit from this tour of europe. the labelling of masters will obviously depend on the quality of the courses provided, but it will also have to take into account the quality of the reception reserved for students. the selection procedure will have to be carried out by a high-level jury, composed of eminent figures from the academic world. at the end of their course, students will have to have learned or used at least two languages. language learning must remain a priority for the european union. as mr prodi pointed out, language learning is one of the main ways of promoting genuine understanding between peoples. the promotion of language learning must continue to be encouraged by all means and this programme offers us a perfect opportunity to do so. second action: the establishment of a system of grants. large grants will be offered to 4 200 students from third countries, either directly or through partnerships between their home university and universities participating in a master's programme. in addition, grants will be offered to 1 000 professors from third countries invited to europe for teaching or research missions of an average duration of three months. third action: the creation of partnerships to strengthen and promote intercultural understanding. higher education institutions will be encouraged to establish cooperation with universities in third countries. the last action is the international promotion of european higher education. a website will be set up specifically for the programme, providing up-to-date information on erasmus mundus masters. to achieve all these objectives, we felt it was appropriate to give ourselves the means to achieve our ambitions; the commission has already proposed that the budget be increased to eur 300 million, taking care not to undermine existing programmes and taking into account the appropriate conditions and means to be determined by the budgetary authority. on all these points, the cooperation with our colleagues from the committee on culture, youth, education, the media and sport and with the rapporteur for opinions has been extremely fruitful. let them be thankful! and here i want to conclude by expressing a wish: that tomorrow young students, academics and researchers from the european union and the rest of the world will find in our continent material to learn from, to train and to understand each other better. in writing. - the main purpose of the text we have just voted is to ensure the health safety of artificial insemination of cattle; but there is another aspect of this activity which has not been sufficiently taken into account until now, and that is the biodiversity or genetic diversity of bovine breeds. the cattle insemination industry, left to the liberal rules of the market, seeks performance at the lowest cost, which leads to pressure to reduce the number of breeders; this has led to increased risk of inbreeding, the threat of extinction for rare species, and the depletion of biodiversity. there is a public service dimension in the genetic selection of animal breeds which is poorly taken into account by a purely commercial organisation of the profession; the maintenance of biodiversity within domestic breeds is one aspect of the multifunctional nature of agriculture which the member states must be keen to support. i therefore ask the member states, while encouraging freedom of enterprise in this profession and while applying the rules necessary for the absolute safety of artificial insemination, to promote the conservation of the most diverse genetic heritage possible in bovine herds.

in writing. - the commission's 2000 and 2001 reports on the application of the principles of subsidiarity and proportionality are distressing. this is a reductive conception of subsidiarity, which should never call into question the community acquis, which should not be in conflict with the commission's plans and which should not be decided by national parliaments. the reduction in the number of community texts reported by the commission since 1990 is merely the mechanical backlash of the end of the single act. but subsidiarity is still being violated today. at present, the court of justice, that is to say a community institution not controlled by the people, is the ultimate judge of subsidiarity, in the usual consistency with the commission. the current convention on the future of europe would like to strengthen this role even further. we disagree. as i said in my contribution on subsidiarity, which i presented to the european parliament's committee on institutional affairs in 1995, the real criterion of subsidiarity is simply the decision which national parliaments must freely take. the people who signed the treaty. they are the ones who should be the judges of its limits.

- the next item is the report (a5-0085/2003) by mrs buitenweg, on behalf of the committee on civil liberties and human rights, on the proposal for a european parliament recommendation to the council on the reform of the drug conventions (com (2003) 0515 - c4-0535/2003 - syn 348) (com (2003) 0514 - c4-0535/2003 - syn 343) (c4-0535/2003 - syn 343)
mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i must say that i am completely astonished by what i have just heard from mr pirker, and i will explain it to you. i would like to begin by congratulating our rapporteur, mrs buitenweg, on her report, which, contrary to what has just been said, is balanced. i have seen that this has not been easy, given the particularly lively discussions which this question has generated during its examination by our committee. as mrs buitenweg has said, there is a real need to assess the effectiveness of existing conventions and also the appropriateness of reclassifying drugs. for example, article 3 of the single convention classifies more than 100 substances into four tables, the first of which groups opium, heroin, cocaine, cannabis and methadone under the same heading. is that really consistent? i put the question to mr pirker. it should also be said here that the buitenweg report is not in any way aimed at deciding the question of the decriminalisation of drugs, not even soft drugs, but only and exclusively raises two questions: the question of the effectiveness and relevance of the current system and the question of the need for a reclassification of products. however, reclassification of products does not in any way mean that cannabis is now being offered for sale or authorised. i challenge mr pirker to prove to the house that this is one of the proposals in mrs buitenweg's report. i would also remind you that the same body adopted the malliori report two months ago, which states that drugs should be classified on a scientific basis, according to the health risks they pose. mrs buitenweg, moreover, refers specifically to this document and i fully support her in this. will we continue to refer to conventions whose earliest date is 1961 and the most recent 1988? we feel that the time has come to evaluate these devices. i repeat that this report is balanced, that it mentions the risks of drug addiction extensively and in a very specific way and that it does not in any way encourage the use of narcotic drugs. on this point too, i challenge mr pirker and some of his colleagues from the epp to find paragraphs in which there is any encouragement to drug addiction. in no way is this report trying to minimize the risks and harm of drugs and, in my view, there is no point in breaking the balance which has been difficult but rightly found in mrs buitenweg's report. i therefore hope that we can achieve the widest possible support for this report, so that we can really advance our common desire to repair the damage caused by drug addiction.

- the next item is the report (a5-0086/2003) by mrs cerdeira morterero, on behalf of the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs, on the amended proposal for a council directive on the right to family reunification (com (2002) 225 - c5-0220/2002 - 1999/0258 (cns)).
- mr president, it is in a climate of security laws and the de facto criminalization of emigration that mrs cerdeirera morterero's report attempts to make positive corrections to the commission's original proposal. this is the case, for example, with the abolition of discrimination in matters of family reunification. but some of my colleagues are asking whether this is a fool's bargain, since the council already reached an agreement in february, which commissioner vitorino welcomed. so let me also express my doubts about the willingness to take account of the opinion of the european parliament. let me also express my deepest concern at the current trend in many eu countries towards tightening up their migration policies. it is clear, for example, why the french government has described this agreement as an important part of the policy of controlling migration flows. if there is to be approximation of national laws, is it on the basis of respect for the rights and protection of third country nationals, in the spirit of the tampere treaties, or will the transposition of this directive on the contrary be used by some as a pretext for a reduction in the level of protection already guaranteed by the member states? by increasing the conditions of access, for example, for children and the selection between applicants for skilled jobs and others, europe is becoming a fortress. this policy does not contribute in any way to the establishment of a european citizenship which gives life to the values of tolerance, democracy and solidarity in compliance with, in particular, the geneva convention and the universal declaration of human rights. on the contrary, immigrants should be able to move freely and receive a welcome that allows them to participate in local life and to enjoy a decent income, which is a real boon for the union. then we'd be far from the invaders' fantasy. the 2002 report of the oecd's permanent migration monitoring system restores the truth. in france, much to the chagrin of the minister of the interior, the total number of permanent arrivals in 2002 was 119 000, a figure lower than in 1998, the main reason for this migration remaining, in 77% of cases, family reunification. finally, like the human rights associations, i would like to condemn the actions which the danish presidency had in some way permitted in its action programme on returns of november 2002. i am talking about sending joint charters with the "undesirables" on board. it has taken mr sarkozy barely four months to get into france with this organization of forced returns, which is unworthy of our time and, above all, far from a humane and just immigration policy.
mr president, the european parliament is voting again today on the council's proposal on family reunification. in this context, it should be recalled that the council already defined a general approach on 27 february. while the right to family life is recognised by international conventions and enshrined in the charter of fundamental rights, it is regrettable to note that this approach of the council seriously calls into question this right for residents from third countries. taking into account the tampere summit which aimed to establish a common approach to ensure, in compliance with human rights instruments, the integration of third country nationals legally residing in the union, this new approach is a real downward revision. as some colleagues have said, it is true that this directive is better than nothing when one knows the difficulties encountered in achieving it. but we cannot help deploring its minimalist appearance, despite all the goodwill of our rapporteur, who is here sincerely thanked for his work. let me, however, make a few criticisms. why exclude persons with temporary or subsidiary protection status? excluded from the asylum system by this proposal, they become rightsless. they are also excluded from all directives relating to third country nationals. furthermore, why limit family reunification to only a legitimate spouse and dependent children under certain conditions? there is no justification for making the admission of minors over 12 years of age subject to the condition of integration, nor for excluding minors over 15 years of age. the definition of a child who is a third country national should be the same as that of another european child. a child is a child. regardless of nationality, he has the right to live with his parents. is this provision not contrary to the international commitments of the member states on the rights of the child? such inconsistencies are unjustified and unjustifiable. as regards the duration of the procedure, once the application for family reunification has been lodged, it must be possible for it to take effect within a reasonable period of time. a three-year wait for marriage is way too long. do you ask europeans to be married for three years before they live together ? the principle of the right to family life is simple. the right to family reunification should be automatic when a foreign national legally residing in a member state of the union holds a residence card valid for one year. in addition, this restrictive proposal risks making family life a torment, especially for women. the directive provides that the grant of a residence permit is limited to a period of one year, renewable under certain conditions. the duration of the document issued should be the same as that of the spouse. the five-year time limit for the granting of an autonomous residence permit to the spouse is far too long. the lack of legal autonomy often places women in total dependence on the husband, which is unacceptable in a europe which defends women's rights. furthermore, access to employment for family members is not a right from the moment of arrival, which forces one spouse to bear all the burdens and blocks any process of social integration of the other spouse. this proposal for a directive is based on a philosophy which is contrary to that adopted last year. not only does it contradict the discourse on integration advocated by many officials, but it also encourages young people of immigrant background to react violently to perceived injustice.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, once again i can only point out the important immigration drift which the text before us represents. the logic is always the same: to encourage immigration to europe more and more and to make the right to family reunification the driving force of this community policy. a month ago, the eu's justice and home affairs council reached a difficult consensus on the directive on family reunification. today the rapporteur proposes to amend this compromise, which she considers too restrictive, because it does not sufficiently promote the right to extended family reunification. indeed, what is being proposed here is to extend the notion of family member to unmarried partners, adult children, and ascendants if they have no other support. but who will judge the materiality of the fact that they have no other support? the simple homosexual association, for example, is here equated with the concept of family. however, it is stated that a long-term and stable relationship will be required. what a joke ! but the breach is open. it's for all the candidates. so, with one person entering, there'll be about fifteen others who can sit with her. we are not insensitive to the situation of separation that some immigrant families are experiencing. but if you want to avoid the resulting uprooting, why do you never consider, in these times of unemployment, the possible organization of family reunification in the countries of origin? and why should we not devote a part of our development credits to this, which all too often actually serve only to take money out of the pockets of the poor in rich countries and give it to the rich in poor countries. is that the real mission of family reunification? should it not rather be organised towards the country of origin of these migrants? more than ever, we denounce this settlement immigration, organized by the member states with the active complicity of the european institutions: the right of asylum for all, the abolition of border controls, the regularization of illegal immigrants, the development of white marriages... this has to stop. it is our duty to put an end to this suicidal policy of europe.
mr president, the report contains proposals which, if they were binding, could reduce the difficulties of family reunification somewhat. it is, however, insufficient and some of the amendments proposed are retrograde and we will reject them. the right to family reunification must be an absolute right. the main concern of the report seems to be to frame this right under the most diverse pretexts in order to avoid that it can facilitate so-called illegal immigration. this humanly despicable concern diminishes the significance of the few positive aspects of the text. the society is so unequal, there is so much poverty in the world, that more and more poor people are trying to escape from hunger and suffering in an attempt to find salvation in the countries of europe, which unfortunately, very often, they do not find. the national states and the european institutions can erect all the physical and legal barbed wire to prevent this movement: they will not prevent it. the coercive measures to reject those fleeing poverty only show the inhumanity of those who take these measures and support them.
- mr president, the proposal for a directive on family reunification has been coming back to the european parliament periodically since 1999, like a sea serpent. the reason for this back and forth is simple: at first the commission makes a lax proposal, the european parliament approves it and bids more, then the council - which seems to be the most responsible of the three - says no and the cycle begins again. this time the commission thinks it has found the unstoppable weapon. it takes a low profile on most of the provisions contested by the council as if it were giving in, but it introduces at the end of the text an article 19 which explains that all these points will be reviewed two years or less later. we see the tactic. the aim, at least initially, is to secure acceptance of a minimum european regulation on family reunification in order to secure recognition of the principle of european law and european intervention. in a second stage, the commission will use these points of reference to return to the charge, especially since article 19 already specifically identifies the provisions which will have to be amended. the council is in danger of passing over this text, with everyone saying - as is too often the case - 'for the time being we will save the main part and we will see what happens in two years' time for the rest. we believe that the council should not be drawn into this. family reunification is now a major source of immigration and it is important that each member state retains the capacity for close monitoring to adapt it to its reception capacities. there can be no question of the states being forced to accept an expansion of this right a priori, as the commission and the european parliament are dreaming of. we therefore believe that this directive would be unnecessary and dangerous for the states, especially since the convention on the future of europe expresses the will to pass all these matters to the qualified majority.

commission. - mr president, as has already been pointed out here, in the debate we are going to have on operational cooperation between member states on the repatriation of illegal residents, joint charter flights will be one of the measures to strengthen operational cooperation provided for in the action programme on repatriation, approved by the council in november 2002 on the basis of a commission communication. legally speaking, such joint charter flights now amount to two or more domestic long-haul operations carried out simultaneously on the same aircraft. these joint charter flights have nothing to do with collective expulsions, which are prohibited by the european convention on human rights and the charter of fundamental rights of the european union. the commission notes that the return of the third-country national concerned to the united kingdom is not subject to the conditions laid down in article 3 of the return directive. each case is assessed on an individual basis, depending on the personal circumstances and legal situation of each person. in other words, each person on board such a flight was subject to an individual procedure which led to an individual rejection of any applications or appeals for legal residence. thus, decisions are based on individual rather than collective motives. the commission has no indication or reason to believe, in the case referred to by mr krivine, that the particular circumstances of each person on that flight were the subject of a violation of any instrument of international law, that is to say, that the persons on that flight did not have their applications individually and effectively examined by the member states which took the expulsion measures.
- thank you for your explanation. i think the problem is very serious because since i asked that question, five joint flights - as you say - have left france. they were transporting groups of people of the same nationality leaving under the same conditions, often handcuffed, sometimes gagged, so much so that two immigrants were even suffocated to death. the government has even decided that these so-called joint flights will now have a red cross doctor on board to assist with the procedure. so my question is , how do you tell the difference between a joint flight and a group flight ? by definition, a group is an aggregate of individuals. when you have forty-two senegalese people together, who is going to determine the criteria to use to know whether they constitute a collective or a sum of individuals? i don't know of any collective that isn't a sum of individuals. but i have the weakness to believe that when you have 42 senegalese or 20 ivorian together - ivorian people who, i point out, are from a country where they risk death - it is about the same. so my question is this: who determines the semantic difference between joint and collective theft ? explain to me what a collective expulsion is, that is, prohibited.

commission. – mr president, concerning the german initiative, the commission stated in its communication, of 14 october 2002, on a common written policy on illegal residents, that there is a clear need for improvement of operational cooperation among member states. the return action programme of the council adopted on 28 november 2002, which is based on our communication, also calls for a comprehensive community return policy, which should be gradually developed, starting with some practical steps for operational cooperation as the matter in hand. in that framework, reference was also made to the german initiative for a council directive on assistance in cases of transit for the purpose of return by air, which i support, as you do. i congratulate mr kirkhope on his report. indeed, a common framework should be set for questions relating to transit during the return process. the commission has presented a proposal on burden-sharing of costs during the return operations. but often it is necessary to use airports of other member states, due to a lack of direct connections to the country of return. in such cases it is important that we establish a clear legal framework for the transit procedures, especially as far as the use and competences of escorts in transit is concerned. nevertheless a fully-fledged common return policy must additionally strive for medium-term legislative measures which will not only smoothen cooperation among member states, such as the binding mutual recognition of return decisions, but will also set certain common minimum standards on expulsion, detention and removal, to guarantee that all member states – not only the 15 but all 25 – abide by and respect human and fundamental rights standards. consequently the commission envisages presenting a proposal for a council directive on minimum standards for return procedures and mutual recognition of return decisions by the end of this year.

in writing. - (fr) we support the right of poland, as well as all the other candidate countries, to join the european union. but the conditions of poland's accession illustrate the inequalities in the treaty of accession. for example, poland is not entitled to the same agricultural aid as the countries of the present eu, despite the fact that farmers make up a large proportion of the population. but the european institutions prefer to subsidize their capitalist agriculture to make profits rather than help the poor peasants of the east to live off their labour. in addition, despite the legal juggling, polish workers have to wait seven years to enter the union and work. it is also inexcusable that the union, which is so unreliable in demanding sacrifices from the working classes in the country, is so ready to make concessions to the polish church. the eu not only accepts the ban on voluntary abortion, which restricts women's freedom, it also prohibits community legislation from amending polish legislation in this area in advance, thus leaving polish women to the whim of a highly reactionary church!
in writing. (fr) once again the vote on the timetable for the european parliament's 2004 sessions has been exploited by those opposed to strasbourg, who want to reduce the number of sessions of the parliament in that city. but once again, this vote is contrary to the treaty. the protocol on the location of the institutions stipulates that the 12 monthly sessions of the plenary session shall be held in strasbourg. traditionally, this number is reduced to 11 sessions in election years. however, the group against strasbourg went even further this time by providing for only 10 sessions. this is partly the result of the absurd action of the socialists, who wanted to cancel the last part-session in april because they did not want to work on 1 may. the paradox is even greater, since the approved timetable envisages the holding of five mini-session in brussels in 2004, which, however, should not theoretically be added to the timetable, unless the 12 normal sessions in strasbourg were overloaded. we call on the french government to take this illegal vote to the court of justice. the european parliament is not really a sovereign body. it has only the specific powers conferred on it by the treaty, which it must comply with.
in writing. - (fr) for our part, we are not going to appear in the european parliament on 1 may, given the special significance of this day as the international workers' day. as regards the rest of the calendar, we have no preferences or particular positions.
(parliament adopted the legislative resolution) the uen group, true to its political line, will oppose any attempt to reduce the duration and/or number of sessions in strasbourg. although in recent years various lobbies have multiplied their efforts to move the seat of the european parliament permanently from strasbourg to brussels - here we are thinking in particular of the reduction of the parliamentary session to four days and the higher number of extraordinary sessions in brussels - the uen group demands respect for the spirit and the letter of the treaties, which stipulate that 12 annual sessions are to be held in strasbourg. it is true that a strasbourg session is usually cancelled during an election year. at the same time, however, it is surprising to note that the number of extraordinary meetings remains unchanged. this is an unusual situation and i have therefore proposed that two extraordinary sessions be cancelled for 2004 in order to reinstate the 12th strasbourg session in accordance with the law in force. i am sure you will understand that this step requires all of us to live up to our responsibilities. for us, it's as simple as that. strasbourg should not be reduced to a mere annex of brussels. strasbourg is and must remain the seat of the european parliament.
in the case of the european parliament, the european council has already decided to hold a debate on the future of the european union. but the treaties and the case law of the court of justice of the european communities on this matter clearly state that the european parliament's calendar must include 12 sessions in strasbourg each year, or 11 in election years, before the decision is taken to add extra mini-sessions in brussels. the calendar adopted for the 2004 election year does not include a strasbourg session, let alone the absurdity of a vote cancelling the strasbourg session originally scheduled to receive the elected members of the new member states of the european union on the same day as the european parliament gives its assent to the accession treaties of these states. in view of the alleged illegality of the european parliament's vote, the french delegation to the ppe-de group demands that the president, mr pat cox, immediately draw the consequences and annul the vote. it called for an emergency meeting of the conference of presidents to be convened to arrange a new vote as soon as possible, in accordance with community law.
in the case of the united kingdom, the commission has already taken the initiative in the form of a proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to carcinogens. the amendments in particular extend the definition of family members eligible for family reunification, speed up the individual's possibility of seeking family reunification and limit the member states' possibilities of refusal. in any case, the commission's original proposal was already very bad in our view, both in its principles and in its provisions. this vote was intended to send a clear signal to the council. although it is not obliged to adopt the amendments of the european parliament (the latter having been consulted only on this matter), the council must nevertheless make it clear that if it endorses the principle of regulation of family reunification at european level, it is moving into a dubious direction. it is obvious that the commission and its allies will continue to push for the council's alleged right to be increased tomorrow. the commission lacks a true understanding of what is in europe's best interests.
in writing. - (fr) we are of course against polygamy and the oppression it entails for women. we cannot accept, however, that the fact that one of the spouses is already living in a host country should be used as a pretext to prohibit the other spouses from entering and staying in that country. behind a moralising exterior, the only thing that is at stake is to create yet another barrier to immigration by breaking personal bonds. although we reject the principle of such a restriction, we voted for the amendment which at least provides for some exceptions where 'the best interests of a minor child so require'. we have also rejected the bullying amendments, such as the use of dna tests against immigrants or the public health argument, which is based on the selfish view that we must refuse to provide the treatment that european countries are able to offer to the populations who do not have access to it. and again, the proposals which represent progress are not binding and instead of approximating national legislation by the best common denominator, the proposals as a whole approximate legislation by the lowest common denominator.

mr president, i would like to say that i am very pleased that the commission has taken the initiative to present this report to the house. the aim was to update the previous report by our colleague catherine lalumière, an update made necessary by the events of september 2001 and by the contribution we wanted to make to the work of our colleagues in the convention. the fact is that it is difficult to assess any european security and defence architecture today, at a time when there is every reason to fear that it has, at least temporarily, been torn apart. my colleagues in the committee on foreign affairs took a different view when they adopted the report on 25 march, in the midst of the crisis, which will be put to the vote in plenary tomorrow. i see at least three reasons. the first is the exercise of a duty of responsibility towards our constituents. the second is the awareness that the present crisis must serve as a lesson on the eve of enlargement. the third and final reason is our desire to clarify the policy of transatlantic cooperation, a policy which we believe the member states are determined to continue to pursue and on which many of us hope that the current differences are much more apparent than real. first, responsibility to our constituents. all the eurobarometers we have been aware of have for years shown that a majority of over two thirds of european citizens are in favour of a common security and defence policy. it was only natural that our colleagues in the committee on foreign affairs should have been similarly sensitive to this call. this is what happened in the vote in committee at the end of a very rich debate which involved the examination of almost 200 amendments. in any event, the application of the new rules of procedure could have allowed a simple vote in plenary, but we agreed that the importance of the subject justified this debate in which we wished to involve the council and the commission. we were very keen, and this will be my second point, to draw the lessons of the present crisis without further delay. europe has not been able to speak with one voice in the un security council, as the mere application of the maastricht treaty required. is this not proof, mr president-in-office of the council, that the time has come to change our institutions to avoid in future the disorder and cacophony which have gradually, and i hope temporarily, become established in the concert of the member states? we know that the citizens themselves, as i have already said, but perhaps even more so the whole world, are waiting for it to take its place in the construction of a multipolar world, so that the fate of the planet does not continue to rest solely on the shoulders of the american president. i would like to make a third point, the most important. is europe prepared to take on the responsibility that is expected of it? i'm not so sure. the choice for her is clearer now than ever. or, as in the cold war, the member states continue to entrust the care of their defence solely to the armed forces of the united states. in that case, they cannot claim to lecture the american people on the use that washington might decide to make of them. or they are finally accepting what the american people have always demanded of them, namely, burden sharing, which obviously requires a greater contribution to a common effort. the secretary-general of the atlantic alliance, lord robertson, denounced the other day in your presence, commissioner patten, the gap between the ambitions of european governments and the means they are willing to devote to their achievement, what he called the 'gap of ambition'. i hope that the current crisis will make them aware of this and decide to start bridging this gap. council mr president, commissioner, members of the european parliament, the recent crisis in iraq has made quite clear europe's backwardness, particularly in foreign and defence policy. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. the crisis can also have a constructive effect on european policies, and in this respect i think that the morillon report comes at a good time, even if it was not visible when it began. the breakdown of the traditional power dichotomy today requires new strategies and security measures. in this context, the proliferation of weapons of mass destruction is not the only source of crises. the european union is not only a threat to the world's security and stability. widespread poverty, organised crime, state violence, deep economic crises can also have negative impacts on global stability and security, such as military or terrorist actions. we must certainly consider whether we are developing the appropriate policies for all these risks and at what time. in parallel with whatever response we choose, we consider it absolutely necessary to base global security on mutual trust, cooperation, consensus through international organizations, alliances, networks. the way we deal with threats to global security will also determine our future in building peace and ensuring a healthy economic environment, with credible answers to global political, economic, and even environmental problems. the european council has already made a number of recommendations on the basis of the conclusions of the european council in brussels, and the council has also made a number of recommendations on the basis of the conclusions of the european council in strasbourg. both the morillon report and other related initiatives, such as the ideas expressed in the morillon report relate to initiatives which have already been launched and are under consideration in the relevant institutions of the union. i will start by addressing the contemporary threats to security, stability, peace, which have taken very different forms from the known threats of the past. the truth is that the esdp mechanism was not designed from the outset to deal with horizontal and asymmetric threats, such as terrorism or the proliferation of weapons of mass destruction. the commission has also proposed that the european parliament and the council should be consulted on the future of the european union's external borders. in this context, two specific objectives have been set as a first step: the use of union military forces to protect the civilian population from terrorist attacks on the one hand, and union military forces deployed in crisis areas on the other. the further development and improvement of military capabilities is undoubtedly a key element of the security and later defence of the union. we attach particular importance to this issue and, as part of the continuation of efforts so far, a capability conference is to be convened to assess and record the progress made in implementing the related action plan, the ecap, and to chart the way forward. the presidency has drawn up a text with guidelines for the practice after the completion of the work of the relevant working groups, the ecap panels. we hope that these initiatives will give new impetus to improving our operational capability in the military sector and, by extension, help to strengthen the basis for the evolution of the esdp. in this connection, the development of the rapid reaction capability is of particular importance and for this reason this issue has been included in the main priorities in the field of the military aspect of the esdp already by the spanish presidency. the operational framework governing the establishment and operation of the rapid reaction units is under consideration in the relevant political and military bodies and we are making every effort to complete it by the end of the greek presidency. it is clear that the strengthening of the union's military capabilities will not be possible without broadening and deepening our cooperation in the field of armaments. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. the decision of the european council, which we took in brussels, had two parts: first, to instruct the council to examine the role of defence research and development in the wider context of the union's defence capabilities and, secondly, to consider the possibility of creating a european armaments agency, an intergovernmental european agency. both these issues are very important steps towards strengthening cooperation in the field of defence. defence research can also be combined with the union's competitiveness policies, fuelling and developing multiple sectors towards stronger growth. the same approach is being taken to develop a comprehensive space policy for the union, which will also apply to security, something which is also mentioned in the morillon report. the developments of the last decade have made it clear that, as many risks are common, so our response must be coordinated their economic and social cohesion. the idea of a civilian peace corps, as mentioned in the morillon report, is a very good one and will help to raise the awareness of the average european citizen about what is happening in the field of security and how we are dealing with it in practice and participating in it. we are seriously considering this idea and it is very likely that the presidency will put forward a text of guidelines. the union's relationship with nato is undoubtedly a component of european security. the european option in dealing with crises is, in any case, to appeal first to the will and action of regional and international organizations, that is, to give priority to dialogue. the recent cooperation agreement between the union and nato is an important step towards the complementarity and mutual reinforcement of the two organisations. i would like to take this opportunity to emphasize the point made in the morillon report that the action of both organizations and in the report, although many of them are very interesting. the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos at work is a very good commission. – mr president, i should first of all like to congratulate general morillon most cordially on a very comprehensive – and certainly timely – contribution to the debate on the development of european security and defence policy. the timeliness was rightly referred to both by my honourable friend and by the minister in the presidency. the number of amendments that the committee considered before adopting this resolution is, in many respects, a testament to the depth of interest, but also frankly to the differences of view, on this key area of european policy. in responding today i must keep in mind the current responsibilities of the commission in security and defence issues. i shall certainly keep them in mind and if i do not mr van orden will remind me of what they are. whatever is recommended in future by the convention, where my colleague, commissioner barnier, has ably led the discussions on defence issues – and i know that he has briefed the committee on foreign affairs, human rights, common security and defence policy in the course of the deliberations on this report – those commission responsibilities are at the moment pretty limited when compared to the range of issues covered in the text before us. the commission is not involved in the purely military aspects of european security and defence policy. that is exclusively for the member states. i shall not therefore comment on the specifically military proposals, including the establishment of a permanent standing military force, a collective defence clause or a joint military college. but the treaty does associate the commission with esdp – article 27 does that in terms – and we are actively involved in all discussions on crisis management operations in the context of esdp, in particular in those that relate to the civilian crisis management instruments, for example policing, the rule of law, civilian administration and civil protection. in this context i am pleased to see that the resolution before us recognises the importance of civilian, as well as military, contributions to crisis management. but it is impossible – this is a point i have made on many occasions in this chamber – to separate purely military matters from related issues in which we in the commission are competent, and have a real contribution to make. military and non-military issues cannot be placed neatly in separate boxes. nor should they be, because they need to be closely coordinated in the service of a single strategy. the commission, for example, may be bankrolling police support in post-conflict situations as in bosnia and herzegovina, where on 1 january the european union took over the police mission from the united nations; or we may be arranging for the training of border services where uncontrolled mass migration is generating conflict; or we may be helping to re-establish administrative structures in countries that are emerging from crises, as we have seen in the balkans and as we can see in afghanistan today. the commission already has an impressive range of instruments and expertise which can be used in crisis situations. new european union instruments may be necessary in the security field, as has been suggested by general morillon. but the most important requirement is that all available instruments should serve agreed european policy objectives in any given situation. current events, i have to say, show that this is far from being the case. another area where the commission has an important role to play relates to defence equipment policy. in my view, defence trade and production cannot and should not be treated as a chasse gardée within the single market. procurement of defence equipment, competition between defence companies, research and development, exports and imports of defence equipment, internal market aspects of defence trade and dual-use goods which have civil and military applications – all these are areas in which the benefits of the single market are of relevance to european industry. there is considerable scope for improvement here. the commission recently adopted a communication to the council and parliament on the defence equipment industry in which it points to some areas where substantial progress is possible in giving european union taxpayers more value for the money they invest in their security. the concerns on duplication and fragmentation in arms production and procurement and the lack of interoperability – identified in the resolution before us – are some of the key issues that we sought to address in our communication. we hope that the work we are initiating as a follow-up to the communication will help to develop the strong and competitive defence industry, transparent market conditions and healthy climate for investments in research and development necessary for the strengthening of esdp. ultimately, much of the credibility of europe's common foreign and security policy depends on the european union's military capacity. the creation of the 60 000-strong 'rapid reaction force' being set up under esdp will certainly help to increase the european union's credibility abroad. and the launch of the first ever european union military operation in the former yugoslav republic of macedonia last month shows that esdp is not just a theoretical construct. but i fully agree with my honourable friend general morillon that it remains difficult for our allies to take europe seriously unless we spend more on our security. it is not enough to argue that europe is picking up its share of the bill by paying most of the world's development aid, true as this may be, or by increasing even further our humanitarian assistance. we also need to invest more in developing our capabilities such as airlift capacity, special forces and battlefield communication equipment. if not, our allies will remain of the opinion that europe cashed in too easily its peace dividend after the fall of the berlin wall. delivery of aid should remain the prime task of the humanitarian organisations to ensure neutrality, independence and impartiality of such humanitarian operations. respect for these principles is paramount for meeting humanitarian needs whenever there is a crisis. the commission therefore welcomes the reference in the report to the guidelines on the use of military and civil defence assets to support united nations humanitarian activities in complex emergencies which were released by the un on 20 march 2003. they fix clear rules regarding the relationship between military and humanitarian actors in un humanitarian operations. the thrust of the guidelines should apply equally to the use of european military and civil defence assets in any humanitarian operation. i would like to say one final word about international humanitarian law, which governs the conduct of hostilities. we believe that international humanitarian law is adapted to today's conflicts, provided that warring parties and all parties to the geneva conventions respect their obligations. i would at this stage express the commission's appreciation of the role of the international committee of the red cross as promoter and guardian of the conventions. finally, i would like to say once again to my honourable friend that this report is almost painfully timely. it raises a number of issues which will go right to the heart of our credibility in europe as we seek to make a greater contribution to international affairs in the years ahead; but, as i have said on previous occasions in this chamber, there comes a moment in politics where one is obliged to put one's money where one's mouth is. we have long since passed that stage when we are talking about security issues.
