- mr president, mr president-in-office of the council, mr commissioner, two years after the report i had the honour of presenting to parliament on the same subject, i am pleased to give my full support to mr morillon's text. after the adoption, as i hope, of a few amendments tabled by our group, we should have no difficulty in voting on the motion for a resolution. i shall therefore limit myself to emphasizing certain points which seem to me particularly important in the context of the very eventful spring of 2003. this is not a good context for the new european security and defence policy, the esdp. since 11 september 2001, we have seen the european union largely sidelined politically and militarily, whether it be in afghanistan or iraq, or the israeli-palestinian conflict. our presence is not non-existent, but limited to civilian and humanitarian actions. it's important, but it's not enough. worse, during this period the union became disunited. despite the praiseworthy efforts of the greek presidency to secure the adoption of common platforms, iraq has divided us: first, on the nature of our transatlantic relations and on our degree of autonomy vis-à-vis the united states; secondly and consequently, on major principles such as the use of force, the place of international law or the role of the united nations. but despite this dismal picture, i would like to say loud and clear that we must not give up. several countries, belgium, germany, france and luxembourg, have already taken the initiative of reviving their security and defence policy. greece, which holds the presidency of the union, is in favour of this. prime minister simitis recently said so. i hope that the convention, together with president giscard d'estaing, will also make proposals after a few weeks of silence and hesitation on this subject. excellent ideas concerning the institutions of foreign and security policy and defence policy have already been expressed by mr dehaene and mr barnier; - mr president, it's always the same. when the european chimeras are shot down in the middle of the flight by reality, our 'europeanist' dreamers launch others, even more absurd, in a kind of forward flight that would be laughable if it were not so serious. with the morillon report, the chimera of today is european defence, which is an old moon. it has already made many simple minds dream throughout the 20th century, with no results whatsoever. already aristide briand was agitating the idea, with the dramatic result of disarming the resistance and the spirit of defense in france. the chimera was revived in 1948 at the hague congress, and then by a certain winston churchill in 1950 with the ced, which was born of his daydreams and which failed. we must also pay tribute to the french parliament for having succeeded in putting an end to it. fifty years later, we are still at the same point, that is, we have not made any progress. we have made so little progress that the essential element of a common defence policy, which would be the creation of a european defence industry, is not only not moving forward but is actually going backwards, since, it should be remembered, most of the weapons europeans buy are not bought from one another: about 60% are bought from the united states. we should start there if we are to talk about defence policy. but, finally, this defence policy is a chimera, because you cannot have a defence policy without a common foreign policy. this was confirmed by the maastricht treaty in title v in 1992, but it has never been implemented in any crisis - rwanda, afghanistan, kosovo. we couldn't do it, because we were united in the american follow-up. and today, the common foreign and security policy is again on the rise. no, ladies and gentlemen, let's not get carried away. europe must be based on reality. the realities, as we see today more than ever, are the states, and the states must not allow themselves to be deprived of what constitutes them: a spirit of defence, an instrument of defence. i shall confine myself to wishing that france, whose global responsibilities are constantly growing, might strengthen its own defence instruments. it is also its only contribution, its best contribution to what remains of europe.

- madam president, between the time when the morillon report was drawn up and today, major international developments have taken place which mean that the defence of europe can no longer be dealt with in a comprehensive and uniform manner. it is no longer possible to pretend that we are still defining a common defence policy, which is intended to implement a common foreign and security policy for all the member states. the clashes in the security council over key issues and the outbreak of another war after the kosovo war, this time against iraq, in violation of the provisions of the san francisco charter, have been a powerful indication of the deep divisions that divide the current and future member states of the european union in matters of foreign policy. two conceptions of europe and its role, two types of foreign policy, two visions of the international order have emerged with great clarity. we must take note of this and we would be wrong to see it at all costs as a circumstantial crisis which, once it has passed, would allow us to return to the old concepts and to resume the essentially semantic games we love about the cfsp and esdp. from now on, all matters relating to foreign affairs and defence at the level of the union can only be considered in terms of variable geometry. this approach has become a must from being optional. it's now the mandatory crossing point. a variable geometry which will also lead to more efficiency and less verbalization. the convention should now use its talents in this direction. it is therefore necessary to distinguish between the proposals in the morillon report, which have been rendered totally obsolete by recent developments, and those which remain relevant. under the first heading i would include paragraph 54 proposing that the european union be granted a permanent seat on the security council. this proposal is clearly contrary to the present needs of europe, which must continue to have two permanent seats to express the two different conceptions, the two main ways in which the european countries are divided. under the second heading, i would like to mention the proposals concerning the essential cooperation to be developed in the first place in the fight against terrorism, which the consequences of the war in iraq will make even more imperative, and secondly in the production and purchase of arms. the current events also provide a powerful indication of the damage that the peace dividend ideology has caused in europe. i therefore welcome the timely reappearance of the concept of community preference in the morillon report, but i am simply sorry that it coincides with its disappearance in another area, which is also strategic, that of the cap, namely food independence or, to use american terminology, food weapons. the security of supply, i quote from the morillon report, must apply to food as well as to arms. we must ensure that commissioner lamy remembers this in the - madam president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, as a member of the gue-ngl, i of course share many of the concerns of the majority of my group, and in particular, like them, i ask myself the same question: how is it possible to make progress in the field of defence without first defining a common foreign policy? i would add that i too am firmly opposed to the very principle of a pre-emptive war such as the one currently being waged in iraq, and i regret the disagreements between european countries on this major issue. however, i think and say that if we do not want to strengthen the monopoly of nato, an organization which we know is dominated by the united states of america, and if we want to be able to resolve conflicts through effective and strong european diplomacy, we must give ourselves the means of a europe of defence. we need a defence europe with clear objectives and principles, with specific missions, with the right capabilities and weapons and with a legitimate decision-making process that is democratically controlled. i believe that conflicts all over the world should be settled through diplomatic means, especially within the framework of the united nations. but to be able to weigh diplomatically and therefore to solve problems through diplomacy, we must have a real military capacity and i am one of those who believe that europe has no right to deprive itself of it. in short, if europe is no longer willing to leave its future in the hands of the leaders of the united states of america, it must give itself the means to do so and the europe of defence must finally be put into practice.

- mr president, commissioner, rapporteur, ladies and gentlemen, we are aware of the development of treatments based on the use of tissues and cells of human origin. they number in the hundreds of thousands each year. it was therefore urgent for the european commission to propose a draft directive to develop new quality and safety standards to increase public confidence in the use of these tissues and cells for use in and on the human body. i therefore wholeheartedly approve and support the approach of the european commission. unfortunately, as has already been said tonight, there are too many amendments which go in all directions, which risk distorting the original draft and thus depriving us of a regulation which is necessary and urgent. that is why, in the debate this evening, on behalf of the gue/ngl, i want to recall the three fundamental principles which lead me to oppose many of the amendments. first principle: a draft directive, the necessity of which is not denied by anyone, should not be used to extend its scope to sectors which will have to have specific regulations or which already have them. and above all, we must not use this project to open up a debate on stem cells, embryonic stem cells, surplus stem cells, research in this field or even on ivf. many of the amendments which we shall not be voting on have these objectives more or less disguised in good intentions. secondly, research and science must be governed by ethical rules to avoid irresponsible and dangerous approaches to the human race, but they must not be hindered by religious prohibitions, wherever they may come from. it's a basic rule of secularism. it is a necessary condition for ensuring progress. and here too there is no shortage of amendments to be rejected in the name of this principle. third principle: the human body should not be sold, bought or stolen. we should all at least agree on this point and agree that this principle implies, firstly, a really explicit voluntary giving of the gift by the donor and, secondly, the explicit protection of the anonymity of the donor and the recipient; the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the rules are applied. however, this does not prevent traceability, which guarantees control of the quality of transplants. and thirdly, the free gift should not be discussed: the body is not a commodity. in conclusion, i would like to reiterate that the development of these therapeutic treatments is such that a european directive is necessary. however, this development also requires, at the same time, that the european parliament, that is to say ourselves, be rigorous and respect the great principles that so many of us have in common and that we cannot accept to be called into question, even insidiously.
- mr president, we welcome many of the points in mr liese's report. we particularly support the amendments which seek to exclude from the scope of this directive tissues and cells derived from human embryos or from genetic engineering, since no european legislation defines the use of gene therapy. however, we have a problem with a compromise: voluntary and unpaid donation of human tissues and cells. we want to make sure that these donations are free. to this end, it is necessary to define precisely in this directive the legitimate and acceptable compensation, namely, for us, the reimbursement of travel expenses and income not received during the journey, the donation and rest that may be necessary, as well as refreshments and other gratuities of this type, but no more. otherwise we leave the door open to compensation, or even remuneration, for these donations, with all the foreseeable deviations in terms of quality and safety, and the risks they pose to the donors and the recipients. as has been said before, the body is not a commodity. our cells and tissues are not for sale. another fundamental principle of this directive concerns anonymity, which must be compatible with the traceability of tissues and cells. the european commission's proposal, supplemented by amendments from the committee on the environment, succeeds in taking both these principles into account. the plenary session of this parliament must not upset this delicate balance by adopting amendments to lift the anonymity of gamete donors and thus, in effect, sperm donors, or to make the tissue and cell distribution files available to the public, and i quote an amendment. the transparency argument is not a good one in this case. the need to trace the tissues and cells intended for transplantation from the donor to the recipient should not be at the expense of anonymity. this would open the door to ethical, eugenic, even racial deviations. finally, we ask the commission, which has not wished to include organs in the scope of this directive, to propose urgently a specific text for the establishment of quality and safety standards for organs. i think that this report is balanced. we must continue to work towards this, including in the next readings.
- mr president, commissioner, i would like to thank the rapporteur, mr peter liese, for his excellent work of information and analysis in cooperation with all his colleagues and with experts of a very high level. cell therapy and tissue transplantation are promising avenues for treating incurable diseases that leave so many people in pain and anxiety. however, mastery of this technique is not enough to meet the expectations of the sick. this is the whole point of this proposal for a directive, the aim of which is to ensure a regulatory framework for safety and quality for human tissues and cells. as regards voluntary and unpaid donation and the anonymity of the donor, the directive cannot impose obligations on the member states under the european treaty, but only recommendations. the gift must be free. who would ever think of trading human products? saving a life is a free and selfless act. donations must also be voluntary and therefore require the written and informed consent of the living donor. it is therefore essential to inform our societies about the appropriateness of these treatments and about the responsibilities of each one in a spirit of solidarity, since it is a question of improving the health of thousands of human beings. the population in our countries is not sufficiently aware of the benefits of donating human tissues and cells. how many lives saved, how many patients cured by bone marrow transplants? the directive must be accompanied by much more detailed information. this information must be more reliable and based on genuine scientific work. for example, how many times have we heard that embryonic stem cells are going to cure incurable diseases, when to date, we have found no literature to prove it? and it would be wrong to say that banning the use of embryonic cells would prevent the saving of lives. there are other alternatives, particularly the adult stem cell technique. this observation raises the question of which cells are concerned by the proposed directive. i agree with the french government on three points. in view of article 152 (4) of the treaty, it is not for us to regulate, through this directive, the use of a particular type of cell, such as germ or embryonic cells. this is a matter for the states. similarly, ethical questions concerning embryos are a matter for national competence. finally, gametes are excluded from the scope of the directive. i shall vote in favour of this report, but i shall be very careful to respect the dignity of both the giver and the receiver.

commission. – may i begin by thanking the committee on agriculture and rural development, and in particular its rapporteur, mrs auroi, for the positive approach adopted towards the commission proposal. this proposal consists of only one amendment added to the last item of the relevant article of ten directives on the marketing of seeds and propagating material. the aim of the proposal is simple – to create a clear legal basis for financing community comparative trials. this initiative is in line with the european parliament proposal to increase the transparency of the commission budget.
the commission has already taken steps to ensure that the community's seed industry is able to compete with the other major producers of seed. as it has stated for the past 25 years, agricultural plants such as cereals, fodder plants, oilseeds and fibre plants have been subjected to community comparative testing on the basis of the applicable legislation. in recent years, this exercise has gained in importance as a result of new legislation on the marketing of fruit, vegetable and ornamental plant propagating material, which lays down, inter alia, the rules for community comparative testing. this system of ex post control, applied to seed and propagating material marketed in the community, is recognised as a very important instrument for harmonising marketing by the member states. however, the improvement thus envisaged will be neither complete nor relevant if the comparative tests financed by the european union are limited to the varieties of seeds and plants currently certified and found in the common catalogue of the union. the commission proposal must take account of the recently adopted legislation on processed products concerning the accidental or technically unavoidable presence of genetically modified seeds in seeds of conventional varieties. moreover, it seems to me that in order to really update these guidelines, three objectives must be achieved. firstly, the proposal must cover all existing seeds, so that there is a complete panel which takes account, alongside traditional seeds, of the specificities of biodiversity and the effects of the introduction of biotechnologies through gmos. secondly, it must bring within the scope of the directive the so-called 'amateur' varieties covered by directive 98/95, which is still not taken into account by all the member states. thirdly, in the interests of democracy, it must allow parliament to be an actor from the beginning to the end of the decision-making process. in this sense, the sensitive issue of the risks of contamination of traditional seeds by gmos must be taken up in the series of directives on the marketing of seeds which we are discussing today. this question cannot be dealt with in committee, because that would exclude members from the debate and proposals on this subject. so, to return to my first point, comparative trials financed by the european union should not be limited to the listed species. preservation varieties and organic seeds should also be able to benefit from these tests. they must be tested in a framework corresponding to these agricultural techniques and therefore more funding is needed. it should be noted that these seeds may not be coated and must be free from any trace of gmos. similar tests are required for plants at risk of contamination by gmos. the present proposal for a directive provides an opportunity to settle questions concerning the proven presence of genetically modified seeds in conventional seeds. the commission has been working for some time on a directive which is to legislate on the additional conditions and requirements concerning the presence of genetically modified seeds in seed lots, planting sites, and the details of the marking of such seeds. unfortunately, the draft of the latest directive does not take sufficient account of directive 2001/18, which has since come into force, on the deliberate release of genetically modified organisms into the environment. to return to point 2, it is important that the species and varieties for conservation mentioned in directive 98/95 be defined and tested for marketing according to specific criteria, which requires an implementing regulation still awaited to date. similarly, farm seed or seed of local origin should be given special flexibility and should be the subject of specific contracts linked to the latter directive. it is my third point that is at the heart of the democratic debate. it is important, as i have tried to do, to reject the reference to precise traceability in the amended articles. it is therefore important to say, seed by seed, that if there are accidental or technically unavoidable traces of gmos in these seeds, a minimum threshold can be set below which they can nevertheless be placed on the market. the value of this threshold shall be established in accordance with article 21 and set at the lowest level possible in the light of the state of the art of scientific knowledge. appropriate measures must therefore be taken during transport and storage of traditional seeds to prove the accidental or technically unavoidable nature of possible contamination by gmos. the directive already provides for the labelling of genetically modified seeds, but it does not address the problem of the risk of traces in traditional seeds, since the rule is that these seeds should not, in principle, contain gmos. this rule is of great importance to agriculture, as the spread of contaminated seeds can have unpredictable economic consequences for both farmers and food producers. finally, the directive already provides that the community may make a financial contribution to the tests provided for in paragraphs 1 and 2. the same treatment should be possible for the specific comparative tests required for seeds and plants produced and grown for organic farming and for the use and conservation of genetic diversity in plants. for the sake of transparency, it is therefore necessary to establish a clear legal basis for any future financial contribution and it is therefore appropriate to provide for community financial measures applicable to such benchmarking which include the necessary mandatory community budgetary expenditure.
the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. i would first like to thank my colleagues and the secretariat of the committee on the environment, public health and consumer protection and the officials of the directorate-general responsible for their very good cooperation. as the commissioner has just said, the european parliament is now required to give its opinion on the second amendment to the sweeteners directive since its adoption in 1994. the competent directorate-general therefore proposes to add two new sweeteners, sucralose and aspartame-acesulfame salt, to the positive list of sweeteners already authorised in the european union. this proposal follows the favourable opinion given in 2000 on these two sweeteners by the scientific committee for food. in the context of this second revision of the sweeteners directive, the european commission has also proposed to revise the use of a third sweetener, cyclamic acid. following a re-evaluation of the scientific committee, it proposes to reduce the thresholds for cyclamates in certain foods and beverages. studies, particularly in denmark, have shown that a child weighing 15 kg or less can very quickly reach the acceptable daily intake (adi) threshold, which can be hazardous to his health. new studies in progress in several member - the next item is the report (a5-0105/2003) by mr nobilia, on behalf of the committee on the environment, public health and consumer protection, on the proposal for a european parliament and council regulation on detergents (com (2002) 485 - c5-0404/2002 - 2002/0216 (cod)).
- commissioner, this proposal for a regulation, which is designed to simplify legislation, is entirely in line with the framework of sustainable development, simply because it is an environmental issue, a question which may also be a matter of public health and consumer policy. this illustrates the links between these three areas of competence. but it is also a question of the internal market, and here we see - as my colleague, karl-heinz florenz, has described it well - again all the economic consequences of such decisions. this is therefore an environmental problem, since pressure should be put on the various actors concerned to significantly reduce the use of detergents, which, when excessive, has adverse consequences on water. it is also a public health issue. in fact, are the consequences on human health of water pollution caused by the discharge of washing water containing detergents really being measured? we all want to reduce significantly the quantities used and the toxicity of the various components of detergents. however, ambitious but achievable targets should be set. and here again we are dealing with a matter of consumer policy, since it is up to the consumers, that is to say each one of us, to rationalize the use we make of detergents. this is achieved by simple measures to reduce the quantities used and to use products more efficiently. the consumer must be better informed about the use of the product and the conditions of use and must be aware of the important responsibility which he has in this area. efforts have already been made by companies in this sector, through codes of good practice or the organisation of information and public awareness campaigns. but these measures are probably still insufficient in view of the environmental issues involved and the current results. i therefore support the rapporteur, mr nobilia, who is already going further than the commission. while we are aware of the need to respect, of course, industrial secrecy - we sometimes touch on a sensitive area - we are asking for more information. we ask that the best information be given without delay to the medical staff who may themselves be called upon to answer and make decisions in this area. of course, i would remind you that medical staff are also bound by professional secrecy. it is essential to continue research in this area to find substances which are equally effective in terms of hygiene but less harmful to the environment. the aim is to find products which are more biodegradable. as regards more specifically the question of animal testing - we have already spoken sufficiently about this in this house and, among other things, when we had to decide on the cosmetics issue - the use of in vitro test methods and other alternative methods should be encouraged as far as possible. of course, the various measures must be closely linked to european legislation, including the legislation we are preparing in the field of chemicals, in order to adopt coherent policies.
- madam president, i should like to congratulate the rapporteur on the quality of his work and on his willingness to reinstate article 174 of the treaty on environmental policy in the text of the regulation. a regulation, particularly in this area, must not be limited to ensuring the free movement of detergents in the internal market. in short, article 95 of the treaty must not take precedence over the prudent and rational use of natural resources. that would be looking at things through the lens of the prism. the new regulation has many positive effects. i will mention only two. improving labelling to ensure that consumers receive the most accurate information possible through clear and legible labels. the restriction of the use of dangerous substances called surfactants, harmful to the environment because they are very little biodegradable and dangerous in terms of public health for those who handle these detergents on a daily basis. i am thinking in particular of substances known to be carcinogenic, mutagenic or toxic. the report also raises the question of the prohibition of animal testing. my position on the subject has not changed. i am in favour of their being abandoned, provided, of course, that safe alternative tests are available, particularly for metabolites. we should not repeat the mistake of the revision of the cosmetics directive, which banned them without ensuring that there were reliable alternatives. as for the derogations, member states must control only the marketing authorizations. i agree with the rapporteur's approach on this point. the commission has also taken care not to harm small and medium-sized enterprises (smes) in a detergent market dominated by four or five heavyweights, for whom the new regulation will not pose any particular problem. on the other hand, smes producing detergents to be manufactured in small quantities, so-called products of the industrial and commercial sector, operate in marginal segments. these companies will have a very hard time getting up to speed.
commission. – mr president, i have listened with great interest to the debate and taken note of the different concerns expressed. perhaps i could group the questions around six groups of amendments on which i can comment one by one. firstly, a number of the amendments seek to improve the wording of the commission's text and can be accepted. i will enumerate them later. secondly, a number of amendments have a link to other legislation. as regards animal testing, the aims of the commission and the parliament are the same. it is on how such aims are to be reflected in the legislation that we differ. the commission cannot accept amendments that introduce policy statements that go beyond the scope of this proposal. many substances and preparations are already adequately regulated by the horizontal chemicals legislation. it is unnecessary and undesirable to refer to them again in the detergents legislation. thirdly, there seems to be a desire to bring forward measures on phosphates, anaerobic biodegradability and organic ingredients other than surfactants. the commission is of the opinion that these are matters where the urgency for action is not so great as to preclude the establishment of a firm scientific base for legislation. the extension of biodegradability testing to all substances and preparations at this stage would be a disproportionate and unjustifiable measure. i will come back to phosphates later. fourthly, on labelling – detergents legislation is supplementary to the horizontal chemicals legislation and must therefore be compatible with it. cosmetics and detergents need to be, and are, separately legislated for. the comparison between a washing-up liquid, which is a detergent, and a chemically similar shampoo, a cosmetic, is a tempting one to make, but it is an exceptional case. no surfactant in an industrial detergent would ever be used in a cosmetic and no cosmetic surfactant would be of any use in a laundry detergent, let alone in an industrial detergent. the purpose of the ingredients data sheet is to provide information to those who need it, e.g. doctors who treat patients suffering from allergies. manufacturers have a legitimate interest in ensuring that confidentiality is maintained. member states also have the right to request ingredient information from manufacturers for use by their poison centres. fifthly, on derogations. the introduction of a lifetime limit for manufacturers for submitting the additional data requested by the member states is a good idea. according to our legal experts the criteria for refusing derogations must be explicitly stated in the text, otherwise a decision to refuse a derogation may not be enforceable in court. a minimum data set is necessary to evaluate the request for derogation; this is what we have specified in annex iv; if, in addition, further data is required by a member state for an evaluation, it can request as much or as little as is needed. in this way we provide for a tiered approach. finally on phosphates. the commission has promised in recital 31 to take action on phosphates if there is a solid scientific basis for doing so. the commission's priority in this matter is to establish a sound scientific basis for action at community level. there is no urgent need at eu level on this matter. those member states that feel particularly vulnerable to the environmental effects of phosphates have already taken national measures. in some cases this was done many years ago and the situation in those countries has stabilised. any action at eu level needs to demonstrate clearly the added value of the present situation. we hope to have a definitive opinion from the scientific committee on toxicology, eco-toxicology and environment on phosphates in detergents before the end of this year. finally, i would like to say that the commission can accept in whole or in part amendments 2, 4, 8, 17 to 19, 22 (partly), 27 (partly), 34 to 37 – but only a part of amendment 37 – and 53. the commission can accept in principle amendments 3, 21, 31, 45, 46 and 52. the other amendments are not acceptable to the commission.

- the next item is the commission statement on the crisis in the international coffee market.
- mr president, the coffee market is in a serious crisis today. the coffee workers are no longer able to live off their production. market prices, set by the four major multinationals with indecent profits, are too low to allow producers to make the profit they need to continue their activity. furthermore, coffee is produced at too high a yield, and its quality is diminished. the situation of coffee producers is not sustainable because there is no international system for stabilizing the prices of coffee and raw materials in general. we must put an end to this spiral of productivism which, in defiance of all social and environmental legislation, leads to the misery of millions of farmers in poor countries. it is a coincidence, some might say, that this crisis is occurring at the same time that stabex has disappeared from the cotonou agreement. the new system of quick cash payments is not helping the coffee-producing countries. the european union, the main importer of coffee, has a primary responsibility in resolving this crisis. the european union must launch an emergency programme, financed from the unused funds of the previous edfs, to make up for the loss of income of the populations and countries concerned. we ask the commission to produce a communication on commodities as a matter of urgency. the commission should also support the quality programme of the international coffee organisation. in the longer term, the european union must implement, for example in the framework of national and regional development plans, a set of measures to combat the volatility of coffee and other commodity prices. the european union must support the diversification of production by farmers in the south and the choice of quality agriculture, and contribute to strengthening the power of coffee producers vis-à-vis the agri-food industries. the commission must above all support the establishment of fair trade structures and facilitate market access for the products produced by them. a commission communication on this subject is becoming increasingly necessary. the question of stabilizing commodity prices, on which a majority of the least developed countries depend, must be addressed in the context of multilateral trade negotiations. the 'development cycle' agreed at doha seems particularly appropriate if the developing countries are to really benefit from world trade, which is currently being carried out rather at their expense. the customs duties on coffee products, which are still in force, must be abolished. the european union must use all its power at the wto ministerial conference in cancún to make trade with developing countries more equitable. we also welcome the french proposal to put the question of raw materials on the agenda of the next g8. the big coffee companies like nestlé, kraft, sara lee and procter and gamble cannot continue to sugarcoat themselves with impunity. they must agree to adopt ethical codes of conduct in line with the ilo and the un and to pay the raw material at its fair price, a price that reflects the social and environmental costs of exploitation and production. fair trade is not just another option for ensuring that coffee growers and workers are paid fairly, but the only sustainable global solution.
mr president, all the tendencies in this parliament are aware of the seriousness of the collapse in the price of coffee on the international market. how can we fail to see this, since these are the lowest prices in real terms recorded in a century? all the trends show the catastrophic consequences of this fall in coffee prices for the economies of a number of the world's poorest countries. but at the same time, all raise their hands in the air in a sign of impotence: and to propose that such an international conference put the question on the agenda, and to give good advice on conversion or diversification, and to offer extension courses to the farmers who are being strangled, and to wish that we would unblock a little something to help the countries most affected! four international trusts - nestlé, kraft, sara lee, and procter and gamble - control half of the world's coffee sales. which means clearly that these four trusts are setting the prices. they are the ones who, in order to make ever-increasing profits, lower the prices paid to producers. to distribute more dividends to their shareholders, they are taking the misery of dozens of poor countries and thus of tens of millions of farmers and their families. i note that the european parliament and the heads of state are powerless in the face of these four trusts and are content to talk about charity at best. and yet the joint resolution dares to advise that the market power of coffee producers should be strengthened. as if the poor peasant of rwanda, ethiopia or haiti could - while the european parliament does not dare to do so - oppose nestlé and its like! if that's not cynicism, what is? and the mere fact that the joint resolution mentions the four coffee trusts responsible for the price cuts gives the eldr group representatives the goosebumps, to the point that they ask for the paragraph citing them to be deleted. hide those trusts so i can 't see them ! there are a lot of truffles in this parliament . and what is true of coffee is also true of other commodities, starting with oil. those who bombed iraq, killing civilians, women and children, claim that they are doing so to free iraq from its dictator. but saddam hussein, the butcher of his own people, has been their hand man for years. they're the ones who armed him and pushed him to war with iran; it is they who sold him the weapons to massacre and gas the kurds and they dare to present the invading troops as liberators, when they are only carrying out the lowly work of the oil and arms trusts. to put an end to the plundering of the planet for the enrichment of a few trusts, to put an end to the extravagant inequalities between the rich in rich countries and the poor in poor countries, to prevent the poor from being murdered by starvation or massacred in wars fought to protect this situation, there is nothing but absolutely nothing else to do but to put an end to the international economic system.
commission. – mr president, i am happy to pass on the message of this debate to my colleagues, mr lamy and mr nielson. i will, however, make a few comments. you must remember that the real problem with the coffee sector is the lack of demand. the supply is essentially about the demand, and for that reason trade negotiations are not the only solution. it is very important that discussions in the world bank/ico context, or in ico itself, lead to solutions. today's problem is that the united states, which is the second biggest coffee consumer, is outside the ico. unless the us is ready to reconsider its position in the context of ico, then the measures will not have the same international impact. as far as the proposal for an action plan before the next meeting and the level of commission participation are concerned, i will pass mrs kinnock's questions to mr lamy and mr nielson. i am sure they will reply accordingly.

in writing. - we are against reproductive cloning. but we are indignant that behind certain formulations which appear to protect the individual or to denounce profit, the european parliament wants, once again, to prohibit therapeutic cloning and, more broadly, medical research on human cells and tissues. this rightly scandalizes and outrages many researchers throughout europe, who risk being banned from continuing their work and, therefore, from bringing science's help to the victims of serious diseases for which there is as yet no cure. to prevent research in this field is to ban in advance, in the name of reactionary designs, everything that could, in the future, help to treat or even cure these diseases. solidarity with these patients and with the researchers has led us to vote against this report and against all the amendments, often drafted in a jesuit-like manner, which are intended to make it worse.
in writing. - i support the initiative taken by germany to propose a directive to improve the organization of the transit of third-country nationals who are expelled from a member state when the aircraft carrying them has to stop over in another member state. in form, this text shows an intelligent use of the right of initiative which article 67 of the ec treaty provisionally reserves to the member states in this area. in theory, this right should be abolished on 1 may 2004 and the commission's monopoly of initiative should be restored in full. we hope that the states will be able to put a stop to this disastrous process at the next intergovernmental conference. unfortunately, the left took the opportunity to push through amendments limiting the right of expulsion, even including a minority opinion calling for "a total stop to expulsions (to countries of origin)... and a right of permanent residence for all in europe". once again we see a spirit which is subtly influencing many european proposals, such as the text on family reunification which the european parliament adopted yesterday. we were therefore obliged to vote against the kirkhope report which, by a strange coincidence, was finally rejected.
in writing. - the french government has just relaunched, in liaison with the german government, the deportation of immigrants from outside the community by charter. yet the scandalous conditions of these deportations, which have led to deaths during the journey, have been exposed, not to mention the imprisonment in the destination countries. it is in this context that the european parliament is being asked to table a draft council directive aimed at harmonising and regulating assistance in the context of removal with or without escort at transit airports in the european union. the report which has been presented to us to validate this codification of expulsions is particularly hypocritical. he does not say a word about the fact that collective expulsions are prohibited by the european convention on human rights and the charter of fundamental rights, thus crediting the national police services with a good consideration of the individual rights of immigrants. it reiterates that the sovereign rights of the member states - in particular as regards the application of enforcement measures to unruly illegally staying third-country nationals - are not affected. for all these reasons, we voted against this resolution and will continue to be involved with all those who want to put an end to these expulsions.
in writing. - the examination of this text on comparative testing and marketing of seeds should be an opportunity to recall some guidelines concerning seeds. every effort should be made to preserve the biodiversity of cultivated plants. left to free competition alone, genetic selection tends to be concentrated in the hands of a few companies, the number of varieties placed on the market is reduced and local varieties disappear. seed companies naturally tend to favour captive, hybrid or genetically modified varieties, which enable them to ensure the profitability of their crops. it is therefore up to the member states to maintain the public service dimension in plant breeding, to ensure the sustainability of local endangered varieties and to allow seed propagation on the farm. finally, the greatest caution should be exercised in the use of plant protection products to coat seeds, a technique which can be harmful to the environment and wildlife, particularly in the case of seeds coated with potent systemic insecticides, which have a disastrous effect on pollinating insects, especially domestic bees.
in writing. - the report before us today is modern and libertarian. the report also calls for the adoption of a new law on the protection of the environment and the protection of the environment from harmful substances. what is desired is a free market in drugs, their liberalization and the decriminalization of drug use offences. how can we not be shocked and horrified by such talk? how can we fail to realise that the damage caused by the use of drugs and other psychotropic substances is increasing in terms of crime, trafficking and death? how can we not accept that drug use increases exponentially with tolerance? in this respect, i would like to congratulate my finnish colleague, mrs marjo matikainen-kallström, who has courageously advocated a zero tolerance policy on drugs. of course, that is the only responsible attitude to take on this matter. let us not touch on the international conventions which lay down the rules and principles of the fight against drugs. the policy to combat drug trafficking and drug use must remain national. and it is not for europe to decide on the basis of scientific studies, which are only valid until further studies challenge them, that it is good to smoke cannabis.
in writing. - the purpose of this report is to break the ice in favour of a better information and communication strategy for the european union. why not ? - why not ? but if the aim, as stated in one of the paragraphs, is to convince all europeans of the european union's virtues in terms of 'security, solidarity, equal opportunities and cohesion', then the party is wrong. no communication strategy can make us forget, for example, that one in eight employees in the union is condemned to unemployment and many to poverty! if the european union were to pursue a policy against collective redundancies, by forcing employers to ensure the maintenance of jobs through their current and past profits, and if unemployment were to fall as a result, a communication strategy would not be necessary: word of mouth would suffice!
in writing. - the vote on a report proposing measures to improve the information of european citizens on the functioning of the european union should in principle be taken for granted. that is not the case with the text presented. the whole of this is based on concern about the eu's lack of popularity, with increasing abstention in the european elections. it mainly criticises the lack of information and the approaches which tend to make the union appear as a permanent arena of confrontation between national interests. as solutions, it proposes communication campaigns to highlight the common european values and the practical benefits of eu membership in everyday life. in our view, the eu's unpopularity is based on the fact that its current priorities are not democracy or solidarity, but the liberalisation of trade, the challenge to public services and the creation of a police fortress europe. the question is not therefore how to organise better institutional propaganda which is out of touch with reality, but how to find ways of presenting the debate on the europe of tomorrow clearly to the citizens and to enable them to make their voices heard at all levels. for this reason we did not vote in favour of the report.
in writing. - i was simply shocked to read this report. this document clearly crosses the line between information and disinformation, communication and propaganda. yes, it is propaganda to say, for example, that the european union's communication strategy must be supported by opinion formers, that information must be targeted to different groups of the population by means of mobilizing means, such as sport, and that messages must be formulated in such a way as to allow them to be easily incorporated into educational systems. the quasi-scientific approach, the recruitment of opinion formers to serve the cause, the instrumentalisation of all available resources, the subtle desire to manipulate the weakest minds through the use of educational systems: all this is totalitarian propaganda. this assembly dishonors itself by adopting a report which calls on the european institutions to squander public money in order to satisfy the lust for power of an oligarchy which wishes to subject reality to its own chimeras (citizenship, conscience, european constitution). however, despite the lavishness of the means at the disposal of the european machine, i want to believe that the peoples will not be fooled by this subliminal federalism.
in writing. - the morillon report proposes a new european security and defence architecture of a unitary and centralised type, which seems both unrealistic and outdated. the report is in fact, from the outset, in the community framework. no development is devoted to what should be the central principle, the freedom of participation of countries and the variable geometry of associations. there is only a reference to 'constructive abstention', a slight flexibility introduced by the treaty of amsterdam to preserve the general centralised framework. on the other hand, the need to develop the powers of the existing european institutions and the inclusion of the costs in the community budget is strongly emphasized (paragraphs 40, 56 and 57 of the resolution). the iraq crisis showed how outdated this montage was. but in any case, this report was not realistic, because it affirmed both the competence of national parliaments in the use of national forces and that of the european parliament in the approval of operations. all of this is contradictory. you have to choose. the only solution for us is the superior legitimacy of the nations and the primary responsibility of their parliaments. everything else has to follow.
in writing. - to advocate a common european army, as the report does, is not without its comicness, at a time when the british army is leading the american army into a dirty war in iraq while the other armies, by political choice or incapacity, say they are opposed to the war. what would a unified european army have done? but behind the tragicomic is the idea that to the divergent national militarisms must be added a supra-european militarism. we reject both because these militarisms are nothing but the periodic bloodshed, the permanent taxation of the people, the wars waged for the benefit of a few big trusts. let no one object to the need to defend the fatherland at the national and continental levels! the french army, for example, has never had to defend the country since 1945. but it has fought a multitude of colonial wars and has been involved in robbery wars around the globe. we therefore voted against this report.
in writing. - the current division between member states on crucial foreign policy issues is regrettable, since it does not allow the union to become a credible actor on the international scene. if the union is to become such an actor, it is essential that it adopt a single line and speak with one voice. if the european union is to defend its objectives and values on the international scene and contribute to peace, freedom and stability in the world, in accordance with the principles of the united nations and international law, it is urgent that it develops a genuine esdp, an integral part of the cfsp. this esdp must be based on the principle of security, security shared by europe and the rest of the world, sustainable security based on equality, justice and reciprocity, security based on respect for human rights, democratic control and international law. a credible actor on the international scene but also a free partner of the united states within the atlantic alliance: that is the key message of this report, and that is why i will support it.
in writing. - the report by general morillon sets out the ambitions of a european union security and defence policy. after a few usual precautions, such as the need to base this policy on equality, justice, reciprocity, human rights, democratic control and international law, and to contribute to freedom, peace, etc., the report reveals its concrete bases, with the police vision of the world that underlies it: instability that would be produced by terrorism, the proliferation of weapons of mass destruction, the trafficking of weapons, drugs and human beings ... as well as illegal immigration, in short by general human evil, and not by social oppression and north-south inequalities. the solutions proposed are therefore to strengthen the military capabilities available in the union, which require the development of a european defence culture as quickly as possible. it is even hoped that by 2009 the european military force will be able to conduct, within the european geographical framework, an operation of the level and intensity of the kosovo conflict. what a peaceful future ! for these reasons we tabled an amendment calling for the rejection of war as an instrument for settling international disputes. in view of its rejection, we voted against the morillon report.
in writing. - it will be remembered that we have debated at length a report on european security, the content of which is essentially totally outdated, and that we have forbidden ourselves, by a large majority, to discuss the war in iraq at a time when its outcome is in play and when its consequences concern our security in the first place. the parliament's silence on the tripartite summit france-germany-russia, which begins tomorrow in st petersburg with the secretary-general of the united nations, will also be noted. is it because it is an intergovernmental initiative, and therefore ideologically incorrect? however, if parliament really cared, as it claims, to see europe exerting its own substantial diplomatic influence in the post-war period, it should attach more importance to the st petersburg summit than to the next european council. the doubling of financial aid to turkey, probably intended to thank ankara for its refusal to lift the occupation of cyprus by its troops, is also noteworthy. it is not necessary to link aid to accession, as parliament has done, but to a constructive attitude on the part of turkey to achieve the reunification of cyprus before nicosia joins the union. if we had done that, we would have worked concretely for the security of europe.

commission. - mr president, i thank the rapporteur and all the speakers for their words and their approaches. i would point out that of the 31 amendments tabled by parliament, 20 can be accepted, in whole or in part, because they involve improvements or clarifications of the text, and in particular those relating to the provision of insurance proof or those relating to overflight and the one relating, for example, to aircraft from third countries. of the 20 that can be accepted, 15 are literally accepted and 5 with appropriate modifications. ladies and gentlemen, i must point out, however, that there are 10 that i cannot accept for the reasons i shall set out below. for example, amendment no 9 on state guarantees, because it would not be in line with our approach to state aid and would clearly distort competition, or amendment no 12 on the validity of insurance, which is not legally viable because insurance could be cancelled during a flight after events such as 9/11 and therefore its application would be impossible to guarantee. amendments nos 13 and 15 on the definition of short-term leases because they fall within the scope of other rules which are not currently being reviewed. amendment no 18, which describes in detail the doubts about the effectiveness of the cover because it is too prescriptive. amendment no 25, which extends the definition of insurer, because it would unduly discriminate against third country insurers and would infringe the community's international obligations in financial services. amendments nos 26 and 28, which extend the application of civil and passenger liability to airline operators, because they could raise difficulties of legal interpretation and, in a matter of this nature, as mr ortuondo has very well pointed out, it is essential that we have the greatest possible clarity, in order to avoid contradictory interpretations. amendment no 27, because it introduces maximum bands instead of minimum insurance amounts. amendment no 29, calling on the commission to harmonize legislation on insurance at airports, because the need for compulsory insurance requirements covering third party damage has not been approved. and amendment no 30 cannot be accepted because the person responsible is often not the person subject to compulsory insurance. i would point out that we are talking about thresholds which are lower than the market currently sets and that since 9 september 2001 insurance costs have been falling steadily, although it is true - and mr nicholson was right about that - that the problem is posed by small companies, with whom there is a case-by-case negotiation. mr vermeer was talking about the open skies issue. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's transport policy is not distorted by the introduction of new technologies. the honourable member is well aware that the commission is trying to secure a negotiating mandate with the united states and the other third countries, which would allow both the necessary flexibility for countries to negotiate new agreements with third countries, which are not always of community interest as a whole, which only affect or interest certain specific countries for special reasons, but at the same time maintain the community as the responsible authority and ultimate bargaining power. i would like to say to the honourable members that the united states, for example, has clearly shown its willingness to start these negotiations in the coming months, if we had a mandate from the commission to do so. i would also point out, as regards flights, that the 1944 chicago convention and the 1994 transit agreement, in article 5 thereof, explicitly allow conditions to be imposed for overflights, not only as regards the payment of certain types of cargo, but also as regards the obligation to take out certain types of insurance. these international agreements therefore clearly allow for the coverage of overflights. as regards the question of the impact study - and i conclude with this, mr president - we have commissioned an impact study on third countries. we're working on it right now. as far as european companies are concerned, we believe that we already have the necessary experience and knowledge. i hope that in the course of the next few debates we will be able to come closer to the honourable members and achieve a result which clarifies and sets the right level of guarantees for everyone and which restores and increases confidence in this type of transport, which is what we all want.

- mr president, the proposal for a directive on environmental liability which has been presented to us today is very disappointing. we welcome european harmonisation in the field of environmental damage, which is often transnational, but it would still require serious progress. however, this text is characterised by an impressive number of shortcomings, exemptions, exclusions and limitations of liability, which would make the new regulation a deception and often even a source of confusion and a reduction in the protection of the citizen, unless the taxpayer is called upon to fill in the gaps. consider two examples. first example: article 3 states that the directive does not apply to the transport of dangerous substances by sea, to damage caused by oil pollution and to damage caused by nuclear power. the reason is that there are already international conventions governing civil liability in all these areas. but these conventions are limited, insufficiently protective or totally inadequate, as we see these days with the ridiculous compensation granted by fipol after the prestige disaster. we therefore ask that this directive not run away from the problem, but that it address it and provide real protection. the second example is gmos. the commission promised us, when we were discussing the directive on the voluntary release of gmos, that the questions of liability and insurance would be dealt with in the general directive on environmental liability, the one we are discussing today. but we were deceived. theoretically, gmos are well covered by this text, but they immediately stand out thanks to article 9, which exempts activities which benefit from an administrative authorisation, of which gmos would be part, precisely because of the directive on intentional release. all this is intolerable, especially at a time when the commission is trying to shift the burden of the problem of the coexistence of the gmo and non-gmo crops it wants to allow onto the member states. in these circumstances, we ask the council not to lift the moratorium until the questions of liability and assurance regarding gmos are clearly resolved for the best protection of the citizen and the environment.
- mr president, to legislate on environmental liability is to open pandora's box, since environmental damage is poorly defined by the directive and its scope of application is vague, particularly in the area of biodiversity, which is already governed by the international conventions of berne and bonn. the repair should be limited to natura 2000 areas and exclude non-profit-making activities such as leisure, which the directive equates with professional activities. the directive does not cover the transport of hydrocarbons or gmos. the compensation must be based on objective and quantifiable criteria, on the nature of the damage and its impact, on the state of the environment at the level of the damage, on local circumstances. the polluter pays principle must be effectively applied and not replaced by the taxpayer pays principle. the responsibility must include gmos, especially as the us is forcing the lifting of the moratorium on imports in the context of the wto negotiations. more generally, what is the point of making the system of liability community-wide, when the danish initiative of the council on the criminalisation of environmental crime falls within the scope of judicial cooperation? this is particularly so since other legal instruments could be used, such as the lugano convention.
- mr president, madam commissioner, we have been waiting for a long time to have an environmental liability regime, a regime that is sufficiently severe but objective and feasible, so that it protects the environment without harming the economy, whether industrial or agricultural. it is also necessary that the application of such liability should avoid any distortion of competition. but i must say that this text seems to me disappointing and rather weak and does not fully meet our expectations. the polluter pays principle is a fundamental principle, but it must be accompanied by financial guarantees. in this text we must not talk about the transport of hydrocarbons by sea, and i regret that. when we see the example of fipol in the sad case of the prestige, when we see the permanent discharges at sea, we think that there is much to be done to make certain professions responsible. and here, our anger is proportional to the extent of the damage to biodiversity. the proposals in this area are not enough and i would also like the commissioner to tell us a little bit about what she thinks of the fipol decision. finally, liability must be proportionate to the fault admitted. we must avoid any joint responsibility which would make others share the responsibility. the taxpayer is not obliged to bear the financial burden of damage caused by others. in conclusion, i do not think that reparations are the only solution. we need more prevention. i welcome the efforts that can be made by companies in this direction through the voluntary agreements which we shall discuss shortly, but i insist that an effective system of financial guarantees be put in place. that's what i wanted to tell you. i am convinced that in conclusion we will have to discuss this environmental liability regime again.
