commission. – mr president, i should like to thank members for all those valuable speeches and constructive ideas on how to improve this proposal. let me begin by commenting on two things: the polluter-pays principle and the scope. several members referred to the long history of this proposal; the debate reflected the different views and the need to find a balanced approach in the end. i also understand that many members want to be more ambitious: to overload this proposal with a lot more. i can understand that, but it is important to see it as a step-by-step approach, because we have a practical view on this. we do not want to overload it with aspects that we are negotiating at the same time in international fora. i am sure that there would be more chance of losing the whole proposal if we were to try to burden it with these aspects. the polluter-pays principle is the guiding principle behind this whole proposal, and that is why it is quoted in the first article. the idea behind it is to create responsibility and, via that, to achieve prevention. it gives that very clear signal. we also touch upon the fact that in many cases it is not possible to find the polluter, or to make the polluter pay. in that case, there has to be remediation. we want to see an insurance system. however, we believe that market forces should be allowed to create that kind of system. we do not want to impose it today in a situation where it is not clear that we would achieve the desired effect. in reply to miss breyer's point: all accidents are covered. i do not know what members' presumptions are about the targets for this legislation, but our presumptions are very much based on the facts that there are too many accidents and too many cases of negligence, and also that short-sighted greed is behind much of the pollution. this is why we have designed the proposal this way. therefore, all accidents are covered and we have also covered cases of negligence; this will create a polluter-pays principle and, in the end, pave the way for prevention. what about the scope? it was very important for us to ensure that we have legal clarity if we want to introduce a new system covering biodiversity, because traditional damage – economic damage or damage to people – is already well covered by the legislation in all member states. we do not have to take over that at community level, but we want to harmonise the rules for covering damage to biodiversity. that was the starting-point. if we want to do this and have a credible system, we need legal clarity and a system which is manageable and which can be applied. if the definition is too wide – as it is proposed, it would cover, in some cases, the whole biosphere – it will be unmanageable. for example, we would have to cover damage to weeds! is that something insurers will be happy to cover? would that be a manageable system? digging the foundations for a house would hurt worms. do we want that to be covered? is that reasonable? you have to be sure about the scope and make a definition that provides legal clarity. we have to see it as a step-by-step approach. i am sure that as we apply this legislation there will be more legal clarity. however, if we are too ambitious at the beginning and think that we can cover the whole biosphere, then we would not be serving environmental interests. on gmos, nuclear and marine pollution: we can see that this is an area in which we would also like to be more ambitious. however, we have a very practical reason for not covering this in this particular proposal. we are negotiating to improve the rules on these areas. we have international fora and conventions that cover these matters. we do not want to duplicate work: we want to be practical. we do not want to overload this system by taking it on here. we need another few years to work on incorporating these aspects. for international activities, there should be international rules. as i have already said, traditional damage is already covered by legislation in member states. what about oil or marine pollution? the polluter shall pay! this is the only rule that can apply. it is a scandal that we have let it go this far. we have seen accident after accident. but, again, this is a truly international activity and we have to work towards international rules that apply the polluter-pays principle. i understand that the director of the iopc fund has announced that claims for compensation would only be covered by up to 15% of this amount. this is not acceptable. the commission is well aware of the situation and this is why we have always supported the attempt to raise the funds available up to eur 1 billion. i understand that this week a diplomatic conference is being held in london to sign a protocol to raise the ceiling of the funds available for compensation. i hope that this conference will be a success; we are all determined to work on marine pollution and to do everything we can. we want to avoid loopholes and also the absurd situation where neither the directive nor international conventions apply. that is why the commission agrees that the directive should apply in all cases where the relevant international convention is not yet in force. for the same reason, where the relevant conventions are not in force, the commission does not support the notion of waiting for five years before the directive is applicable. it has also been proposed that after a five-year transitional period, the commission should develop proposals so that the directive applies eventually in a complementary manner to the international conventions where liability or compensation is insufficiently regulated within those conventions. the commission does not believe that letting the directive play the role of filling in possible gaps in existing conventions would be either constructive or workable. the conventions contain exclusivity clauses that bind the states' parties to the conventions and prevent them from imposing any complementary legal instruments, so member states would have to denounce conventions they had ratified to be able to follow community rules. before letting it come to that, it would surely be preferable to try to improve those conventions by renegotiating them in the proper international context. what about regulatory compliance and state-of-the-art and development risks? some amendments have been tabled that seek to maintain the so-called permit and state-of-the-art or development risk defences as proper defences and, as far as permit defences are concerned, with a formulation that would better specify its scope. other amendments aim instead to introduce regulatory compliance and state-of-the-art as mitigating factors. the commission believes that proper defences, with the proposed improved wording, constitute a preferable solution in terms of insurability and legal certainty. the commission considers it useful, however, to better specify the scope of the so-called permit defence to avoid any suggestion that this might be tantamount to a blank cheque to pollute, because this is not the idea. the commission does not find it appropriate to impose liability on the competent authority when damage is caused by a permitted activity, nor does it find it appropriate that there should be a link between the state-of-the-art defence and any environmental audit and management system. i am sure that these issues will come back during further decision-making on this issue. amendments have been tabled to impose either proportional liability or joint and several liability. the commission considers, however, that member states should retain the right to opt for either joint and several, or for proportional liability, or a mix of both, according to their national legal traditions. i recall in that respect that the proposal offers some safeguards to operators, since it provides that operators who are able to establish the extent to which the damage results from their activities, be required to bear only such costs as relate to that part of the damage. it has been proposed that the commission should present a proposal to supplement the regulatory framework on liability for damage caused by gmos. apart from the fact that such a requirement would unduly impinge on the commission's right of initiative, the commission is currently considering the issue of economic damage to conventional and organic farmers in the context of the so-called coexistence debate. the outcome of that debate should not be prejudged here. again, this is what will cover traditional damage. on financial security: amendments have been tabled either to propose that financial security become compulsory after the directive enters into force, or to oppose such a move towards compulsory financial security. i think we can agree that financial security will become an important factor in the proper implementation of the directive. member states and market operators, as well as the commission, will have an important role to play in encouraging a timely emergence of financial assurance systems, products and markets to that effect. having said this, it is clear to me that member states should have the possibility to develop financial assurance solutions at their own pace; solutions which are well adapted to their own needs and institutional conditions. in addition, financial markets should be given time and leeway to develop market solutions following the demand for insurance that is very likely to take off once the new liability regime is established. in the light of this, it appears premature to impose fully-fledged financial security for all annex i operators within a few years. that said, it would certainty be fruitful to revisit the situation when the commission carries out its general review of the implementation of the directive. there is general agreement that the polluter-pays principle should imply, for the liable operator as polluter, to pay for all the damage it causes to the environment. in addition, there is a clear need for a common understanding within the community that the costs of environmental damage should be borne by the polluter. furthermore, the rules set out in the proposal specify the full range of remediation actions to be carried out by the liable operator. amendments have now been tabled to narrow down the scope of damage remediation by suppressing the remediation of interim losses, together with suppressing the concept of a natural resource service. deleting elements from this range of actions would inevitably result in the polluter not having to carry the full cost of the damage he causes. finally, in the difficult context of this debate on environmental liability, the commission has tried to reach an overall balance which has already been built on compromise solutions. at this stage the commission is still of the opinion that the proposal is fair and workable in many respects and should be supported. i am also aware, however, that we are still at the beginning of the legislative process, and thus entirely conscious of the need for all the institutions involved in this process to reach agreement in due course. such an agreement implies necessarily the willingness of all parties to find appropriate and satisfactory compromises. the debate has reflected this need to ensure that we bridge the different views and find a workable solution in the end. i shall hand the commission's position on all the amendments to parliament's services for publication commission's position on parliament's amendments: see annex.. however, i should like to say one word about the amendments we have accepted. in addition to the technical amendments that the commission can support, i would single out the amendments to articles 4 and 5. the commission can accept these – at least in principle. these two articles are at the core of the proposal since they specify via whom and how preventive and remediation measures should be taken.
in writing. - the proposal for a directive on 'environmental responsibility' is very important to ensure better protection of the environment and to combat all types of pollution. from the 2002 azf disaster in toulouse to the erika and prestige oil tankers, these disasters have cost lives and caused serious and lasting environmental damage. the report by the legal affairs committee proposes a more conciliatory approach to the interests of business by weakening the original proposal for a directive. on the contrary, the provisions envisaged must be reinforced with means of protection, by making polluters bear the burden of the damage caused to the environment, by giving the possibility to ngos and citizens to bring legal proceedings, and by including in the directive the damage caused by gmos. at a time when fipol has just announced a ridiculous 15% compensation rate for the damage caused by the prestige, rightly creating astonishment and anger among the population and associations, europe now has a responsibility to make a completely different voice heard. it must convey a strong message of justice and determination.
mr president, mr corbett's report is designed to strengthen parliament's powers of control over the texts implementing legislative acts prepared by the commission in the framework of what is mysteriously called comitology. the epp endorses the report's guidelines and supports in particular the idea that in the event of disagreement between parliament and the commission on a draft implementing text, the commission should not overlook this opposition. if the commission did not follow parliament on this point, the epp would gladly join the rapporteur in his request for referral back to committee. we have two points of disagreement with mr corbett's report. first, it provides that if parliament does not agree with the text proposed by the commission, the commission may simply withdraw its text without preparing a new one and without taking a legislative initiative. we think that this power is quite excessive. it is tantamount to a genuine authorization to strike enforcement acts and we cannot support it. our requests for separate voting are designed to deny this possibility. secondly, mr corbett's report suggests that if the commission were to initiate a new legislative initiative because it considers it impossible to overcome its disagreement with parliament by simply amending its text, the text prepared by the commission would be provisionally applied until the new legislative text is adopted. we do not think this is acceptable. it seems to us to be quite unfair to allow the commission to ignore parliament's opposition for a very long time, even though the disagreement between the two institutions is so serious and so deep that it cannot be overcome by a simple amendment of the draft, but would require the use of a legislative procedure. to give the commission the power to impose, even for a few months or years, the contested text would be to officially recognise the commission's power to ignore or violate the law. these are the two reserves we have. we have not tabled any amendments, but simply requests for separate votes which actually seek to correct the report on this point, which we also approve and for which we congratulate the rapporteur, because it is a remarkable piece of work.
commission. – mr president, first of all let me stress that the proposed amendments and the speeches made indicate that much thought and effort has gone into the examination of this proposal, which aims to enhance the role of the european parliament in the institutional triangle. as far as possible, the commission will take into account the detailed amendments proposed by the committee on constitutional affairs. the commission can accept, in whole or in part, amendments nos 1, 2 (in part), 4, 7, 8, 11 (in part), 13, 14, 18 and 19. however, the commission cannot accept amendments nos 3, 10 or 11 (in part), as they could complicate the commission's negotiations with the council. the commission's proposal aims to give the european parliament and the council equal rights as co-legislators in controlling the commission; but the proposal cannot go further than or beyond the scope of the present treaty, which does not provide for explicit delegation of legislative power to the commission. the commission, as the sole executive, should be able to retain full responsibility for adopting executive instruments. this political responsibility goes hand in hand with the freedom of the commission to adopt a decision, taking on board or not the objections raised by the legislator. the deletion of 'possibly' would tie the hands of the commission and prevent it from exercising its responsibility as the executive. the withdrawal option, as formulated in mr corbett's amendments nos 3, 10 and 11, would effectively amount to replacing the freedom of adoption by the commission by an explicit withdrawal or non-action by the commission. if the commission's views are not in line with those of the legislator, the commission would be obliged to renounce the adoption of an implementing measure. substitution of the commission's responsibility and freedom to adopt an implementing measure via the non-action option would also send the wrong political signal to stakeholders. the proposal is, on the contrary, based on the assumption that action is needed and that the commission will take responsibility for it. given the scope afforded by the current treaty, these amendments are therefore not acceptable to the commission. the proposal indeed goes as far as possible towards granting the european parliament the control rights that, as a co-legislator, it should possess. the reform, as i have just mentioned, cannot go as far as a more thoroughgoing reform conducted in the process of amending the treaty. in the framework of the european convention, the commission has explicitly suggested that the council and the european parliament should, under delegation of legislative powers, have the possibility to oppose a text proposed by the commission. in this scenario the latter would indeed either renounce its text, modify it or present a legislative proposal. to conclude, i can assure you that the commission will endeavour to achieve progress on this issue in the council. i would like to conclude that the commission needs parliament's support in negotiating the strengthening of the european parliament's prerogatives with the council. i am confident that the commission can count on parliament's continued support in the process of clarifying the roles and competences of the executive and the legislator.

in writing. - the proposal for a decision on the implementing powers conferred by the council on the commission - prepared by the commission itself - is in line with the wishes of the european parliament, which has just warmly endorsed it. parliament has long wanted to be given the right to control implementing measures on an equal footing with the council, at least for texts adopted under codecision. this ambition may surprise because in many parliamentary democracies, including france, the elected assembly does not control the details of the measures taken to implement laws, reserving only, if necessary, to call into question the responsibility of the government. but perhaps the attitude of the european parliament, which is primarily motivated by the desire to compete with the council, reveals something quite different: that the commission is not a real government, and that it is not a real parliament. today, after some progress, particularly in 1999, the commission wants to complete the process and push the council to give full control to parliament. it forgets only one thing: this equality is not provided for in article 202 of the treaty, which gives the council the main power. that is why we voted against the proposal.
in writing. - we voted with a number of reservations in favour of the sacconi report on environmental agreements concluded at community level, which provides for a new instrument to simplify and speed up legislative work at european level: voluntary agreements. these agreements, which form part of the sixth community environment action programme, may take two forms: self-regulation and co-regulation. we do not think it appropriate to favour co-regulation, as the rapporteur recommends. it is not of higher value than self-regulation. the commission does not have to be the judge and jury in the conditions for the implementation of these agreements. moreover, voluntary agreements should not be seen as instruments complementing the existing community legislative arsenal. voluntary agreements are flexible instruments which have their place in the legislative instruments. we welcome the fact that the commission's initiative took the form of a non-binding communication. we want the commission to continue along this path.

in writing. - the manders report claims to be based on the polluter pays principle: companies that damage the environment must bear the costs of the damage they have caused. we voted in favour of this report because some of the amendments are sensible. there is still a major problem with its implementation. it is not enough for parliament to vote on its recommendations for them to come into force, nor is it enough for the competent authority to be appointed for the operator to assume its responsibilities. especially when the operator is a multinational group that has the means to circumvent them and the competent authority is used to complying with its requirements, as was seen in france with the company totalfinaelf (erika oil spill, azf explosion). the nuances which the rapporteur has drawn up on the responsibility of the polluter up to a certain point would be laughable if the behaviour of these large groups, which are particularly attentive to their profit-making, did not have dramatic consequences for the population. nor is it enough to have financial guarantees in place. fipol, which is supposed to cover the risks of oil tankers, has just announced that it will only reimburse 15% of the damage to the prestige, because its coffers are empty. to appease the anger of the victims, the french government did not consider turning against the charterer but made the taxpayers pay. this means that, in the face of the harsh reality of a profit-oriented society, this report will remain powerless.
in writing. - the issues raised by environmental liability and specific liability for shipping are, despite appearances, of a different nature. the text voted by parliament will cause confusion. the concept of environmental liability, which is still in its infancy, is based on the need to identify the person responsible and to establish a causal link between the event giving rise to the pollution: it involves lengthy procedures and late compensation. the system of no-fault liability laid down by the clc/fipol international conventions has the advantage for victims of designating a person responsible who must be insured and of creating a compensation fund which, in theory, can be mobilised immediately in the event of pollution. however, the experience of recent oil spills shows that this system must be extended to shipping companies and to biodiversity damage, and that fipol must be significantly upgraded and made permanent. these requests should be made to who by the member states most directly concerned and most determined to act. if they fail, it will be up to these same states to demand that the european union act unilaterally, as the united states has done, by taking over these indispensable improvements.

mr president, the enlarged europe's neighbourhood policy, which the council and the commission have just spoken to us about, seems to us very interesting because it is part of a new, more flexible approach, that of general but graduated and differentiated cooperation, adapted to the case of each neighbouring country. at this stage, however, it raises four questions for us. first, the content of neighbourhood agreements has sometimes been defined by the phrase 'everything but the institutions', which can be misinterpreted as 'everything but the decision-making power'. this ambiguity should therefore be removed. secondly, on the substance, there was also talk of the priority extension of the four freedoms of movement in the single market. isn't this commitment in advance very unwise? of course, other objectives are even more important, such as safety. thirdly, the new neighbourhood policy seems to be reserved for neighbouring non-candidate countries. turkey is not on this list, but it is not clear why, as its accession has not yet been formally accepted. fourthly, in this neighbourhood policy, the european union does not start from scratch. it does not start from scratch since the current members already have relations with their neighbours, especially those who are immediately adjacent. how will european policy be articulated with existing national policies? should not the member states which are closest to us be given a decisive voice or a privileged right to see the new european policy?

- mr president, commissioner, europe has never defined its limits. she started at six, she could have started at seven or eight. even today, in the draft constitution, article 3 says: 'the union is open to all european states whose peoples share the same values', but it does not specify what a european state is. it is never good to not indicate the borders to the people, because it worries them more than it reassures them. so, everybody has their own boundaries in mind. for some, including myself, they stay in the countries of the maghreb, who are our neighbours and friends. so it's good to plan the best partnerships with them. the borders also stop at belarus, moldova and ukraine, because these countries are part of a whole, as is russia. they are neighbouring and friendly countries. for many, the borders also do not include turkey and the caucasus countries. we made this promise of integration 40 years ago, but it is not certain that the peoples will follow us. in this case, our neighbours would be iran, iraq and syria. i think we should offer this group the best possible partnerships. in any case, if europe is to have a bright future, it must be able to put an end to its geography. you know the saying, "too much kissing, too few hugs".
- mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, the key element in the debate on foot-and-mouth disease today is, in my view, the constraints imposed by the oie on trade sanctions against countries which no longer enjoy the status of 'free from foot-and-mouth disease'. it is these rules that make the disease so terrifying for farmers, because of the very high economic losses it causes. it should be remembered that foot-and-mouth disease in livestock is not dangerous to humans. it's not a public health problem. i therefore support our rapporteur's proposal in his amendment no 5 to recital 14 that member states should submit proposals to the oie to change the trade sanctions linked to these situations. to be more precise, this evolution of oie rules must go in two directions. first, we must take account of the progress made in vaccines - marker vaccines, which distinguish a vaccinated animal from an infected animal, and vaccines with a wider spectrum - and remember that products - milk or meat - from a vaccinated animal do not present any danger to human health, nor any risk of contagion. there is therefore no longer any reason to discriminate against these products or the countries in which they circulate. this development of the rules will also make it possible to reconsider the problem of prophylactic vaccination, which should be allowed by the member states in cases where, for reasons of their own, farmers wish to do so. i am thinking in particular of animals of high genetic value, breeders, small breeds of interest to biodiversity. secondly, the member states must be allowed to regionalize their farming areas and it must not be allowed that an outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease in alsace - my example is of course theoretical - prevents brittany from exporting its excellent animal products. finally, and i regret that the point i raised in the work of our temporary committee on foot-and-mouth disease was not taken up by the rapporteur, let us not lose sight of the fact that certain developments in european agriculture, which have been encouraged by the deviations of a certain cap, are in themselves risk factors for the spread of epizootic diseases. i am talking about the increase in the size of farms, the unconsidered intensification, the generalization of off-shore livestock farming, the specialisation of regions, the transport of animals over long distances: all these factors that contribute to creating very high densities of animals increase the risk. at the moment, mr president, when this parliament is going to have to decide on the mid-term review of the cap, let us be determined to correct these deviations rather than amplify them, by favouring farms on a human scale, extensive livestock farming in the less favoured regions, the local integration of the supply chains, local slaughterhouses, in short, a farming with a human face.
- madam president, in its broad guidelines for economic policy for the period 2003-05, the commission presents a set of recommendations which, in themselves, seem to us to be quite sound. ensure commission. - (es) madam president, thank you very much to everyone who has taken part in this debate. unfortunately, given the time available, we cannot go into all the points raised in detail, but i would like to make a few points which i think are important. first of all, i thank parliament for its cooperation and i am aware of the difficulties it is facing. i would also have liked to see us discussing the broad economic policy guidelines and the employment guidelines together today. unfortunately, that has not been the case. i am even aware of the short time available to parliament, but the commission and the council are also limited in that respect. it should not be forgotten that the commission's proposals must be based on the decisions of the spring european council and it is therefore very difficult to start this kind of work before april. secondly, the fundamental debate today is whether the economic policy we have decided is right for the present situation or whether the present situation should lead us to a change of economic policy. i think that two things are mixed up in the debate here: economic policy and economic policy instruments. i think that if we look at the behaviour of macroeconomic policy during this period, we will see, in my view, that it is helping to deal with the crisis. monetary policy has naturally changed, and even fiscal policy is now clearly more expansionary than it was in the margins accepted by the stability and growth pact. i shall come back to this point later. i believe, however, that the present situation should not make us retreat from structural reforms, which are nothing other than the modernisation of our economies. is the stability and growth pact a brake on the current economy? does it present a difficulty? i think that, with excessive simplification, a rigid stability pact has been proposed, which does not allow for any room for manoeuvre - which does not correspond to reality - and is based on an assumption which is also not correct, namely that discretionary fiscal policies are correct for any economic situation. rather, i think economic theory tells us something different, and that is that they are only correct in very specific circumstances. i think it is worth reflecting on a point which i consider to be fundamental, and that is that we should see that precisely the countries which are having the most difficulty are those which have the greatest deficits today. is the deficit therefore a cause of the bad economic situation or is the bad economic situation a cause of the deficit? i think this is a debate which can be illuminated by other elements, such as developments in japan, or even the very impact on the united states of the measures taken by the present administration. i still believe that the stability and growth pact is the best instrument we can have for an appropriate, flexible - in so far as it allows us to use automatic stabilisers - and automatic fiscal policy, so as to avoid any kind of voluntarism which can have negative impacts in the end. in my view, the analysis of economic policy which we have put forward has in some cases gone too far into the anecdotal, the detailed and even the caricatural. it is not a policy based solely - or, let us say, at all - on wage restraint - wages are always set in accordance with the evolution of productivity - nor is it a policy whose fundamental element is employment. the policy is made up of three fundamental instruments, which i have already mentioned: sound macroeconomic policies, structural reforms and environmental, social and economic sustainability in the medium and long term. even when we talk about structural employment policies, we are not talking solely and exclusively about the flexibility of the labour market. we are talking about population trends, the rate of activity and, of course, labour markets adapted to the new situation. of course, the economic policy guidelines are not contradictory to lisbon. they are one of the instruments - not the only one - which enable us to put lisbon into action. i am surprised at the concern to redefine new programmes of action and new lists of things to do. i am also surprised at the references that are sometimes made to the need to know more about what is happening. i assume that parliament is aware that the commission's summary report on the implementation of lisbon was published in january. and in this report you can have all the information you want about the achievement of each of the objectives by each of the member states. you even have lists, with charts, that highlight which countries have done better and which have done worse, and you have, perfectly defined with lists, the three worst countries and the three best countries in each of the objectives. all these issues therefore exist, just as there is a report on the implementation of the broad economic policy guidelines every year, in which you can see exactly where the shortcomings are. so our fundamental problem is not knowing where we are, but wanting to change the situation in which we find ourselves. and that is a point which, as a consequence of our own system, is the responsibility of each of the member states. the system we have in place is based on a policy of peer pressure, as i said in my supplementary speech, and that is obviously a fundamental point. some of you have referred to the open method of coordination, a method which, in my view, should be applied in those cases where there are no methods of its own in the treaty. so it's a useful method, which should be agreed, but it's a limited method. i am sorry that time does not permit us to go into further details, but i would like to thank all of you for your participation in this morning's debate.

mr president, the resolution proposed to us by the erika mann report includes, in paragraph 21, a call for the complete communitization of european trade policy with exclusive community competence, majority voting in the council and co-decision with the european parliament. we cannot follow this community fundamentalism, guided by the idea that only supranational mechanisms are relevant to this policy, in order to promote global openness and the transcendence of nations. but global openness, as useful as it may be, is not the only thing. it must also be recognised that the member states have social models and fundamental interests to protect. we must therefore give them the means to do so and find the right balance between european policy and national interests, between the control of the european parliament and the control of the national parliaments. but in our view, the erika mann report does not strike that balance. in particular, it should be recognised that decisions by qualified majority in the council can have adverse effects. let us take a recent example: the convention on the future of europe is considering the possibility of subjecting all trade policy to the majority rule, thus removing the derogations recognised by the treaty of nice for certain essential services, in particular cultural services, which the treaty has kept within the scope of unanimity. the french government protested and asked for the unanimity to be maintained on the grounds that it was more protective. we approve. but why admit it here and not elsewhere? at the same time, an association of mainly american large companies, the international communications round table, is writing to the convention and the commission to praise the majority rule. it is clear that this rule would have the effect of bypassing certain national resistance and thus of dismantling our defenses. we therefore ask the convention to take a more comprehensive and balanced view. first, there is a need to involve national parliaments more closely. secondly, the majority procedure should only be used to decide on safeguard measures. on the contrary, whenever it comes to lowering our protections, decisions should be taken unanimously so as not to harm anyone.

the rapporteur. - mr president, i would first of all like to thank my colleagues who have worked very hard on this report, mrs de keyser, in particular, on behalf of the committee on foreign affairs, and mrs zrihen. i also thank the european commission and mrs gonzalo, who has given us all the information we needed. i would remind you that the meda programme is the instrument for implementing the mediterranean policy defined by the barcelona process in 1995. the first phase was carried out by the meda i programme (1995-1999) and the second by the meda ii programme, an ongoing programme, defined by the valdivielso and mine reports, in 2000. this new regulation entered into force on 15 december 2000 and we were able to analyse its operation until the end of 2002. the conclusions on meda i had raised many reservations, with the overall payment-to-commitment ratio from 1995 to 1999 being only 26%. the main causes of this relative failure were identified: the length of the negotiations and the complexity of the programme procedures, the multiannual nature of certain operations, the limited administrative capacity of the meda countries, together with, it must be said, the lack of administrative resources of the executive commission to manage this programme, which obliged it to delegate to technical assistance offices, whose intervention was not conclusive. meda ii does not simply promote the creation of a free trade area at the mediterranean level by 2010, but adds a social, cultural and environmental dimension to mediterranean economic cooperation. the programme has a total financial envelope of eur 12.75 billion for the period 2000-06, divided between the european union and loans from the european investment bank. in brief, on the basis of the documents we have presented, the analysis of the situation leads us to draw the following conclusions. firstly, we see a clear improvement in meda ii compared to meda i, thanks to the creation of the europe aid cooperation office for external relations. the overall ratio of payments to commitments for meda i has thus risen from 26% to 37.4% in 2000, 53% in 2001 and 92.9% in 2002, or 59% overall for meda ii. this was achieved by dismantling technical assistance offices and setting up eight delegations (algeria, tunisia, morocco, egypt, jordan, syria, lebanon and the west bank), with one representation for gaza only. these delegations are more operational, with commission representatives and well-identified resource centres in each country. secondly, the comitology has been simplified. a methodological guide was established in march 2002. thirdly, as we have repeatedly recommended, parliament is very attentive to the link between the allocation of aid and the respect of human rights policy by the various countries, on which we ask for an annual report. fourthly, we want regular monitoring of the democratic expression in the choice of projects, not just through bilateral negotiations between the european union and the states concerned, but also by ensuring the participation of civil society, ngos and respect for gender criteria, particularly with regard to the participation of women. fifthly, we stress the need to develop south-south relations further than bilateral relations, which still absorb more than 85% of the appropriations. sixth, we take into account the ongoing work of the european convention to address the five challenges for the meda countries: demography, employment and migration, globalisation, the scarcity of natural resources and the environmental challenge, human rights. seventhly, we suggest using the sixth framework programme for r & d to carry out research in the field of environment and agriculture to ensure food sovereignty, especially water management, and to put more emphasis on renewable energy. we want more attention to be paid to agricultural diversity, to the implementation of projects for farmers, traders, consumers and smes. finally, we want all the means of the information and communication society to be developed, in particular electronic communication. finally, we should note that all this meda action is now taking place in the difficult context of the post-war situation in iraq, the resolution of the difficult problems in the middle east, the peace process, in particular between israel and palestine, and the new balance established by the treaty of nice with enlargement to twenty-five, in relation to which we must continue to ensure that it is not a pretext for penalizing mediterranean cooperation. this is why we support the creation of a euro-mediterranean foundation for dialogue between cultures and civilizations, as well as the migration observatory, the consideration of the creation of a euro-mediterranean investment bank and a euro-mediterranean parliamentary assembly with a structuring role in a well-integrated and monitored euro-mediterranean cooperation policy.
mr president, the proposal for guidelines for employment policies which the commission is presenting to parliament for consultation is a document based on pious generalities: improving the overall employment rate, that of women and the elderly, improving the quality and productivity of work, strengthening social cohesion and integration, all generalities which we have heard a hundred times already, which teach us nothing and which, no doubt, will also teach nothing to the governments of the member states. the coordinated employment strategy could have been useful, but it would have required going into greater detail, talking about more specific problems and comparing countries. it should have been noted, for example, that the unemployment rate in the eurozone countries is approaching 9%, while that of the non-euro countries is close to 5%. is there really no conclusion to be drawn from this? even within the euro area, the differences are very wide. apart from luxembourg, which is an exceptional case, we see, at one extreme, austria at 4.2% or ireland at 4.5% and, at the other extreme, france at 9.3% and spain at 11.9%. in the face of such differences, can we really draw guidelines that apply to all without falling into abstraction or even artificiality? i would prefer that the spirit of open coordination, which is that of diversity, the exchange of good practice, be better respected and that there be concrete talk about successful experiences that should be disseminated.
mr president, mr hernández mollar's report is full of good intentions and we will probably vote for it, but it is also full of a very curious naivety. how can we conclude legal agreements - and even discuss the law - with a state - the united states - that ignores and flouts the law, the very notion of law? how can we envisage the extradition of our nationals to a country, a state, which does not comply, or is increasingly not complying, with the same legal standards as ours? this is the question raised in this report. we are dealing with a state which applies the death penalty and to which we are considering extraditing nationals. a state that does not respect fundamental rights, in particular in the context of anti-terrorism laws; a state that is steadily increasing the number of cases brought before its military courts, so that we may eventually see citizens of our nations tried by a us military court; a state whose regulations on the transfer of personal data flagrantly violate our laws, so that, in the end, we may ask why we are passing laws on this subject, as on many others, if it is to blame a state that deliberately violates them. a state, last but not least, which behaves as in the old days when tribes kidnapped citizens of our nations, imprisoned them without even bothering to charge them - i am thinking of guantanamo, of course, but i believe there are other examples - and even, certainly, engaged in some acts of torture, far from the curiosity of journalists, alas! in reality, we are dealing with a state which does not respect the law and we have, in my view, no legal, at least judicial and criminal, link with it. i doubt, however, that the european union is capable of adopting a firm stance, since it has itself fallen into this trap, and is observing a kind of passivity towards the united states which will eventually lead us into overwhelming situations. we can see some examples of this.

in writing. - the european parliament has just rejected the proposal for a council decision which was intended to lay down practical arrangements for the application of the directive on the mutual recognition between member states of decisions which each of them may have to take in order to remove third-country nationals. fortunately, parliament was consulted only for its opinion, and this draft will therefore finally be able to continue its adoption procedure. we believe that it is justified in substance, and the european parliament is trying to start a bad fight. the majority of this house argued that article 63 (3) of the ec treaty could not constitute a valid legal basis: it does mention the adoption of common measures for the repatriation of persons staying illegally, but this provision would allow for substantive measures, not procedural measures. this is a peculiar distinction, which even the legal affairs committee was unable to accept. in reality, the european parliament is showing its usual pro-immigration bias: what it dislikes most about this project is that it could facilitate the repatriation of illegal immigrants. of course, we didn't follow him.

in writing. - lifelong learning, work, older people are very important topics on which this report focuses and employment strategies are essential. we want more jobs, but we also want better jobs. the fight against poverty is fundamental. we cannot accept that at the moment there are still families living below the poverty line. it's a matter of solidarity. the objectives to be achieved must be attainable. we must invest in quality services so that women can reconcile family and professional life. a more effective partnership must unite the member states. to promote women's participation in social life and the labour market, a series of concrete actions should be defined to provide services that meet the needs of childcare, but also help families with dependants. it is important to invest in public services to meet the needs of families and society as a whole, and it is essential that all relevant actors are involved in the implementation of the employment strategy. in addition, efficient public services require fair taxes.
in writing. - the committee on employment and social affairs proposes that we adopt the draft council directive establishing a comprehensive employment policy for the european union by 2010. this policy is part of the lisbon strategy to make europe the most competitive and dynamic knowledge-based economy in the world, capable of sustainable economic growth accompanied by a quantitative and qualitative improvement in employment and greater social cohesion. the amendments to this legislative resolution improve the original text in some respects, in particular with regard to the objectives of gender equality and the consideration of qualifications and vocational training. however, these amendments do not call into question the liberal logic of lowering corporate taxation and flexibility of labour. more importantly, the resolution maintains the objective of achieving a five-year increase in the effective average retirement age at community level by 2010, even as millions of people in france and other european countries demonstrate against this logic and for the safeguarding of their pension systems. for this reason i did not vote in favour of the report.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to reiterate, on behalf of all my colleagues in the french socialist delegation and on my own behalf, our position on the report on the status of members of parliament. the completion of the current enlargement process makes its adoption urgent. we are in favour of the principles underlying this approach, even if we disagree with certain provisions concerning the amount and taxation of members' remuneration. it was necessary to improve the readability of the members' compensation system, but the proposed text does not seem to us to fully meet this imperative. the french socialist delegation therefore wished to amend the text by voting on amendment 8 to article 7 of the draft statute, an amendment which it had tabled with other political groups. in our view, an intelligent implementation of this principle implies that benefits should be adapted to the differences in living standards between member states, even if some inequalities need to be corrected. we regret that this amendment was not adopted. in the current context, an increase in the allowances of members of the european parliament is likely to be extremely unwelcome, at a time when the legitimacy of the pay gap between the economic and political elites and the rest of the population is in question.
in writing. - under the new article 190 (5) of the ec treaty, introduced by the treaty of nice, our parliament has just prepared a draft unified statute for members of the european parliament, which should be submitted to the council for decision by qualified majority, and no longer by unanimity. the text deals with a number of technical questions which had to be settled in any event within the framework of the autonomy granted to the european parliament to organise its proper internal functioning. but it also goes much further by introducing a statute which unifies all aspects of the member's situation at european level and cuts essential links with his or her country of origin, including remuneration. we have said it a hundred times, the member of the european parliament must be paid - as today - by the citizens of his country, who elected him and whom he is supposed to represent. the current approach of the european parliament implicitly corresponds to the objective of establishing a super-state, where meps would represent the union as a whole, and not the country that elected them. this is a fundamental change, albeit a surreptitious one, of which our electorate is once again unaware. we refused to vote on this bill out of loyalty to them.
in writing. - at a time when the peoples of europe are facing so many difficulties (unemployment, insecurity, precariousness, etc.), i am not convinced that they will appreciate the value of parliament's determination to adopt its uniform statute for members of the european parliament. i think this is a completely secondary concern, for both material and ideological reasons. as regards the material aspect, there is no point in going into it at length, but i consider it indecent to take this opportunity to give meps a whole series of exorbitant perks and privileges. the ideological aspect is clear: the primary objective of this status is to completely detach the elected representative from his or her home state. even though we, the representatives of our respective peoples, are legally in this parliament, we are presented as representatives of a mythical european people, in other words, the uprooted. all this is part of the logic under which this parliament once voted in favour of a uniform electoral procedure, the principle of transnational electoral constituencies or european political parties. this report proves once again that euro-federalism is far from the reality of the peoples.
in writing. - since my election to the european parliament i have heard a great deal about the status of members. i think that our colleague mr rothley and the whole legal affairs committee have spent a lot of time and energy on this, too much in my opinion, because, as with the statute for european political parties, i have the impression that it is a lot of money. these are not the great democratic advances that will bring the european union closer to its citizens. what is the point of these proposals which amend a text of superior legal value and which will therefore remain inapplicable? what is the purpose of this attempt at uniformity which creates a gap between the elected representatives of the present 15 member states, the new and the old, and those of the 10 states which will join us in a year's time? many want status to improve an image tarnished by the abuses of a few. unfortunately, nothing in this statute can be considered as an effective improvement in transparency. on the other hand, if we offer the representatives of the peoples of the member states a european system which derogates from national rights, we will only widen the gap which we are trying to bridge. that is why i voted against this draft statute.
in writing. - we voted against the mann report firstly because it calls for the complete 'communitisation' of the european union's trade policy, which would be harmful as i said in yesterday's debate. but we also reject this report because of the commercial strategy it advocates, which we believe is wrong on at least two important points. first, it makes it quite clear that the objective of opening up international trade is to lead to global integration, including 'regulatory convergence'. while it is possible to support the idea of increased trade for the benefit of all, it must also be added - which is not stated in the report - that each country, or each regional area, has the right to protect its model of society. secondly, it is far too lenient towards the european union's trade policy, and in particular its adoption of all sorts of free trade areas. these areas are useful if they reflect the desire for controlled openness. but in reality, as far as europe is concerned, they are so numerous and so intertwined that no one knows their real effects and that they are rather becoming a cause of uncontrolled trade relations.
in writing. - through a commercial strategy, is it a certain world view that prevails: pure trade liberalization leading to the aggravation of inequalities or the fight for real development? however, as the mann report reiterates, the rationale behind the establishment of regional free trade areas (ftas) is essentially to ensure political and economic stability for the eu with the countries concerned (the 'strategic geopolitical interests') so that nothing interferes with the sacred free movement of goods, services and capital. but what about people's access to fundamental rights? what about an assessment of the social, environmental, cultural and economic consequences of these liberalisations? what about genuine cooperation on equal terms and respecting the specificities of each partner? the wto rules should not police the eu's still privileged relations with its partners. the eu cannot reduce its policy towards entire countries and regions to the prospect of free trade, as is too often the case in the mediterranean, for example, when there is an urgent need to establish a genuine political dialogue and to build economic and social cooperation free of any conception of domination.
in writing. - with mr piétrasanta's report, the european parliament must give its opinion on the state of relations between europe and its mediterranean partners. this report raises the fundamental issues underlying the partnership and provides relevant answers to which i subscribe, including the need to emphasise the political dimension of the euro-mediterranean partnership to promote democratisation and peace, support for mediterranean civil societies, the systematic integration of the issue of human rights in monitoring, the establishment of a genuine euro-mediterranean parliamentary assembly at the next euromed ministerial conference in naples in december 2003. i will vote in favour of this report to strongly support the integration of these objectives into the meda programme. but this programme is not enough today to summarise the relations between the eu and its mediterranean partners. indeed, no additional resources are currently envisaged (for 2003, the meda regional financing plan will have €32 million and the 'euro-mediterranean investment and partnership facility' €25 million), while the disproportion between europe's financial effort for the ten new members and its commitment to the mediterranean is spectacular, if not scandalous: €185 per capita aid for the east, half a euro per head for the mediterranean. in writing. - the eu-us agreements on judicial cooperation in criminal matters and extradition are absolutely necessary, particularly in the fight against terrorism. however, they raise for the first time the question of the interpretation of articles 38 and 24 of the eu treaty, introduced by the treaty of nice, concerning the conclusion of international agreements by the european union in the fields of the second and third pillars. these articles were drafted and adopted with culpable negligence, despite the warnings i had given in my counter-report on the treaty of nice. we are now seeing the consequences: national parliaments once had the right to ratify such international conventions, but now they lose it, without the european parliament gaining an equivalent right. it is true that the states are now seeking to regain national powers of review through the 'constitutional reserve' which may give them the opportunity to come back before their national parliaments. but it is a very imperfect solution. this is the result of badly negotiated treaties. the convention on the future of europe should correct this and bring national parliaments back into the game. unfortunately, it seems to be going the other way.
in writing. - while this agreement could have been a real step forward in the fight against major international crime and terrorism, this parliament thinks it useful to attach extravagant conditions and humiliating considerations to its support for the united states! the reservations about the lack of democratic control or the requirement of a reference to the charter of fundamental rights seem almost quaint in the light of the serious accusations against the united states. it is almost like a dream to read that the judicial system of some states in the united states does not offer the same level of guarantees as the measures of the european court of human rights and the eu are intended to provide for the member states of the european union! and what about these comments about the inappropriateness of an agreement with the united states, when several citizens of the union are being held at the military base in guantanamo illegally and without any guarantee of a fair trial. when it reaches such proportions and results in such absurdities - how can terrorists be equated with ordinary prisoners? - evangelicalism borders on stupidity.
mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, as a double rapporteur, i shall begin, if you will allow me, by presenting the report on the reform of the cereals com adopted by a very large majority in our committee on agriculture and rural development, and then proceed with the presentation of my second report, also adopted by a very large majority, on the reform of the dried fodder com. let us start with the cereals com. in its reform proposal, the european commission, completely departing from the framework of the mid-term review of agenda 2000, envisaged a real dismantling of all the essential constituent elements of the cmc. what are the commission's proposals? firstly, the reduction, or rather the continuation of the reduction, of the intervention price until it is below the cost price, which is an approach that is both uneconomic and unsustainable. then, the abolition of monthly increases. secondly, the abolition of intervention for rye, the abolition of the minimum price for starch potatoes, the abolition of production refunds for starch. the committee on agriculture and rural development considered that this dismantling of the oldest and most emblematic of the common market organisations was neither appropriate nor justified. as regards the intervention price, i, as rapporteur, had proposed that account be taken of inflation, which has been at 25.5% since the 1992 reform and which brings the actual fall in internal cereals prices, in real terms, to 56%. the intervention price for cereals, it should be recalled, is an index of the income of hundreds of thousands of farmers. our committee did not want a further fall, which is not justified by anything, not even by the evolution of world prices, which the commission itself believes will rise in the coming years. the absence of the price reductions recommended by our committee does not call for any financial compensation and therefore renders the degressive approach pointless. as regards the monthly increases, our committee on agriculture and rural development wanted to point out that they correspond to a real economic and financial burden, that of storage, including the modernisation of silos and their updating to standards, particularly in terms of safety, and that their abolition would amount to an additional, uncompensated, reduction in the intervention price. consequently, consistency required that the two commission proposals concerning the intervention price and the monthly increases be treated in the same way. as regards rye, for which there is a real problem of surpluses, we propose to reduce the amounts allocated to intervention so that in future the cultivation of this cereal can be concentrated in regions where it is the last line of defence before the barren and where no profitable alternative exists. as regards starch and potato starch, commissioner, we find it difficult to understand the european commission's insistence on wanting to abolish the mechanisms that allow european industry to compete on equal terms with imports. this is a real gift to the starch producers of third countries, without any counterpart for the european union. the proposals of the committee on agriculture and rural development therefore do not go in the direction of the negative measures put forward by the commission, which do not seem to us to offer any positive development prospects for the cereals sector. now, if you will, let us turn to the common organization of the market in dried fodder. i have never before seen a statement of reasons for a proposal from the european commission based on such weak arguments. on the basis of an outdated remark in a report by the court of auditors, the executive commission intended to abolish this common organisation of the market as from the 2008/09 marketing year on the grounds that, and i quote the court of auditors' report: 'this production is based mainly on the use of fossil fuels for dehydration and, in some member states, on the use of irrigation'. what a light-hearted and careless way of putting the future of an entire industry in question on such a thin foundation! and not just any sector, a sector which provides 15% of the forage protein produced in the community, a sector which concerns 150 000 producers and 500 000 hectares, a sector which, for its dehydration component, consists of 350 units for processing and packaging fodder, the majority of which are owned by farmers in the form of cooperatives, and which concerns no less than 15 000 jobs. have you calculated, commissioner, the amount of public rural development budgets that would have to be mobilised to maintain the activity and jobs in rural areas that the euthanasia of this sector would destroy? our committee on agriculture therefore had no difficulty in convincing itself that, in the context of the union's shortage of fodder protein, it would be completely irresponsible to abolish aid for dried fodder. if parliament adopts the report proposed to it by its committee on agriculture, it will clearly reaffirm the position it had already adopted in the stevenson report, which called on the commission to find and quickly put in place the means necessary to reduce this very serious handicap, this strategic dependence, this monstrous deficit in vegetable protein which reaches more than 75% of our needs. the americans, i would remind you, did not have the courage and did not hesitate to introduce, after the blair house agreements, direct aid for soybeans without the wto getting upset. our committee on agriculture also considered that the environmental impact of dried fodder could not be limited to a vague static consideration of the consumption of fossil fuels. if all economic activities which use fossil fuels were to be eliminated, you would have had to walk from brussels, commissioner. by contrast, alfalfa, which accounts for more than 80% of dried fodder production in the union, has outstanding qualities in two key areas - soil renewal and the economics of plant protection products. in addition, no alfalfa varieties are genetically modified in europe. this production, which ensures that the feed produced is perfectly traceable, thus replaces imports, which raise many questions about gmos. as for dehydration, the use of fossil fuels has already been significantly reduced in the past years. but it is true that there is still room for improvement. we therefore propose, in agreement with the industry, the conclusion of progress contracts through which dehydration units can commit themselves to improving their performance, their yield and their energy balance. we believe it is more constructive to introduce eco-conditionality schemes for this sector than to withdraw all aid. finally, our committee felt that further agronomic and environmental progress could be made by this profession in this sector. this is why we propose the creation of a research fund funded by a small levy on the aid allocated to the sector. these, mr president, commissioner, seem to us to be the positive directions in which the executive commission should move, thus offering a particularly sensitive and strategic sector a very different perspective from the destruction, without any other form of trial, of a common market organization which has so far managed to preserve one of the few sectors available to the union in the field of plant proteins.

- mr president-in-office of the council, mr commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, the mid-term review was a great adventure and it is not a bad thing that we, the members of the committee on agriculture and rural development, have reached a compromise which, i think, could satisfy the farmers. we wanted the political guidelines to be readable by all and that is why we provided the cunha report with a clear preamble. for us greens, the positive aspect of this compromise is that it strengthens rural development. the serious improvement proposed today allows european farmers to retain the positive aspects of multi-functionality by strengthening rural development, with the modulation system making it possible to move from the first to the second pillar. i am thinking in particular of amendment no 12 to rule 44. this modulation proposal uses a territorial criterion for the application of different percentage points taking into account disadvantaged areas. as the rapporteur says in his explanatory statement, the objective must be to strengthen the structure of producer organizations. in addition, this amendment obliges the member states to commit themselves to rural development, since they will only receive 100% of the eaggf guarantee section amounts if they commit themselves to compulsory national co-financing. this will encourage states to properly finance all the social, food quality and environmental aspects of rural development. in this respect, the model of territorial exploitation contracts introduced by france was an excellent precursor. it should be noted, as this is essential for the future, that the member states can use this modulation to finance the national contribution to the installation - as necessary - of young farmers. similarly, states can choose - and we believe they should - to finance compensatory payments to less-favoured areas, as well as areas subject to environmental constraints or agro-environmental measures. all this without prejudice to the overall amount allocated by the state to the second pillar. this strengthening of rural development is therefore in the right direction for two reasons: the first is to strengthen good agricultural practices, more extensive practices, protecting consumer health, respecting the environment and biodiversity and producing good social added value; the second is to protect the rural world from the vagaries of aggressive trade liberalism advocated by the wto. thus, the multifunctional specificities of european agriculture, or the enhancement of products specific to a particular region, will be able to continue to be remunerated under the second pillar, which best protects small producers in disadvantaged areas. in addition, the difference in the rate of decline in direct payments between fragile areas, where it is 6%, and other areas, where it reaches 8%. this strengthening of the second pillar must, if it is to be fully effective, preserve the milk quotas which have proved their effectiveness in safeguarding mountain livestock. natural pastures must also be protected and strengthened, but in addition, we must continue to support fodder and, more generally, protein crops necessary for healthy and high-quality livestock farming - alfalfa mentioned by mr souchet - and maintain the necessary facilities. protein crops should therefore be able to be grown on all frozen land, since europe is in short supply in this area and the cultivation of plant proteins is beneficial for soil quality, the environment and the quality of animal feed. on the sensitive issue of decoupling, it was necessary to decide between those who wanted total decoupling and those who did not want anything. it seems to us that the compromise which is being made step by step opens up a perspective which everyone can accept.

- commissioner fischler, you have a lot of talent, firstly in the perfect packaging of your reform. you call it a mid-term review, which is a mid-term liquidation. and you justify it with popular, i dare say populist clichés: animal welfare, sustainable development, food quality or environmental protection. in reality, rural development will not be sustainable, because young people will not settle down. as for quality, it will be the world's food that we will be aligning our prices with. but the technical assembly of your cap 2004 is also very talented. you're presenting it as a new development, thanks to decoupling. but already in 1992 farmers' incomes were decoupled from agricultural prices, and now direct aid is decoupled from agricultural production itself. the reform is basically summed up in the following: we pay the hand and the knife. but how long will we continue to pay out these decoupled, partially decoupled, modulated, controlled, audited and 'eco-conditioned' direct aids? and that's where you have a lot of talent, even a supreme, machiavellian talent. the cap is now 40 years old. your objective is to make it last for another 10 years, in 2013-2014, and all the curves stop in 2013. the cap is only funded until 2012. milk quotas are stopped around 2013-2014. in 2013, the majority of farmers who are now 50 years old will be retired. in the meantime, they're quiet for 10 years. and if they're quiet for 10 years, they'll be paid for 10 years, except for the young. so they have no reason to protest! and if they don't protest, there's no rioting in the countryside. if there are no disturbances in the countryside, the french, who are the main opponents of the reform, have no reason not to vote for it. and the united states itself, in cancun, will accept your reform with the group of 15, because it is a moratorium. as a result, the distinction between compulsory and non-compulsory expenditure has been removed from the european constitution itself. consequently, parliament will have the final say on agricultural spending and here there is an ultra-liberal majority. therefore, here, before 2013, a majority will abolish decoupled, partially decoupled, modulated or non-modulated direct aids. and the european farmers will be eliminated because they will be in a market where the american farmers will be financially watered down. we shall then be left with a small-scale agriculture, which will necessarily be austrian. that is why, commissioner, you are the perfect man, you are the man of the hour, you are sissi the farmer.
- mr president, by accepting, even with a number of reservations, the logic of decoupling proposed by the european commission, the cunha report invites us to take a first step in the wrong direction. why would you do that? because decoupling, by introducing a radical cut-off between the farmer's remuneration and the act of production, would transform direct aids into rents linked to the land, fixed in their amount, constituting a kind of negative tax which is difficult to justify in the eyes of citizens and taxpayers, increasing the price of land in an undue and uneconomic way, thus making it more difficult for young people to enter the farming profession and to settle down. decoupling would also have negative consequences on the regional location of crops and would therefore be a factor of relocation rather than of land use planning. the decoupling is designed to improve our negotiating position at the wto, but it is difficult to see how the announcement of reform before the negotiations could give us more weight. finally, by removing any link between production and state aid, we are prohibiting any measures to guide and control the markets, which is the basis of all our coms. so we must abandon this crazy and useless idea of decoupling. total decoupling would be a total error and partial decoupling a partial error. partial decoupling would be an incomprehensible compromise, a bureaucratic monster and an unsustainable system. it would make a cap even more complex, which it is urgent to simplify. it would create a new cursor, the decoupling rate, which many hands would certainly move towards total decoupling at the expense of our agriculture, our independence and our food security.

you were right, commissioner, to prefer movement to the status quo, anticipation to waiting. your reform is courageous, because it breaks with the logic of incentives to production which it advocates through decoupling. it is ambitious, by reinforcing the multifunctional character of european agriculture. it is relevant in the light of the future wto deadlines and the forthcoming enlargement of europe. but it is also unfair, as its inspiration is exclusively continental and it does not take sufficient account of the diversity of regional situations, particularly with regard to production in the outermost regions. these regions have not yet reached the original cap objective of achieving a certain degree of agricultural self-sufficiency. their markets are far from saturated. they need incentives to develop their holdings. the proposed measures, if applied mechanically to the outermost regions, would undoubtedly put a brake on the dynamism we have seen in recent years. it is not a question of putting the outermost regions in a bubble, it is simply a question of taking their specificity into account. the legal basis is article 299 (2). the political will is still needed. the committee on agriculture and rural development of the european parliament took up its responsibilities by adopting, on 21 may, an amendment which i proposed in order not to subject the outermost regions to the systematic and mechanical application of the reform. the commission and the council must now take theirs. while we must learn from history and adapt our agricultural policy to the challenges of the 21st century, it would be intolerable if, in the name of generous principles, this reform were to be the death knell of the union's most fragile farms.
