the signing of the treaty of accession of ten new countries and the probable conclusion of the work of the convention. but i want to focus on a third major event, which transcends all the others: the union's identity crisis has burst into flames. what do we want to do together? this existential question remains more than ever unanswered. this is true of our ambitions within the union. do we really want to set ourselves the objective, as the convention bureau proposes to inscribe in the future constitution of the union, of balanced economic growth and social justice, full employment, a high standard of living, social protection, equal opportunities for all? in that case, why refuse to open the debate on a change in the european central bank's priorities? nor price stability at a time when recession is in danger, but securing jobs, training and pensions for all, financing useful infrastructure, such as large-scale railways, and more generally genuinely fair and sustainable development. why confine public services to the precarious status of an exception to the free competition rule, instead of making the promotion of high-quality services of general interest a priority of the union as such, and thus appearing in the constitution? why should we continue to exclude any prospect of taxing capital movements and financial income? this kind of blatant contradiction between the affirmation of objectives that meet expectations and the refusal of the means to achieve them is at the heart of the crisis of confidence of our citizens in the european institutions. what do we really want? we must answer frankly and take responsibility for our choices so that europeans can weigh in on the debate in full knowledge of the facts. as albert camus wrote, "to call things by their wrong names is to add to the misery of the world". this identity crisis is equally evident in the union's role in the world. we've known that since the war on iraq. before the conflict, the dissenting but frank voices at least allowed our public opinion to see clearly and to be involved in this confrontation of options. they have done so spectacularly and so closely, from west to west, that we see this as a break in the history of the union, the only hope for future change. on the other hand, since the demonstration of strength by the world superpower, in defiance of the law and the will of the international community, everything seems to be happening as if the european union were rebuilding its unity on the basis of resigned or enthusiastic subordination to the strongest. the european parliament has been asked to take a decision on the question of the future of the european union, and the council has been asked to take a decision on the future of the european union. we received confirmation this morning, and i regret it. if george bush decides to monopolize the management of the middle east road map, with all the risks inherent in his complicity with sharon and his reservations about the very substance of the commitments to be made, the european union, which is the co-initiator of this fragile hope for peace, is thrown off the stage without a hitch. the united states rejects the international criminal court, maintains exceptional military courts, and, as mr enrique barón crespo has pointed out, holds european citizens in a zone of non-absolute law at guantanamo, but the council is preparing an extradition and mutual legal assistance agreement with washington, turning a blind eye to all these abuses of the law. if our american partners renew the offensive to lift the moratorium on gmos in the name of defending, i quote, 'the interests of american agriculture', europe immediately begins to waver, while being careful not to apply the trade retaliatory measures authorised by the wto itself against the ill-considered tax advantages granted to exporters across the atlantic. for all these reasons, my group is of the opinion, mr president, that the greek presidency would be doing europe a service by clearly putting the question of what we want to do together and what means we are using to achieve this on the table of the european council in thessaloniki. in any case, in our societies, the question is now being asked and that is a very good thing. i quoted a french author earlier. i will conclude with a german quote from the great hölderlin: "where danger increases, salvation also increases". the danger to europe is clear. let us be the ones who try to save it.
- mr president, at the european council in thessaloniki on 20 and 21 june, the president of the convention should give his conclusions, but he will no doubt ask for a prolongation of the work. i think we should consider this proposal with caution. it is essential that governments do not get caught between a delayed date for the conclusion of the convention and an unalterable deadline for the end of the igc. the convention is an interesting forum for discussion, but the fact remains that only democratically responsible governments should have the last word at the intergovernmental conference and should not be tied up in advance. in this respect, we strongly disagree with the commission's request, expressed earlier, that the convention should submit to the council a single text without any alternative. this means that the council would not have freedom of choice, that democratic power would be transferred from the governments to a convention without democratic legitimacy. we do not want that europe. we want the opposite: to re-root europe in its nations. the work of the convention - to draft a complete european constitution - is indeed enormous, but it is the convention that has chosen to do so. the mandate given by the council of nice did not speak of drafting a constitution and that of laeken mentioned this possibility only conditionally and in the long term, i.e. not for the time being. we think those councils were right. europe is not built to adopt the constitution of a super-state and that is why the convention is currently facing so many difficulties. the result is a voluminous document, difficult to master, full of problems, which will have to be refocused on the real priority for europe at the moment, the one that has been too much neglected since the beginning at the convention: better control by national democracies. this may require a return to the original community method, now largely forgotten, which was based on two pillars: the pillar of encouraging cooperation, in particular with the commission, and the pillar of respect for national sovereignty, in particular with the council. the fundamental flaw in the construction of europe today is the weakening of this second pillar. it is now necessary to strengthen it if we are to re-establish the link with the peoples, with national democracies. in this respect, the convention is steadily going backwards. the control of subsidiarity by the national parliaments has been stripped of its meaning. the peoples' congress is gone. the commission is strongly opposed to the permanent presidency of the council. we must put an end to this continuous and disastrous undermining of national democracies by rehabilitating the council and giving national parliaments a right of veto.

in writing. - i share the rapporteur's concern to clean up the fleet of vessels carrying dangerous goods. the commission itself admits that more than 4 000 vessels are considered to be at risk. it is urgent to require shipowners to withdraw these garbage vessels and to comply with stricter technical and social standards. however, in view of the recent shipwrecks of the erika and the prestige, i consider that the european union is still too timid in the necessary fight against maritime insecurity. the proposed deadlines are still unsatisfactory: the minimum age for sailing on the prestige class (category 1) oil tankers is set at 23 years from 2005; for category 3 and 2 ships (generally built between 1982 and 1986), the age limit is 28 years from 2010. even with these measures, the risk of disaster remains. instead, all dangerous ships should have been banned from navigation and public policy should have shifted production from shipyards to the construction and development of modern and safe ships. the european union should have been given new tools in its fight against the complacency system. but above all, member states should make a real commitment to applying existing legislation. without this minimum, all prescriptions sound like wishful thinking.

- madam president, i did not know that idealism was the dominant philosophy in the european parliament. it is not enough to say day, night and morning that we want a transatlantic relationship to be one. the first transatlantic relationship was determined by the reality of the opposition - this is an idea expressed by mr patten at the end of his speech - between communist totalitarianism and the west. this situation died with the collapse of communism. so if we want transatlantic relations, we must redefine them, we must ask ourselves whether the united states and europe today necessarily have the same interests. is it compulsory as it was in the communist era? once the question is asked, it is clear that, geostrategically, economically, the americans and the europeans do not share the same vision and do not have the same interests. on this basis, a new transatlantic relationship cannot be a charm - we want it, we want it, we want it - but it must be defined in a totally new way. let's take a very simple example. today we have the euro. if we are sincere, the euro is a currency that separates europe from the united states, because the euro is the first currency competing with the dollar. so, economically, strategically, we have different interests and if we want to get out of the economic slump, if we want to get a revival through europe, we must at some point ask, at the global level, a question that is central to europe: are we doomed to pay our energy bills, our oil bills, in dollars? the rapporteur. - madam president, madam commissioner, i am happy to present my report this evening - in a rather empty chamber, you will admit it with me - because the issue of women and sport, which is the responsibility of both the committee on women's rights and equal opportunities and the committee on culture, youth, education, the media and sport, is at the crossroads of my commitments in this parliament. it is an own-initiative report which, in short, deals with the foundations of our democracy, since sport itself has been one of the key elements in the construction of democracy since antiquity. i am glad that this report will be completed under the greek presidency. i would like to briefly recall the various contextual elements of this own-initiative report, as i proposed it at the outset. first, it must be acknowledged that there is a very wide disparity between the situations of men and women, girls and boys, in the matter of sport and access to sport. whether it is high-level sport or recreational sport. there is a disparity here which we are forced to acknowledge. secondly, sport is and remains a space for self-fulfilment, at all ages of life, and in this respect the issue of equal opportunities is of particular importance. thirdly, since there are disparities in situations, it is true that to give equal opportunities to little girls and boys, men and women and adolescents or young adults, it is necessary to take into account a rather difficult element: the disparity and asymmetry between the two sexes in relation to sport. some people will tell me that these findings are outdated. i would remind you that both the army and the police are required to organise competitions and to provide different performances for both sexes. this shows a kind of attempt, say, of equity between bodies that are not the same, to access the same opportunities. i have tried to explain this idea in particular in my recital m. it is very difficult, from different situations, to reach a situation of equality or balance, call it what you will. so, in my view, these three contextual elements have been the guiding principles behind the drafting of this report. i would remind you that a report on women and sport was presented to parliament 13 years ago. i had hoped to pioneer, but no, i must admit that others before me have raised this problem and i am glad of that. there are three areas where this equality of opportunity or self-realisation takes place: school, leisure and high-level sport. perhaps this is where i wanted to innovate in relation to the previous report. all three areas must be taken into account for the development of sport. schools are places of role models, places of education shared by boys and girls, and places where opportunities must be opened up rather than closed. all the professionals told me that the school plays a fundamental role in women's access to sport. the leisure area is for some - i would say especially for some - a luxury. in order to be able to exercise as a leisure activity, one must have the time, the means and the possibility of access to it. infrastructure for girls, adolescents, young women and women is much less important than for boys and men. the disparity is large given that for women who are already busy with their dual work and family lives, access to leisure sport is a luxury. that's a point i wanted to make. as for high-level sport, you have to know it first. it is not always easy to keep up with what is happening in women's top-level sport. the media don't always report it as they could, or as they should, or as we would like. in addition, there are health problems specific to women's high-level sports. hormonal imbalances and disorders can cause future difficulties in motherhood or premature aging. all the professionals have given me a lot of warning about these health problems. as one sociologist put it, contrary to popular belief, exercise is not necessarily good for health. finally, everyone stresses the need for women to be more involved in decision-making. it is also a fundamental element. in conclusion, i would like to say that i have been working a lot with the various political groups in recent times. i thank them for their availability. i also thank the greek presidency for organising a meeting on women and sport in thessaloniki on 8 march, which i attended. i would also like to thank the greek presidency for including my proposal for a 'women and sport' unit in its statement at the end of this meeting. i would also like to thank the ioc, which has been extremely helpful, and the european women and sport network (ews), which has been very helpful. the last idea i would like to express is in line with what everyone, all the professionals, have told me: please defend diversity in sport. this is our future. the report is called women and sport, but its objective is the mixing of men and women, girls and boys in this exercise which is a happiness and must remain a happiness for both sexes.

- the next item is the report (a5-0159/2003) by mrs jöns, on behalf of the committee on women's rights and equal opportunities, on breast cancer in the european union [2002/2279 (ini) ].
mr president, like you, i would like to greet our male colleagues in the house because, as mr mussa said, the pathology in question affects men too. because when this disease affects us, it affects our spouses, our families, our children. in addition, it is surrounded by a psychological climate which has an impact on the lives of those around us. the available data - even if they are difficult to compare, as our rapporteur points out, in the absence of uniform criteria - show that breast cancer is stagnating or increasing in different countries of the european union. this pathology is, as mentioned, one of the main causes of death among women aged 35 to 55, which is why early detection and comprehensive care of patients should be defined as european priorities. this is what mrs jöns' report tells us, which advocates the implementation of screening campaigns, carried out - and this is very, very important - in the framework of multidisciplinary units, which, if necessary, of course, allow medical care, but also psychological and social care, which is sometimes also an asset in treating the disease, by quality staff, during and after treatment. in france, a cancer steering committee published a report in january 2003, which recently led to the development of a national plan by the president of the republic to combat cancer, and which bears striking similarities to your report, both in terms of findings and objectives to be achieved. given the physical and psychological stresses of breast cancer treatment and to ensure an optimal quality of life for women, it is essential to act upstream to encourage women to undergo regular screening at all ages through appropriate information and prevention policies. this is why we cannot but agree with the need to coordinate national policies, to continue developing european guidelines for mammography, to intensify research and review the issue of gene patenting by the european patent office and to set up registries other than the existing national registries. the report by karin jöns, as adopted by the committee on women's rights and equal opportunities, therefore seems to meet this objective. that is why the epp group decided to vote in favour of this report, because it shows a certain courage, i must say, and since we are fortunate to have a woman commissioner today and we know that the fifth framework programme has set up eur 400 million, why not make cancer, madam commissioner, a major european cause as from 2004? it would be a mobilizing response to the proposal for a conference made by mrs jöns.
- mr president, madam commissioner, we have here today a proposal for a regulation which is an indispensable and very important element, as well as a logical consequence of the effort to improve food safety undertaken since the various crises which we have unfortunately experienced in the food sector in europe. although - and i would like to remind you - the european food chain is one of the safest in the world, we felt it necessary to adopt provisions on traceability and labelling. all the decisions that are taken are a sign of the political will of the european parliament, but they are of no use if they are not properly implemented. in the field of food safety, as in many others, what is often lacking is effective enforcement of existing laws or regulations. i congratulate our rapporteur, mr schnellhardt, on the quality of his work on this subject, with the aim of establishing a rigorous monitoring system for products of european origin as well as for imported products. the new concept that has been much discussed in this house, the farm-to-table concept developed by the european commission, will only be fully satisfactory if there is continuous and sufficient monitoring of food placed on the market from production to consumption. to restore consumer confidence, consumers must be able to say to themselves when they buy meat or any other foodstuff that they can rely without fear on the information provided on the product label. the consumer must be able to be sure that the product he is going to consume is healthy. to do this, as our rapporteur has explained, it is essential to develop both independent official controls and to strengthen the own responsibility of the operators in the sector. i would like to stress the role of veterinarians and the necessary independence of inspection activities. we also need to use common sense in adopting regulations which take account of the size of the companies and do not penalise small farms, because we have this problem with smes. i am glad that amendments have been voted in this direction, just as i am glad that the commissioner has mentioned the need for flexibility. it is clear that these adjustments must not be made at the expense of consumer safety. the proper transmission of information and the regular updating of the lists of approved establishments will greatly facilitate controls and coordination between member states. i think that all of this is done with the aim of building consumer confidence and should ensure that safer products are brought to market for each and every one of us consumers.
- mr president, madam commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, the key point in food safety is the official control of products of animal origin intended for human consumption, which is the subject of the schnellhardt report we are considering today. the four annexes to the regulation deal with fresh meat, molluscs, fisheries and milk and milk products. i shall simply mention the few points which are most important to me. first, a derogation must be included in the regulation for primary production. i believe that the primary production of food for private use, as well as the direct supply by the producer to the final consumer or to local shops and restaurants in small quantities, should be considered as traditional food production which should benefit from specific marketing methods. i therefore support amendments nos 11 and 12 from the committee on the environment, public health and consumer policy. in addition, the competent authorities in each member state are, in my view, best placed to assess the situation and to issue prescriptions which will ensure the best protection for the consumer. it seems to me also essential to incorporate the concept of small craft establishments into the regulation, which should allow for sufficient flexibility without calling into question or reducing consumer food safety. this concept of small establishments guarantees the maintenance of small slaughterhouses distributed in a balanced way throughout the territory. so let us not go to too strict and too burdensome regulations, which will lead to the closure of local slaughterhouses. the maintenance of these slaughterhouses would simplify matters since there would be no need to legislate on the maximum distances and hours of transport of livestock by truck. let's face it: only by shortening the food chain will we make progress. to this end, it is important to reward producers and operators with a better balance sheet result by granting them a reduction in the costs of official controls. this must not, of course, be at the expense of food security. the issue of licensing is another difficult one. who is to blame? community or national level? so where does subsidiarity fit in? i prefer the option of dual competence which will require member states to keep the list of approved establishments up to date, while highlighting their own national control regulations. on the other hand, it seems to me counterproductive for the commission to require the member states to transmit the names of establishments in a single format by means of telematics, since the simple exchange of lists between member states is sufficient. similarly, there is no justification for the standardisation of administrative sanctions for breaches of hygiene principles. administrative closures of slaughterhouses, such as the publication of penalties, are the sole responsibility of the member states. the difficult problem of importing animal products from third countries is effectively addressed. member states will have at their disposal a list of approved, inspected and certified establishments, taking into account the hygiene, manufacturing and storage rules applied in third countries. i am more concerned about animal welfare, which must not take precedence over food safety, and about the preeminent role of the veterinary inspector. i think that official auxiliaries should be able to participate in ante mortem inspections at the slaughterhouse. this is already the case in france and i cannot understand why this should be called into question. i support the rapporteur on amendments nos 111 to 114 concerning game meat, which propose an analysis of residues which are not the result of hunting itself. i have reservations about the commission's proposal, particularly the presence of old open fractures. a priori, if they're old, these fractures are no longer open, so they're healed. there are no more food-related risks. as regards the formation of gas in the gastrointestinal tract, as you know, hunters, as a precaution, immediately detect game and i do not see how the veterinarian, inspector or official could therefore check the presence of gas in the gastrointestinal tract. as regards the presence of the listed health-hazardous parasites, i think it would be advisable to attach the list of these in the annex, in order to avoid difficulties of interpretation.

in writing. - i voted against the cunha report which approves the broad lines of the fischler proposal which, as a mid-term review of agenda 2000, proposes a radical reform of the cap based on decoupling aid, modulation and cross-compliance with environmental requirements. i cannot support this reform, which clearly aims to further liberalize agricultural policy, to continue to lower the prices of agricultural products, to dissociate the farmer's income from his production, in order to anticipate possible wto requirements. in short, it is organizing the destruction of european agriculture, and first and foremost french agriculture, in the name of a devious globalism. whereas the cap should have been more stable, with greater responsibility for its actors and based on remunerative prices, this text will lead agriculture towards ever greater concentration, accompanied by a kind of functionalisation of agriculture condemned either to hyperproductivity or to salaried gardening.
in writing. - the principle of decoupling direct aid, whether it is total, as the european commission wants, or partial 'at first', as the cunha report recommends, is wrong. it will make the cap even more complex and bureaucratic. it completely ignores the fact that direct aid to farmers is 'compensatory' aid for the price and income cuts inflicted on farmers by previous reforms. it turns these aids into rents which are disconnected from agricultural activity and therefore unjustifiable in the eyes of the taxpayers. it is draining the instruments of control and production guidance which are the cmo of their effectiveness and weakening europe's negotiating position in the wto. it is true that the commission is accustomed, when it wants to destroy a common policy, to a strategy of implementing a reform so impractical and unsustainable that it is in fact only a step towards the outright disappearance of the public policy it claimed to adapt. the only point of satisfaction was the adoption of my amendment on energy and industrial crops on arable land, which should help to consolidate the emerging sectors.
in writing. - in this debate, my position is clear. first, the current cap is certainly not perfect. it's expensive and sometimes unfair. however, it is to this cap that we owe the existence of agriculture in europe today. secondly, the cap may need to be reformed to adapt to the current european and global situation. it must be better targeted on quality, environmental and rural employment objectives. however, what is being proposed to us, cleverly disguised under the guise of justice and ecology (in the name of the famous 'decoupling'), will inevitably lead, within 10 years, to the disappearance of the cap and, in its wake, to the disappearance of a truly diversified and self-sufficient european agriculture. that is why i cannot accept the proposals that have been made to us.
in writing. - we voted against the oostlander report on turkey's application for membership, although the rapporteur has shown a certain willingness to nuance the usual positions of the council and the commission. so it seems that the message from the grassroots is starting to influence some of the parliamentarians a little bit. in particular, the report seems to appreciate the immense work that remains to be done to implant values similar to those of the european union, not only in the state superstructures of turkey (which would imply the dismantling of the authoritarian state), but also in the depths of its population. but in the end, the oostlander report does not dare to break the taboo, and continues to pretend to believe that by the end of 2004 it will be possible to open accession negotiations with turkey, if it makes efforts to meet the copenhagen criteria by then. we think that we should be more realistic and not underestimate the profound differences between turkey and europe. in any case, we ask that the peoples not be put once again before the fait accompli and that they be consulted before any negotiations are opened.

in writing. - i challenge anyone reading the smet report to understand what the 'open method of coordination' is exactly. this is not the rapporteur's fault, since the convention itself, which had intended to include a definition of this working method in its text of the 'european constitution', finally abandoned it in view of the difficulties of the year (article i-14 of the current draft). it was the lisbon council in march 2000 that introduced the term, but with a definition that was too vague. the intention is quite clear: to set up a flexible coordination system allowing governments to get closer together, exchange experience, and, where appropriate, set global guidelines, but then remain flexible in their implementation. unfortunately, from that point on, interpretations differ. we believe that this method should be developed as an alternative to rigid harmonization within the scope of the treaty. the 'integrationists' on the contrary want to use it to undermine national competences, and even to make the procedure more rigid by transforming it into a kind of top-down planning method, accompanied by binding numerical indicators. this is a complete misunderstanding.

the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council and parliament. the european commission, which is the guarantor of the application of community law, must maintain a privileged relationship with the citizen who, as a witness or actual or alleged victim of an infringement of community law, lodges a complaint with its services. the communication which underpins this report attests to the commission's commitment to transparency and efficiency. it publishes, as it had undertaken to do, the consolidated set of its internal procedural rules governing its relations with the complainant. she also ensures that she remains in contact with him throughout the examination of his complaint, following a strict timetable. it was in particular following an own-initiative inquiry and criticism of the european ombudsman, following the unwelcome closure of a complaint, and also following a repeated request from the european parliament that the european commission reconsidered its administrative methods in dealing with its relations with the complainant. it should be recalled that the commission has a discretionary power in the assessment of a complaint at the stage of initiating the infringement procedure and at the stage of referral to the court of justice. the aim is not to review the handling of complaints but to provide citizens with information, in particular on the progress of the examination of their complaint. we are pleased to see that the commission's proposal is totally in the right direction. we consider the administrative measures taken by the commission in the context of the examination of complaints to be particularly valuable and to allow the complainant to be regularly informed of the state of play of the procedure. moreover, the maximum period of one year that the commission undertakes to respect in order to respond to each case seems to us to be quite reasonable, given the number of complaints lodged and their complexity. however, i think there is one thing missing from this communication, namely the double filing of a complaint and a petition. as you know, the commission is not the only body responsible for answering citizens' questions about the proper functioning of the institutions and the proper application of community law. the european ombudsman, the european parliament, through its committee on petitions, are also increasingly being consulted. it is therefore possible that a complaint lodged by a citizen may also be the subject of a petition to parliament, lodged by the same citizen. this is what i call double filing, whereby each person is treated differently according to the institutions to which he or she is subject, and according to a different timetable, which, as you will understand, is a source of confusion for both the citizen and the institutions themselves. it seems desirable and logical that decisions taken by community institutions concerning complaints, appeals or petitions should be coordinated at the level of the institutions concerned, in the clear interest of efficiency for the citizen. we therefore urge the commission to review the interinstitutional agreement of 1989. it should also be borne in mind that since that date the ombudsman function has been introduced and the right of petition has been recognised in a large number of member states, which has considerably increased the number of appeals. despite the commission's competence in dealing with complaints, citizens cannot do without the committee on petitions, which provides more political attention and a response to the problems raised, but the commission and parliament are, of course, complementary in order to ensure the required effectiveness. the information needs will increase in the coming years with the arrival of ten new member states in the community. let me end by mentioning one of the commission's most promising achievements: the creation of solvit. solvit aims to resolve very quickly - and when i say very quickly it is in ten weeks, with four additional weeks in case of additional problems - recurrent crossborder problems concerning the internal market and thus prevent legal action. the originality of solvit is to involve the member states in a partnership with the commission for the examination of the dossier. it is a guarantee of integration which is, moreover, becoming increasingly successful and the commission should be congratulated on this step forward, the ultimate aim of which is to simplify the lives of citizens in compliance with community law. today it is not at all clear how the proposed text will answer that question. worse still, it is foreseeable that before long another treaty would be needed to resolve the power conflicts or to - mr president, i would like to congratulate mr wijkman and thank him for his interest in dialogue and for listening to the amendments tabled in the committee on development and cooperation. the accession of the poor to energy has become a priority, as the johannesburg summit rightly stated, even though the vital needs of the population in this area are far from being met and the trend remains uneven, due in particular to the consumption of fossil fuels in developed countries, in particular in the united states, which is excessive and very unbalanced compared to that of developing countries. life expectancy and development are so closely linked to access to energy that many people see it as a fundamental human right. this right must be recognised, guaranteed and protected. how can we contribute to the existence and development of an efficient energy sector in developing countries without policies that favour strong cooperation for the exchange of know-how, with the primary objective of meeting the vital needs of the population? - mr president, commissioner byrne, ladies and gentlemen, i generally agree with the recommendations of our rapporteur, mrs keppelhoff-wiechert, on the matter of additives in animal feed. it is clear that we must move towards the elimination of these antibiotics, which have been modestly renamed growth factors and are systematically incorporated as additives in certain foods. the trivialization of these antibiotics is in fact creating the risk of the development of unwanted antibiotic resistance, which is dangerous for human health. on the other hand, there seems to be no need to impose the elimination of coccidiostats which remain indispensable for poultry farming and i support the latest provisions proposed by our rapporteur on this matter. as for the issues raised by labelling, i believe that they cannot be solved by regulation alone and that the decisive factor is trust between the food manufacturer and the farmer who uses it. i would like to remind you, on the occasion of this debate on additives in animal feed, that feeding farm animals with industrially produced compound feeds is not the general solution, fortunately. the ruminants - sheep, dairy cows and suckler cows - are fed mainly on farm produce. for laying hens, this is more than 25% of the feed produced on the farm. only for poultry and pigs have feedingstuffs been almost entirely outsourced and industrialised in some regions. i would like to see some discussion about the merits of this development. it is obviously in the interest of this powerful industry, but is it in the interest of the consumer? is it in the farmer's interest? is it in the interests of the environment? is it in the public interest? does it go in the direction of animal welfare? it seems to me that the answer is five times no and that on the contrary, common sense would encourage the consumption of farm animals. consumers would be more reassured to consume animal products - milk, meat and eggs - using farm-based rather than industrial feed. it is a question of image, taste, traceability and probably also food safety, because farmers would never have given their cows meat meal themselves. for the farmer, this would be a way of capturing additional added value and avoiding double negotiation, that of selling his crop production and that of buying his compound feed. it would also have the opportunity to improve its image and to increase its commercial value. our environment would benefit from an obvious transport saving, that of the journey of the lorry that comes to the farm to buy the maize or the pea for fodder and that of the lorry that comes to the same farm to deliver the compound feed. the great benefit to the community would be to reduce the monstrous vegetable protein deficit that is plaguing our food security by replacing imported soybeans with locally produced oleoprotein crops. i would add that if agri-environmental aid were granted to farms producing oleoprotein for the self-consumption of their own livestock, it should be easy to get it accepted under the green box so dear to commissioner fischler. from the point of view of animal welfare, it would mean more time spent grazing, healthier, fresher and more varied food. it would therefore perhaps be a good thing, mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, if the european union and the member states, while not denying the usefulness of legislation on additives in animal feed, spent more energy on encouraging the feeding of farm animals than on regulating and controlling the production of industrial feed.

in writing. - we voted against the leinen report on the status and funding of european political parties because we think it is indecent to take money from taxpayers to keep these artificial bodies going, whose main purpose is to make people believe that there is a real european political scene, participating in a european democracy. in reality, it is largely a deception. if the so-called european political parties really have the solid base they claim, then they accept to be financed by that base, the citizens and the national political parties. furthermore, the proposed system of "status" may result in political control of parties, which has extremely vague legal references and is unworthy of a free society. this is so true that the promoters and beneficiaries of the project themselves are reluctant to see their names involved. the commission would like the european parliament to manage the system, because it is obviously political in nature. parliament, not concerned about damaging its image, would like the commission to do so. to simplify matters, why not give up this bad plan?
in writing. - i abstained on this report for two reasons. the main reason is that the regulation on the statute and funding of european political parties allows donations by legal persons to european political parties. i cannot accept such a proposal because it makes it impossible for the parties to be independent of the economic circles. the influence of economic lobbies on political parties and political orientations is already significant, and direct funding, even with a ceiling, will further increase their influence on political parties. moreover, the funding of national political parties by european political parties is not guaranteed by the authorisation of cross-border actions. finally, it is no longer a question of european political parties but of political parties at european level. i decided to abstain and not to vote against this report because i believe that the adoption of such a statute is a positive and strong signal towards a closer union, a truly shared destiny. the european political parties, financed by public subsidies and by the contributions of their members, are one of the means offered to citizens to support and achieve this ever closer union of peoples.
in writing. - in addition to the questions which remain, particularly on the commission's role in the allocation and control of appropriations, some points raise serious problems. this is the case with the obligation on european parties to respect the principles of democracy and the rule of law and the fundamental rights and principles contained in the charter of fundamental rights of the european union and the treaties. i am very concerned about the possible consequences of such a provision, which contains in its seed the principle of the prohibition of political parties - ipso facto, that is what excluding a party from public funding is all about. this liberticidal measure is all the more shocking because it leaves room for arbitrariness. how can we expect parliament to carry out an objective examination of the status, programme and activities of a political party? it must also be stressed that the europe of parties towards which the project is moving will not be synonymous with european democracy. nothing would be worse than to see a system within the european union developed dominated by parties eager for power, a system which in france signaled the bankruptcy of the third and fourth republics.

mr president, i would like to thank the rapporteur for his report, which is a very good report, and i would like to thank the rapporteur for his report. these reversals are linked to the uniqueness of this case. as in the previous case, we are dealing with a case in which freedom of expression is at stake. mr musotto is being prosecuted for having made certain remarks on italian television just after his election by universal suffrage, but before parliament met in its constituent session. the problem is that if we follow the text to the letter, it was not yet "truly" parliamentary at the time it was expressed. this strict, even restrictive interpretation should lead us to lift the immunity of someone who was not a member of parliament at the time of the facts. this solution may be legally pure. but it is morally and legally deeply shocking. in law, there is the letter, but also the spirit. however, there is no doubt that at the time when he was questioned by the press, mr musotto was already considered to be a member of parliament, since the journalist began his question by addressing him as 'mr member of parliament'. it is therefore indisputable that he was questioned and answered as a member of parliament and any solution which would seek to deny him the benefit of immunity or to fail to defend his immunity would, in my view, be contrary, if not to the letter, at least to the spirit of the text. this was the unanimous opinion of the legal affairs committee after lengthy debate. as the rapporteur said in a previous report, we must not interpret national rights in cases where freedom of thought or expression is at issue. whatever he said, we must defend mr musotto's parliamentary immunity: the independence of our institution is at stake! i too think that it is not good to rely exclusively on national rights. in the present case, it appears that italian law grants immunity to someone who has just been elected by universal suffrage. in interpreting the treaties broadly, the legal affairs committee has acted with great wisdom, courage and consistency, because its position is in line with decisions taken in similar situations in the past. however, we have accompanied our report and conclusion with a remark to suggest to the convention and the next intergovernmental conference that the textual anomaly be corrected by an amendment of the text of article 3 of the 1976 act. such a revision would ensure optimum protection for members of parliament to guarantee them real freedom of expression and would fill the existing legal vacuum by making the exercise of the mandate coincide with the proclamation of the results of the european parliament elections. the letter and spirit of the texts would thus be reconciled. that is why, mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i am defending mr musotto's immunity.
- mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, the report we are considering today is essential for the harmonization of financial markets, since it will allow securities to be listed on all european markets. but it is also essential because it guarantees the uniform information necessary for the transparency and security of the markets and thus their proper functioning. it also aims to ensure that all stakeholders are well informed about listed securities. the compromise reached by the greek presidency is undoubtedly a point of balance which can be welcomed, since it makes it possible to reconcile the different european approaches to market regulation. but when i hear my british colleague arguing in favour of the language regime, i get a certain suspicion. i understand that a dutchman, a frenchman or an italian can argue for a language system which is not a protection of markets; i imagine a different conception of market protection in the mouth of a londoner. more seriously, at this stage of the parliamentary proceedings, i would like to address two questions which, it seems to me, are not details, but are still very much essential questions. the first is the choice of the competent authority for convertibles, in other words, essentially eurobonds. it seems to me that by allowing companies to choose the competent authority, we encourage the so-called regulatory one. the issuing companies will naturally go to the least-caring authorities. we therefore risk weakening the markets. i've accepted the difference between debt and equity. the small investors are not affected by the bonds. so we can tolerate less strictness. on the other hand, it seems unacceptable to me to accept free choice for convertibles. these provide access to the capital of a company and are one of the two forms of capital increase. moreover, these securities are intended to be held by the public and will be increasingly so in the future. the compromise reached by the presidency seems satisfactory on this point. the second difficulty is the delegation of powers by the authority. in the states where such a delegation exists, the stock exchanges to which these tasks are delegated have often become private for-profit entities. they are thus de facto both judge and party in the examination of the prospectuses. this clearly raises problems as regards the quality of the examination of the prospectus and possible distortions of competition. the eight-year period provided for in the presidency package for member states to adjust to this industrial reality seems to me to be the most acceptable. this should make it possible to terminate this delegation. these two questions remain essential. a few other details should also be mentioned here: the possibility for smes or natural persons considered as qualified investors to waive this status; the fact that if a competent authority has not examined a prospectus within the given deadline, it is considered to be adopted; the problem of languages, which i have briefly mentioned. in conclusion, mr president, i hope that parliament will vote in favour of the compromise of the greek presidency, which is a mutually acceptable solution.

- in the debate between the council and parliament on public procurement in the european union, what is striking is how the most bitter enemies of statism forget their reluctance when it comes to competing for state contracts. they're interested in the state's money. indeed, how could the large building and public works trusts have built financial empires without the state's orders? how would the arms trusts survive without public money? the so-called market economy is a state-supported economy. the fact that harmonisation in public procurement is progressing so slowly is no coincidence. the big industrial groups would like to keep captive access to their national state's money and access to the public money of the neighboring country. as for the conditions for awarding contracts, the rules which are beginning to be laid down show a cynicism which borders on sincerity in their administrative aridity. the tendering conditions are based solely on the economic interest of the tender. environmental and health requirements, as greenpeace and friends of the earth rightly denounce, are forgotten, as are the working conditions and pay of workers in companies that pocket public money. and so many other things have been forgotten, including archaeological research. finally, the general interests of society were forgotten! all that matters is profitability. social organisation is reduced to a balance sheet. furthermore, under the pretext of coordinating the procedures for the water, energy, transport and postal services contracts, the council seeks to make it clear that these are precisely markets and not vital services for society as a whole. no, you can't! these services of water, energy, transport and postal services must be and remain public services. they cannot be granted to these private groups who are concerned with their profits and not with the interests of the users. commission. mr president, thank you for giving me the floor a second time on this important matter. i would like to reply to some of the points raised. i would like to elucidate what i said earlier so that no misunderstandings remain between what this parliament would like to see the commission do, and what the commission itself intends to do. firstly i refer to what mr maccormick said right at the beginning of this debate, which was also repeated by other speakers. mr maccormick referred to the current state of jurisprudence. in accordance with that jurisprudence, the common position already clarifies that environmental characteristics and social clauses may be used as award criteria and that it is not necessary that each and every award criterion taken individually can be shown to provide an economic benefit for the contracting authorities or entities. it is sufficient that taken as a whole the award criteria can carry out their proper function, which is to allow an objective evaluation and comparison of the intrinsic qualities of the products or services offered and by the award of the contract to the most economically advantageous tender. here i would also refer to mr harbour's remarks, with which the commission agrees. secondly, mrs thors and mr junker referred to production methods. i should like to reply that regarding the amendments which aimed to insert explicit references to production methods, the commission is of the opinion that it is superfluous to do so since production methods are a part of the environmental characteristics which, as i have just said, are already allowed for. furthermore, they are explicitly referred to as examples of legitimate technical specifications. i then come to my third point, which was also raised by mr maccormick. in article 53 the words 'for the contracting authority' are explained by recital 44 as meaning that the best tender will be assessed according to what the contracting authority will have defined as its requirements. recital 44 further clarifies that this encompasses requirements addressed to satisfy the needs of the public concern in the case of the ruling about the need to limit air pollution for the population of the city of helsinki. mr koukiadis gave us a further example of valid award criteria under article 53 – the needs of handicapped people, which should be taken into account. in the case of transport services – for example better access to buses for handicapped people – would certainly be a valid criterion. there is no doubt about that. my fifth point refers to the phrase 'economically most advantageous', which mr herman schmid and a number of speakers mentioned. in reply to those comments, the most economically advantageous tender would be the result of a combination of economic but also qualitative criteria, and the latter would serve not necessarily to calculate the costs for the contracting authority, but would certainly help that contracting authority to make up its mind. my penultimate point refers to labels, which mr jonckheer mentioned. as the common positions clearly show, the commission is in favour of clarifying the role of eco-labels in public procurement and the possibility of referring to them when defining technical specifications. it should be kept in mind, however, that unlike 'ordinary' european standards, european eco-labels do not replace other competing eco-labels such as pluri-national ones. the commission's proposals on eco-labels had foreseen such replacement, but this was not accepted during the legislative process. the current situation is, therefore, that different eco-labels may exist side by side even if they cover the same aspects. it would therefore not be appropriate – indeed, it would be contrary to established policy in the environmental field – to introduce a preference for european eco-labels over other eco-labels. the commission is conscious that references to the performances underlying eco-labels rather than to simply require the labels themselves may be more complicated for purchasers. this task has been rendered easier through a database created by the commission which lists the different performances defined in eco-labels that can be used in connection with award procedures. i can add that a practical guide to green procurement will be published later this year. finally, i should like to deal with the questions put by mrs thorning-schmidt and mr hughes as to why the commission is going back on current law as interpreted by the court of justice in the helsinki buses case. my answer quite simply is as follows: it is simply not true that the common positions are more restrictive than the interpretation of current law given by the court of justice in the helsinki buses case. on the contrary, through the combination of recitals and articles, the common positions consolidate and clarify the possibilities offered by current law. they do not add anything to or subtract anything from current possibilities, but they have the merit of setting these out explicitly instead of having to rely on interpretations of jurisprudence with all the ensuing possibilities for different use and consequent legal uncertainty on this crucial issue. moreover, they clarify that under the same conditions as set out by the court of justice, the use of social award criteria is also legitimate. i should like to end by expressing the hope that in its vote parliament will support the common position so that we can get these directives onto the statute book as quickly as possible.

- the agenda calls for joint debate on: - recommendation (a5-0202/2003) for second reading, on behalf of the committee on the environment, public health and consumer policy, on the common position of the council with a view to the adoption of a regulation of the european parliament and of the council on genetically modified food and feed [5204/3/2003 - c5-0133/2003 - 2001/0173 (cod)) (rapporteur: mrs scheele), and - recommendation (a5-0204/2003), on behalf of the committee on the environment, public health and consumer policy, on the common position of the council with a view to the adoption of a regulation of the european parliament and of the council on the traceability and labelling of genetically modified organisms and the traceability of products intended for human or animal consumption as from 2001 (rapporteur: mrs mellis) and amending directive 2001/18/ec (directive 2001/18/ec) (rapporteur: mr mellis) [1580/01/2003] (c8-0180/01 (cod))
- the gmo regulations should be a major step forward in terms of biosecurity, freedom of choice and consumer information. the two texts under discussion today do not provide any further guidance. the most critical point is the thresholds for the presence of gmos that are allowed when the presence is accidental or technically unavoidable. the council proposes 0.9%. it's too much! we should return to the position adopted by parliament at first reading, which is 0.5% at the most. as for unauthorised gmos, how can the council legalize them in the food chain by proposing a threshold of 0.5% when they are banned in the union? the question of contamination of crops also needs to be addressed. the commission places the responsibility on the member states, while reserving the right to develop guidelines for the coexistence of conventional and genetically modified crops at a later stage. in the immediate future, member states must be able to take emergency measures on a sovereign basis, for example administrative suspensions of authorisations in the event of a risk to public health or environmental contamination. i also think that seeds should be excluded from the regulation, distinguishing between living gmos which must be covered by directive 2001/18/ec - which makes their traceability compulsory - and genetically modified food. finally, a genuine system of liability for the introduction of gmos into agriculture and the environment will have to be defined. i think that the polluter pays principle is applicable here. the farmer using gmos will have to repair the damage caused to conventional farming. in conclusion, i fully support the european moratorium on the complaint lodged by the united states with the wto.
- madam president, we must take the full measure of the problems raised by gmos and above all not reduce them to the sole question of the rapid profitability of the costly research carried out by a few multinational seed companies. first, the question of gmos poses a major sovereignty problem: citizens' sovereignty over the commercial exploitation of scientific discoveries, farmers' sovereignty over what they sow, consumers' sovereignty over their food, states' sovereignty over what they control. secondly, gmos present two major risks. the first concerns human health: there is a risk that the transgene introduced into the plant codes for the synthesis of a toxic protein. the mad cow prion has shown us that certain unwanted proteins can have very long-term toxic effects. the second risk is environmental: the risk of spreading unwanted genes to wild flora and the rhizosphere. the extreme recklessness of the americans who spread gmos over millions of hectares without taking the precaution of properly assessing the risk is deplorable. thirdly, we must ask who benefits from gmos. the benefits for the consumer and the environment are currently nil, as the reduction in pesticide consumption that gmos were supposed to provide is still expected. the farmer's benefit is small: some savings in seed preparation, treatment and weeding but at the cost of increased dependence on seed and plant health companies. for developing countries, the benefit is only theoretical, because the firms have only worked for solvent markets, which makes the american criticism of european countries on this point unacceptable. so it is actually the seed companies that are making the most real profits, and therefore the american multinationals, which are the most advanced in this field. what do you need to do? keep looking, of course. exploring both the potential and the risks of transgenesis, although this technology is extremely expensive and seems more suited to very large-scale crops with very low diversity, which are not characteristic of european agriculture, at least before the fischler plan. the commission's proposal is to be submitted to the council and the council for approval, and the council will be able to accept it.
- madam president, commissioner byrne reminded us earlier that we are meeting today after two years of emotional and controversial work on this important question of gmos, on which our parliament must decide without delay. we should be rational, consistent and firm about what is, after all, a great improvement. however, our discussions today show that there is still a great deal of difference of opinion. while ensuring the proper functioning of the internal market, we must help our farmers in their choices and, above all, ensure a high level of consumer protection. we still have to convince him of the validity of our decisions! the exercise requires us to adopt strict rules on the authorisation and control procedure, i.e. european harmonisation of the scientific criteria for authorisation and full traceability of products to ensure the safety of animal and human food. this too is achieved through communication which is not concerned with ideology. the consumer is often worried because of the lack of accurate information. the need for credible communication to the general public is all the more pressing. the labelling must be clear and legible to allow consumers to make the right choices. the consumer must be sure that all gmos in the products he buys have been assessed in a strict manner for safety reasons. he will then have the choice of buying the products he wants. these texts call for the moratorium to be lifted. once all the guarantees of safety and traceability are in place, the moratorium must be lifted. if we do not do this, we risk once again putting the brakes on research in europe and causing our best researchers to leave for the usa or asia.
- madam president, commissioner, with the two reports by our colleagues trakatellis and scheele, we are dealing once again with gmos, but from the small end of the spectrum. we are talking about traceability, labelling, zero tolerance, maximum thresholds, consumer choice, health, the environment and precautions. meanwhile, who's dealing with gmos in washington? that the bush administration treats gmos as a matter of sovereignty: economic, industrial, scientific, food. as with bananas, hormone-rich meats, oilseeds, grains, chickens, the united states is making gmos another battle in the transatlantic agricultural war. and in the meantime, what do we do? the legal system against imperialism. the real question then, madam president, is not scientific, health or environmental. the question has been the same for 40 years: does europe of 450 million people want to be independent? in the persian gulf, it answered no by submitting to the american war. in the gulf of mexico, in cancun, on 14 september, if she says no, it will be an agricultural and tropical munich, but europe is feminine: she loves to be vassal.
- madam president, the feverishness of the sowers in lobbying to convince members to reject the amendments adopted by the committee on the environment, public health and consumer policy is the only reason why we are voting for them despite the limitations of the texts concerned. we are in favour of the most comprehensive traceability and labelling of gmos for food and feed so that the consumer can judge and choose. the problem is not genetic modification itself, nor the research carried out in this direction. the problem is that the exploitation of these products is entirely in the hands of large agro-food trusts, which society cannot trust at all, because they do not seek genetic modification in the interests of men and society, but in terms of what it will bring them. so i also take this opportunity to protest against the imprisonment of josé bové in france. josé bové has at least had the merit of reducing the mistrust towards the use that can be made of gmos. he was convicted of opinion offences and of militant activities. he must be released.
- at a time when josé bové has just been arrested in scandalous conditions for plucking some genetically modified plants, we must not lose sight of the political background of this second reading, namely the feverish will of the commission and the member states, especially since the united states' complaint to the wto in this regard, to lift the 1999 moratorium on gmos. the most positive aspect of this compromise is that it allows member states to take all the measures necessary to avoid contamination of conventional and organic crops by gmos. it would still be necessary for these states to show the necessary political will. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the use of genetically modified organisms (gmos) in foodstuffs. the tolerance for the incidental presence of gmos varies between 0.3 and 0.5% for each species, while the threshold should be the same for all species, namely 0.1%. such a threshold is essential to ensure the varietal purity, traceability and labelling of all seeds along the production chain, and to maintain genuinely gmo-free supply chains. the responsibility of those who introduce gmos into the environment, in particular the seed industries, including european ones, must be clearly established under the polluter-pays principle: the cost of repairing damage must be borne by gmo agriculture. as it is impossible to know precisely the radius of contamination of pollen from a genetically modified plant, it is in the interest of the growers of these plants to find good insurance, unless they manage to educate the bees so that they can be very selective in their harvesting.
- madam president, commissioners, according to a recent eurobarometer survey, more than 70% of europeans do not want to consume gmos. it was therefore necessary to respond to european consumers by adopting legislation on labelling, which should leave everyone the opportunity to choose their food. i would have a few reservations, however. the first concerns the 0.9% threshold. why, when a lower level is technically detectable - the 0.5% threshold being retained for unauthorised gmos - refuse to be less demanding? unless this 0.9% presence is already a reality even before the moratorium is lifted. the second reservation concerns consumer choice. will this choice be guaranteed in time, when we do not envisage binding legislation on the subject of coexistence but leave it to the member states to take appropriate measures? perhaps we already know that this coexistence is impossible, that we cannot regulate the flight of bees or the direction and strength of the wind and that gmo crops are irreversible? if this is the case, we are taking a big risk for europeans, because we cannot limit the subject of gmos to a matter of consumer choice and ignore public health and environmental problems. finally, to date no one has been able to put forward strong, undeniable and convincing arguments to justify the interest and harmlessness of gmos. the commission has already taken a number of initiatives in this area. gmos are just one application of biotechnology. refusing to allow gmos to spread in europe is not to be against progress or against gene therapies, it is to prefer the precautionary principle to the ramblings of the sorcerer's apprentice. everyone knows that economic and financial interests still prevail in this area and that the agricultural and environmental future of the european union is at stake under pressure from the united states and negotiations within the wto. this is regrettable, because it must be borne in mind that the united states has not yet ratified the cartagena protocol. it is felt that all this debate and our votes tomorrow are preparing us to accept the lifting of the moratorium without much discussion. our vote will therefore be much more political than it appears and we would be guilty before the citizens if we did not demand, before any decision is taken, to be better informed of the real risks that the cultivation of gmos will have on the environment and on the health of the population.
