- madam president, in france, josé bové is paying with his freedom for his commitment to the prevention of gmos and the precautionary principle. the sanction is totally unacceptable, especially when we compare the threat it poses to society with the threat gmos pose to our future health. we know this better than anyone else, because we have a responsibility to ensure that our fellow citizens have a genuine choice whether to consume or not to consume gmos. we must not be intimidated by the lies and pressure of mr bush, who is being driven by the pro-gmo agribusiness which denies choice to its own consumers. let's move forward, let's dare to change the loopholes in our regulations. we must be very clear that we do not want unauthorised gmos to be placed on the market. as regards the labelling of authorised gmos, we know that the food industry is able to detect up to 0.1% of gmos. this is the way we must go. however, without a guarantee of coexistence between gm and non-gm crops, the best regulations in the world will be useless if gmos are everywhere in nature. it is absolutely urgent to allow free choice of consumption and to protect the environment, to preserve gm-free crops and to ensure that they remain so. that's the real challenge. let us not deceive ourselves: without a guarantee of coexistence, there will be no choice.
commission. mr president, i am delighted to be able to announce to you that, earlier today, the commission adopted a communication on the g10 medicines initiative. for those of you who are not familiar with g10, i would like to briefly explain the background to this initiative. in recent years there has been growing evidence that the european-based pharmaceutical industry was losing competitiveness compared with its american-based counterparts. this is not only serious for our economy but of vital importance to public health and, especially, european patients. millions of europeans use medicines everyday. achieving real and long-lasting benefits to patients is a key objective of pharmaceutical policy. we must support member states to make authorised medicines, especially the newer and more innovative ones, available and affordable to all those who need them as quickly as possible. however, some of the statistics concerning the industry make difficult reading; those pertaining to research and development, for example: critical to our industry, to our science base and to our patients. in 1990 europe was the world leader in pharmaceutical research and development and innovation. now the us has overtaken europe in the discovery of new chemical or biological entities. this has not happened by chance. since 1990, research and development expenditure in the us has grown at a dramatic rate. between 1990 and 2000, research and development expenditure grew at twice the rate in the us compared with europe. by 1997 america had overtaken europe in terms of total research and development expenditure. g10 medicines were born out of this background. in recognition of the critical role the industry plays in both the industrial and health sectors, commissioner byrne and i established the high level group on innovation and the provision of medicines – g10 medicines. it is a small group of high-level representatives from member states, industry, mutual health funds and patients. the group was given the challenging remit of reaching consensus on ways of improving the competitiveness of the pharmaceutical industry in the context of achieving social and public health objectives. to many people’s surprise, the group was able to report back in may last year, with 14 wide-ranging recommendations. in the communication adopted today we set out how we plan to take these recommendations forward. there are five broad themes we pursue in the communication which we intend to take forward in parallel. benefits to patients are at the heart of g10. we will look at ways of improving patient information on medicines, strengthening the role of patients in public health decision-making and so forth. i am sure that in that area my colleague mr byrne will say more. developing a competitive european-based industry takes us back to the origins of g10. we examine ways of improving access to innovative medicines and the need to speed up national negotiations on reimbursement and pricing, greater price competition for medicines that are not part of the state sector and measures to develop competitive generic and non-prescription markets. with regard to strengthening the eu science base: if we fail to support innovation we will pay a heavy economic, social and public health price. we look at ways we can develop incentives for research, including the use of virtual institutes for health to stimulate and organise health and biotechnology research and development. we also link in to the many initiatives under the commission’s existing sixth framework programme. as for medicines in an enlarged union, with the forthcoming enlargement the union is facing one of its greatest challenges and opportunities. we look at ways of meeting the challenge through providing a level playing field for intellectual property protection and providing support for the new member states to implement the new legislative framework. as regards member states learning from each other, benchmarking will provide a practical mechanism for monitoring the implementation of the recommendations, as well as providing a forum for member states to share best practice. so, what is the driving force for implementing the proposals in the communication? the main driving force will be the pharmaceutical review supported by the life sciences and biotechnology action plan and the public health programme. you will be well aware of these, and the pharmaceutical review will obviously have its second reading in the autumn. however, the unique aspect of g10 is the vehicle it provided to look at areas of national competence that have an impact on competitiveness and public health. there is only so much we can achieve at european level. in the communication we set out areas where we believe that a european reflection could benefit member states as well as helping to achieve our g10 goals. in particular, we propose an examination of national pricing and reimbursement systems. although this is clearly within the competence of member states we believe that the injection of more market measures, while ensuring national safeguards to control expenditure on pharmaceuticals, could bring benefits to patients and the industry in terms of quicker access to the markets. overall, i believe the communication, together with the other initiatives i have mentioned, provides a framework for turning around the competitiveness of our pharmaceutical industry while reinforcing european public health.
commission. mr president, in the g10 communication adopted today by the commission we see patients and public health placed at the centre of the debate on the future direction of european pharmaceuticals policy. this rebalancing of policy-making between legitimate industrial innovation and health needs is an important step in the right direction. you have previously heard me say here that our health is our wealth. the development of rising public health standards, the extension of disease-free life-years and the increase in life expectancy are shaping features of modern economic development, and pharmaceutical innovation has played a significant role in all of this. similarly, from a patient point of view, innovation has yielded dramatic improvements in the dignity and quality of life of patients in recent decades. now patients are taking a more active role in seeking out information and products. but at a point where health expenditure is rising, the population is ageing and patients' expectations are increasing, we need to have a strategic vision of how to move forward in this complex field. there are a number of interlinked issues here. for patients, there is a desire to have more effective, more humane products, brought to market more quickly. there is a desire to have better information on the comparative advantages of products and early warning of adverse reactions. for patients, the availability of clear and authoritative information from the leaflet inside the package, to online at the level of a european health portal, is essential. for those who finance the health system, there is a need for sustainable budgeting, affordable medicines, manageable demand and responsible behaviour from patients, prescribers and producers alike. from a public health point of view there is a need to ensure that medicines maintain high quality and safety standards and that adverse reactions are quickly identified and tackled. there is a need to work towards more rational prescribing and consumption patterns, to ensure that we can tackle anti-microbial resistance. in addition there is a need to ensure that research develops products which tackle health requirements as distinct from lifestyle issues. for example, more must be done to develop products that tackle rare diseases and childhood illnesses. and, in an ageing society, medicines will play an important role in ensuring active and healthy ageing – with all its attendant economic and human benefits. for the industries involved, there are a range of specific issues which are being presented to you today. but we need to be aware that an increasingly global industry is less likely to prioritise investment in research for the treatments which europeans will need in 10-20 years' time if they are dealing with a fragmented and unpredictable market. in other words, whilst there will be no shortage of sure-fire lifestyle wonder drugs like viagra, how can we be sure that the medicines needed to tackle arthritis, alzheimer's and obesity, to name but a few, will be developed? it is only by moving towards a more predictable market environment across europe that we will be in a position to convince industry to take the needs of europeans seriously in the years ahead. the high level committee on health has stated that the public health goal of pharmaceuticals policy is 'to make readily accessible, efficacious, high quality and safe medicines, including their most recent innovative ones, to all those who need them, regardless of income or social status'. each of these issues has been addressed in this communication. we have effectively highlighted patients' needs for better information and their need for a stronger voice to influence policy. efforts in both these areas will support their growing role as important decision-makers for health care. the establishment of an eu-funded european patients' platform in february this year is an important step. we have also targeted the medicines themselves, to build up systems that ensure their safety, quality and efficacy. here the g10 put the need for stronger systems of pharmacovigilance and relative effectiveness firmly on the agenda. in this way we aim to improve the rational use of medicines. this is a public health goal that underpins our vision for the pharmaceuticals sector. relative effectiveness is a very important issue for the european union. in june 2000 the council underlined the importance of added therapeutic value both in terms of health protection and from an industrial policy perspective. effective medicines must get quickly to the people who need them. this means identifying which medicines are genuinely effective, not just in the controlled environment of a clinical trial, but in general use amongst the wider population. this is the critical issue at stake here. relative effectiveness is one key tool towards rational use. but, clearly, we have to consider the role of other actors too. how can we improve rational use of pharmaceuticals at the level of the health care prescriber and the consumer? a parallel question might be: how can we know if we have improved the rational use of pharmaceuticals? this brings me to the issue of benchmarking. the recommendation to develop indicators for public health has set us a big challenge. for example, to investigate indicators that could monitor what is happening at the health-care prescriber level. ultimately, the intention is to have a set of indicators that can shed light on what is happening in the pharmaceuticals sector of member states in terms of the extent to which public health needs are being met and in this way to inform policy development at national and european level. finally, the discussion on enlargement is particularly timely. the accession treaties have been signed. although enlargement is one specific recommendation of the g10, clearly our responses to each recommendation need to adequately reflect the changing environment within the european union. the g10 is a first important step to developing a strategic vision of the future health needs of europeans which is affordable, effective, transparent, inclusive and safe. properly pursued it will be good for the health of all concerned.
commission. mr president, i must emphasise that the two proposals are separate as far as the review is concerned. the review is supported by g10 and now has the support of the member states. the g10 process goes further, and so far there has not been any broad discussion in the member states about that. there is, firstly, a proposal from the group and today there are the recommendations from the commission. next week the italian presidency is organising a conference on g10 on the basis of the commission recommendations. we hope that the dissemination of these messages goes forward. as i said, it is now important to get the review through. that is important for research-based industries because it strengthens their position; it accelerates the access to markets for new products; it acts as a counterbalance; and it also means that generics will be more competitive when the patents expire.

- mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, the successive food crises have undermined consumer confidence and food safety is now a genuine political issue, becoming a constituent part of the overall security of citizens. in this respect, the provision of substantial information on the composition of foods is considered essential and accurate and appropriate labelling is essential, in particular for ingredients that may cause allergies. the problem is relatively simple for allergens present as such in the final product. on the other hand, is it reasonable to require the labelling of ingredients such as technological aids, used in particular in the manufacture of alcoholic beverages, which are involved in the manufacturing process but do not end up in the final product? - mr president, the european parliament has already spoken twice on the question of child soldiers, in 1999 and 2000. so why use the emergency procedure today for a new resolution which, of course, goes further, since it covers not only child soldiers but also all forms of child trafficking? well, because the problem is growing and the european union is not showing enough determination. 300,000 children, boys and girls, are enlisted in combat units in over thirty countries. every year, 1.2 million children are trafficked, and trafficking is now a booming 'industry' worth nearly €3 billion a year. after drug trafficking and small arms trafficking, it is the third most lucrative criminal activity in the world. the fight against this senseless scourge of the 21st century should be a major focus of the union's development policy. this is not the case - alas! at international level, however, there is a growing mobilisation, as evidenced by the entry into force in 2002 of the optional protocol to the united nations convention on the sale, prostitution and pornography of children. we urge the council to encourage the member states, which are still too few to have done so, to ratify this protocol. we also call for the rights of the child to become a political priority of the union, reflected in budgetary arbitrage by an adequate budgetary allocation on a specific line, in order to enhance its effectiveness and readability, as well as a common strategy. of course, the council of 10 december 2002 has accepted the principle, but the text must be published and operational without delay. to this end, our resolution proposes a number of ways, such as the appointment of a high representative for the rights of the child, a policy of cooperation based on prevention, support and protection of victims, better cooperation with countries of origin and international mandates against the organisers and perpetrators of this unnamed trafficking.
the commission is not prepared to accept the amendments tabled by the committee on budgets. the commission welcomes the draft report on the rights of the child drawn up for the acp-eu joint parliamentary assembly. it highlights the enormous challenge facing the international community in protecting children's rights. first, on the subject of child soldiers: the european union supports the un special representative and welcomes the initiatives of the un security council, in particular resolution 1460 of 30 january 2003. the european union calls on all states to ratify the optional protocol to the convention on the rights of the child and to accelerate the ratification of the rome statute of the international criminal court, which defines the recruitment and use of children under the age of 15 or their use in hostile conflicts as a war crime. at political level, the european union is seeking a common position on the issue of child soldiers. in december 2002, the council approved the development of a strategy or guidelines on this subject. unicef and other stakeholders then organised a meeting of children's rights experts on 14 march 2003. the recommendations made at this meeting emphasise, inter alia, the importance of a pre- and post-conflict strategy and the need to make this issue a cross-cutting issue in the whole european union decision-making process. the council working party on human rights will in due course consider what steps should be taken next. the following is to be said about european funding for measures to help children in armed conflict: for echo, children are a key focus of humanitarian aid. this commitment is reflected in concrete projects, advocacy and research activities. children are one of the three priorities of echo's strategy for the current year. secondly, to combat trafficking in children: the european union has taken a number of initiatives at legislative, political and financial levels. in 2002, the council adopted the framework decision on combating trafficking in human beings and reached political agreement on the draft framework decision on combating the sexual exploitation of children and child pornography. on the initiative of the commission, the european conference on the prevention and combating of trafficking in human beings - a global challenge for the 21st century - was held from 18 to 20 september last year. the brussels declaration was a concrete outcome of the conference. the commission then decided on 25 march 2003 to set up an advisory group of experts on trafficking in human beings, which will assist the commission in putting forward further concrete proposals at european level. in particular, the group should submit a report to the commission based on the recommendation of the brussels declaration. in 2002, the stop ii programme funded 16 projects to combat trafficking in human beings and sexual exploitation, with a total of more than eur 1.7 million. the tacis and cards programmes also support projects to combat trafficking in human beings in eastern and south-eastern europe, and an action plan against trafficking in human beings has also been developed in the framework of the eu-africa dialogue. third, in the area of 'children and development', the commission pursues the millennium development goals as its objectives, in particular the achievement of universal primary education and the reduction of infant and child mortality. although children are not specifically targeted by our development policy, they benefit from extensive resources in the areas of education, health, aids and population policy. finally, the cotonou agreement contains specific provisions for the protection of young people, particularly in the fight against child labour. in order to promote these objectives, the commission has also strengthened its cooperation with the world labour organisation as a whole. in conclusion, i would like to note that the report contains many interesting proposals for strengthening the european union's commitment to children's rights. the community does not currently have specific competence in this area. we are, however, looking forward with interest to the outcome of the discussions on the draft constitutional treaty, the convention for europe, which for the first time makes the protection of children's rights a specific objective of the european union. thank you for your attention.

in writing. - the italian presidency has identified immigration policy and the fight against illegal immigration as one of its priorities, and we assure it of our support. we hope in particular that it will be clearer and more resolute than the council of thessaloniki two weeks ago. although it devoted a large part of its conclusions to immigration policy - seven and a half pages, compared with one and a half pages for the convention! - the council was particularly obscure, if not impossible to understand, defining its objective in particular as a 'two-way process' aimed at both combating illegal immigration and 'searching for legal migration routes'. europe needs a clear and firm policy on border controls, returning illegals to their countries and reforming the right to asylum to put an end to abuses. in this respect, we regret that the thessaloniki council did not really deal with the uk's request to create transit centres for asylum applications at the external borders of the union and 'regional protection zones' close to the countries of origin of applicants. we are counting on the italian presidency to take this matter forward.
in writing. - during this second reading of the draft regulation on genetically modified food and feed (scheele report), i voted in favour of the following amendments, which are considerably more stringent than those adopted by the council:- amendments lowering the labelling threshold for authorised gmos from 0.9 to 0.5%, in particular amendment 19; - amendments to remove the tolerance of unauthorised gmos in the food chain, when their percentage is less than 0.5%, in particular amendment 43 (by the way, one wonders how the council can propose a threshold of 0.5% here, when it claims that it is technically impossible when it comes to the threshold for the labelling of authorised gmos); - amendments calling on the member states to take measures to prevent the non-contamination of traditional crops by gm crops (compromise amendments 44 and 45); - amendments authorising member states to take emergency measures to restrict or prohibit the use of an authorised gmo, when it is later found to present a risk (e.g. amendment 40). beyond these technical issues, i will set out my position in principle in my explanation of vote on the side report on the traceability of gmos.
in writing. - in the series of amendments which came up for second reading we voted in favour of everything that goes in the direction of transparency and the most complete possible labelling. we voted against the compromise amendments which would in fact support the lifting of the moratorium.
in writing. - on the subject of gmos, we do not want europe to make a careless commitment, as the united states has done, to the thoughtless and uncontrolled large-scale distribution of genetically modified organisms, guided by the sole interest of the firms that produce them. but we also do not want it to be left out of the picture of a technology which may hold some hope for the feeding of mankind. faced with a technology that allows man to manipulate the genome, that is to say to act on the very heart of life, it is essential that society should ask itself questions and that the necessary ethical debates should not be ignored. it is the duty of the public authorities to legislate and regulate. the sovereignty of states implies that they retain the power to admit into their territory only products which are desired, chosen and corresponding to a real need. the cartagena protocol on biodiversity recognizes this right. let us use it to the full to maintain our control over the cultivation of gmos in europe. the freedom of choice of the consumer and the producer also implies that the necessary measures are taken to ensure the coexistence of production using gmos and production not using gmos.
in writing. - the trakatellis report on the traceability and labelling of gmos, like the scheele report, is an opportunity for us to address a serious warning to the commission and the member states. we feel that they are only waiting for the final adoption of the traceability regulations to lift the moratorium currently imposed on gmos in europe. the adoption of this regulation would therefore serve as a guarantee, even though two other essential conditions are still not fulfilled: the existence of a clear definition of liability (with corresponding financial guarantees) for damage that may be caused by gmos and the entry into force of rules - which do not exist at present - that safeguard the non-contamination of traditional crops by gm crops. the last point is essential: it is recalled that the trade union leader josé bové was convicted in france for plucking transgenic maize plants, an act considered as a violation of a private property right. but was not this violation preceded by another, much more serious violation, namely, the risk of contamination by gmos to neighbouring private properties and to the natural environment in general, which is common property?
in writing. - in the name of the precautionary principle and because the development of gmos reminds me of the sorcerer's apprentice in the service of easy money and an outdated productivism, i am today hostile to the practice and development of gmos. moreover, since gmos exist, whether one is for or against, one cannot be - and i cannot be - against improved traceability and labelling. this improvement is a lesser evil, which should not make us forget the fundamental question.
in writing. - everyone is in favour of labelling foodstuffs containing gmos, in order to inform the consumer and ensure traceability of these products along the production and distribution chain. however, these measures are particularly disconcerting because labelling, controls and other inspections will hardly be able to prevent the spread of pollen, the interpenetration of the two food circuits, namely with and without gmos, and finally the victory of the biotechnologies of the multinational monsanto and other large american seed companies. the pharisaism of european leaders, who pretend to control the gmo phenomenon for health reasons as uncertain as the positive contributions that these genetically modified products would bring to world agriculture, is doubled by a calendar irony. the european parliament is speaking out on the subject at a time when the french agricultural leader, josé bové, a world symbol of the warning about the real or overestimated dangers of gmos, is being imprisoned for excessive and disproportionate means. labelling for gmos, closure for anti-gmos, this sums up the ambiguity of these biotechnologies and the european position.
in writing. - traceability is the basic principle on which consumer protection and respect for their free choice in relation to gmos must be based. this traceability requires the introduction of systems for the recognition of the identity of gmos, i.e. procedures ensuring that it is possible to know, at all stages of the production and marketing chain, who has placed the products on the market and to know their origin. companies are also required to report whether a product is derived from gmos, to keep such information on identity and traceability and to make it available to the competent authorities. as regards the presence of authorised gmos, we support the most stringent thresholds, on the understanding that the rate chosen must be realistic, i.e. based on technical and measurable criteria. this requirement will need to be maintained in a progressive manner as detection and analysis methods become more sophisticated. finally, it is necessary to ensure that operators who choose not to use gmos can derive a commercial advantage from their choice.
in writing. - i voted in favour of the amendments adopted by the committee on the environment, as they significantly improve the council's common position and provide strong guarantees on traceability and labelling, aimed at preserving the consumer's freedom of choice between gmo and non-gmo products. contrary to the decision of my political group and the majority of the european parliament, i voted against compromise amendments 44 and 45 agreed with the council. the latter leave it to the discretion of the member states to adopt measures concerning the coexistence of the gmo and non-gmo sectors. however, as a result of the rejection of amendment 40 to the scheele report, member states are prohibited from restricting or prohibiting, on valid grounds, genetically modified food and its importation which present a risk to human or animal health or to the environment. where is the consumer's freedom of choice guaranteed? it turns out that the sole purpose of this legislation is to allow the european moratorium on gmos to be lifted as soon as possible. a large majority of the european parliament, as well as the european council, have just adopted legislation that is ineffective and will force gmos on europeans against their will.
in writing. - the common position on the indication of ingredients in foodstuffs is satisfactory with one exception. the commission's proposal is to be amended to include the following: the common position is in fact quite disproportionate in requiring that all substances used in the manufacturing process be indicated on the labels. especially when these substances leave no trace in the finished product. this is the case for famous drinks that give life to entire regions, such as beer and wine, which could thus be labelled as containing egg and fish derivatives. this has ruined the reputation of these fine drinks, which have been safely consumed for centuries. the amendments tabled, which are along the same lines as those we tabled for the vote in the committee on the environment, call for these technological aids to be subjected to precise scientific tests proving their allergenic effects. at this point, nothing is proven, everything is assumed. let us therefore wait for the first results before making labelling of these technological aids compulsory. yes to transparency to inform consumers about the composition of products while opposing over-labelling, which is disastrous for agro-food chains vital to france and many other countries.
in writing. - after salmonellosis, listeriosis and other foodborne infections, health policy in northern europe is now focusing on allergies to ingredients in food. hence the need for a directive on the labelling of these allergenic additives. but since wine is treated as a food, labelling would also be required for bottles in the name of the right to information on the risks of intolerance, in particular for eggs and fish referred to in annex iiia, listing the 20 risk ingredients. in order to eliminate suspensions in the wine during the production process, egg or fish-based glues are used. but it is clear that they disappear with the flocculation deposits they allow. there is therefore no reason to put these technological aids on a label, since there are no allergens at the end of the chain. with the friends of the winegrowers and common sense, we have tabled the amendments necessary to remove wine from this phobic and neurotic labelling requirement.
in writing. - the examination of this commission proposal, which aims to revise the sole objectives of recycling and re-use of packaging and packaging waste, is a laborious exercise for our assembly. the situation in each country, and even in each locality, is very different. the member states' performance in meeting the objectives laid down in the 1994 directive is uneven. the efforts they would now have to make to achieve the objectives set out in the commission's proposal are therefore very different from one member state to another, not to mention the specific case of the candidate countries. the council has therefore so far only reached a common position, which the rapporteur considers to be very insufficient. i personally cannot share his view. we cannot deny reality, even if it does not correspond to our ideals. in an ideal virtual world, mrs corbey would have had my support and i could have been even bolder than she was. but in the very real world we live in, every decision has consequences and implies costs that weigh on the taxpayers and the consumers that we all are. it would have been counterproductive to vote today on provisions which have never been quantified and which impose obligations on all our member states which are not realistic. in writing. - i voted for this bill. i am not particularly in favour of this worldwide system of selling "rights to pollute". the practical experience i have had with industrialists in my sector shows that these economic actors can make a significant effort to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. however, i wanted to make amendments to the original proposal submitted by the european commission. it seemed very important to extend the scope of the directive to the chemicals and aluminium sectors. i have tabled amendments to this effect. i therefore deeply regret that the council of ministers has not accepted the position adopted by my colleagues on this point and is thus delaying the inclusion of the chemical and aluminium sectors.
- mr president, there are many uncertainties about the cancun conference, whose preparatory negotiations are far from being concluded, particularly in the areas supposed to be favourable to the developing countries. the dismantling of agricultural subsidies is very limited, and this shows that the rich countries, and above all the united states, are not ready to give up their privileges, even though they are committed to the development cycle. the european union, obsessed with its own interests, also downplayed the reform of the cap. revision of the trips agreement to ban the patenting of living things should be a priority for cancun. applying to all forms of life, intellectual property rights violate the sovereignty of states and peoples to protect their resources and know-how and deny the very existence of public goods. negotiators, listen to the call of the africa group, if you want cancun to be a success, and abandon the singapore outcome. the absence of solutions to the famous paragraph 6 of the doha declaration on access to medicines shows that our governments, under pressure from the pharmaceutical companies, are afraid to adopt a courageous and genuinely humanist stance. once again, there is a great risk that a compromise solution which would have been considered unacceptable a priori will be finally accepted. in egypt last week, the americans seemed to take a step forward by waiving a restrictive list of diseases. there is also the problem of the countries eligible. what is meant by sufficient production capacity? - commissioner, you have reformed the common agricultural policy in order to give europe a margin of manoeuvre in the wto negotiations. the compromise reached in luxembourg last week largely follows the commission's recommendations. let me ask you a few questions. can you tell me today what new horizons this reform opens up in negotiation? can you tell me what agriculture will gain from this, despite a reform which will have very negative consequences for our farmers? european consumers are expressing increasingly high demands for food safety, product quality and production conditions. these are translated into increasingly stringent constraints on farmers in respect of the environment and animal welfare. do you think you can meet their expectations by requiring that only products meeting the same requirements enter the european market? otherwise, it would create a distortion of competition in our own markets which would be detrimental to our products. in the field of public health, the union has opted for a ban on hormone-treated meat. will you stand firm on this position which we do not wish to be called into question under any circumstances? our agriculture also produces very high quality foodstuffs, which are recognised by designations of origin and often represent the spearhead of regional economies. how do you propose to promote them to our wto partners? finally, we support the eu moratorium on gmos in response to the complaint lodged by the united states. we are counting on you, commissioner, to take a firm and aggressive stance in defence of european agriculture, consumer demands and refusal of any concessions on the opening up of markets. to give in to liberalism would be to condemn european agriculture.

they are indispensable - but, as mr delors said, competition is not enough, we must build cooperation and solidarity between us if we are to have a functioning economy and play a role in the governance of the world economy. if we do not have this will and these concepts, let us at least work on institutional reforms, let us try to equip ourselves with institutional tools. you proposed a single representation of the euro area and put forward the idea of a minister for economic affairs who would play his role both internally and externally and who would be placed in the commission. of course, i can only support these proposals which are going in the right direction.
- madam president, the gasòliba i böhm report takes a positive view of the functioning of the euro area since 1999, and identifies many advantages, but also some rare and hypothetical disadvantages. we can be a little more specific, however: the real benefits are there and they were known from the start: for example, the disappearance of currency fluctuations between the countries of the euro area, which has undoubtedly saved us from some crises in the recent period. but there are downsides. these include twice as low growth and twice as high unemployment in the euro area as in the non-euro area. this difference may have several causes, but one of them is most certainly the rigidity introduced by the unified interest and exchange rates applied to economies whose needs remain very different. another disadvantage, which is rarely mentioned, is the lack of incentive for structural reforms, which results from the sharing of responsibilities. in the past, national mismanagement could lead to a currency crisis that required corrective action. today, the responsibilities of the virtuous and the delinquent countries are blended in the single currency, so that some can defer reforms as long as the euro has credit. it was indeed intended that the disappearance of the foreign exchange market disciplines would be compensated by the disciplines of the stability pact, but it is now clear that these administrative disciplines cannot suffice to replace those of the market. as for the strengthening of overall economic coordination and the european budget drawn up on federal principles, which the report calls for, we should not count too much on this in the immediate future, as is shown by the few results achieved by the convention on this chapter. it would not be in accordance with the maastricht treaty. in other words, madam president, the eurozone's ship is floating, but it is not navigable and no one knows where it is going. i hope it's not to the superstate.

- madam president, i would first of all like to thank the rapporteur very warmly for this gender budgeting, because it seems to me that, thanks to this document, we are taking an important step, as the commissioner said. the rapporteur explained that gender budgeting practices were already being applied in countries outside and inside europe. i therefore hope, commissioner, that we will give our full support to this report. i would like to say to my colleague who thinks that we are playing with ideology when we talk about this issue that it is an economic issue. if i take the example of the pension issue, which affects most of our countries in europe and, in recent months, particularly france, gender budgeting makes it possible to make a diagnosis of the situation. for example, it is found that while the gender pay gap is 25%, the gap rises to 47% by the time of retirement. that's a diagnosis this study allows us to make. however, this diagnosis is not enough, because the angry spirits will say: 'well, it's going to cost us money!' economic gender equality costs money, whether it's job equality, pension equality, or many other issues. i would like to remind those sad minds that there is another way to look at the inequality between men and women: economic inequality between men and women costs money! better analysis and practice of equality for financial issues would reduce rather than increase a cost. i say this for those who think we are ideologizing. they are wrong, we are also doing economy through this question.

in writing. - the thessaloniki council launched a reflection on the union's security strategy on the basis of a report by the high representative ('a secure europe in a better world') which seeks, in a very interesting way, to take account of certain recent developments. in particular, the document highlights the new threats: terrorism, weapons of mass destruction, criminal or failing states, and organized crime. it shows that, because of increased interdependence, geographically distant destabilisation can have dangerous repercussions for us, directly or indirectly. finally, he stressed that often a 'preventive engagement' (which is not necessarily military) 'can help to avoid serious problems in the future'. these considerations could provide a good basis for a posteriori justification for intervention in iraq, which provoked the anger of the chairman of the communist group. but i do approve of this effort to be clear-headed. however, i believe that the high representative's report underestimates the threat of increasing and uncontrolled migration flows for the future. moreover, the text seems unrealistic as regards the possibilities for a unified foreign policy in europe without a sharp reduction in democracy.
in writing. - we have refused to accept the outcome of the thessaloniki european council. first, we exclude immigration issues as the main problem in europe. at a time when immigrants who are victims of poverty, political repression or conflict are dying every day outside the walls of fortress europe, whether in sfax or lampedusa, we reaffirm the principle of free movement and free establishment. the creation of transit centres, regional protection zones and the intensification of police and border enforcement have proved inhumane and ineffective. secondly, we do not recognise the legality or legitimacy of the proposal for a constitution for europe by giscard d'estaing. this text, which emerged from the undemocratic process of the convention, is nothing but the expression of the tenets of a market europe, a europe of democratic and social regression. this project, after having been in the hands of the eurocrats, is now in the hands of the heads of state or government. if the citizens of europe want a constitution, they need a constituent process based on democracy, social rights, public services and the general interest. by voting against the resolution, we are defending that perspective.
in writing. - with the official presentation of the convention's work, the thessaloniki summit will of course remain a landmark european council. the result for the convention is ambitious but unsurprising. the convention, which was set up to provide the european union with a constitution, is a text of a clearly federalist nature. the question now is what will become of this text. although the draft constitution is not legally binding on the participants in the next igc, there is a risk that political pressure will be strong to force the adoption of the constitution on the states. in such a situation, i hope that the national governments - which retain the exclusive competence to revise the treaties - will resist the oukases of ultra-federalist circles and will show the necessary authority to preserve their prerogatives. in addition, whatever the outcome of the igc, i hope that in the member states where the referendum procedure exists, the new treaty will be submitted directly to the people. this is a democratic requirement
in writing. - we abstained on the ghilardotti report which advocated gender budgeting, i.e. public budgets which take account of the 'gender perspective' and are therefore supposed to establish a little more equality between men and women. the intention is good but the means are not. this is all the more so when one is in line with the broad economic guidelines of the member states of the european union, which, contrary to what the author of the report claims, do not reduce inequalities in europe, but on the contrary contribute to their aggravation. the european parliamentarians, in their ivory tower, can imagine whatever they want. the reality is very different. by increasingly giving free rein to large industrial and financial groups, by destroying public services or by attacking social protection, the eu states are not reducing inequalities, they are deepening them. by refusing to put an end to redundancies, by advocating wage moderation, by reducing the amount of pensions, their action worsens the evils suffered by women, such as being more often than men victims of unemployment, precariousness, forced part-time work. in writing. - public budgets are currently drawn up on an administrative basis, with appropriations being allocated by ministry. but there are presentations by major function, by programme or by economic breakdown. since 1995, in the name of gender equality, it has been proposed to prepare budgets on a gender basis. it is gender budgeting, which would answer two questions. first, how are the budgeted expenditures divided between women and men: who pays? second, who pays? who pays the taxes? this bold vision needs to be expanded to even more justice. we need a generational budgeting. in society, which generations, young, retired, working, fourth generation, pay taxes? which generations benefit most from public spending? but above all, we need class budgeting, categorical budgeting. what social groups bear the burden of taxation? the employees, the pensioners? finally, the big taboo: who benefits from the budget? rich or poor? the middle class? old people, peasants, small people, fat people? the question of justice is there, it is not hormonal but social.
in writing. - the creation of the single european sky to allow for an optimal and unified use of european airspace in the face of sky saturation and the resulting delays is based on good feeling. however, the fragmentation of european airspace is not the only cause of delays. the commercial practices of carriers, which increase the number of small aircraft on the most profitable routes, are a major contributor. the infringement of the principle of subsidiarity by the requirement of organic separation between the regulator and the operator prevents member states from organising their national navigation control system as they see fit, possibly within the framework of the second pillar of the cfsp with a corollary of harmonisation with nato. the commission's proposal to change the allocation of airspace between civil and military uses must not favour purely commercial interests at the expense of security. what will be the result of a community-wide duplication of eurocontrol's powers? its current operation is organized efficiently in terms of safety and flow management. will we not create a technocratic and administrative 'monster' which will once again remove the citizen from the centre of decision-making?
in writing. - we rejected parliament's amendments which sought to liberalize and deregulate air transport in europe. we are not satisfied with the council's position, however, which endorses the abolition of the notion of a mission of general interest and of public service obligations. as is often the case in these matters, after consulting the trade unions in the sector, we resign ourselves to the policy of the lesser evil, knowing that the member states chose at the barcelona european council to deal a fatal 'totally liberal' blow to users and employees. the question of the single european sky should have been raised not in the pursuit of commercial interests but in the context of effective harmonisation on the basis of the best european standards for operating systems and environmental and social standards. this would have made the single sky a given for all citizens and not a new market for a minority of industrialists and shareholders.
in writing. - we rejected all amendments which seriously undermine the staff regulations, the quality of services and, more generally, the public service remit. we have no confidence in the market rules to harmonize or improve air transport. parliament's amendments are part of the liberal ideology. under the guise of harmonisation, they fragment the european sky into several entities and open the way to competition between service providers. we have therefore voted against the requirement to extend the single sky to lower space. we rejected the commission's arbitration in the case of a dispute over the creation of crossborder space blocks and the imposition of sanctions on the provider. we are concerned about the relatively short duration of the concession for providers (5 to 10 years) and the strong return of financial incentives. the single european sky of the commission and the council will, in these circumstances, be a source of precariousness and insecurity. in the long run, the single sky is a regression for users and employees, as opposed to a public service coordinated at european level, integrating the long term and using the most advanced techniques.
in writing. - we would have voted for the amendments which seek better compensation for passengers, but since almost all amendments are voted as a whole, we did not want to support those which exempt certain service providers, such as tour operators, or which seek to reduce the obligations of airlines. we are particularly opposed to the fact that the latter are held responsible in the event of a strike. it would be unthinkable for air transport employers to escape their obligations when it is their wage and employment policy that is the cause of these strikes.
in writing. - we voted for this report because we cannot but agree with the denunciation of this abject situation of the transformation of children into slave soldiers. but at the same time, we are disgusted by the hypocrisy of a text coming from political representatives of rich countries whose ruling class has so much responsibility for the misery of these countries. what, for example, do statements about "a strategy to combat poverty" or the promise, which is known to be false, to facilitate access for these children "to medical care, social benefits and schooling" mean? moreover, while the european parliament expresses its indignation, the member states of the union continue to maintain relations with the leaders of these countries. for example, to take just one recent example, the fact that the president in office in liberia is using child soldiers did not prevent the leaders of the french state from receiving him with honours four years ago. the rule of armed gangs has never stopped the arms companies from selling weapons to the regime, nor the jewelry companies from recovering smuggled diamonds. while the massacre of civilians and the dehumanization of child soldiers continues, the looting continues.

in writing. - the european parliament's concern about the situation in chechnya is understandable. is this a reason to ignore the most basic principles of international law, such as russia's national sovereignty, non-interference in its internal affairs, the right of russian political authorities to take the necessary measures to guarantee the territorial integrity and indivisibility of the state? i do not think so, especially since the reasons given for the usual condemnation of the events in chechnya seem to me to be completely wrong. even if some people sometimes forget, we are dealing here with a legitimate fight against terrorism. but contrary to what the human rights humanitarianism of a handful of irresponsible people would have us believe, there are no good or bad terrorists. there are terrorists, that is to say fanatics who, in contempt of human dignity, commit murderous attacks against innocent people. so yes, a political solution is desirable in chechnya - and i welcome vladimir putin's efforts in this direction - but it will only be credible if the terrorist factions give up violence once and for all. that's my hope.
in writing. - the fifth wto ministerial conference to be held in cancun next september seems to be governed, once again, by the imperatives of free trade rather than rebalancing in favour of respect for national sovereignty. on the procedural side, the commission seems to want to use the negotiating mandate granted in 1999 for seattle, which was already of little relevance at the time and is now completely outdated. the european parliament is consulted only by this resolution, which concludes a short one-hour debate and has no binding legal force. the negotiations will therefore once again be opened without transparency, which is a bad omen. in the end, for us, what is at stake is the right of each people to regulate the society in which it lives. this includes the right to choose its own agricultural model (as dominique souchet said very well in yesterday's debate), the right to choose the way in which its public services operate (and their limits), the right to safeguard its independence or to apply the precautionary principle by prohibiting certain imports, and the right to freely apply a regional preference or a preference in favour of poor countries in order to express a choice of solidarity.
in writing. - we obviously voted against the joint resolution on the wto because we are against the capitalist system, as well as all the international organizations which represent it. we also voted against or abstained on most of the amendments because, while they express good intentions to make the capitalist world a better place, they are just part of the general cheating. capitalism cannot be improved by the rust of a few amendments from the european parliament.
in writing. - we vote against the joint resolution on the forthcoming world trade organization conference. this resolution takes up the positions traditionally defended by the european commission in favour of widening the scope of negotiations in the wto. on the so-called singapore issues, it advocated the formal opening of negotiations on competition, investment, trade facilitation and public procurement. this would give the wto greater powers. the resolution also considered that the reform of global governance could be satisfactorily achieved by establishing a more balanced and better articulated relationship between the wto and other international organisations. this is a misunderstanding of what the wto is. it was set up with the aim of promoting trade liberalization. it was designed to ensure the predominance of the imperialist countries within it. it is imposing itself as an undemocratic force, its decisions, taken without any popular control, having to be transposed into national or community legislation. the wto is a war machine for the money powers. it is not enough to rebalance the relationship to solve such a problem! democratic reform of international trade will be against the wto, not with it.
in writing. - the blokland report welcomes the appreciation of the euro against the dollar but warns that the intensification of this trend must not jeopardise exports. he points to a black hole in monetary union: no one knows exactly what the exchange rate target for the euro is. in any case, it is not for the ecb to define this, since the ecb is only responsible for maintaining price stability. the demand for a large-scale study of the euro confirms that the ecb does not seem to be taking a spontaneous interest in this issue. this ignorance, which is claimed or even asserted, confirms our analysis of the euro: it is not an instrument designed to support a better coordinated economic policy and more favourable to employment. it is essentially an economic policing tool aimed at putting pressure on wages and social budgets. it is therefore not surprising that this report, like the gasòliba i böhm report, is a strong reminder of the strictest orthodoxy, particularly in budgetary matters. far from deploring the breakdown of the stability pact, we see that its principles are both inapplicable in practice and profoundly harmful in their effects. that is why we voted against these two reports, which are nothing but a compulsive repetition of patterns that have long been shaken by the economic situation.
in writing. - this report does not derogate from the principle applicable to the examination of annual reports, which requires that the institution concerned be flattered. this time, the 'bold' rapporteur dares to deplore the fact that the introduction of the euro has had what he modestly calls an impact on inflation. the ecb is also asked to be cautious about the speed with which markets react to or ignore its monetary policy decisions. this is all the "negative" aspects of a report which, for the rest, is a thorough analysis of the ecb's activities. the ecb is praised for having responded correctly to economic and financial developments, and for the appreciation of the euro against the dollar. the ecb is now reaping the dividends of its constant allegiance to federalist and monetarist dogmas. in these circumstances, it is not surprising that passages concerning the ecb's independence are being used, let alone the attack on member states which have broken the stability and growth pact, which risks undermining the credibility of the euro area! i am not surprised, incidentally, that i reject this report.
in writing. - all is well in the best of all worlds! this is, in essence, the spirit of this report on the international role of the euro area. while everyone is worried about the appreciation of the euro against the dollar - a phenomenon which is severely penalising our exporters - and while some are questioning the criteria for interpreting the stability pact, and while the commission is increasing threats against states which cannot comply with the overwhelming constraints of maastricht, the rapporteur speaks of the euro as an important success of european integration on the road to greater prosperity and european identity, and sees only the independence of the central bank and the policy of price stability. in his view, the euro is such a success that a single representative of the euro area should be appointed to international political institutions! in short, once again the european parliament is being carried away by an ideological and demagogic interpretation of the observable situation. all this is truly astounding, and it shows an incredible blindness to economic realities. this report is off the table and i shall naturally vote against it.
the commission (es) mr president, as you know, the commission adopted on 2 april 2003 a decision confirming an infringement of the competition rules by six beef federations. the corresponding fines were imposed, amounting to approximately eur 17 million. this is an agreement concluded in france between four farmers' federations and two slaughterhouse federations at the end of 2001. the agreement consisted of a minimum price undertaking and a suspension-limitation of imports from other member states. it took the form first of a public written agreement and then of a secret oral agreement after the commission sent letters of formal notice. these agreements were concluded against a background of low prices on the beef market due to the crisis in the sector. on the basis of information provided by the directorate-general for agriculture, the directorate-general for competition opened an investigation and sent requests for information in mid-november 2001. on this basis, the commission - and i want to emphasize this - initially merely sent warning letters at the end of november 2001. all parties to the agreement then gave written assurances to the commission that they would terminate the illegal agreement. but the commission found indications that the parties were keeping the agreement secret. the surprise inspections carried out in mid-december 2001 confirmed the commission's suspicions. the parties were given the opportunity to make written and oral submissions. the decision of 2 april 2003 concludes, on the basis of settled case-law of the court of justice, that, first, there is a price agreement which is incompatible with the provisions of article 81 of the treaty and, second, there is an agreement suspending imports from the other member states, which is also incompatible with the community competition rules. the documents discovered by the commission in the course of the investigation show that, moreover, all the organisations concerned knew that the agreement they were concluding was illegal and that they were exposed to interference by the competition authorities. the commission imposed fines of eur 12 million on the fnsa, the main french agricultural federation, and fines of up to eur 480 000 on one of the slaughterhouse federations. let me remind you that in the case of very serious infringements of the competition rules, the commission imposes fines, the basic amount of which for each participant is, in principle, at least eur 20 million. the three main criticisms of the commission's decision are: firstly, that it is an attack on freedom of association; secondly, that the amount of the fine is excessive, given the context of the crisis; and thirdly, the commission's inaction in the second mad cow crisis. i will try to answer these three arguments. as regards freedom of association, the commission considers that the scope of the decision has been exaggerated. freedom of association is a fundamental freedom, recognised by all, as the commission reiterates in its decision. but this freedom does not give the right to do anything: a trade union cannot have as its legitimate activity the conclusion of an agreement on prices and limitation of imports in contravention of the principles of the common market. that's all the decision says. the amount of the fine is fixed according to the seriousness of the infringement and the aggravating circumstances. the matter was not without seriousness and aggravating circumstances, even the most serious ones. in this respect, it should be recalled that the farmers, by means of acts of physical violence, forced the slaughterhouses to sign the illegal agreement. it should also be recalled that the parties, after having given written assurances that the agreement would not be renewed, in fact continued to apply it in secret. the commission has also taken account of the difficult economic situation in the agricultural sector, the dual crisis of mad cow disease and foot-and-mouth disease, to which mr bernié referred in his speech to this house on 7 april, and it is precisely this particular situation which has led, for the first time, to a reduction of the fine by 60%, a significant percentage. the third criticism is that it was the commission itself that failed to take adequate measures to deal with the mad cow crisis. in this connection, it should be recalled that the commission has increased its market stabilisation measures. the intervention mechanisms were used extensively, including the conditions for their application, and specific crisis mechanisms were created to enable member states to withdraw additional quantities of channels from the market. in a few months, about 10% of european consumption was thus withdrawn from the market. more than eur 1 billion from the community budget was used for this operation and the commission also authorised member states to grant national aid to the farmers most affected. in the case of france, the commission approved over eur 300 million in state aid. finally, it should be recalled that, although the crisis in the beef and veal sector affected the whole of europe, the commission has no record of the parties in any other member state having considered it necessary to create an illegal cartel. the decision, setting out in detail the facts as established by the commission and its legal conclusions, will be published in the near future.
- commissioner, i asked the commission for this explanation because i was shocked by the fine you want to impose on the french agricultural unions. it condemns trade unionism twice: on the one hand, you condemn the initiative capacity of a sector which enables it to establish solidarities to face a very exceptional crisis; on the other hand, you condemn the very existence of the unions, since the amount of the fine exceeds their budgetary capacity. the french cattle sector has 200 000 farmers with an average annual income of less than 8 000 euros. by autumn 2001, prices had fallen by more than 45%, while, paradoxically, consumer beef prices continued to rise. moreover, european solidarity has not worked and the french market has been saturated by low-priced meat arriving from other member states. in this context of a very exceptional crisis, there was no longer even a market. the french agricultural unions have agreed, with the agreement of the minister and the french ministry of agriculture, to fix a minimum price. a price at a level which did not allow for any margin to be made available. it could not in any way have been a secret agreement since the same evening as the agreement was signed, the french unions held a press conference. this is not, therefore, the creation of a cartel, despite what has been reported in the press, but rather a solidarity approach to avoid the disappearance of a part of agricultural production: that of quality beef. if europe had not failed in its mission to ensure market stability, french farmers would not have had to replace it. in exceptional circumstances, exceptional measures. in conclusion, commissioner, i would like to ask you a few questions. can you tell me what measures the commission has taken and why they have failed? have you really taken account of the distress of farmers and the risk of the disappearance of a quality sector? can you tell me on what basis you have estimated the fine at eur 16.7 million, which seems to me to be a very high figure? do you not consider that the commission's position is contrary to the principle of fixing a minimum price? finally, do you not think that, in a context where the agricultural unions have asked for arbitration by the european court of justice, the commission should play the cool hand by withdrawing these penalties in the circumstances?
- commissioner, i disagree with your analysis. we must remember the dramatic situation in the european union in the autumn of 2001, at the time of the terrible mad cow crisis: an exacerbated consumer fear led to a precipitous fall in beef consumption, a collapse in prices to levels unknown until then. the catering industry, the supermarkets, the slaughterhouses, they refused beef. desperate farmers saw their stock piled up and their fodder resources depleted and threatened public order. and what was the european commission proposing? weak and ineffective measures, far from being adequate to the scale of the crisis and the disturbances it was generating. it proposed voluntary slaughter-destruction measures, which were not applied by some member states, notably germany and the netherlands, which exported their problems to france by refusing to come to the aid of their own farmers. in this context, the measures taken in france by common agreement between the public authorities and the profession, which consisted in fixing a buying grid with the slaughterhouses at price levels corresponding to the buying-for-destruction prices fixed by the commission and calling on importers to stop their beef imports, were perfectly adapted to the situation and had an immediate calming effect. the allegation of collusion raised by the commission therefore appears to be totally out of date and scandalous in relation to the gravity of the situation at the time and, to put it bluntly, both absurd and irresponsible. i therefore urge the commission to abandon these senseless prosecutions and to devote all its energy to tracing the real hidden cartels which are really undermining freedom of competition.

limit fraud as much as possible. at the aforementioned meeting, the commission undertook, and i think this line must be maintained, to propose a draft text on this issue within the year. that would be the council and we can accept the new text.
mr president, the text we are considering today is in fact directly linked to the fundamental question of maritime safety and we must approach it with the recent disasters that have struck our coasts in mind and which are clearly linked to issues of insufficient training of crews. the increase in recent years in shipwrecks caused by human error, as well as in fatal collisions and escape attempts, is a sign both of serious shortcomings in the training of crews and of the absence of the basic culture of demanding solidarity among seafarers. our fishermen are working today in the fear of a collision with a merchant ship. unfortunately, these collisions have become common along our coasts. we also note, and i am thinking in particular of the case of the french fishing vessel cistude, which was gutted just a year ago by the norwegian freighter bow eagle, the difficulty of the families of seafarers who were victims of these accidents in obtaining compensation for the damage they suffer. in this case, the offence of absconding, which led to the deaths of several seamen, should be punished only by a light prison sentence. in fact, the recruitment of crews in third countries and in fact from manning agencies, these recruitment agencies which, according to some, are more concerned with collecting high commissions on the salary of seamen they provide to shipowners than with ensuring their qualifications, must be considered a bad idea. a genuine prevention of disasters in which the human factor plays a decisive role must therefore be organized around two aspects and not one. the first is a voluntary component of training crews composed of nationals of the member states of the european union, before encouraging and facilitating the recruitment of seafarers from third countries, as this directive aims to do. the real causes of the current shortage of qualified seafarers in the union must be seriously examined and a proactive policy developed to correct this negative trend. that is why i find amendments nos 1 and 2 tabled by the committee quite relevant. the second aspect of this prevention concerns the absolute need to ensure the highest possible guarantees of quality and effective training when foreign seamen are recruited by ships flying the flag of a member state of the union. although this is difficult, it would be desirable to have control extended to the level of training establishments, as suggested by amendments nos 12 and 15; i also think that it is appropriate to introduce a progressive check to avoid the provisions of the directive being frozen for a long period, as proposed in amendment no 23. but why should we want to discharge the member states of their responsibilities in this area, which is primarily a matter of security? the european maritime safety agency will certainly be able to provide useful expertise in the assessment of training. but why should this evaluation of third countries be reserved exclusively for the commission and the agency? finally, mr president, why would you want to deprive member states of the right to revoke recognition visas when they consider it essential for their in writing. - vat, like all indirect taxes, is a scandal. it is a tax paid at the same rate by the poorest and the richest, by the unemployed and the billionaire. in other words, the real problem is not the "administrative cooperation" between states, as the author of the report proposes, but the fact that the share of vat in state revenue is much higher than that of income tax, which is at least somewhat proportional to the income of the taxpayer. we demand the complete abolition of vat and its replacement by a tax on income and wealth, which should be graduated sufficiently to ensure that the tax paid by the rich classes compensates for the shortfall in income generated by the abolition of indirect taxes. we voted against this report.
in writing. - this report takes up in substance, if not in form, the complaints of dutch employers against european provisions which might have the effect, not of preventing, but of making it a little less easy to dismiss their employees residing in another member state. this situation, although the result of a combination of exceptional circumstances, is considered intolerable by employers and the dutch authorities, as is the rapporteur who calls on the commission to 'look into (this) problem'. as if the european authorities needed such encouragement to trample on the rights of workers, whose hearts, concerns and actions are already too much in favour of employers! we have of course voted against this report.
in writing. - air transport is one of the many illustrations of the fact that the so-called european union is above all the result of rivalries of interests between states and their trusts and large groups. the european authorities would like europe to be a bloc in global competition. they can't do it. and not more so in the airline sector than elsewhere because the big european airlines are also competing with each other. when they have an interest in associating or concluding agreements with non-european companies, particularly american ones, the opinion of the european institutions cannot prevent them from doing so. the report's author, a supporter of free competition, would like to reconcile the search for added value for community airlines with the domestication of the savagery of rivalries. the defence of capitalist europe may be trying to square the circle, but we are voting against this report because we are against this system based on competition, regulated or not, because it is a huge source of waste.
in writing. - we voted against this report. not because we would reject a european agreement with china on shipping, but because the agreement in question bears the stamp of inequality in europe's imperialist relations with the rest of the world. the main points of this agreement are clear, which takes account of the interests of european shipping companies and their shareholders, as well as the interests of the companies linked to them. all this, without the rapporteur, as natural as it must seem to him, even pretending to care about the way in which the shipping industry's supporters, these workers, who are often asian, are treated and the sufferings of which ship owners, especially european ones, and the large groups for which they operate, are fed.
in writing. - this society, fundamentally unequal because of the inequality between social classes, secretes a multitude of other inequalities. thus, certain regions which, because of their geographical location, do not offer all the facilities from the point of view of capitalist profit, inevitably benefit from less investment. the advocates of the liberal economy themselves have no other means of compensating for this inequality than to appeal to the state or, what amounts to the same thing, to the european institutions. we would not be against this type of compensation if it compensated for the disadvantages of the working classes which stem from the very functioning of the capitalist economy. however, the destructive forces of the capitalist economy are more powerful than the ridiculous resolutions of the european parliament. even if subsidies are voted for the less favoured regions, it is not said that in the end it is these regions and their working classes who benefit. the report presents the outermost regions as a model for isolated mountain regions. despite the aid and subsidies, both national and european, reunion, guadeloupe and martinique, to name a few, have a particularly high unemployment rate and particularly low wages.
