- the next item is the report (a5-0226/2003) by mr lambert, on behalf of the committee on employment and social affairs, on the proposal for a european parliament and council regulation on the coordination of social security systems (com (98) 779 - c4-0137/1999 - 1998/0360 (cod)).
- madam president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, the report by our colleague mr jean lambert contains a number of very interesting measures. the main objective of this report is to ensure that people moving within the union are not disadvantaged in their social security rights. for us in the house, who are very much looking forward to the increase in cultural and human exchanges within the framework of the free movement of persons, this report is a step in the right direction. regulatory simplification, coordination and harmonisation of procedures based on the application of the principle of equal treatment, which grants employees and self-employed persons of other member states the same rights as citizens of the competent state, all contribute to the construction of europe. some of the measures in the report are particularly noteworthy. i personally think that they are in line with the evolution of our societies. i am thinking in particular of the desire to regulate motherhood and fatherhood together, the proposal to include third-country nationals in the scope of the directive, and the definition of household members which applies to unmarried partners in a lasting relationship, regardless of their sex. while i and my group support this report, i would like to stress the paradox, madam commissioner, between the will shown and the threats of a regression in the social security systems in many european countries. france, italy and germany, for example, are on the verge of or already affected by reforms aimed at breaking up existing social protection systems, under the pretext of excessive budget deficits in the light of the maastricht criteria. the increase in the scope of action of private bodies is leading to a decrease or even a disappearance of national solidarities, which are a serious danger for the future. yet the principles and objectives that underpinned the establishment of social security systems in europe are still relevant to developing a european social model that has proven itself in enabling growth and the well-being of people for decades. i would add that these objectives are even more necessary in the light of the increase in precariousness and poverty in europe today. according to a recent eurostat study, 15% of the eu population is at risk of poverty and social exclusion. if all social transfers are removed, the rate rises to 24% and the situation is likely to worsen. the question we face today in europe goes far beyond the establishment of coordination, which is essential. it is a genuine choice of society. do we want a model of economic and social development based on fairness and solidarity, which will enable us to foster growth, or are we heading towards the disappearance of all social systems, at the risk of increasing the number of the precarious, the poor and the excluded? choosing the former would require the establishment of genuine european social governance, based on harmonisation from the top down. this would of course also involve reviewing the maastricht criteria.

- mr president, ladies and gentlemen, after having welcomed the excellent remarks made by president pasqua, i would like to remind you that history teaches us that it is better to make constitutions after making revolutions, rather than the other way around. unfortunately, this has not been the case in the drafting of this so-called european constitution, which for the moment is really a friendly little musical party between old and new, small and large, within the european institutions and between the european institutions themselves. but there were many revolutions within our reach. we could have made an economic and social revolution, overturning the stupid dogmas - i quote president prodi - which, established in maastricht and reinforced in amsterdam, condemn europe and especially euroland to deflation and unemployment, as we see more and more every day. we could have made a political revolution by declaring our independence, affirming our vision of a multilateral world and defending the central role of the united nations in world affairs. we could have even made a cultural revolution by opposing the right of peoples to choose their own way of life and their own solidarity to the commercial organization of the world. above all, we could have made a democratic revolution that would have made europe an extension of our national democracies, instead of organising their withering away, by creating a genuine political space specific to europe, through the congress you proposed and by resorting to the referendum. however, mr president, to do so, it would probably have been necessary to draw more inspiration from rousseau than from montesquieu. everyone knows, mr president, that you have chosen a turtle as your emblem, a symbol of punctuality, of perseverance, perhaps, but not really of the revolution. that's too bad. that is why i doubt, mr president, that the peoples of europe and the citizens of europe - - mr president of the convention, you once asked the convention a question which was both pertinent and impertinent, to which we never received an answer. when you presented the report of the working party on legal personality, you asked: 'but what exactly should be given legal personality? to a state or to an international organization? " it was a great question, but it was a little disturbing. the convention never responded, preferring to remain ambiguous. however, if it was possible to say at the beginning that the construction of europe was sui generis in nature, that it was an unidentified legal object, today, with the passage of the treaties and especially with the end of the convention, the object is becoming more and more identifiable. it is, in fact, a state, a central supranational decision-making authority with its unique institutional framework, its superior law to national constitutions, its decision-making procedure based on common law by majority vote and even, now, its constitution with its supreme constitutional court. perhaps some of its elements, in some respects, considered in isolation, may be part of an international organization. but when they are all brought together with this strength, this generality, this intensity, they obviously form the shape of a european state. i would therefore like to ask you, mr president, whether you think that this european superstate is really what our peoples want. those of you who quoted the polls earlier, you know the answer is "no". our peoples certainly want european cooperation, they even want more policies with transnational impact to be dealt with at european level. but at the same time they want their country to retain its freedom of decision, the freedom of choice of its national democracy, the only democracy in the full sense of the word to date. in these circumstances, mr president of the convention, do you not think that the european superstate is a very bad answer to a good question?
in writing. - a right of withdrawal recognized at the end of part i and 'constitutional' amendments to be ratified unanimously at the end of part iv, the 'european constitution' set two reasonable benchmarks in a text which, from the outset, however, went to the absurdity of a legal hold-up by stealing the name 'constitution' to make its intergovernmental nature be forgotten. with more than 400 articles, progress is being made in the following areas: a classification of legal acts into european laws, framework laws or delegated laws, a minister for foreign affairs, three presidents - of the european council, the council of ministers and the commission - and a whole orchestra of institutional instruments in which, if we cannot identify the leader, we can locate the big money of the european parliament, which is gaining in volume without gaining in political credibility. but while making a lot of noise with its institutional hardware, the european constitution fails to cover two of its major silences: on the one hand, the silence on the necessary protection of democracies crushed by the power of the media, from the empires of murdoch to that of berlusconi and, on the other hand, the silence on the protection of taxpayers against taxes that will be increasingly confiscatory.
, in writing. - mr giscard d'estaing stressed that the central point of the draft constitution drawn up by the convention was the recognition of the 'dual nature' of the european union, which becomes the emanation of both citizens and states. this special distinction implies that states are separate entities from the will of the citizens. it therefore prepares the way for the eventual challenge to the democratic legitimacy of the states and changes the nature of the union, which has hitherto been a union of states representing their peoples. a very perverse germ was thus introduced into the new "constitutional treaty". it is based on a mythical entity, the european citizen, who is not unlike the old proletariat, to whom one can lend whatever intentions one wishes. mr giscard d'estaing was right when he said that the citizens of europe were looking forward to a european constitution, a european foreign policy, a european foreign minister, etc. on this basis, any slip-up is possible, especially since the amnesiac barbarism characterizes this new man who is the european citizen, as evidenced by the refusal of the conventionalists to mention in their text the historical role played by christianity in the true constitution of europe.
in writing. - the sinking of the tricolor and the prestige have been a stark reminder of the urgency and need to make maritime safety a major issue, and therefore of the importance of ensuring a high level of training for seafarers on european ships, including seafarers from third countries. the possibility of bringing seafarers from third countries into the union is of real interest to the european fleet. of the approximately 140 000 seamen serving on ships flying the flag of a member state of the european union, about one third (i.e. 47 000) come from a third country. in addition, in many member states, shipowners have difficulty finding nationally trained staff. this proposal, which aims to replace the current procedure for the recognition of certificates of competency by the member state with a procedure for recognition at commission level, with the assistance of the european maritime safety agency, is therefore a major step forward in ensuring the highest possible level of safety. i shall pay particular attention to the amendments on seafarers' skills, access to training, the evaluation report and the fight against fraudulent practices.
in writing. - i voted in favour of this directive. i welcome this proposal. today, unfortunately, we are faced with a shortage of personnel in the european union, and particularly in france, for all maritime professions. we are therefore forced to use third country nationals. it is therefore necessary to ensure that these people have received quality training. this level of training has a very important impact on maritime safety. the shipwreck is not the only cause of the disasters we have experienced. human error, lack of experience and lack of communication between staff increase the risks at sea. in the face of these realities, it is necessary to harmonise the rules for the recognition of qualifications and to introduce the use of a single language on board ships. we must also think about the future. at a time when the european economy is stagnating and unemployment is no longer falling, the various professions in this sector need to be promoted, particularly among young europeans, to encourage vocations. this will enable our european companies to employ eu nationals who will be engaged in these maritime professions.

in writing. - the report of the legal affairs committee is based on the principle that these proposals are not intended to 'directly lay down criminal rules or to achieve criminal harmonisation'. this is the right starting point and is the result of serious preparatory work and reflection by the legal affairs committee. the commission's opinion was based in particular on a hearing of criminal law experts who confirmed the major upheavals and difficulties that such harmonisation would create. unfortunately, the report's follow-up takes us in exactly the opposite direction, relying on the extensive interpretations of the court of justice, calling on the commission to lodge complaints in its capacity as guardian of the treaties and asking the intergovernmental conference to define a community criminal jurisdiction. for this reason, the members of the edd group, representing the interests of hunting, fishing, nature and traditions, voted against this report, which, in accordance with a technique often used in this house, ultimately requires us to do what we say we do not want to do.

the rapporteur. - mr president, first of all, i am honoured to present to you the annual report on the situation of fundamental rights. it is a synthesis of the fundamental values on which the european union is founded. this synthesis is recognised and appears in part ii of the text of the draft constitution drawn up by the convention. i believe that under article 7 of the treaty on european union, the european institutions can monitor, each in accordance with its own area of competence, the strict observance of human rights and fundamental freedoms by the member states. i hope that, as a result of this vote, the legally binding nature of the charter, once it has been implemented, will allow direct and individual referral to the court of justice and the european union by european citizens. i say this because i, for my part, wanted to involve citizens in the drafting of this charter. i have thus associated two schools, one german and one french, with the first hearing, and they have been following the work for six months now. i then wanted to bring together all the major non-governmental organisations - amnesty international, human rights watch, the international federation for human rights - but also representatives of national parliaments, including those of the candidate countries. i think this has enabled me to add to the information and to verify it on my own travels. too much information, far from being a handicap, can be enriching. it is also in this sense that i wanted the report to highlight the strong points. first of all, i wanted to reflect on one of the biggest rifts that europe has experienced since the fall of the berlin wall, namely the impact of 9/11, both within and outside the union. i also had the opportunity to go on a three-week study trip to the united states. as i traveled through this country, i saw how many negative effects of 9/11 still remain. people are afraid and, most importantly, everyone recognizes that an unprecedented wave of islamophobia is taking place: it is their honor to recognize it. churches, judges, citizens, ngos have even been protecting muslims. i think that from this point of view we should also learn a lesson. why should this be a lesson for us? because, in my opinion, too often we forget the primary objective of terrorists: to destabilize the rule of law. but whenever we do something that is not in the direction of strengthening the rule of law, somewhere we are participating in the terrorist objective which is precisely to destabilize the rule of law. secondly, it is important to bear in mind, in the context of defending the first fundamental right, the right to life, which constitutes the first chapter of the charter of fundamental rights, the need for all of us to remain united in the fight against terrorism. i think that is the least of it, especially since the terrorists strike blindly. an anecdote came to mind while working on this report. in 1994, i had the good fortune to be received by nelson mandela, who was about to take power in south africa. just as he was about to take power, a report was released that listed the anc as a terrorist organization. it should also be remembered that the german occupation did not consider the resistance fighters as terrorists. the un has identified more than 142 definitions of terrorism. somewhere in there, you want to say, "to each his own". the fact remains, mr president, that terrorism today is, i believe, a real source of conflict in all its forms and can lead societies to become frivolous, to close in on themselves. it is therefore our responsibility to ensure that, within the framework we have, solutions are found as quickly as possible. i am thinking in particular of the concern that citizens, european nationals, are now being held in what i would call the utmost secrecy in cuba because they are suspected of having committed terrorist acts. so fighting terrorism is also helping to maintain the rule of law. the second thing that concerned me was the situation in prison. i think it is particularly shocking, at the beginning of the millennium, to see what is happening in the prisons of the european union, where the situation is far from satisfactory. there is an almost universal prison overcrowding. in france alone, 60,000 prisoners for 50,000 places. another concern is the threats to freedom of expression. i am thinking in particular of the economic mega-groups and the case of italy. finally, equality. in this context, it is urgent that more european political parties sign the charter of european political parties for a non-racial and non-racist society, adopted in 1998. in addition, the transposition by the member states of the directives adopted by the council on combating discrimination of all kinds at the workplace is often incomplete or non-existent. other topics, such as solidarity, civil and social rights, equality between men and women, equality in the workplace, seem to me to overlap with european citizenship and justice. there is still too much progress to be made. i did not want to point the finger at any particular country. i simply wanted to bring together the best of each of our countries.
- mr president, in addition to congratulating mr sylla on his work, i should like to make two comments on the method which i think should be used in this report. firstly, i would like to point out that this is the third report after an extremely important reform, which our parliament wants, which is actually to read the situation of fundamental rights in the union in the light of the charter, which brings with it a number of obligations. we have the means - a network of experts who produce a report, normally a working group - but the keyword is the whole charter and nothing but the charter. this naturally obliges the rapporteur and all those who would like this report to be adopted very widely to ensure that it does not become a pretext for militancy, that it does not become an opportunity to put forward personal opinions, or that it does not serve as a fodder for the action of lobbies that have nothing to do with it. not just the charter, but the whole charter! i think this principle should be reaffirmed. my second point concerns countries. this report is in two parts because that is the european union's regulation. in reality the report forms a whole and therefore the resolution should contain only the substance of the report and only highlight what parliament would like public opinion to take into account. this would avoid nationalistic reflexes on the part of a number of our colleagues who cannot bear to see their country mentioned. i think that, from this point of view too, we would be better off keeping only the important points in the resolution, which actually correspond to why parliament has chosen to make this report. it has chosen to do so as the guardian of public freedoms and to be able to answer the question: has the charter of fundamental rights as it is written, and not as it would like to be written, been respected, during the year under review, in the territory of the union? this is the subject of the report. it is very important not to forget these questions of method if we want this report to be adopted with the widest possible political support.

should we consider occitan, for example, in the south of france, or its differentiated components such as provençal or gascon, as such? but above all, we must not forget that many of our national languages are themselves endangered. the fact that the european parliament itself provides its own delegations travelling abroad with an interpretation service in english only, as was recently the case for the delegation to japan, leads me to believe that we are on a dangerous track. my own language, french, is unfortunately losing ground every day as a language of international communication, but others are also threatened in their existence. i am thinking of the irish gaelic and the baltic languages which narrowly escaped russification. the development of regional languages, of course, and that is my conclusion, mr president, but let us be careful not to damage or weaken our national languages. let us beware of any artificial reconstruction of abstract languages that are far removed from regional realities. we must not set up a system of authority and constraint. it is on this triple condition that regional languages will contribute to our cultural wealth.
- the next item is the report (a5-0251/2003) by mr perry, on behalf of the committee on culture, youth, education, the media and sport, on 'television without frontiers' (2003/2033 (ini)).
- mr president, i would first like to congratulate our colleague, mr roy perry, on the quality of the work he has done on an essential and, moreover, extremely sensitive subject. it's true he's used to difficult cases. we are all aware of the real cultural and economic challenges posed by the 'television without frontiers' directive for each of the member states of the union and the candidate countries. we therefore support the reasonable position of the european commission, which rightly sought to obtain the opinion of each member state before any decision to review. the directive may need to be improved from time to time to take account of technological developments, but care must be taken to ensure that these adjustments are not made in a hurried manner. if we look objectively at the situation on the audiovisual market, we can see that national markets are gradually adapting to new technologies. recent technological developments have not really changed the audiovisual landscape, which remains largely dominated by traditional television. any future development of the directive must in no way lead to a change in its content. a revision calling into question the cultural objectives on which all the member states had reached agreement, under the pretext of extending the scope of the directive to all broadcasting media, would in reality amount to a complete change in the original objectives of the directive, namely the defence and promotion of cultural diversity. the essential provisions of this directive must not be called into question. the promotion, circulation and dissemination of european works within europe, the production and dissemination of works by independent producers, the existence of television broadcasting quotas, the guarantee of protection for minors, measures against excessive advertising - all these principles must continue to be the basis of community audiovisual policy. the 'television without frontiers' directive is a legal instrument which has proved its worth and is now being applied satisfactorily. the revision of the directive will only be justified if it brings about real improvements in a few areas, such as the worrying issue of media concentration, which obviously undermines pluralism. this directive must remain an effective tool for the promotion of cultural diversity and not become a legal instrument allowing exclusively the promotion of commercial channels where we would see, for example, advertising in continuous transmission in defiance of the works broadcast. beyond economic and financial issues, which are of course essential, there is simply the question of our cultures, our identities and the values we believe in.
- thank you, mr president, madam commissioner, ladies and gentlemen. this is a difficult and evolving case. we can thank mr perry for the work he has done and at the same time not know whether or not to revise this directive. this has been made clear by both the professionals and the commission. this series of articles deals with the problem of defining and understanding the transport of images, the evolution and acceleration of which we do not currently control. what concerns me is the lack of a definition of a "work". the 'television without frontiers' directive gives a negative definition. we know what it's not. it is not information, it is not advertising, it is not this, it is not that. it's produced by x or manufactured by y. i would like to know what it is - and i think some professionals would like to know what it is. this may help to settle the debate on reality tv in france and other european countries. the problem is to define the margin of the audiovisual work. there are not only works that are very easy to define like documentaries or films. i don't know how to define reality tv. this is a serious concern. the second point that i think this debate raises is the circulation of works. the circulation of works and artists - as i had stressed in the report on the living spectacle - is a recurring problem in the cultural field. in the context of television without frontiers, it is amplified by concentration and non-national character. how can we get the non-national works into each of our countries? we shall have to decide on this fundamental question. mr perry, you have paid a great deal of attention in your report to the question of media concentration, which can prevent the circulation of non-national works. i am very pleased that you have stressed this point, which i think is essential and which we must also consider very seriously.
- mr president, the fundamental problem which is currently arising in the audiovisual debate is that we dare not define the quality we want to defend. when we talk about european works, for example, we include talk shows which are completely ridiculous, on the pretext that they are european productions. until we have the courage to define - and geneviève fraisse is right - what a work is, that is, what we want to defend, our television will not be able to defend european production and european works in europe, for lack of the appropriate instruments. second, with regard to concentration, the problem is very simple. if we do not define what we cannot accept democratically in europe, we shall have an increasing concentration and domination of non-european forces in the market. for these two reasons, i believe that the european union must have the courage to define what a work is and what the boundary, in a democracy, should be between political power and the power of the media.

- the next item is the report (a5-0276/2003) by mrs zorba, on behalf of the committee on culture, youth, education, the media and sport, on the cultural industries (com (2002) 2127 final).
commission. - mr president, i should first like to thank mrs zorba for her excellent report. it is timely to underline the importance of the phenomenon of european cultural industries not only from an economic point of view - as has been said - but also because of the potential they represent for cultural diversity in europe. it is a pity that we do not always realise the economic weight of the european cultural industries. i'm talking about the media, the music, the publishing. a 2001 study of the employment potential of the sector estimated that 4.8 million people were employed in the broadest sense of the creative industries, representing 3.1% of the eu. the european audiovisual sector alone directly employs over one million people. thus, beyond their contribution to diversity, cultural industries make a large contribution to the economy. of course, they play an obvious social and cultural role, because they are different industries. they're related to creation. it is not a question of producing and selling products like any other but cultural goods. these goods are the vectors of an identity, they are vectors of reference. so, in relation to the cultural industries, the normal industrial policy cannot play the same role, because it is inadequate. we have to go further. cultural diversity presupposes a strong and diversified industrial fabric guaranteeing the pluralism of the cultural offer in a globalised market. this phenomenon alone shows the importance that must be attached to this sector of activity which concerns our identities. i would like to highlight a few key actions to show you that europe is taking care of this sector not only in the context of cultural programmes but also far beyond. you all know about the media programme and the work we do for film. but did you know, for example, that in the culture 2000 programme, support for publishing houses to encourage literary translation has supported 1 300 translations in recent years? did you know that the structural funds are extremely committed to the development of the cultural industry? in the swedish town of hultsfred, for example, the erdf has co-financed projects to develop the music industry. since then, it has become the rock capital of sweden! as you can see, european aid can lead to a real concerted and concentrated development of the cultural industries. in your report you are asking for a communication on the structural funds and culture, a communication which will highlight this type of action. i should also like to point out that since 2002 we have been developing experimental actions to support the music and book industries. for example, we are planning to develop the export of european music beyond our continent. you can see, ladies and gentlemen, that these cultural industries are supported only by programmes and actions of the european union. i would add that we will soon have a unique opportunity to strengthen this action. that will be when we discuss the extension of the media and culture programmes and the new generation of our programmes. to this end, very systematic action will have to be taken, with the help of parliament, so that the creativity of this sector promotes economic and cultural diversity and thus our european roots.
- mr president, i should like to begin by congratulating mrs zorba on her very interesting initiative of devoting a report to the cultural industries. indeed, we are now seeing the emergence of cultural industries which have an increasingly important economic dimension and at the same time play a vital role in europe's cultural diversity and identity. one of the problems raised by this report is the complete absence of a precise definition of cultural industries and of any industrial strategy for europe in this field. the european commission must study these questions and make proposals, perhaps through the green paper. in the future, support for cultural industries in regional and urban economic development projects should be strengthened, through the structural funds, but also by encouraging private-public partnerships. similarly, the european union will have to put in place measures to support smes and the self-employed, who play an important role in the fields of artistic creation and production. finally, i would like to stress the importance of the printed press, and in particular the regional daily printed press. it is the best guarantee of linguistic and cultural diversity and the one that is largely forgotten in the cultural policies of the union. it is essential that the commission, in the course of drawing up its green paper, finally make proposals for active support for this sector, which is also essential for pluralism. in the same spirit, the commission will have to propose specific measures to combat media concentration. in conclusion, i believe it is time to mobilise our efforts so that the draft unesco convention on cultural diversity can be launched soon. more than ever, we need to promote a european cultural spirit to foster creativity and to make the cultural diversity live without which europe could neither exist nor shine abroad.

in writing. - i am a strong advocate of maintaining and even developing cultural diversity in europe, particularly at the time of enlargement to 25. and since languages are the primary component of this diversity, i am in favour of linguistic enlargement, whatever the material and technical difficulties that may arise. i am afraid, moreover, of the double-dealing of those who advocate the multiplication of languages in order to better impose, in practice, the monopoly of english. we must therefore work on the question of languages, in particular by looking objectively at esperanto again. the monopoly of english is not good for europe or for britain, whose language will become "a language of the kitchen".

in writing. - this year again i see that this report on human rights in the world is far from achieving the objectives it should have. who can fail to see that the moral lessons given to each other, the unfair accusations, the risky accusations, are all acts of inadmissible interference in the internal affairs of the states concerned and, consequently, are not likely to bring about a positive change in the situation? furthermore, in the name of what does this parliament judge the diplomacy of the member states in denouncing those who 'support anti-democratic regimes in different parts of the world, when economic, military interests ... are at stake at their national level'? as the delusional remarks on the fight against international terrorism, which is stigmatised in this report on the grounds that it 'is a serious threat to the protection of human rights' (!), finally show, moralising evangelicalism always trumps objective realism. if there is one area where naive idealism often proves disastrous, it is foreign policy. it is high time that europe recognized this geopolitical constant and quickly stopped its fruitless inquisitorial campaigns.
in writing. - mr fodé sylla's report on the situation of fundamental rights in the union, which is based on extremist proposals, gives an idea of what might happen if the union gained a more solid competence in this area (as proposed by the convention). the commission's proposals on immigration are as follows: extension of the right of asylum; wider legal channels of immigration; relaxation of naturalisation procedures; extension of the concept of european citizenship to legal immigrants from outside the community; the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the rights of the disabled are respected. these proposals are accompanied by severe and peremptory judgments on a specific european country, which is ordered to make amends to rehabilitate itself. in the meantime, france is being asked to ratify the charter for regional and minority languages, which the previous socialist government had signed. i hope she never does. it is clear that if the charter of fundamental rights were to become binding, the union would have the means, thanks to it and to article 7 teu, to impose a genuine rights policy geared - or rather disoriented - towards the disruption of our societies.
in writing. - what the european authorities pompously call fundamental rights is at best only a vague notion whose content is reduced to little for the workers and the most vulnerable of the inhabitants of this europe. and, with a few exceptions, the report does not record progress but retreat in this area, because, more often than not, the policies are intended and applied by states which would like us to believe that they are the guarantors of real rights for the people of europe. the people who are denied the most basic individual, economic, social or political rights in this society are first and foremost the 'little ones', and the ones who are harshest treated are women, children, the disabled, the elderly, homosexuals, asylum seekers, immigrants, members of national minorities, etc. for millions of workers, the prospects are unemployment, low wages, the arbitrariness of employers, exploitation, and death at work. where do they find the fundamental rights on which the european union is founded? our vote in favour of the report was motivated by the accuracy of its critical description of the actual state of human rights in europe, but it does not imply that we share the illusions of its author about the capacity of the european institutions to fundamentally change things.

in writing. - the question of water services will not be discussed at the wto meeting in cancun. it's a shame. the lannoye report examines the commission's proposal to create, among other things, a european water fund for the acp countries. these countries are, it should be remembered, major trading partners. they are also affected by a cruel lack of access to safe drinking water and sanitation. access to water is a right, as is the possibility for people living in rural areas in our member states to have basic public services (post office, education, clinic, etc.) at their disposal. access to water must therefore remain a public service and not be managed on a purely commercial basis. the 1980s were marked by the failure of the imf and the world bank policies on aid conditionality. only countries that privatize their water and electricity distribution networks received aid from international institutions. the commission is about to make the same management mistake with the european water fund. i support the lannoye report in its critical analysis of the commission's programme.
in writing. - i approved the lannoye report on water management in developing countries because it rightly emphasises the urgency of the problem: today, out of six billion people, 1.7 billion do not have access to clean water, and 30,000 die every day. the johannesburg conference set the target of halving the number of people without access to safe drinking water by 2015, and europe must work together to achieve this. that is why we particularly approve the creation of a european water fund for the acp countries in general and african countries in particular. the projects supported by this fund will have to be defined, not from above, but with the national authorities and the populations concerned at the bottom. priority should be given to a management model based on public-private partnership, in which the public sets the general framework for private sector action and its objectives. however, the lannoye report remains wary of the actions of private enterprises. i think that privatisation of water management, even on a small scale, if it is used well, should allow for more rational management.

in writing. - while access to water has recently been proclaimed a human right, the number of people without access to safe drinking water worldwide has been increasing steadily in recent years, reaching 1.7 billion today. we must recognise and tackle the causes of water scarcity, whether it be intensive and productivist agriculture, export-oriented economies that often undermine local economic development, or the liberalisation of public services in the water sector, often a condition imposed by the world bank and the imf on countries in the south to receive loans. the costs of water services have also become unaffordable for the poorest populations. to remedy these divergences, we want, in the north and in the south, the establishment of new modes of production and consumption based on sustainable water management. we want to promote ecological agriculture and new irrigation systems. in the face of the tragedy facing the people and the total inadequacy of the responses provided so far, the creation of a european water fund for the acp countries is a good initiative. access to drinking water and sanitation services must be defined by national authorities with the participation, through civil society associations and movements, of the populations concerned.

the commission (es) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i should like to begin by thanking all the speakers for their very interesting speeches. let's be honest with each other. for a long time, the best policy for maritime safety in the european union was precisely the absence of maritime safety. i shall refer to the last 15 years only, because that is when we have the single act - and therefore majority voting - in the field of transport. and i'm only going to refer to the most spectacular cases. 1987: casón, europe, chemicals, 23 dead; 1989: exxon valdez, in the united states, 40 000 tonnes of oil spilled; 1991: haven, in europe, 144 000 tonnes of oil; 1992: aegean sea, europe, 74 000 tonnes of crude; 1993: braer, also in europe, 85 000 tonnes of oil spilled; 1996: sea empress, 70 000 tonnes of oil spilled also in europe; 1997: the nakhodka spill occurs in japan, with 19 000 tonnes of crude; in 1999 the erika spills 20 000 tonnes of heavy oil in europe and in 2002 the prestige, also in europe, 63 000 tonnes of heavy oil. it is important to note that in 1987 (casón), 1991 (haven), 1992 (mar aegean), 1993 (braer) and 1996 (sea empress) there were national, regional and european governments. there was a commission, a parliament and a council of ministers and nothing was done. that's what happens, your honours. we must wait until 1999, with this commission and this parliament, for action to be taken. in 1981, immediately after the exxon valdez sinking, the united states introduced the oil pollution act (opa); if we had done the same here in europe in 1987, 1991 or 1992, the accidents of the braer, the sea empress, the erika and the prestige, to name only the most serious, would certainly have been avoided. ladies and gentlemen, we must prevent this from happening again. there are two aspects: prevention and dealing with disaster, if it occurs. mr sterckx's report is very comprehensive, and i congratulated him on it. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the safety of ships is not compromised by the fact that the ships are not equipped with safety belts. i am not at all comforted by the fact that we are polluting the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the use of the term 'competent authority' to cover the whole of the european union. - mr president, commissioner, this directive and this debate are terribly complex, and doubly complex, legal complexity and computer complexity. yet, their stakes are high. economically, tens of billions of dollars, philosophically, the status of human knowledge among men. in 6,000 years of history, the immense knowledge of mankind has progressed by copying. the necessary condition was that the products of knowledge, whether music, mathematics or anything else, should be freely and gratuitously accessible. copyright pays the creator without challenging these principles. when man uses material or uses the forces of nature, the definitions, have led to a proliferation of such patents. the legal status of these thousands of patents is unclear and this poses a huge danger to millions of individual creators or small mr president, ladies and gentlemen, this morning's debate comes after a turbulent period in which the world of computer users, inventors and innovators has been defending tooth and nail its right to difference, freedom and creativity. at the heart of this debate is patentability with its advantages (when the patent protects the inventor) and its major disadvantages, which are linked to the creation of often conservative monopolies to the detriment of young creators. i continue to personally support this movement which seems to me to be in the same direction as all the alternative movements which are fighting for a less rigid and less commercial society. since this debate began, we have made progress with draft amendments which significantly improve the original draft. recognising that in order to be patentable, a computer-implemented invention must be capable of industrial application is a step in the right direction. it was necessary to clarify that patents should not be allowed for mere computer programs. however, the nuances introduced and the many inaccuracies cannot be ignored. at this stage of the debate, even if there is a risk that these amendments will not be voted on or taken up, it is clear that not all the problems have been solved, far from it. i will therefore be personally vigilant when voting and remain prepared to vote against the project if the improvements are merely a cosmetic attempt to mask the hold-up of creative minds by big business. in this respect, commissioner bolkestein's last sentence, which is blackmail, will not diminish my deep distrust.
- mr president, ladies and gentlemen, what is this about? to protect the intellectual property resulting from computer innovation. two legal procedures are opposed: patentability on the one hand and copyright on the other. in our view, and i believe, commissioner, in the view of the vast majority of speakers in this house, the normal form of protection is copyright. if a journalist, a novelist, sees his text protected by copyright, he cannot claim to own the syntax, morphology, vocabulary and grammar of the language he uses. the same must be true of software, because software uses language. it is true, commissioner, that in your speech - extremely aggressive, even threatening, in relation to the criticism raised by your draft directive - you stated that software as such was not covered by patentability. but you can't take people for fools. and the least that can be said is that your directive is ambiguous, because the definition you give of computer-implemented invention, article 2 (a), can perfectly apply to software. of course, in article 4 of the draft directive, you seem to limit patentability to inventions which are, i quote, 'capable of industrial application'. but here's a concept you're not defining. it is well known that american multinationals have been successful in patenting such trivial things as the use of a click on a button to close a window on a screen, or the idea of alerting a user by a melody that he has received an e-mail, or the underlining by a colour of words that need correction in a word processor - and word processing is susceptible to industrial applications in typography or printing. i will quote again the electronic shopping cart in an internet store. young designers have even managed to drop the 35-hour workweek imposed by the previous government in my country. so why is such a text being proposed in this house? are the interests of the european patent office, which is financed on the basis of the number of patents filed, completely foreign to this? in reality, commissioner, there was a strategic choice to be made: either to align oneself with the patentability practice of the american multinationals - which is what you seem to be beginning to do - or to defend the specificity of european law and deny any effect to abusive patents. it is obvious that you have not made this second choice and your directive can be considered as not being in line with the legitimate interests of european creators.

commission. mr president, since there are many amendments, i do not propose to go through them all one by one, indicating the commission's response. with your permission i should like to provide you with a list of the amendments by number, showing which of them the commission can accept, which we cannot accept and which we could accept with suitable rewording commission's position on amendments by parliament: see annex.. on this understanding i should like to confine myself to some remarks of a general nature and hope to end with some more specific remarks to address questions raised by members of parliament. turning first to the mccarthy report itself, i have already indicated that we are favourably disposed to most of the amendments that have been made in it. however, i should like to speak about two specific amendments that raise important issues. the first is amendment no 20 - the insertion of a new article 6a on interoperability. at first sight this looks reasonable. on closer examination, however, it is plain, at least to the commission, that the exception as proposed might empty some patents of their value. in fact it could potentially render them totally worthless. i believe this would be disproportionate and in addition may be against our international obligations under the trips agreement. nevertheless we could look favourably on a provision that dealt with interoperability, provided that these important issues are dealt with. the wording used at the end of amendment no 76 might form the basis of a compromise because it evokes the trips agreement. the second point worth special mention is amendment no 18 - the addition of a new paragraph to article 5, dealing with computer program claims. that is something that the commission did not put into its original proposal. this was not an oversight but something that we considered long and hard. we were concerned that allowing computer product claims was a step on a slippery slope to allowing computer programs on their own to be patentable, something that is clearly contrary to the european patent convention and to the views of the vast majority of the members who spoke this morning. after reflection, however - and let me not disguise that a lot of this reflection was prompted by the work of this parliament - we consider that such a clause might work within the commission's overall objectives, if – and only if – we can word the article in a very careful and cautious way. unfortunately, i cannot be as positive about most of the amendments which have been tabled to the mccarthy report and which have to be considered here today. the problem with many such measures is that even if they were considered to be worth looking at, they all have one thing in common: they introduce a special regime for computer-related inventions. in patent law and practice it is a fundamental principle that inventions ought to be assessed in a neutral manner with regard to the type of technology on which they rely. the patent examiner will of course examine each individual invention for its inventive element, but he or she has no preconceptions that an invention that uses a certain type of technology is per se innovative or not. this principle is in fact enshrined in international law, in particular the trips agreement, where it is stated that patents shall be available in all fields of technology and patent rights enjoyable without discrimination on that basis. there are some amendments which pose less of a problem for the commission and we might therefore accept them. i am thinking especially of certain of the amendments directed at the report which the commission must prepare on the operation of this directive, although i should emphasise that the commission is not prepared to accept that, in this respect, 'anything goes'. anything which imposes unreasonable demands, given the limited resources at the commission's disposal, could not meet with our approval. the need to remain within the scope of the directive should also be borne in mind. some of the amendments proposed are too broad in their effects. that said, i shall make a few brief remarks. firstly to mr rocard, who said that the proposal does not guarantee that there will be no software patenting as such. the proposal lays down a specific hurdle that must be cleared before any invention can be patented. the invention must make a non-obvious technical contribution: this guarantees that non-technical software will never be patented but genuine technical inventions will get the protection they deserve. i also say this to mr maccormick who asked me to ensure the directive is watertight against leakage. this requirement of the technical contribution does so. i hope this will satisfy mr de clercq. my second specific remark is addressed to mrs echerer, who said that if a small part of a problem is patentable then the whole problem is patentable. patents are about solutions to technical problems and a patent has to cover the whole, not just a small part, of the solution to a problem. it is only infringed if the whole solution is used. it does not, therefore, monopolise every separate component part which contributes to the solution. on the matter of smes, which many members mentioned: in so far as smes are users of patents, i wish to stress that nothing becomes patentable that is not patentable now. as smes may be inventors of software, they also need to be protected and would get the protection they deserve under the directive. i say this to mr oreja and mrs thyssen in particular. let me echo the words of mr wuermeling who said: 'whoever opposes this directive must know that the present practice will be continued.' therefore, if you do not want the present practice to continue, please vote in favour of this directive. lastly, the commission would once again like to thank mrs mccarthy for her report . although it is not identical to the commission's original proposal, –it could, subject to the comments i have made, achieve the balance that we require. i thank all members for their attention and you, in particular, mr president. - this debate is over. the vote will take place tomorrow at 12 noon. documents received: see minutes. the following shall be considered as a written declaration:
in writing. - the introduction of new provisions on the legal status of political groups is yet another recognition of the latter. in principle, there is nothing to prevent the status of political groups in the european parliament from being further strengthened - but the desire, shown in recent years, to eliminate all forms of national representation in the european parliament, in the exclusive interest of a narrowly partisan representation, is to be deplored. however, let us not go too far in making parliament the home of a future 'government of parties'. the influence of the major political parties in this house is already very (too) large; the commission's proposal is to be adopted by the council on the basis of a proposal from the commission. we have seen worrying abuses here recently, abuses by certain groups which, in particular because of their federalist ideology, occupy a dominant political position. i am thinking here of the dissolution of the tdi group, a political act of extreme gravity when we know that the banning of parties is no longer even a practice in the member states! such a drift must not happen again. i am concerned to see that the proposed text is again considering this liberticidal hypothesis. we must be moderate!
in writing. - austria, using the right of initiative which is still provisionally reserved to the member states in the field of immigration policy, has just put forward a useful proposal: to draw up a list of european countries considered safe from the point of view of respect for human rights, so that they can be entrusted with the processing of asylum applications lodged in a country of the union by persons who have first crossed their territory. this measure seems to be simplifying, common sense, consistent with the need for better cooperation between the countries of the continent in the face of the influx of refugees of all kinds. this austrian initiative, which we supported, did not please the european parliament, which rejected it on various more or less specific legal grounds, for example that this text anticipated a future, broader directive on asylum procedures. the real reason is something else entirely. as can be seen from the explanatory memorandum, the european parliament clings to a narrow view of the geneva convention, based on an absolute 'non-refoulement principle' without nuance or condition. it is this narrow vision that must be challenged today if we are to really tackle the problems of asylum.
in writing. - we voted against the initiative of the republic of austria which advocates a particularly restrictive application of the right of asylum. as for the schmidt report, we do not support its call for 'bringing the solution to the problem of safe third countries'. we believe that the problem is not to draw up a somewhat longer list of states whose decision to grant asylum would be acceptable to the european union. the right of asylum must be unrestricted. and we reject any restrictive application of the geneva convention and the principle of non-refoulement.
in writing. - if the initiative of the republic of austria must be rejected, it is for reasons which are more fundamental than those which are relevant to the recitals of the rapporteur. in substance, the concept of 'safe third states' is contrary to the international obligations arising from the 1951 geneva convention. this is particularly evident in the case of roma fleeing racism and discrimination in countries such as romania and slovakia, which are considered "safe" by the eu. as the rapporteur acknowledges: 'even if a list of safe third countries were to be drawn up, an asylum application cannot be automatically rejected on the grounds that this would be contrary to the geneva convention.' it is already common practice to declare an asylum application to be 'manifestly unfounded'. the list of 'safe countries' will serve as a pretext for further encouragement of expeditious examinations and systematic disposals. the principle of non-refoulement is violated by the project to keep refugees in their regions of origin. it's a pushback that doesn't say its name. in france, the villepin law calls this "internal asylum"! it means preferring refugee camps to refugee shelters. the austrian initiative must be rejected because it effectively authorises the erosion of the right to asylum in europe and anticipates how, in the context of the elaboration of european legislation, the member states intend to abandon the respect for the right to asylum and the geneva convention.
in writing. - we voted against the appointment of jean-claude trichet as president of the european central bank because, during his hearing, he did not show any willingness to make a political change in the face of the near-stagnation in which the heart of the euro area is sinking. instead, he stressed that there was no recession in the strict sense, which is true, and that the euro area's key rates are "the lowest in more than half a century", which is also true. the implicit message he was sending us was that he could not do much more as president of the ecb. he is not entirely wrong: the slowdown in which france and germany are sinking is probably impossible to correct by the instruments of conventional monetary policy, because it is partly caused by the very structure of the single currency, a rigid framework applied uniformly to different economies. in view of this situation, the ecb president may have little room for manoeuvre. but is it not a just punishment of history to trap one of the very people who invented the maastricht system?
in writing. - our negative vote on 'the appointment of jean-claude trichet as president of the european central bank' is addressed primarily to the institution but also to the individual. the european central bank is responsible for applying a monetary and credit policy entirely favourable to the big business of the european union and, therefore, entirely unfavourable to the popular classes. we are against the very function of this institution, whoever is in charge of it. but we didn't want to bail the man out either. before being appointed to his future post, jean-claude trichet was governor of the banque de france for ten years. as such, he is responsible for a 'restructuring' plan under way at the banque de france, a plan which has resulted in the closure of half of the branches and the elimination of more than 2 000 jobs, or more than a quarter of the workforce. a man who takes on such a task deserves no more support than the institution he is about to take over.
in writing. - we voted against the nomination of jean-claude trichet as president of the european central bank because he has been the embodiment for some 15 years of the doctrine of competitive disinflation, which has inspired the neoliberal policies pursued in our country. it was under his influence that wages were blocked to allow financial profits to capture an increasing share of the wealth produced. this policy has stifled growth and encouraged the rise of mass unemployment. we would therefore not like to see this fatal dogmatism transposed to the community level. but we are not making a personal issue of it: we would probably vote against any other candidate, because it is the very conception of the european central bank that we are challenging on two essential points. such an institution should not be given an unnecessarily rigid 2% inflation target which blindly chooses finance over employment. and the ecb should be placed under genuine democratic control which goes beyond the 'operette' democracy of voting full powers to a man who will now be uncontrollable.
in writing. - the appointment of the future president of the european central bank is an act of the utmost importance because, in addition to the personality of the candidate, it is also, and above all, a monetary policy that we are called upon to decide. in this case, while i am obviously pleased that a frenchman will soon become president of the central bank, i cannot at the same time ignore the fact that mr trichet, since he is the one in question, embodies and claims a strict budgetary orthodoxy. mr trichet said it bluntly at his hearing before the economic and monetary affairs committee: against all odds he intends to perpetuate the legacy of mr duisenberg, that is to say, a monetarism as rigid as it is inappropriate. however, this option cannot be approved. at a time when many member states are no longer able to comply with a stability pact whose constraints appear, in the current situation, to be completely out of step with the harsh realities of the economic situation, i cannot support the appointment of a candidate who is clearly suffering from the same disease as his predecessor: autism.
in writing. - i tabled an amendment calling for the rejection of the european commission's proposal on the approximation of measures concerning the security of supply of petroleum products. i do not think that this proposal is an appropriate or effective response to the oil crisis. the increase in the minimum stock level from 90 to 120 days would have been an expensive measure to implement in several states, due to the current insufficiency of storage infrastructure in the union. moreover, the increase in the level of these stocks would not have been sufficiently substantial to allow the union to exert pressure on oil markets vis-à-vis the producing countries. finally, the establishment of public oil storage agencies transferred substantial burdens to the member states, even as the european commission increased its capacity to intervene in the management of these stocks. such an approach, which deprives states of their prerogatives in managing energy supplies, was therefore unacceptable. by rejecting this text, we have sanctioned a false good idea, which was based on solutions that were as simplistic as they were ineffective.
in writing. - despite the displeasure of all kinds of sovereignists, it is more logical to build up energy reserves at the level of the union as a whole than at the level of each of the small and medium-sized states which make up it. but why is it necessary to stock up? according to the report's authors, this is not against any natural cataclysm cutting off supply routes, but "above all to guard against economic dangers arising from the instability of markets". the european union is thus obliged to protect itself against the consequences of the economic system on which its very existence is based. we will therefore not take part in this debate on the worshipers of the market economy, of which we are not a part.
in writing. - we supported the report by timothy kirkhope on the german initiative to strengthen cooperation between member states when measures are taken to remove third-country nationals illegally staying in the union by air. these are useful but relatively technical measures, which mr kirkhope, the former secretary of state for immigration in the last british conservative government, had the greatest difficulty in getting the commission and the european parliament to accept. we have heard from the left-wing benches unlimited statements denouncing "deportations", "inhuman methods" or "collective expulsions". all this has nothing to do with reality, because these measures of removal are obviously regulated by law. in particular, it is not a question of collective expulsions (the expulsion of an entire social group without regard to individuals) but of individual expulsions, controlled by the courts, of persons in an illegal situation. in this respect, the minority view of mr krivine, ms boumediene-thiery and others, who see these expulsions as a 'violation of migrants' rights' and who clearly dream of opening europe's borders to immigration from all over the world, is instructive.
in writing. - we join the minority opinion of the committee on civil liberties and human rights in denouncing this report which proposes to organise the mechanisms for deporting migrants 'illegally staying' more efficiently. the house is asked to further increase the repressive scope of the original initiative by deleting a passage denying transit for expulsion in cases where the deported migrant 'risks inhuman or degrading treatment, torture or death'. the european parliament, in voting on this report, endorses and endorses the policy of most national states which seek to expel from their territory migrants to whom local legislation does not allow the necessary residence permits. we demand, on the contrary, a total halt to deportations, the release of all those who are imprisoned pending deportation and the granting of legal papers to all "undocumented" persons and the right to reside in europe permanently.
in writing. - the text proposed to us, far from being a security measure, is intended to regulate the conditions for the transit of persons who are in an irregular situation on the territory of the union and who are subject to expulsion. the proposal for a directive, which was already withdrawn last april and referred back to committee for reconsideration, is obviously provoking a wave of indignation from the left, the greens and the third world. the reason is simple: it is immoral and inhuman to deport illegal aliens back to their country of origin! in the minority opinion annexed to mr kirkhope's report, they do not hesitate to denounce with horror fortress europe or the mechanisms of deportation which illustrate the cynicism of a racist policy which places the interests of the state above the aspiration of human beings for a better life. we might laugh at this, but in reality we are tired of hearing and hearing again all these speeches full of human rights, these good feelings that today, everywhere in europe, we see the same things: uncontrolled immigration, overwhelmed states that no longer know what to do with their illegal immigrants and have no other solution than to open temporary accommodation centres (which are temporary only in their title). in writing. - the sinking of the prestige, which caused a major ecological and economic disaster, is a stark reminder of the urgency of making maritime safety a major issue at european and global level. a whole series of measures must be taken quickly to prevent future accidents like the prestige. the first of these measures is the application of and monitoring of compliance with existing community and international legislation. the measures provided for in the two erika packages must be implemented without delay. these agreements can be supplemented and will be more effective if people from the fisheries and aquaculture sectors are involved in the negotiations. this disaster is not, as some people would have us believe, a 'simple' spanish affair. i therefore think it is essential that a temporary committee be set up. it is essential, if we are to avoid such a disaster happening again, to know as objectively as possible the causes and consequences of what has happened here: this is a matter of the credibility of parliament and the dynamic role that europe must play in maritime safety.
in writing. - i voted in favour of the report by mr sterckx, which provides a comprehensive overview of the information currently available on the prestige accident and whose proposals are relevant. it is essential that member states transpose the erika legislation into their national law as quickly as possible and ensure that it is complied with. if these rules had been put into effect earlier, the prestige could have been saved from sinking. similarly, the international legislation in force must be strictly respected and monitored. on behalf of the polluter-pays principle, i support the rapporteur's idea of criminal liability for all actors involved, including policy-makers, in maritime disasters. it is essential that all member states ratify the protocol on the fipol complementary fund, which will provide eur 1 billion for victims' compensation from 2004. i regret, however, that the cope fund has been blocked at council level insofar as it would have allowed for accelerated compensation for the victims of the prestige and perhaps other disasters. a high level of compensation for victims of maritime disasters should be ensured through the fipol fund, the cope fund being able to provide a more flexible european contribution.

commission. - madam president, ladies and gentlemen, i thank the european parliament for inviting me to this evening. i always welcome the opportunities offered to me to discuss with parliament the competition policy issues on which i have the honour of appearing periodically before the economic and monetary affairs committee of the parliament. the subject of your invitation this evening, madam president, is a specific matter under consideration and on which i must therefore exercise a certain discretion. i am at your disposal to explain any questions that may arise. what has the european commission done so far in the alstom case? she made a decision and she decided not to make another one. the decision to initiate the examination procedure concerns the support measures adopted by the french state on 2 august, in the framework of an agreement with alstom and a number of banks, and subsequently notified to the commission. this decision to open the procedure was taken by the college on 17 september. she's just like everyone else. i now come to the decision not taken. it concerns a specific element of the support plan decided upon and announced on 2 august but not yet implemented: a state participation in alstom's capital. the commission could not accept an immediate participation by the french republic in alstom's capital because this type of measure, unlike other liquidity injections, was liable to have irreversible consequences on the markets on which the alstom group is active. on 17 september, the commission therefore found that the conditions were met for the french authorities to be ordered not to implement a state participation in alstom's own funds. however, the commission wished to give france one last opportunity before proceeding with the injunction. to this end, it empowered me to adopt and implement, by 22 september at the latest and in agreement with president prodi, an injunction to suspend certain aids, unless the french authorities publicly undertook to refrain from taking measures involving automatically and irreversibly a state participation in the capital of the alstom group, without the prior approval of the commission required by community state aid rules. following successful and rapid contacts with the french authorities, i was able to note yesterday that they had agreed to amend the support plan in a way that satisfies the condition set by the commission. the french state will therefore not immediately become a shareholder in alstom and will not adopt measures which could constitute capital, that is to say, structural measures which the commission cannot accept without prejudice to the conclusions of the competition inquiry which it will carry out. the state's participation in the capital increase will be replaced by a subordinated fixed-term security redeemable in shares. this is a liquidity measure which can be converted into equity only if the commission decides that the state's participation in the capital increase does not raise competition concerns on the relevant markets. since france had agreed to renounce its automatic participation in alstom's capital and had undertaken to no longer put the commission in the position of having reached a fait accompli, there was no longer any need for me to exercise the power of ordering suspension conferred on me by the college of commissioners. that is the commission's failure to take a decision. the commission welcomes the constructive attitude of the french authorities and, in particular, i would like to stress this, of mr francis mer, minister for the economy, finance and industry. it was our duty to prevent the conditions of competition on the market from being changed immediately and irreversibly in favour of alstom before the commission had even begun to examine the impact of the aid on the markets concerned. the amendments made are likely to result in an increase in the overall volume of aid to be granted. this fact demonstrates the multiplier effect of a capital increase and its irreversible effects. in other words, it would never have been possible to restore the status quo. i would point out that the amount of aid will also be a key element which will be taken into consideration by the commission when examining the merits of the case. of course, the fact that it is not necessary to exercise the stay order does not mean, at this stage, that the commission has approved the aid. the examination of the measures as a whole will now come into play. the examination of the merits will be able to be initiated in a constructive spirit and as rapidly as possible in view of the complexity of the case. the aim is to allow for a restructuring of the company which at the same time preserves the proper functioning of the internal market, the only guarantee of sustainable employment. during this examination, the commission will verify the long-term viability of the company and the proportionality between the amount of aid granted and the counterparts which france will be prepared to accept in order to preserve the conditions of competition on the markets in question. i would like to emphasize, ladies and gentlemen, that this is by no means a position of principle on the part of the commission concerning the rules governing the ownership of undertakings in the member states. you know as well as i do that the treaty provides for and therefore requires the strictest neutrality in the matter of public or private ownership of companies. i am therefore well aware that the purpose of the suspension was not to prevent the entry of the french state as such into alstom's capital. the commission took the view that the aim was to prevent aid measures from having irreversible consequences on the markets concerned without the commission's prior approval, in breach of the treaty rules on state aid. please do not say that the commission is against public ownership of companies. as i have always stressed, it is not the commission which asks a member state to open up the capital of public undertakings as the french government does, for example for électricité de france. these are choices which are entirely up to the member state concerned. what the commission has a duty to enforce, under the treaties, is that companies, public or private, comply with the competition rules. i would like to emphasize the quality of the cooperation inspired by a spirit of constructive trust - as i have already said - with the french government and, in particular, the minister for the sea. in addition, some of the reactions and comments from french political and economic circles heard in recent days will merit a more detailed analysis. i understand the union's feelings. i am well aware of the importance of the alstom group in the european industrial and social fabric. i do not understand the reference made here and there in the french debate in recent days to the notarial behaviour and the alleged lack of political awareness on the part of the european commission. is there not a political value in safeguarding a single market without distortion of competition, a necessary, if not sufficient, but necessary, element of a social market economy? is it not politically expedient to prevent a state from overstepping the rules of the single market, which benefits european businesses themselves and the opportunities for growth, including employment? is it not politically necessary to give confidence to the whole of europe by showing the citizens of the small and future member states that the commission, in its role as guardian of the treaty, is not hard on the small and weak on the big?
