mr president, we are generally satisfied with mr whitehead's report and with the fact that the council has generally accepted our amendments. the commission has also proposed that the commission should be given the task of drawing up a report on the implementation of the directive. the definition of these bodies should be strict. the report goes along with this, while ensuring the involvement of a panel of organisations. of course, organisations with the necessary technical expertise must be selected, but the independence of the representative bodies must also be ensured. it is therefore imperative that lobbyists - industrial, commercial, professional or otherwise - do not see these bodies as a means of indirectly influencing the policy of the union. on the other hand, we must maintain our relations with the cooperatives whose charter takes account of the interests of the consumer. relations with consumer protection organisations must be developed as closely as possible to the citizen. we cannot therefore simply give priority to relations with community or national organisations and offer only support to bodies with a regional dimension: they must have real representation in the consumer committee and the corresponding financial support. the committee will also ensure even wider representation of civil society. the extension of the area of competence is important. the food sector organisations are now joined by protection organisations in the service sectors and more broadly in the non-food sectors. access to information is an essential guarantee of consumer protection. this is why we have demanded and obtained easily accessible public databases. citizens must be able to know the exact history of products, their origin, their production methods, etc. this is achieved, among other things, by improving labelling, which is an effective means of ensuring consumer information. but we have to go further. if we want to ensure that safe products are placed on the market, we must no longer simply inform people about the risks but organise risk reduction. this is only possible by developing comparative evaluations focused on sustainable and responsible production and consumption: this is the real consumer protection policy.
- mr president, commissioner, our colleague andersson's report emphasizes the need to take account of the poverty of the many pensioners, or the inequalities between men and women in regard to pensions. it advocates minimum pensions with a guarantee of an adequate level, and an increase in the level of employment for women in the context of equal opportunities. i agree with my group on these points in the report. it even indicates that it is concerned to ensure a balance between social concerns and financial imperatives. unfortunately, this commitment is contradictory and leads the rapporteur, in the name of financial criteria, to call into question the basic social acquis. the vote in committee was not unanimous. we did not vote for this report in the committee because it supports the commission's proposal to raise the retirement age. this is part of the liberal approach which has been advocated for several european councils for more flexibility and longer working hours. we are opposed to this type of reform which imposes a lengthening of the time limit and which does not solve the question of employment in any way. the report claims that the states have taken steps in the right direction, that is, in the direction of enlargement. the majority of employees in france, austria and germany have expressed their rejection of this extension of working time and of pensions by capitalisation. would we want to settle the european debate on pensions without the citizens? we are tabled amendments with my group which attempt to take account of these aspirations. with these amendments we are of course opposing the raising of the legal retirement age and the extension of contributions. we are also opposed to the capitalisation pension, which in no way guarantees income and dismantles the principle of solidarity in the distribution systems. we propose that the burden of work and dependent children be taken into account in the calculation of contributions. finally, we propose to study new forms of financing of statutory pension schemes. the argument of increasing longevity is used to introduce the system by capitalisation; it does not adequately disguise the financial appetites of multinational corporations for this option. other, more supportive and sustainable ways of addressing the issue of long-term financing are possible. we propose, for example, to extend social security contributions to all financial incomes with a modulation according to whether or not firms are job creators. these do not seem to me to be entirely irresponsible proposals. in conclusion, i would say that in the face of the challenge to the choices made by the heads of state and government in europe, it is now a matter of listening to the demands and not going against the tide, otherwise european citizens will drift further and further away from the union.
mr president, the proposals in this report merely reflect the retrograde policy pursued by all the member states of the european union in the field of pensions. by seeking to raise the actual retirement age, by wishing to extend the working life, and even by proposing to replace retirement with the distribution of pensions by pension funds, the rapporteur justifies and harmonises all the attacks on employees. the rapporteur is cynical in observing that the increase in the number of pensioners and their longevity will put considerable pressure on pension schemes financed by distributions. should we therefore wish for a shorter life expectancy and fewer retirements to save money? if the fruits of productivity were distributed differently, by favouring the big business and the richest a little less to allow workers who have spent their lives enriching them to age with dignity, there would be no problem in providing a decent pension for a growing number of pensioners. but your economy is not designed to meet the needs of the majority as best it can, but to enrich the minority more effectively.

- mr president, the new directive on investment services aims to regulate competition between three major structures, the stock exchanges, the internet and the companies that do business internationally. their competition for processing transactions will intensify in the context of the european financial market which is becoming more integrated. it is well known that the city of london, which is also an aircraft carrier for the american investment banks, has a strong lead in terms of internationalisation. other companies such as deutsche bank or abn-amro are entering the business with ambitious business plans. i observe that in carrying out our task as legislators we have singularly lacked a sound economic analysis to clarify the nature of the competition involved and its implications. do we want, for example, the small european cities from the south to the east to be run by a few global players from london? we are here to account for the general interest and not the interests of any particular country. this is why we have supported two main principles: quality of information and fair competition. internalisation firms capture masses of resources, but they do not form the market. they manipulate him, but they need him. pre-trade transparency is therefore crucial for the quality of price formation, in particular to prevent volatility, speculation and insider dealing. the commission proposal applied this principle of pre-trade transparency which mrs villiers initially wanted to remove. then she accepted it. she has shown great professionalism, i must say. it has moved but a large number of traps and mines have been voted in the commission on its initiative, which drain much of the substance of this requirement of transparency and create legal uncertainty. this concerns the definition of the firms carrying out the internalisation, the obligations, the size of the orders, the exemption for eligible counterparties and the concept of price improvement. the report as it stands proposes less regulation than the united states has. that is why we have asked for a number of separate votes to remove the wording which we consider harmful, and our aim is not to reach a first reading conclusion at any cost, or simply to seek a compromise between interests, but to provide a resolution which really serves the general interest.
- mr president, the basis of this report was a clash. there was a difference between two philosophies. the first was to consider that investment firms - firms which practice internalisation - should be allowed to establish a strictly bilateral relationship with their clients, which had the disadvantage of not allowing those clients to benefit from the best possible price on the market, or even to know that best price, or even simply to ensure price formation, which can only result from a general confrontation of supply and demand. the second philosophy, that of regulated markets, was that consumer protection consisted in placing all offers and requests in competition on a single and transparent market, so that customers could know the price and obtain the best possible price. were these two philosophies compatible? yes, provided that the policies of investment companies are subject to common rules. the commission's text was very satisfactory on this point. i am not sure, unlike mr bolkestein, that mrs villiers' report is a significant improvement on your original text. but we can live with this compromise, because it is, as has been pointed out here, relatively satisfactory. it enables us to stand up for true principles and to act. two reservations to this, however. first, the question of price improvement. it is not a question of whether the customer has the best price. of course he has to have the best price! what is at issue in price improvement is the possibility for investment firms to charge a price different from the one they display and thus prevent the market from contributing to the formation of fair prices. secondly, we cannot accept a portfolio transaction which, in order to remove a transaction from the directive, involves the addition of securities of different types which have no relation to each other. with these two essential reservations, on which some of us will vote differently from what is proposed, we consider mrs villiers' report to be satisfactory and i would gladly congratulate the rapporteur if i had the feeling - and this is a reservation - that she had adopted, throughout the negotiations between the groups, a completely loyal attitude.
- mr president, everyone greets the rapporteur, so i do too, and i measure the distance travelled between what she called the 'prodi amendment' and the text on the table today, even though extra-continental influences weighed heavily in our discussion. the objectives of the directive are well known to all of us: to put the financial sector at the service of the best possible allocation of the financing resources of our economy. i believe that the text we have drawn up is awaited by all operators on this basis. i have a few more important observations to make. to protect lay investors, financial firms need to take the trouble to check their knowledge and resources. execution only is not a continental practice. the commission has also proposed that the eu should be able to impose a tax on the use of the euro. for competition to be effective, information must be available to all players. transparency is therefore essential. there should be no exception to pre-negotiation transparency and i can accept that it does not concern limit orders and is restricted to standard size orders, but it seems to me that the possibility of price improvement, which mr jean-louis bourlanges has already mentioned, is an extremely worrying element. finally, it seems to me that in the vote on thursday we should try to restore what was the position of our parliament on the 'delivery' regulation, that is to say, to ask the commission to draw up a directive on this point.
- mr president, ladies and gentlemen, in the apocalypse of st. john, the number of the damned is 666. well, in our draft constitution, it is 473, part four, article 7, paragraph 3. it is the revision clause, or rather the perpetuity clause, since it will now require double unanimity at the igc and at the level of ratification to change the slightest comma. it's like the impossible is etched in the marble. i would also point out that this article is not covered by the consensus, since in the urgency of the last few days it was not clearly debated in the convention's plenary. is this conventional text a treaty or a constitution? in a treaty, the terms are amended by the unanimous consent of the contracting parties. in a constitution, these terms are changed by a qualified or even overqualified majority, but never by unanimity. so if we want a constitution, we will certainly have to change and find a new clause so that we can evolve this thing, for example through a bridge clause of which our draft constitution is already very rich. our rapporteurs themselves, although the report on this point is terribly weak, say that destruction is possible if we do not change things. we have no right to the future of others. article 4.7.3 should therefore be amended.
- i believe that we are experiencing a real crisis of confidence at european level. i want to see proof of this in the massive and frank rejection of the euro by the swedes, the bitter defeat of commissioner lamy in cancun, the rather ridiculous standoff between the commission in brussels and france, both on the stability pact and on the alstom case. the only thing that remains in the european union's stores is this draft constitution, which will now be submitted to the states. personally, i would not take too much position between the choices of parliament, the commission or even the states, because it seems to me that the problem is not between the european institutions, it is between these european institutions and the european peoples. that is why it seems to me essential, and i regret that mr tsatsos' report does not make a much more frank reference to it, that this constitution, this draft, be put to a referendum in all european countries at the same time as the european elections. because think about that choice! if it is a constitution, it needs a referendum and if there is no referendum, it will not be a constitution.

why did the fifth ministerial conference fail? first of all, it must be recognised that the ambiguities contained in the negotiating agenda and the knots that had not been dissolved in doha tightened the noose in cancún, and this was particularly the case with the two main issues, agriculture and the singapore issues. in both cases, we are dragging the ambiguities with us from doha. as regards the text on agriculture, too many parts of it were made ambiguous during the fourth ministerial conference itself, even in the last minutes, in the last sentences. on the other hand, something speculative happened with the postponement of the decisions on the singapore issues, which were the subject of a heated debate in doha and then risked creating a possible negotiating impasse. the fourth world conference resolved these ambiguities by the decision of the qatari presidency to extend the negotiations for another 36 hours on these very issues. as is well known, the formula adopted at the time allowed for a more or less effective inclusion in the individual undertaking, but without a specific negotiated commitment. this means, apertis verbis, that the success of doha is probably due to the international state of necessity. it was the extraordinary nature of doha, the proximity of the tragic events of 11 september, that made the fourth ministerial conference a success. but perhaps the wto crisis, which began in seattle, was only anesthetized in doha and reemerged in cancun, coincidentally on the same issues as in doha. these are two somewhat speculative chapters: on the one hand, on agriculture, europe and the other northern countries have made a cultural exception, which is perfectly legitimate but which is still in conflict with the aspirations of the main developing countries, which accuse us of protectionism and market distortion. on the other hand, there are the singapore issues, i.e. the other issues of the governance of globalisation, which are a priority for europe and the big investor countries, but which the developing countries consider to be invading their prerogatives, so they have also made them - at least some of them - a kind of cultural exception, at least for now. the second question is: who's responsible? there is certainly a responsibility first and foremost on the part of the negotiating parties, who have not acted on the basis favour of the different players - led to a polarization of positions which exacerbated the negotiations. for the same reasons, some african countries have tried - and perhaps had to - take an original and offensive line by promoting thematic initiatives, such as the one on cotton, and by tightening their positions on traditional chapters as well. in the background, there is a clear structural problem with the wto: the commission's proposal is to be seen as a step in the right direction, and i would like to thank the rapporteur for the work he has done in the committee on budgets, and i would like to thank the rapporteur for the work he has done in the committee on budgets. commissioner pascal lamy, in the immediate aftermath of the summit, spoke of medieval organisation. in the whether europe has done all it can. we europeans, for our part, have prepared ourselves well - at least that is what we thought - firstly with the reform of the common agricultural policy, in the face commission. - mr president, it is customary to say that trade negotiations are a 'win-win' game in that the gains of the participants, if successful, exceed the costs they accept. well, what's true in success is the opposite in failure. just as the members of the world trade organisation would have all won in cancun if they had succeeded, the failure of this ministerial conference means that we fischler and i would like to inform you this afternoon of the commission's analysis of the positions we have taken in the discussions and of the conclusions we draw from this event, at least at this stage of our reflections. what was it about cancun? we told you before we left: we are halfway through the negotiating programme adopted in doha at the end of 2001. if we have not succeeded, it is simply because the distances between the negotiating positions could not be sufficiently reduced. la palice would have said the same. we were supposed to be halfway there, we're barely a third of the way there. then why? no, not as in seattle, because of insufficient preparation, but because the momentum of the negotiations did not start before cancun or at cancun. this dynamic is what makes it possible to reduce differences by gradually creating the prospect of a positive outcome, and it is what makes an increasing number of delegations see a greater interest in success than in failure. we all know, however, around the wto table, that each of us has a very precise pharmacist's scale, so precise that even a slight weighting will correct the imbalance. well, ladies and gentlemen, it is the game of weights that is the cause of the failure of cancun. then whose fault is it? to refute the proverb that success has many parents and failure is usually an orphan, my answer to this difficult question is that it is all our fault, or more precisely the fault of the judgment that all the negotiators present have had on how best to fulfil their mandate. to illustrate this abstract point, i will briefly review the positions of the four most visible actors in cancun: the european union, the united states, the g21 and the african and least developed countries group. the european union was strongly in favour of the success of the doha programme, and therefore of success in cancun, which is an uncomfortable tactical position, as everyone knows, when it comes to exchanging concessions or setting up rules that we europeans love. and we paid a lot of money for it. we paid the price in doha, reluctantly agreeing not to negotiate the links between basic social clauses and trade rules and moderating our environmental ambitions. we paid between doha and cancun, softening our positions on investment, competition, trade facilitation and public procurement. we have paid for this since the reform of the common agricultural policy by accepting additional multilateral disciplines on our support for agriculture, for the benefit of developing countries, and by accepting further opening up of our agricultural market, which has enabled us to engage the united states in the same way. finally, i will not mention access to medicines, where we had to persuade our pharmaceutical industry of the urgency of exemptions from patent rights, which fortunately remain vested since they were negotiated separately. but there are limits to concessions. with the agreement of the council, the member states and your delegates on the ground, we have removed these limits in cancun on two points of the programme: investment and competition. but in the absence of significant moves by the other actors, the chairman of the conference concluded in failure, without the negotiation having really started on the long list of issues that remained on the table. let us turn to the united states, which, for its part, also knows how to monitor its pharmacist balance. i feel that the removal of additional access to the agricultural and industrial market in line with their initial ambitions, which were vast, has thrown a precarious balance off balance. but what tipped the balance was the prospect of separate negotiations on a very politically sensitive product, cotton. i believe they would have agreed to meet the demands of the four african countries, which clearly feel they are being harmed by the us support system, if commitments to reduce this support had been made in the agricultural negotiations. the negotiating process has unfortunately failed to reach this point on the agenda. the group of 21, which included brazil, india, china, south africa, mexico and 12 latin american countries, was born, in my opinion, of two parents, a politician father and a farmer mother. the political father is the will to assert the voice of the developing countries at the wto, in the face of a so-called american-european duopoly. this is a strange duopoly, considering the long-standing differences between the us and european positions on access to medicines, singapore issues, geographical indications, the implications of the convention on biological diversity for the wto, the reform of the dispute settlement mechanism and market access in agriculture. i'll stop there. the political father of the g21 was therefore probably more far-sighted than the world trade organisation. i believe that this coalition has been an expression of the will of the major emerging countries to assert themselves more in international debates. they couldn't do it at the un about iraq. they did it in cancun about trade. but the agricultural mother of the g21 was there, as it is true that measured by the wto, the us and europe are the main providers of agricultural support. however, there is one limitation which the abortion of the discussion did not allow to be addressed: the difference between agricultural subsidies which disrupt trade and those which do not. this is a key frontier for the future common agricultural policy. to make a good point and complete the characters surrounding the birth of the g21, it would probably also be necessary to mention the presence of an industrial uncle, of very high tariff size, very impressive for our exporters and in fact not eager to shrink. for the g21, the combined weight of the political success of its assertion of existence and of defensive concerns which, being mercantile in nature, are no less legitimate in the wto, has therefore, in my view, weighed more heavily on agriculture than the prospects of a success, however attractive. to conclude this brief discussion, let us turn to our friends in the least developed countries of africa. in our view, the disadvantages of the erosion of their trade preferences in our markets, which are indisputable in the event of a reduction in what remains of our multilateral protections, outweighed the benefits at hand in other areas. this explains the rejection of the compromise proposed by the conference president, which consisted in keeping only those matters relating to the transparency of commercial transactions and public procurement among the so-called singapore issues. this refusal, let us not forget, was denounced by korea, which wanted to retain investment and competition in the negotiations, probably to compensate for the agricultural concessions which were even more difficult for them and for japan than for others. with this brief presentation of the main positions in the house, i believe i have shown that it is exaggerated and even inaccurate to explain the failure of cancun by a sudden north-south split in the wto. ladies and gentlemen, in cancun there was no north and south facing each other, but north and south facing each other without ever meeting. before coming to the conclusions we draw for the moment from this failure for all of us, i would like to reiterate to you that the european union negotiated in cancún in good faith and added new concessions to those we had already put on the table. we can be criticised for this good faith, but this is a question of the image of the european union on which neither franz fischler nor i am prepared to compromise. we can also be blamed, i read and heard, for moving too slowly. but too slowly in relation to who or in relation to what? compared to the total immobility of all the other major participants, none of whom moved an inch? i would gladly accept this criticism if the process of discussion had, at some point, picked up speed. i believe we have enough witnesses to prove that it was not. the shock is important, let's not hide it. as with any political shock - and cancun is a political shock - we must go back to the basics and ask ourselves some questions about the union's international trade policy, in order to check whether or not the foundation on which we have built it over several decades remains unchanged. the first question is: do we keep as a benchmark this dynamic balance between the opening up of markets and the creation of rules without which this opening up is neither real nor in line with our values? this question must be asked, because the appetite for open markets around the wto table is becoming dangerously selective. modernization of existing rules or the adoption of new rules in areas that are dear to us, such as the environment, is confronted with the heterogeneity of policy choices that are the other face of the growing participation of nations in international trade. the second question, which has just been put by the presidency, is whether we are still committed to these priorities of multilateralism, which is the hallmark of the union's external policies. is this preference shared by our partners? if they're not, are we powerful enough to change their minds? are bilateral or regional agreements still complementary to the progress of multilateral disciplines or should they replace them in the event of a standstill, which would leave the wto dispute settlement mechanism with the task of interpreting inevitably incomplete rules and thus, in time, take the place of the international legislator, the ministerial conference, which today brings together the 148 member states? thirdly, how should we approach the future of our trade preference systems, which the european union has largely set up for the benefit of developing countries and with a differentiation concern to concentrate the benefit on those who need it most? the fourth and final question is: are the wto, its principles and its organisation still relevant to today's world? given its principle of equality of rights and duties of members, tempered by special treatment and differentiated by the asymmetries in the level of protection that remain between the north and the south. the european parliament has been a key player in the debate on the future of the european union, and its organisation has made it increasingly difficult to reach consensus among its growing membership on questions which are technical but which have major political consequences, since they now affect, immediately or in the medium term, the lives of billions of women and men. these are the few questions, ladies and gentlemen, that we must consider together before returning, if necessary, to more tactical or operational terms, before imagining new compromises, which are indispensable if our priority is to keep globalization under control and make it fairer and more equitable. the european commission is counting on you and the council of ministers to help it find the right answers to these questions. it is counting on all of you and, of course, first of all on those whom you delegated to cancun, who are here tonight and with whom we have worked hand in hand.
the commission is not prepared to accept the amendments tabled by the committee on budgets, which are not in line with the commission's proposals. pascal lamy and i are in complete agreement on this. unfortunately, cancun was a failure. this failure is damaging to us all and is of course a setback for the entire doha development agenda. the idea that agricultural policies in the industrialized countries were ultimately responsible for the failure is wrong. the negotiating parties have not even had the opportunity to raise this issue in a final round of negotiations. in the months leading up to cancún, much of the responsibility for a successful round of negotiations in cancún was attributed to the eu. firstly, we were told that we had to reform our common agricultural policy in order to make the negotiations a success. we did, and we got a lot of international applause for it. afterwards, we were told that the talks would fail if we did not resolve our differences with the americans. we have therefore drawn up a compromise document with the united states in august which has created a solid negotiating structure for the success of the negotiations. the bottom line is that we are all losers in the failure of the talks, and in the end the developing countries are probably the net losers in the agricultural negotiations. this is particularly true of the g21 countries, which were the most opposed to the approach proposed by mr pérez del castillo. the package offered in cancún would have enabled the developing countries to integrate their economies more closely into the world trading system and thus to benefit accordingly from the advantages of the world trading system. because the package offered in cancún would have led to a meaningful continuation of the reform of the agricultural trade system. in particular, and this was one of the main objectives of the developing countries in the agricultural negotiations, it would have led to drastic cuts in subsidies that - mr president, commissioners, our first task is therefore to make a proper diagnosis. the union may have made mistakes, but i would not be the one to shout haro at the baudet, i would not kick my mule. we can and must discuss tactics, but in substance it is true that our negotiators respected the mandate, made many concessions, withdrew from the negotiations on investment and competition. it was the last thing to do. but, as i shall say, the realities of the situation require us to review our mandate in depth. in cancun, there were other elephants and other mules. but the united states has stood behind us, when they had no will to engage. india and many other countries are not interested in the doha agenda, brazil is interested, especially on agriculture, but it has given priority to its political emergence. a misdiagnosis can be extremely dangerous for the future in the face of great challenges. we must beware of internal pressure to abandon the common agricultural policy. good reform requires moving towards the elimination of export subsidies, certainly not of long-term support. the european parliament has been very active in this area, and i think that the commission has been very active in this area. let us beware of a certain north-south angelicism. like many others, i see the conjunction of free traders and large agricultural exporters in the south. i also think it would be suicidal for employment in europe not to see that china, and tomorrow others, are emerging with big comparative advantages. second question: what should we do? mr president, commissioner, mr president of the council, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your work. cancun has shown: firstly, the demand for market opening without taking account of the existence of serious social differences is simply unrealistic. the starting point in each wto member state is so different that equal conditions for all do not promote justice but increase injustice, thus moving away from the stated objective of fair trade rather than towards it. secondly, of course, the differences between the industrialized and developing countries are particularly great, but these blocs are not homogeneous either, just as the european union is not a homogeneous entity. and since we all know how difficult it is to achieve results within the european union, we should also understand how much more difficult it is in a community of 148 countries. thirdly, in negotiations, one must always put oneself in the position of the negotiating partner, i.e. one must be prepared to make concessions to the weaker party without expecting anything in return. but if you negotiate on the bazaar principle - - madam president, the failure of the cancun ministerial conference on 14 september has caused many to fear that the first victim will be the multilateral approach to international trade negotiations. that would be a shame. we are convinced that world trade and international life in general must be based on simple multilateral rules that are respected by all and enforced by transparent international organizations. but what rules? this is the whole problem because since 1995 and the marrakesh agreements, the wto has been living on a great underlying principle: systematically opening markets and global free trade, which is supposed to bring the greatest benefits to all, in all cases. this is the rule, which is being challenged by more and more countries, which has just exploded in cancun and we must be aware of it if we want to rebuild something. to rebuild, of course, we must maintain the rule of free trade, but supplement it with another: that of the sovereignty of each national democracy or each trade preference zone, which must be free to adjust trade according to its needs, particularly in agriculture. the lessons of the cancun failure must now be learned and the specific nature of these issues must be acknowledged, which should perhaps even be removed from the wto and placed under the control of a specific international organisation. in any case, the fundamental rules must be the right of each country or area to preserve its agricultural model, its food independence and the health of its population. which implies two twin imperatives. first, accept the total disappearance of agricultural export subsidies in the long term. let us not hide our faces, let us be frank, it is a moral necessity. secondly, to admit just as frankly the legitimacy of community preference in the form of import levies or internal aid when it is necessary to achieve the social objectives we have democratically set ourselves. these two simultaneous franchises are necessary if we are to start from scratch, but they also involve a thorough review of the internal reform of the european agricultural policy which was prepared too quickly in the cancun perspective. this reform must now be re-examined and reoriented in the light of the lessons we have learned from this failure.

in writing. - the resolution just voted by the european parliament following the failure of the wto conference in cancun provides no substantive diagnosis, nor any clear direction for the future. in particular, it does not say that this failure is the result of a growing rejection of free trade and that work must now be done to establish fairer rules for international trade; whereas the european union, which has been a zealous servant of this free trade, in particular by insisting on the inclusion in the negotiations of singaporean issues (rules on investment, public procurement, etc.) which the developing countries did not want, has largely contributed to this failure; the commission in particular is also largely responsible for having used in these international negotiations the same autistic method as it uses internally vis-à-vis those who want a different policy. and the reform of the common agricultural policy, which was prepared in anticipation of cancún and which we strongly condemned, is now largely obsolete. the european union must take account of the new data and prepare another reform, more suitable to protect our agricultural model.
in writing. - unlike a majority of meps, i am one of those who rejoice at the failure of cancun, not because i am against globalisation on principle (i am even philosophically in favour of the free movement of ideas and people), but because i am against globalisation without rules or rather against globalisation whose rules are economic, financial and strictly structured by the law of the strongest. i would add that this summit has shown that the alternative world view and its advocates have succeeded in moving beyond simple rejection to genuinely alternative proposals. that is why i refuse to join a resolution which, to a large extent, regrets this failure. this new signal was needed so that the world's top leaders would finally understand that they will never again have full and complete freedom to impose their ideas and practices on us.
in writing. - the failure of this 5th wto conference offers a unique opportunity to rethink the union's trade policy: since the good intentions and efforts of the european delegation cannot be questioned, it might be time to recognize that it is the framework and specifications of this type of organisation which are the cause of this inefficiency today. as unjust as it may seem, this sanction provides the european union with the means to put an end to its dogmatism in this area and to look at foreign trade again as an object of negotiation between sovereign states, and not as a new stage in the triumphal march of the whole community. how can we not see in the ldcs' refusal the only possible manifestation of their freedom? how can we fail to understand that the indigestible "global negotiation" which serves as a postulate before each new cycle, offers little room for manoeuvre to the nations at the top to evaluate the europe/us agreements or to take responsibility for a failure? it will not be a miracle if the wto is given a cosmetic treatment for every answer: it does not need to be put back on track, but needs to change direction.

- mr president, by asking the commission this oral question on the pressing problem of the mass mortality of bees, my colleagues dominique souchet and astrid lulling are once again sounding the alarm, and i wholeheartedly support their approach. for several years now, since 1995 to be exact, we have been witnessing in france totally abnormal problems of decline in bee colonies. the situation is getting worse every year, the extent of the affected areas and the number of hives are increasing steadily, and now it can be said that many european countries are affected. it is clear from the examination that this mortality of bees is not a classic pathology. several other hypotheses were investigated, such as climate, general pollution or misuse of plant protection products. but while they may sometimes bear some responsibility, they can by no means explain the full extent of the wrong. i do not agree with the view you have just expressed, commissioner. in fact, according to experts and professionals, one main cause is well identified: the environment of the apiaries, when it includes fields of honey, rapeseed, sunflower, maize, whose seeds have been treated with insecticides of the gaucho or regent type. of course, the industrial manufacturers reply that the link is not formally established, but experience shows the complete coincidence between the disorders of the bees - loss of sense of orientation, tremors, inability to plunder and finally death - and the presence nearby of crops from seeds treated with gaucho or regent. the more observations there are, the more these conclusions are confirmed. however, nothing decisive has yet come from the public authorities, apart from words of appeasement, the launch of studies and some specific measures such as, in france, the temporary suspension of the gaucho's authorisation for the treatment of sunflower seeds. this is why the european parliament's committee on agriculture, again at the instigation of dominique souchet and astrid lulling, organised a hearing on the subject on 28 april. the lessons we have learned are alarming, because the bee problem may just be the most visible part of a larger problem of pollinating insects, entomophagy and soil fauna. so the gaucho and regent molecules could be harmful, not just to bees but to a much wider environment. and we're not stopping there! since molecules are present in agricultural products used for human or animal food, there is also reason to be concerned about our own health. this is why, in the face of this risk of widespread poisoning of the ecosystem - and perhaps of people - we demand the application of the precautionary principle. i have just heard the commission's replies to the oral question by mr souchet and mrs lulling. i think it's way too much of a wait-and-see. the precautionary principle implies, in our view, that the use of the products in question should be prohibited, at least for all honey crops. measures will also have to be taken to ensure that beekeepers are compensated and able to rebuild their hives.

in writing. - despite the good intentions, the report and the interinstitutional agreement on better lawmaking are not convincing. the major declarations on respect for subsidiarity are in contrast to the convention's proposals, supported by the european parliament, which entrust the court of justice with ultimate control. in a democracy, it is unacceptable for the court of justice to decide whether national parliaments are justified in opposing a commission proposal. moreover, the technique of the interinstitutional agreement, the respect of which depends on the goodwill of the institutions, is in itself a detriment to the legal quality and certainty which this exercise purports to seek. the elected members of the edd group cannot approve these texts.
in writing. - i voted for the frassoni report, "better lawmaking". pending the entry into force of the european constitution, which will bring undeniable progress in the transparency of community procedures and respect for the distribution of competences and the principle of subsidiarity, i believe it necessary to improve legislative practice within the framework of the treaties currently in force. in this respect, the interinstitutional agreement between the commission, the council and the european parliament is good news, because it offers more clarity and consistency while respecting the powers, procedures and general principles of our positive law. all too often the texts adopted by our assembly remain difficult to access for the uninitiated. we can do better, the interinstitutional agreement paves the way for such an ambition already mentioned in the white paper on governance. now it's just a matter of making it happen.
in writing. - considering the space industry only in terms of competition in a market, mainly with the united states, this report is quite symbolic. it is clear that he wants more use to be made of public funds, i.e. taxpayers' money, to help european companies to maintain or gain market share. and to make it even more effective, he advocates commands in the military sector, which would also allow industrialists to take advantage of the knowledge already acquired in this field and which would go in the direction of setting up a european military force independent of that of the united states. this military force is considered by some to be indispensable for conducting what they call 'peacekeeping operations' which are nothing but operations to defend the interests of european industrialists and financiers. such a report, with its clarity, is like an admission that the european institutions have no other goals than to mobilise public knowledge and funds in the interests of european private capital, in the space sector as in the rest. we can of course only vote against a report which is so full of these concerns.
in writing. - i supported and voted for this report which recognises the efforts made by some european states to ensure that space policies exist in europe today. the results are impressive! however, if we are to avoid serious difficulties and ultimately the law of the strongest prevail, we must move rapidly towards a controlled communitarianisation, as is the case in the field of research. it is not a question of 'doing instead of ...', but of enabling the implementation of european added value. space will increasingly be present in all aspects of citizens' daily lives. europe must be in space! space will always be a driver of industrial innovation. europe's industrial future therefore also depends on our investment in space. these are just a few of the reasons why i support and vote for it.
in writing. - i voted with satisfaction and relief in favour of the excellent report by my colleague, mr guido bodrato, on the green paper on european space policy. satisfaction, because what is at stake is european autonomy: a strategically sovereign europe must have its own military and space capabilities. the vote is a relief because it shows that the european institutions are aware of the concerns of industrialists and politicians in the face of the recent economic deterioration in this sector and the rise of our international competitors. europe will rise to the challenge of space if it takes strong action in the white paper to be presented in december and if manufacturers restructure themselves to become more competitive. to do this we will need a revival of public investment, otherwise our large groups will not be able to retain their human and technical resources and we will lose skills. this vote by the european parliament, after the decisive support given to the galileo and ariane v programmes, shows that the european union is able to defend its vital strategic interests and, beyond that, wants to contribute to the knowledge of the universe which cannot leave mankind indifferent.
in writing. - it is a joy to see the council, the commission, parliament and the national states struggling in attempts to regulate their sacrosanct competitive market. the concentrations which all claim to control are in fact only the logical outcome of this competition where the bigger ones naturally eat the smaller ones. and whether it is the commission or the national states that pretend to control these struggles between financial sharks is of no importance from the point of view of the workers. in any case, capitalist groups already dominate the economy and know how to influence and, at worst, ignore or circumvent the ridiculous decisions taken by the european institutions. what the report calls 'control of concentrations between undertakings' has no other purpose than to defend the interests of certain capitalists against others. at no point is it a question of controlling mergers so that they are useful to society, that they do not harm employees and consumers. at no time is there any reference to the dramatic consequences for the people of these factory closures, restructurings and social plans which accompany mergers. this is to express our absolute rejection of the concerns in the report which we voted against.
in writing. - the della vedova report is a significant part of the commission's ideology, which has been taken up in its own way by the liberal majority in this parliament. the real problems posed by the acceleration of the overall movement of concentration of enterprises are treated exclusively as threats to competition. the risks for consumers (high prices, opacity, etc.) or for the employees of these enterprises (transfer of production to the so-called social less, abandonment of activities, redundancies on the stock exchange, etc.) are not taken into account as such. as if free competition had proved adequate to these risks! in france, the latest mergers, from vivendi to air france, from alstom to péchiney, have shown how much the concerns of the national and european institutions are outweighed by the needs. for us, however, these are the first components of the general interest. taking them into account would certainly make a revision of the european merger control procedure interesting, but the option taken here remains a prisoner of the dogma of 'fair competition'. that is why we voted against this resolution, which by its deadlock insults the employees concerned and, more generally, all citizens.
in writing. - continuing its work on the revision of competition law, the commission is proposing a major amendment to the merger regulation. this initiative should be fully welcomed. for several years now, european companies, now joined by the community judicature, have been pointing out the shortcomings of regulation no 4064/89. the procedure for examining concentrations was too long and the notion of dominance was too vague: these two factors, to name but a few, were clearly not such as to enable the operations which were becoming increasingly necessary for the global competitiveness of european firms to be carried out. the commission proposal, supplemented by the amendments adopted by parliament, should normally enable the major european industrial groups to maintain their position and to play on equal terms with their american competitors. the commission will still have to demonstrate, in applying the new text, genuine european ambition, and to abandon the narrowly accounting approach which, until recently, led it to refuse certain industrial marriages. a legal text is nothing apart from the interpretation which is given to it. i therefore hope that the commission will start its own cultural revolution and, in particular, that it will abandon this procedural zeal which has done so much harm to european businesses and workers.
in writing. - i abstained on the resolution on the transfer of personal data by airlines to the us authorities in the case of transatlantic flights for the purpose of searching for terrorists or 'serious crimes and misdemeanours'. the european parliament, in the name of the protection of privacy, asks that these transmissions be suspended until an appropriate international agreement is concluded. the intention is good, but the motivations are exaggerated, and the result disproportionate. exaggerated motivations because the resolution overestimates the risks (this data is not so personal, since the interested parties have already communicated it to the airlines), and tends to restrict the categories of wanted criminals (why accept this communication for the search for terrorists, and not for murderers or rapists?). the result of european reluctance would be to prohibit airlines from communicating all the data concerned, which would put them in an untenable situation, and to complicate the indispensable fight against terrorism. i therefore believe that our proposals should have been reversed: to accept the disclosure of data for a transitional period, at the end of which a fair and transparent international agreement should be concluded.
in writing. - the european parliament resolution on the mass mortality of bees is rather disappointing because, once again, it merely mentions a possible link between these phenomena and the use of certain pesticides, gaucho and regent, for seed treatment. it proposes further studies and the setting up of an expert committee. as for the emergency measures, it merely calls, in a very vague and allusive way, for 'preventive measures with regard to the use of the new generations of residual neurotoxic products'. in the debate which preceded this resolution on 25 september, i considered that the latest studies, such as the practical experience of beekeepers, now show that there is a direct link between the death of bees and the use of these insecticides. this does not mean that other causes, such as general pollution in rural and urban areas, cannot have an influence. but they should not be used to mask the insecticide's effect. their use should therefore be suspended, at least temporarily, as a precautionary measure. i did not wish to mix my vote with that of the waiting party, but i voted for this resolution, which was also improved by an amendment by dominique souchet.
in writing. - beekeepers are sounding the alarm: bee populations have been falling for years to a level that puts pollination at risk. why the health crisis? the varroa parasite is probably responsible, as in germany in 2002, where it destroyed 40% of the herd. but the gaucho pesticides, bayer and regent's imidacloprid and basf's fipronil, are responsible for a very large proportion of these excess deaths. the german bayer had the audacity to sue the former vice-president of the union of french beekeepers for "defamation" in june 2003, but the facts are there: when honey crops, sunflower, corn or rapeseed, are treated with these pesticides in the vicinity of bee colonies, they show serious behavioural disorders and die en masse. the precautionary principle requires that these two neurotoxic pesticides be suspended as a minimum as a matter of urgency, pending serious in vivo studies, not in vitro studies, with expert bee biologists and representatives of beekeepers. compensation must be paid to the affected beekeepers and the unreasonable importation of foreign honey, which is sometimes cheated and always dumped, must be stopped.
in writing. - i am very pleased that the resolution which mrs lulling and i drew up in response to the alarming information we received from european beekeepers has been adopted by a large majority in this parliament. this resolution has the merit of clearly raising the issue of the serious consequences of the use of new generations of molecules with potent neurotoxic effects in the coating of seeds of large crops on bee health and human nutrition. parliament called on the commission to step up its efforts to combat inertial forces by making two main requests. the resolution recognises that the current authorisation protocols for plant protection products are no longer suited to the new types of molecules appearing on the market and calls for their updating by providing for new specific tests on bee health and the risks of food contamination, taking into account scientific studies on possible transmissions of these molecules throughout the food chain. the resolution also calls for compensation for beekeepers who have suffered significant production losses, and for aid to restore devastated flocks. the ball is now in the commission's court, which should aim to boost european honey production.

- mr president, what is quality bathing water and who decides? these are the questions which arise in the wake of the maaten report on the proposal for a directive on bathing water quality. should europe legislate in this area, and on what basis, given that neither public health nor tourism are community competences but remain the competence of the states? the only positive thing in my opinion is that the public is better informed. but why tighten up microbiological thresholds and not provide for any chemical quality threshold? it is also important to emphasise the difficulty of identifying all the sources of pollution, especially in estuary environments, located at the mouths of watersheds of a very large area drained by rivers. why extend the directive to water and leisure activities? will we eventually ban surfing, windsurfing, kayaking or rowing because the water is unfit for swimming? these activities are often carried out outside the bathing water and sometimes outside the bathing season. why centralize data on the commission's website, which seems unnecessary and costly? who takes their computer on holiday to see if it can swim in microbiological safety? local radio and traditional, easily updated, billboards are, in my view, more than enough to inform the general public. finally, the proposal to define the beach as a place usually visited by more than a hundred swimmers for at least twenty days during the bathing season is almost ridiculous. who will do the counting? as usual, of course, no one talks about the cost of the operations and the high economic impact of a ban on bathing. it is not for the directive to define the cases in which bathing will be prohibited, since this decision is the exclusive responsibility of the member states. subsidiarity must be respected, especially since the who has just published a practical guide on bathing water which could serve as a reference for the member states. we will therefore support the proposal to reject the directive.

the rapporteur. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, we have all been working together for two years now on the birth of erasmus mundus. i would therefore like to thank the commission, the council and all my colleagues in the committee on culture, youth, education, the media and sport for the work that has been done. with the erasmus mundus programme for the period 2004-2008, the european union will have a new instrument for exchange and cooperation in the field of higher education, with a view to strengthening links between european universities and creating a genuine european higher education area, the only one capable of attracting students, teachers and researchers from all over the world. i would like to remind you in a few words of the main actions of this programme. the first is to create 250 european masters, called erasmus mundus masters, with the label and support of the european union. these master's degrees, selected for a period of five years, will involve at least three higher education institutions from three member states. they will lead to the award of officially recognised double or multiple diplomas. students who take these master's degrees will have to study at least at two of the three associated universities. the second action is to create erasmus mundus scholarships for 4 200 students from third countries to europe. the amount of these grants is significant. it is on the same level as the fulbright scholarships in the united states. these students will receive an average of eur 1 600 per month for postgraduate study under erasmus mundus. the third action is directed at teaching staff. one thousand professors or researchers from all over the world will be able to visit european universities for teaching or research missions lasting on average three months. they will receive a grant of 13,000 euros for their mission. the fourth action is to develop partnerships between higher education institutions in third countries and european universities. these partnerships will be based on joint projects of a maximum duration of three years. they will focus in particular on the outward mobility of european students and teaching staff. the fifth and final action is the international promotion of european higher education. to make erasmus mundus known throughout the world, the european union will provide financial support for international promotion actions and the creation of services to facilitate information and access to european universities for students from third countries. finally, i would like to emphasize the priorities which have been defended by the european parliament and on which we have been agreed by the council and the commission. first priority: the name of the programme, originally erasmus world, has been changed to erasmus mundus, thus allowing a better identification with the european union. second priority: to preserve cultural and linguistic diversity, we have given students the opportunity to learn at least two of the languages spoken in the countries where the universities are located. third priority: we wanted the erasmus mundus master to take into account not only the quality of the training offered, but also the quality of the conditions under which the students are received. fourth priority: we also insisted on the recognition of diplomas and studies, which is essential if we are to make progress towards a european higher education area. the free movement of graduates within the union should be fully allowed. this tour of europe for students from third countries will be available to european students who wish to do so. finally, fifth priority - the fifth priority which we, the european parliament, have defended - we have reached agreement on a budget which is commensurate with the ambitions of this programme. the council of education ministers proposed €180 million for this programme. the commission proposed to allocate €200 million to this. parliament succeeded in securing a budget of eur 230 million for this second reading. i would like to say again, madam commissioner, how much i appreciated the positive spirit with which we all worked together, the european parliament, the commission and the council. i think we can be satisfied with the progress of the erasmus mundus programme. i hope that erasmus mundus will be as successful and popular as its little brother erasmus and that the europe of knowledge we all aspire to will become a reality.

commission. – mr president, this proposal aims to authorise member states to ratify the 1996 hague convention on child protection in the interest of the european community. it is a follow-up decision to the decision of 19 december 2002 which, exceptionally, allowed member states to sign this convention in the interest of the community. the current proposal concerns the second and final stage of this procedure, that is, the ratification procedure. the scope of the convention, which was concluded in 1996 within the framework of the hague conference on private international law, is very similar to that of the council regulation on parental responsibility, which was approved by the council on 3 october and will apply between member states as of 1 march 2005. the new regulation creates a common judicial area in the field of divorce and parental responsibility. it contains specific provisions to facilitate cross-border visiting rights and to deter child abduction within the community. it is widely recognised that the convention would make a valuable contribution to the protection of children in situations that transcend the boundaries of the community, thus usefully complementing the regulation on parental responsibility. the similarity between the two instruments will facilitate the parallel application of the two instruments that share the aim of offering increased protection to children who are resident within the community or third states respectively. the commission would like to express its gratitude to parliament in general, and to the rapporteur, mrs hermange, in particular, not only for their continued support of the commission's work in the field of parental responsibility, but also for their enormous efforts in this particular case. the commission is aware that parliament has done everything in its power to speed up the procedure, including changing the date for the plenary vote from december, as originally scheduled, to today. the work of the rapporteur and the responsible committee has thus taken place under considerable time pressure. the commission takes note favourably of the amendments proposed and is extremely grateful for these efforts which will enable the council to adopt this proposal in early november, at the same time as the regulation on parental responsibility, thus ensuring parallelism between the two instruments.

the european parliament will always have to ensure that the best interests of the child remain, in line with the recent conclusions of the un world summit on children, a paramount consideration, not in writing. - (pt) this report sets out the plan to be used to endorse and implement the policy of restructuring in situ training methods and the means of producing teaching and learning materials (which now falls within the sphere of competence of the multimedia industry). this is in response to the example set by the experiences and policies of countries that have gone further along the path of privatising schools and commercialising education. in these countries, the companies that provide such goods and services are more experienced and have already accumulated considerable economic weight and cultural influence. the support given by this report to measures which de-structure conventional modes of education, in particular in situ education, is apparent in several respects. these measures are combined with the underfunding of educational institutions to facilitate the dismantling of public education systems. in addition, they open the way for private organisations to provide informal educational methods, such as distance learning, which have little value as an educational qualification, and for ad hoc contracts with workers trained in such informal 'educational systems'. doubts remain as to the composition of the commission's advisory committee, although it naturally includes 'experts', thus circumventing the representative authority of governments. the explosion of programmes such as elearning, leonardo, socrates, and so on, tends to reduce the room for manoeuvre, the authority of each member state, of each educational institution. these programmes reduce the very purpose of education to a secondary role or to a means to other ends.

- madam president, mr president of the council, madam commissioner, there are undoubtedly changes and innovations in this european budget for 2004: it is a budget, as it has been said, with 25 members, with a new nomenclature, based on activities, objectives and destinations. this is not necessarily an improvement in readability when, for example, there are 215 activities instead of the distinction between administrative and operational expenditure. the new feature of the abolition of the distinction between compulsory and non-compulsory expenditure will also be added soon, and one of these days the edf will be budgetized. on that day, moreover, will we be able to continue here in the european parliament to expedite the debate in two hours and to expedite the vote on the 100 billion euro in two hours as well? why do we spend 640 million euros in afghanistan, turkey and iraq (which we were not obliged to destroy...), when we cannot build high-speed trains or major transport systems? this is a perversion of solidarity, which in turn reveals a fourth deficit, namely a deficit of coherence. this is a europe which, in lisbon, wants to be the world's leading knowledge power (nikita khrushchev wanted to be ahead of america as early as 1960!). this is the europe of erasmus mundus, which wants to be a planetary university, the europe of great works like pericles, the europe of universal foreign policy, the shiva with a thousand arms, cotonou or mercosur, in asia, in south africa, everything but arms, the poor and even the rich. but this europe the size of the planet has a provincial budget of €100 billion, or 1% of its gdp, which is not even increasing. in the contradiction between these global ambitions and the absurdity of this budget, the question arises as to where the truth of europe lies. the answer is in the budgets: year after year, europe is being talked about in grand speeches which, in reality, are short-lived.

reserved about more advanced demands. history has often shown that an effective foreign policy is not accompanied by extensive parliamentary powers. a meeting is a place for debate and discussion and, where appropriate, decision-making. parliamentary time is by its very nature a long time, whereas foreign policy has to be conducted on a daily basis. in addition, parliament is also sometimes a place of conflict between groups which are necessarily heterogeneous. i believe that in the expression of its foreign policy, a community has an interest in showing itself as united as possible. it should be noted that in all democratic countries the role of national parliaments in foreign policy is governed by specific rules. finally, a final remark: the strengthening of parliamentary prerogatives would not be in the direction of a greater readability of europe's foreign policy. let us not develop some tangle of additional competences which would make our action a little more difficult to - mr president, it is good that the commission has finally agreed to the idea of splitting cod and hake, whereas it had originally intended to treat the two stocks in a single recovery plan, which in writing. - once again, the european parliament has just approved in its preliminary draft budget an item entitled '3710 - contributions to european political parties', with a memorandum. we voted against it. for several years now, our assembly has been eager to finance the so-called 'european' political parties with public money. but this was impossible, because there was no legal basis. the treaty of nice has provided one (article 191-4 tec), but the implementing regulation is still lacking. but it is not easy to write because it wants to introduce gross discrimination between 'integrationist' political parties and others, but also between strictly european political parties and those who, on a national basis, work at european level. it would thus contradict article 191-4 of the treaty, even as amended by nice, which gives a broad definition of the beneficiaries of funding, since it concerns parties 'at european level' (contrary to what the current wording of heading 3710 would have us believe). to avoid this new obstacle, the draft european constitution makes one further amendment: it is subtly aimed at political parties at european level (article i-45-4). but unfortunately for the federalists, this text is still far from being adopted.

in writing. - i voted against the proposal to extend the liberalisation of rail transport across europe. while the effects of directive 2001/12 on access rights to the trans-european freight rail network could not be assessed, as they are being transposed in the member states, the european commission and mr jarzembowski propose to accelerate the full liberalisation of rail transport. it is simplistic to claim that the loss of rail competitiveness is due to the lack of liberalisation. there was no need to liberalise rail passenger transport to develop competitive and safe lines. the cooperation between operators, as regards the thalys, is working. what europe lacks is an industrial policy, the development of cooperation between public service operators, investment budgets of the member states and the union in the trans-european networks. despite the improvements made, mr sterckx's report confirms what the council of ministers has accepted: the subordination of safety to profitability. i support the savary report on the creation of a european railway agency whose board would include representatives of the employees' organisations and take account of environmental, social and safety aspects in line with the ainardi proposals.
in recent years, the trafficking of human organs has increased considerably. human trafficking has been organized to harvest organs from living donors. patients from the european union buy organs from donors in third countries, taking advantage of their dismay at extreme poverty. in this context, the proposal for a framework decision is to be welcomed. organ donation from living people is a real source of abuse and often means exploiting poverty. the use of living donors should therefore only be a last resort when transplantation of organs from deceased persons is impossible. i therefore tabled an amendment to punish any organ harvesting from living donors who do not have close personal relationships, as defined by law. in the absence of such relationships, such donations could be made only under the conditions laid down by law and after authorisation by an appropriate independent body. organ donation from living donors must be highly supervised and closely monitored to protect people in vulnerable situations and to avoid the unacceptable exploitation of human beings for their organs.
in writing. - the european council of 16 and 17 october deleted from its conclusions the idea of an immigration policy based on quotas, as proposed by the italian presidency. we deeply regret this, because such a policy would have been the first step towards controlling immigration, since to implement quotas, one must first be able to count and control. among the opponents, jacques chirac, on behalf of france, declared that he was "a priori hostile to the very principle of quotas", at the risk of appearing reluctant to the very idea of limiting immigration. other opponents had better reasons: the commission's intention was to use the initiative to build an integrated european policy on quotas, removing the powers of the states to determine the number of immigrant workers they are likely to take in. it also wanted to offer additional quotas to third countries that agreed to take back their illegal immigrants. it would have been a strange bargain, rewarding those who would have wronged us, when it is their strict duty to reprove their offenders. it is not surprising that under these conditions some states have preferred to scuttle the quota policy.
